doi:10.64898/2026.10.08.757540.title: Ordinal position in auditory sequences is encoded in population dynamics in macaque frontal cortex
doi:10.64898/2026.10.08.757540.authors: Errington SP, Agayby B, Berger JI, Griffiths TD, Petkov CI, Kikuchi Y.
doi:10.64898/2026.10.08.757540.abstract: The ability to extract structure from sensory sequences requires tracking not only stimulus identity but also ordinal position within a sequence. How and where ordinal information is represented in the primate brain remains unclear. Here, we recorded activity in populations of single neurons simultaneously from auditory cortex and ventrolateral prefrontal cortex in macaques passively listening to structured auditory sequences. Population-level analyses revealed that frontal cortex activity evolved progressively across the sequence, occupying distinct regions of neural state space for successive ordinal positions. In contrast, auditory cortex population activity reset with each element, producing stereotyped, stimulus-locked trajectories. Consistent with this dissociation, frontal cortex populations robustly decoded ordinal position independently of stimulus identity, whereas auditory cortex showed weak positional decoding despite strong identity representations. Frontal neurons further exhibited longer intrinsic timescales and reduced synchronization to element presentation, supporting integration of information across multiple elements. Together, these findings identify frontal cortex activity as a key substrate for ordinal position encoding during auditory sequence processing, while auditory cortex primarily supports element-specific sensory representations.

doi:10.64898/2026.10.05.756650.title: "Mine" or "yours"? Acoustic structure of food calls predicts sharing decisions in marmosets
doi:10.64898/2026.10.05.756650.authors: Wierucka, K.; Winiger, S.; Sehner, S.; Burkart, J. M.
doi:10.64898/2026.10.05.756650.abstract: Foraging and feeding are often associated with vocalisations across animal species. Food calls may function to claim ownership of resources or recruit others to feeding sites, yet their potential role in facilitating food sharing remains poorly understood. This study investigates the relationship between food calls and food-sharing behaviour in common marmosets (Callithrix jacchus), focusing on adult-infant interactions, where food transfers are most frequent. We analysed over 1000 food interactions across six groups, categorising events as non-sharing (without begging or despite begging) or sharing (proactive, resisted, or facilitated). We examined the spectro-temporal structure of food calls produced immediately before each interaction. Food transfers were more likely to occur when preceded by a food call, suggesting a functional link between food calls and sharing. Random forest models reliably classified food calls according to interaction type, while generalized linear mixed models identified acoustic variation associated with sharing outcomes. Our results suggest that food calls encode information to either encourage or deter conspecific (infant) approach, influencing food transfer outcomes. These findings highlight the role of food calls in modulating social interactions around food in marmosets, advancing our understanding of vocal communication and its integration with cooperative behaviours in primates.

doi:10.64898/2026.09.30.755565.title: Attractor dynamics underlie sequence working memory in data-constrained recurrent neural networks
doi:10.64898/2026.09.30.755565.abstract: Sequences of stimuli can be maintained in working memory by encoding each item, together with its position, as a distinct pattern of neural population activity. Competing hypotheses about the underlying dynamics have been proposed: patterns of activity might be supported either by stable attractor states that persist over time, or by transient sequential dynamics. To investigate the dynamics underlying sequence memory, we developed a framework for fitting low-rank recurrent neural networks (RNNs) to multi-session recordings of spiking activity, and applied it to 2,488 units recorded across 30 sessions in two macaques. Our data-constrained RNNs generated population spiking activity which closely resembled neural data and recovered single-unit tuning properties across sessions. Consistent with prior work, fitted networks represented items presented at different sequence positions in separate low-dimensional subspaces in the neural activity, alongside a dominant temporal component. The RNNs enabled direct investigation of the underlying dynamics: By isolating the temporal and stimulus subspaces, we found a manifold of fixed points emerged during the memory retention period. Targeted perturbation analyses confirmed that activity within this manifold is consistent with attractor-like dynamics, and predict that brief optogenetic perturbations delivered along this attractive manifold can selectively induce persistent shifts in neural activity and decoded behavior. Together, our results indicate that sequence working memory is organized by position-specific coding subspaces, within which attractor states maintain persistent representations, while activity evolves along time-varying dimensions.

doi:10.1523/jneurosci.2108-25.2026.title: Synchronous Activity in the Auditory Forebrain Represents Temporal Landmarks in Vocal Communication Signals.
doi:10.1523/jneurosci.2108-25.2026.authors: Ahmadi A, Robotka H, Gahr M, Theunissen F.
doi:10.1523/jneurosci.2108-25.2026.abstract: Precise temporal segmentation of sound is critical for identifying and interpreting complex acoustic signals such as human speech (Pisoni and Luce, 1987) and bird song (Gentner, 2008). Using the zebra finch model system, we investigated the neural coding of the songs' temporal features. We recorded neural activity from avian primary and secondary auditory cortex-like brain areas using electrode arrays in awake birds (4 males and 3 females) exposed to conspecific songs. By applying a deep-learning approach with bidirectional long-short-term memory networks (Daly, 2023), we demonstrate that not only the amplitude envelope of song stimuli but also discrete, time-locked envelope landmarks can be decoded from multi-channel neuronal responses to songs. The times of envelope peak amplitude and peak slope were decoded with average accuracies of 40% and maximum accuracies of 70% at 20-ms time scales. The decoding of these landmarks enabled the segmentation of song into syllables with maximum accuracy of 90% at 10-ms time scales. Decoding accuracy for temporal events was greater in the primary auditory than in the secondary auditory area, suggesting a serial processing of the segmentation and identification operation. These findings reveal that neural entrainment to salient temporal events in vocal communication signals is a ubiquitous, specialized feature of the vertebrate primary auditory forebrain (Mesgarani et al., 2009; Heelan et al., 2019) providing a mechanism for segmenting continuous acoustic streams into behaviorally relevant units for higher-order processing. Significance Statement To decipher speech or vocal communication signals, humans and animals must segment continuous sound streams into identifiable syllables or call-types. We found that amplitude envelope of songs and the time of salient acoustic landmarks can be decoded with high-accuracy from the activity of neurons in the auditory cortex analog of songbirds. These landmarks can be used to segment the song into its component syllables. We found higher fidelity for the representation of the envelope of the sound in primary relative to secondary auditory regions. We postulate that this functional organization corresponds to the order of auditory computations where the segmentation task precedes the identification task.

doi:10.64898/2026.10.05.756828.title: Spoken language comprehension relies on context-dependent neural weighting of syntax and prosody
doi:10.64898/2026.10.05.756828.abstract: Comprehending spoken language requires extracting syntactic structure and meaning from a continuous acoustic signal. Psycholinguistic evidence points to a key role for prosody in this process. However, because interactions between prosody and syntax are typically demonstrated using carefully controlled sentence constructions, it remains unclear whether such interactions constitute a general, default property of spoken language processing. Addressing this question requires naturalistic, broad-coverage data. Here, we combined experimental psycholinguistics with naturalistic neuroscience to investigate the joint neural encoding of syntax and prosody in MEG recordings of 26 participants (19 female) listening to narrative speech. Linguistic annotations revealed that strong prosodic boundaries tend to coincide with syntactic phrase closures, and that the strength of prosodic boundaries scales with the number of phrases closed. Using time-resolved regression with temporal response functions, we modeled how these features relate to delta-band neural activity during continuous speech processing. Our results reveal a bidirectional interaction between syntax and prosody. Prosodic marking modulates the neural processing of syntax, with phrase closures being encoded more strongly when accompanied by strong prosodic boundaries. Conversely, syntactic structure shapes prosodic encoding, such that boundary strength is neurally encoded primarily at points of syntactic phrase closure. These findings demonstrate that syntax and prosody are encoded not independently, but in a context-dependent and mutually constraining manner, highlighting their joint role in guiding structure building during naturalistic spoken language comprehension. Significance statement How the brain transforms continuous sensory stimulation into structured representations is a central question in cognitive neuroscience. Spoken language comprehension provides a particularly compelling case: as the acoustic signal alone underdetermines linguistic meaning, the brain must integrate bottom-up sensory information with top-down linguistic knowledge, such as syntax. Here, we recorded brain activity during audiobook listening to examine how syntax and prosody jointly shape neural responses to narrative speech. We find evidence for a bidirectional neural interaction: prosody modulates the neural encoding of syntax, and syntactic context shapes the neural encoding of prosody. These findings suggest that the brain flexibly integrates bottom-up and top-down information depending on how informative each cue is for extracting structured meaning from naturalistic speech.

doi:10.20944/preprints202610.1130.v1.title: Unsupervised Acoustic Stimulation at Home in Users with Self-Reported Maintenance Insomnia Symptoms
doi:10.20944/preprints202610.1130.v1.authors: Cerny F, Jongejan SL, Cox R, van der Heijden AC, Talamini LM.
doi:10.20944/preprints202610.1130.v1.abstract: Closed-loop acoustic stimulation can enhance slow-wave sleep and sleep spindle activity, but evidence has largely been obtained under controlled laboratory conditions. Translat-ing this approach to the home environment is important for developing scalable interven-tions for the myriad of disorders featuring deep sleep reduction, including insomnia. We evaluated the feasibility and electrophysiological effects of modeling-based closed-loop neurostimulation (M-CLNS) using a self-applied wireless EEG headband (ZMax) during unsupervised home use in adults with self-reported maintenance insomnia symptoms. Sixty-two participants completed two habituation nights followed by two counterbalanced five-night periods of stimulation or sham. Forty-nine participants contributed 330 record-ings that met signal-quality criteria. Acoustic stimuli were phase-locked to the onset of the positive slow oscillation deflection (0°). Across 230,139 phase-targeting events, stimula-tion was delivered close to the intended phase for both stimulation (mean −10.2° ± 74.5°) and sham (−4.1° ± 72.4°). Compared with sham, stimulation elicited a significant stimu-lus-locked SO response and increased spectral power in both the SO (0.5–4 Hz) and sleep-spindle (9–14 Hz) bands. Sleep architecture was not measurably altered. These findings demonstrate the feasibility of phase-targeted acoustic stimulation using wearable EEG during repeated unsupervised home use. This scalable approach provides a founda-tion for longitudinal studies investigating whether sustained enhancement of SO activity can improve sleep and daytime functioning or alleviate insomnia symptoms.

doi:10.64898/2026.09.29.753775.title: Auditory and visual mismatch negativity responses to numerical and non-numerical magnitudes in adults
doi:10.64898/2026.09.29.753775.authors: Mobeen S, Koponen T, Torppa M, Hämäläinen J, Lohvansuu K.
doi:10.64898/2026.09.29.753775.abstract: We investigated how auditory and visual presentation of small numerical magnitudes and non- numerical magnitudes are passively processed at the neural level. Earlier research suggests automatic processing of quantities occurs rapidly in the brain. However, there are no studies on passive, pre-attentive change detection of magnitudes utilizing mismatch negativity (MMN) across sensory modalities in same participants, important to understand amodal processing of magnitudes. We recorded EEG in passive auditory and visual multi-feature oddball and control paradigms from the same adult individuals (N=104/105, respectively). In the auditory paradigm, the standard stimulus was a 2-part sound, while the deviant stimuli varied in frequency, intensity, gap length, and number of sounds (1-part and 3-part stimuli). In the visual paradigm, the standard stimulus was a dot array containing two medium-sized dots, while the deviant stimuli varied in numerosity (1 or 3 dots) and dot size (small or large). The results for the auditory paradigm showed significant MMN across all features, including comparisons with deviant-alone control stimuli, except for the 2-part vs. 1-part contrast. The results for the visual paradigm suggested differences in processing across all features apart from large and medium-size stimuli. These results replicate earlier MMN findings that the brain distinguishes pre-attentively changes in sound frequency, amplitude and gap. Auditorily presented small numerical magnitudes also showed pre-attentive processing but less robustly to the contrast 2 vs. 1. Visual pre-attentive processing of small numerical magnitudes was also observed. Together these findings could be interpreted to support the existence of abstract, pre- attentive processing of numerical magnitudes. Highlights • Auditory and visual processing of numerical and non-numerical magnitudes was examined with EEG • Auditory non-numerical magnitudes and medium vs. small dots replicated earlier MMN studies • aMMN and vMMN showed pre-attentive processing of changes in small numerosities 2 vs. 3 and 2 vs. 1 • 2 vs. 1 tone processing was less robust than 2 vs. 3 or the processing of the visual contrasts • The brain processes changes in small non-symbolic magnitudes pre-attentively

doi:10.1111/ejn.70710.title: Mismatch Responses to Prosodic Changes in Children With Developmental Language Disorder: A Longitudinal Approach.
doi:10.1111/ejn.70710.authors: Themas L, Schaadt G, Lippus P, Padrik M, Kask L, Vaher U, Männamaa M, Kreegipuu K.
doi:10.1111/ejn.70710.abstract: Developmental language disorder is characterized by difficulties in auditory processing and prosody discrimination. Estonian word prosody features a unique three-way quantity distinction, characterized by changes in syllable duration and pitch contour, which differentiate word meaning and grammatical cases. In this study, we examined the Mismatch Responses longitudinally in 23 children with developmental language disorder and 25 age and biological sex matched typically developing peers (age at first measurement 4;6-6;5 years; age at second measurement 5;6-7;5 years). A multifeature paradigm was used in which all stimuli were meaningful words; two deviants differed from the standard, one in syllable duration and the other in both syllable duration and pitch contour. We also tested the discrimination of these prosodic features with behavioral tasks at both measurements. For duration discrimination, an early positive mismatch response diminished from first to second measurement, while a subsequent negative mismatch response increased. Significant longitudinal changes were observed in the typically developing group but not in children with developmental language disorder, while direct comparisons of maturational trajectories did not reveal significant group differences. For the duration and pitch contrast, in both groups and at both assessments, no mismatch response was detected. Additionally, no association was observed at the individual level between maturational changes in mismatch responses and behavioral discrimination at either measurement. These findings provide insights into the maturation of prosodic change detection processes and contribute to a better understanding of developmental language disorder and its manifestations.

doi:10.64898/2026.10.05.756641.title: Categorical rhythmic patterns do not predict song preference in zebra finches
doi:10.64898/2026.10.05.756641.abstract: Categorical rhythmic patterns are fundamental features found in language and music across cultures. In humans, these rhythmic patterns occur in both vocal production and perceptual preference, highlighting a link between rhythmic production and preference. Categorical rhythmic patterns have recently been identified in animal vocalisations too, but whether rhythm production is linked with rhythmic preferences in non-human animals remains unclear. Within this context, zebra finches (Taeniopygia castanotis) are of particular interest, as both sexes develop a song preference, and their song has been suggested to exhibit an isochronous temporal structure. Here, we tested for the first time whether zebra finches prefer songs containing discrete rhythmic patterns, using operant preference tests with either two or four rhythmic patterns. Our results show that no categorical rhythmic pattern was consistently preferred across the population, although responses varied among individuals. These findings indicate that categorical rhythmic patterns are unlikely to be a primary driver of song preference in zebra finches. Together with previous work in other vocal-learning birds, our results suggest that preferences for categorical rhythmic patterns may not be universal and could instead reflect species-specific features of vocal displays rather than the rhythmic categories characteristic of human music.

doi:10.64898/2026.10.03.756368.title: Successor representation supports structural learning of syllable sequences
doi:10.64898/2026.10.03.756368.authors: Liu J, Wang Y, Feng J, Zhao H, He Q, Yang X, Liang B.
doi:10.64898/2026.10.03.756368.abstract: Humans efficiently learn the temporal structure of speech, yet the underlying cognitive mechanisms remain unclear. Recent research in visuospatial sequential memory has proposed the successor representation (SR), important in reinforcement learning, which encodes multi-step transitional relationships. To test whether SR also supports the structural learning of rapidly changing speech syllable sequences, we adapted a pyramid-structured sequential learning paradigm using syllable streams presented at a natural speech rate (∼ 4 Hz). Participants exhibited robust structural learning, evidenced by asymmetric memory performance modulated by adjacent transitional probabilities. Notably, the SR model captured recognition performance for non-adjacent syllable pairs. Moreover, SR-based learning effects generalized across all syllable sequences, regardless of adjacency. Furthermore, the effectiveness of SR learning was associated with cognitive flexibility and working memory capacity. Together, these findings suggest that humans rely on effortful SR-like mechanisms for the structural learning of syllable sequences, highlighting a modality-general computational principle for sequential learning across various temporal modulation scales.

doi:10.1523/jneurosci.0198-26.2026.title: Flexible Modulation of Premotor mu Rhythm Waveform Shape Predicts Human Motor Sequence Learning.
doi:10.1523/jneurosci.0198-26.2026.authors: Suresh T, Khatri U, Hussain SJ.
doi:10.1523/jneurosci.0198-26.2026.abstract: Motor sequence learning recruits a distributed sensorimotor network. Within this network, the premotor cortex (PMC) encodes and represents sequence information while the primary motor cortex (M1) executes movement sequences. Like M1, PMC neuronal populations exhibit mu (8-13 Hz) rhythms, which are typically nonsinusoidal. Previous studies showed that mu rhythm phase gates corticospinal transmission, sensitivity to LTP-like plasticity, and learning-related corticospinal plasticity. However, these studies treated mu peak and trough phases as discrete functional states and focused exclusively on M1. Here, we characterized mu phase-dependent mechanisms of motor sequence learning by measuring waveform shape, which is a more holistic measure that treats peak and trough phases as continuous components of the same oscillatory cycle. Using cycle-by-cycle analysis of resting EEG, we quantified the peak-trough symmetry of mu rhythms recorded over premotor regions during, before, and after healthy adults (25 females, 11 males) practiced a serial reaction time task containing a repeating, embedded sequence (sequence group) or no sequence (no-sequence group). As learning progressed, premotor mu rhythms became more symmetric in the sequence than the no-sequence group; these symmetry increases were also more positively correlated with skill acquisition in the sequence than the no-sequence group. Furthermore, premotor mu asymmetry before task exposure predicted sequence acquisition, such that participants with longer baseline trough phases acquired greater skill and showed larger learning-related increases in mu peak-trough symmetry. Overall, these findings provide first evidence that motor sequence learning reshapes premotor mu rhythms, consistent with learning-related redistribution of cortical excitability across the mu cycle.

doi:10.64898/2026.10.14.26365371.title: Effects of Cannabidiol on Auditory Mismatch Negativity in Autistic Children
doi:10.64898/2026.10.14.26365371.authors: Budhiraja K, Parrella N, Hill AT, Downey LA, Catchlove S, Enticott PG, Ford TC.
doi:10.64898/2026.10.14.26365371.abstract: Pharmacological treatments targeting core autistic features remain limited. In neurotypical adults, cannabidiol (CBD) alters mismatch negativity (MMN), an electrophysiological marker of automatic auditory deviance detection that has been associated with autistic traits. The effects of CBD on MMN, as measured using electroencephalography (EEG), in autistic children remain unknown. This secondary analysis of a pilot randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover trial examined the effects of 12 weeks of oral CBD oil on MMN during a duration-deviant auditory oddball task. We hypothesised that CBD would produce more negative MMN amplitudes and shorter peak latencies relative to placebo. Nineteen autistic children (6-12 years, 8 female) received CBD (dose) and placebo in randomised order, separated by an 8-week washout. Age-adjusted linear mixed-effects models tested Time (baseline, follow-up) × Treatment (CBD, placebo) effects on mean MMN amplitude and peak latency separately at Fz and FCz. Exploratory Spearman correlations examined baseline associations between MMN and Developmental Behaviour Checklist-2 (DBC-2) Social Relating scores. At FCz, latency decreased following CBD but increased following placebo but did not survive FDR correction ( p = .029 , p FDR = .058) and no other interactions were significant. Higher baseline DBC-2 Social Relating scores were associated with more negative MMN amplitude at FCz ( ρ = -.58, p FDR = .028) and Fz ( ρ = -.59, p FDR = .028). These findings provide tentative evidence that CBD may modulate MMN latency in autistic children. Larger trials should clarify CBD’s effects on MMN and further examine the association between MMN amplitude and social-relating difficulties.

doi:10.64898/2026.09.28.753104.title: The representation of vocalizations in structured noise in the mouse auditory cortex
doi:10.64898/2026.09.28.753104.authors: Cai Z, Peters J, Arends S, Englitz B.
doi:10.64898/2026.09.28.753104.abstract: Efficient processing of complex acoustic signals within noisy environments is a fundamental challenge for the auditory system. This study investigates the cortical representation of structured noise and vocalizations embedded in it using widefield calcium imaging with the high-speed Calcium indicator jGCaMP8m in the mouse auditory cortex. The spectrotemporal statistics of the structured noise were controllable, including its temporal variance and cross-frequency correlations. We find that structured noise invokes spatially and temporally complex neural responses across the auditory cortex that reflect the spectrotemporal properties of the noise. We identified partially distinct noise response components: noise onset responses showed stronger overlap with primary than secondary areas, while later suppression components did not show a significant primary-secondary bias. Vocalization-evoked responses were significantly attenuated in the presence of noise compared to silent contexts, exhibiting reduced onset magnitude and altered adaptation dynamics. Using decoding we find the neural representation of vocalizations to become more discriminable with longer preceding noise exposure. Furthermore, structured noise cochleograms could be reconstructed from neural population activity, with performance depending on stimulus statistics, tending to be higher in primary than secondary auditory cortex while remaining substantial across both. These findings suggest that the mouse auditory cortex represents acoustic targets in noise through context-dependent and spatially distributed population activity, shaped by both the statistical structure and temporal history of the acoustic background. Highlights Structured noise invokes a spatially and temporally complex neural response across auditory cortex Spectrotemporal properties of the noise can be reconstructed from the spatiotemporal response Decoding quality for vocalizations improves with exposure to the noise during passive listening Acoustic information is distributed across auditory cortex rather than confined to a single subdivision

doi:10.1016/j.neuroscience.2026.09.033.title: Transcranial magneto-acoustic stimulation ameliorates cortico-subthalamic circuit dysfunction in MPTP-induced Parkinsonian mice: a cross-scale characterization.
doi:10.1016/j.neuroscience.2026.09.033.authors: Zhang S, Liu P, Xu Y, Mi J, Yue K, Zhang X, Zhai S, Wang Y, Xu G.
doi:10.1016/j.neuroscience.2026.09.033.abstract: Parkinson's disease (PD) is characterized by abnormal oscillatory activity and altered interregional coupling within the cortico-subthalamic (M1-STN) circuit. Transcranial magneto-acoustic stimulation (TMAS) combines focused ultrasound with a static magnetic field, but its modeled physical responses and circuit-level effects remain incompletely characterized. We integrated multiphysics simulations with behavioral testing, simultaneous M1-STN local field potential recordings, Golgi-Cox staining, and histological analyses in MPTP-induced parkinsonian mice. Simulations predicted an acoustic field concentrated in M1, magneto-acoustically induced motional source-current hotspots mainly in superficial cortex, and small passive membrane-potential polarization (approximately ± 0.03 mV) during one 400-ms active sonication period. The estimated mechanical index (∼0.71) and temperature rise (≤3 °C) indicated relatively low predicted mechanical and thermal risk; H&E examination showed no overt cortical histopathological abnormalities. In vivo, TMAS partially ameliorated selected behavioral deficits, attenuated abnormal aperiodic-adjusted beta activity in M1 and STN with region-dependent low-gamma effects, reduced beta-gamma phase-amplitude coupling, and reduced pathologically elevated M1-STN coherence after local bipolar re-referencing. TMAS also increased cortical dendritic spine density and partially attenuated MPTP-related reductions in SNc TH-positive neurons and striatal TH-positive fiber immunoreactivity. These results provide a cross-scale characterization of TMAS-associated physical, electrophysiological, behavioral, and structural changes. Because the acute simulations and chronic biological outcomes were not causally linked and component-specific controls were not included, the findings reflect effects associated with the overall TMAS paradigm rather than proof of a single physical mechanism.

doi:10.64898/2026.09.19.752870.title: Supra-regular recursion in primate vocal sequences
doi:10.64898/2026.09.19.752870.authors: Nitschke, R.; Krapp, L. S.; Cathcart, C.; Gallot, Q.; Bosshard, A. B.; Burkart, J. M.; Berthet, M.; Townsend, S. W.; Surbeck, M.; Zuberbühler, K.; Bickel, B.
doi:10.64898/2026.09.19.752870.abstract: Complex syntax is the widely accepted demarcation between animal and human communication. Although animal vocal systems occasionally contain pockets of syntax-like structures, their grammars are thought to be at best regular, whereas human language is supra-regular, i.e., including at least context-free computational complexity. Leveraging a new likelihood method for probabilistic formal grammars, we show that the call sequences of three phylogenetically diverse nonhuman primates (bonobos, olive colobus monkeys, common marmosets) include parts that are most likely generated by supra-regular recursive grammars, similar to human language. These findings challenge syntax as the major transition in hominid evolution and opens up prospects for alternative evolutionary scenarios.

doi:10.1152/jn.90042.2026.title: Automated inference of respiratory and syringeal biomechanical trajectories from birdsong acoustics.
doi:10.1152/jn.90042.2026.authors: Ostrowski LM, Méndez JM, Tostado-Marcos P, Cooper BG, Gentner TQ.
doi:10.1152/jn.90042.2026.abstract: Songbirds, in particular zebra finches ( Taeniopygia guttata ), provide a powerful model for investigating the neural mechanisms of learned vocal behavior. Researchers typically rely on the acoustic structure of birdsong to quantify vocal behavior. As a more direct measure of motor control, we present VIBE: Vocal acoustic Inversion to Biomechanical Estimates, an open-source pipeline that recovers the biomechanical control parameters of song production from the pitch and amplitude of the acoustic waveform. Biomechanical models of the songbird syrinx describe vocal production with two continuously varying parameters: α and β, representing subsyringeal air sac pressure and syringeal muscle tension, respectively. Recovering these parameters from song acoustics provides a motor-based coordinate system against which neural activity or other dependent variables can be directly compared. Because α and β are the coupled control parameters of a nonlinear oscillator, their joint recovery is non-trivial. VIBE addresses this through iterative optimization of the governing normal-form equations. We validate VIBE against recorded air sac pressure across 44 songs from twelve birds, showing that the recovered α corresponds to empirically measured air sac pressure. Pairing VIBE with Neuropixels recordings from RA in five birds, we find that RA activity is well predicted by the recovered parameters, and that α and β add predictive power beyond the acoustic features of song. By recovering biomechanical control parameters from the acoustic signal, VIBE makes the biomechanical coordinate system of song production accessible to the broader songbird research community.

doi:10.1016/j.brainres.2026.150566.title: Toward selective vowel-tone integration in non-tonal L2 learners of Mandarin: Evidence from MMN additivity.
doi:10.1016/j.brainres.2026.150566.authors: Mao Y, Li M, Cai X.
doi:10.1016/j.brainres.2026.150566.abstract: Syllable perception requires the continuous integration of segmental (consonants and vowels) and suprasegmental (lexical tones) information. While native listeners of tonal languages exhibit pre-attentive integration of these dimensions, it remains unclear whether non-tonal second language (L2) learners can develop such integration through L2 experience. The present study employed electroencephalogram (EEG) to record mismatch negativity (MMN) responses in a passive oddball paradigm, investigating the perceptual integration of consonants, vowels, and tones. Twenty-four native Mandarin listeners (L1 group) and fifteen non-tonal L2 learners of Mandarin (L2 group) were recruited. Stimuli included a standard syllable (/da1/), three single-deviants (/ga1/, /du1/, /da4/), and three double-deviants (/gu1/, /ga4/, /du4/). MMN additivity analyses compared original double-deviant MMN amplitudes against the sum of corresponding single-deviant MMN amplitudes. The L1 group exhibited robust sub-additive MMN patterns across all double-deviant combinations (consonant-vowel [CV], consonant-tone [CT], and vowel-tone [VT]), demonstrating integrated processing across all phonological dimensions. The L2 group showed delayed MMN peak latencies and reduced pre-attentive sensitivity to single consonant and single tone deviations. Crucially, they exhibited additivity for CV and CT combinations (independent processing), but a selective sub-additive trend for the VT combination, which we interpret as preliminary evidence for vowel-tone integration. These findings provide tentative support for the TTRACE model and refine the dimensional transfer hypothesis, suggesting that non-tonal L1 biases may be partially overcome through L2 experience when phonological dimensions share tight acoustic proximity within the syllable nucleus (i.e., vowel-tone integration). Non-tonal L2 learners display a developmental pattern rooted in acoustic salience and bottom-up physical binding.

doi:10.1016/j.neubiorev.2026.106997.title: Music as neuromodulation: A systematic review with insights from human intracranial electrophysiology.
doi:10.1016/j.neubiorev.2026.106997.authors: Far R, Theivendirarajah K, Kim K, Flaten E, Satkunendrarajah K, Milosevic L, Melloni L, Jacoby N, Valiante TA.
doi:10.1016/j.neubiorev.2026.106997.abstract: Music engages a wide range of cognitive and affective processes; however, the precise mechanisms by which music shapes brain activity remain incompletely understood. Human intracranial electrophysiology (iEEG) provides a unique opportunity to answer this question through direct recordings of neural activity with high spatial and temporal resolution. Here, we systematically review the intracranial literature on music perception and its cell- and circuit-level neural effects, identifying common principles extending across experimental paradigms and brain regions. Following PRISMA guidelines, three databases were queried for published literature describing quantitative modulations of neural activity in response to music exposure. We performed a narrative synthesis of study characteristics, main interventions and outcomes, and study quality. Integrating all studies, we outline a conceptual framework in which music is processed in an anatomically distributed fashion across multiple levels of abstraction. Within auditory cortex, iEEG studies demonstrate robust evidence for the encoding of basic acoustic features, while moderate evidence supports the predictive processing of musical expectations. In contrast, evidence remains sparse for the generation of emotional, mnemonic, and action-related representations of music in more distant cortical and subcortical regions. Studies of electrical stimulation mapping and single-unit neural activity also represent key areas for future research. Altogether, we propose that music can be understood as a neuromodulator that dynamically coordinates neural activity across sensory, association, limbic, and motor systems. We position music as a powerful model system for investigating sensory perception and integration in a complex, real-world context, while spotlighting iEEG as a valuable tool in this ongoing exploration.

doi:10.31234/osf.io/z7624_v1.title: Aging and Hearing Loss in Emotional Prosody Processing: Divergent Neural Adaptation and Behavioral Performance
doi:10.31234/osf.io/z7624_v1.authors: Lin Y, Lu Y, Ding H, Zhang Y.
doi:10.31234/osf.io/z7624_v1.abstract: Emotional prosody perception is vulnerable in later adulthood, yet the contributions of central aging and peripheral hearing loss remain unclear. Across two experiments, we combined event-related potentials (ERPs) , time-frequency analyses and behavioral measures to examine how aging and hearing sensitvity shape emotional prosody processing. Experiment 1 used acoustically matched speech and nonspeech stimuli in a passive oddball paradigm to assess preattentive processing. Experiment 2 examined explicit emotion identification and implicit stimulus judgment to evaluate goal-directed performance and its associations with neural responses. Aging was associated with reduced neural differentiation between emotions and lower behavioral efficiency, alongside enhanced P3a amplitude. Older adults also responded more slowly than younger adults during emotion identification. Hearing sensitivity showed no significant main effect on accuracy or reaction time, despite associations with delayed early neural processing and stronger theta- and alpha-band activity. Hearing-related neural effects were most evident in older adults and varied across emotions and stimulus types. Brain–behavior associations were selective: reduced mismatch negativity (MMN) was associated with slower responses during stimulus identification, whereas longer MMN latencies were associated with lower accuracy and slower responses during emotion identification. These findings indicate that aging and hearing loss have distinct yet interacting associations with emotional prosody processing, with neural responses not necessarily corresponding to behavioral performance. We propose an “asymmetric adaptation” account in which neural responses to degraded auditory input reorganize selectively across processing stages and contexts, potentially explaining this neural-behavioral divergence and informing more sensitive assessment of socioemotional communication in later adulthood.

doi:10.31234/osf.io/qyxvm_v1.title: Relationships Between Auditory Statistical Learning and Reading Skills in Children with Reading Difficulties
doi:10.31234/osf.io/qyxvm_v1.authors: Hu A, Siles B, Montoute M, Chan KHY, Young-Hong S, Van Horne A, Christiansen MH, Qi Z.
doi:10.31234/osf.io/qyxvm_v1.abstract: Purpose. This study evaluated the psychometric implications of a novel gamified SL task for school-aged children with reading difficulties and examined the relationships between auditory syllable-based statistical learning (SL) and literacy skills.Methods. Two groups of children aged 7–11 with reading difficulty were recruited. In Experiment 1, 13 children piloted a child-friendly, non-gamified auditory SL task at two timepoints, with learning assessed via a two-alternative forced-choice (2AFC) test at both timepoints and a statistically induced chunking recall (SICR) test at Timepoint 2. In Experiment 2, 22 children completed a gamified version of the SL task, with learning assessed via 2AFC and SICR at both timepoints and reading skills (nonword and sight-word fluency) assessed at Timepoint 1.Results. Children showed learning at the group level across timepoints, as measured by SICR in both gamified and non-gamified tasks, and as measured by 2AFC in the gamified task only. SICR showed higher internal consistency than 2AFC across tasks. Test-retest reliability for 2AFC was higher for the gamified (r = .64) than non-gamified (r = .14) task. Children’s performance on 2AFC and SICR in the gamified task were significantly associated with their nonword and sight-word reading fluency.Conclusions. Gamification and the use of a statistically induced chunking recall task in an auditory SL task improved the task’s psychometric properties in school-aged children with reading difficulties. Auditory SL was also associated with concurrent reading skills in these children, suggesting that the implicit learning of regularities in spoken language input may additionally support reading development.

doi:10.64898/2026.09.21.753161.title: A systems-level model of sleep-dependent memory-consolidation failure in neurodegeneration: the spindle–slow-oscillation decoupling cascade dissociates amyloid and tau
doi:10.64898/2026.09.21.753161.authors: Masry B, Shahin A, Malek ZS.
doi:10.64898/2026.09.21.753161.abstract: During non-rapid-eye-movement (NREM) sleep, the temporal coupling of cortical slow oscillations (SOs), thalamic spindles, and hippocampal sharp-wave ripples drives the consolidation of declarative memories. This coupling degrades in ageing and Alzheimer’s disease (AD), and although A β and tau leave dissociable signatures in human sleep, the mechanisms by which progressive pathology dismantles the consolidation machinery are difficult to isolate experimentally, and have not to our knowledge been reproduced in a model that can be perturbed directly. We built a systems-level model in which cortical SOs and thalamic spindles are generated by reduced oscillators, hippocampal ripples replay encoded spike sequences, and the measured per-event SO–spindle timing alignment causally gates spike-timing-dependent plasticity on cortical sequence synapses. A post-sleep cued-recall test reads out consolidation. Five neurodegeneration parameters (amyloid, tau, synaptic density, GABAergic inhibition, cholinergic tone) map to distinct mechanisms grounded in the human and animal literature. The model reproduces graded healthy consolidation and a progressive collapse in which coupling, slow-wave power, spindle power and recall fall monotonically and the overnight memory effect flips from consolidation to net forgetting, with weak memories failing first. Scrambling SO–spindle timing while holding oscillation power fixed abolishes consolidation, establishing that coupling timing, rather than oscillation power, is what the plasticity gate depends on within the model. A β and tau impair memory through orthogonal signatures (A β collapses slow-wave power while sparing replay order, tau the reverse) and this orthogonality holds across the entire A β × tau plane and survives simultaneous ±50% resampling of every mapping coefficient (40/40 samples), so it is not an artefact of a single calibration point. The model yields a falsifiable clinical prediction: closed-loop slow-oscillation enhancement rescues memory only when the deficit is amplitude/coupling-dominated, not when it is replay(tau)-dominated, despite normalising slow-wave power in both cases. Because the therapy arms dissociate coupling from memory benefit, the model also cautions against adopting SO–spindle coupling as a standalone surrogate endpoint. Author summary Sleep strengthens new memories through a precisely timed dialogue between three brain rhythms: cortical slow waves, thalamic sleep spindles, and hippocampal ripples. This timing breaks down in Alzheimer’s disease, but it has been unclear how the two hallmark pathologies of the disease (amyloid plaques and tau tangles) each contribute, and whether the same treatment would help both. We built a computer model that reproduces the rhythms and, crucially, lets the measured timing between slow waves and spindles control how strongly memories are written into cortex. As we gradually increase simulated pathology, the rhythms uncouple, memory consolidation fails, and overnight the model begins to forget rather than remember, exactly the trajectory seen in patients. When we scramble only the timing of the rhythms while leaving their strength untouched, consolidation collapses, showing that timing itself carries the memory benefit. The model separates amyloid (which weakens slow waves) from tau (which corrupts the hippocampal replay that timing is supposed to gate), and predicts that a leading experimental therapy (slow-wave stimulation during sleep) will help amyloid-dominated patients but fail tau-dominated patients even though it restores their slow waves. This prediction is directly testable and could guide patient selection for sleep-based interventions.

doi:10.64898/2026.10.01.26364332.title: Spatial hearing in adults with sequential bilateral cochlear implants: a longitudinal prospective cohort study
doi:10.64898/2026.10.01.26364332.authors: Valzolgher C, Ghiselli S, Epifania MO, Gullotta J, Zanetti D, Lilli G, Di Berardino F, Pozzi M, Ciorba A, Borin M, Brunelli N, Musumano LB, Frau GN, Tromballi G, Chini A, Rosi T, Malerba P, Cuda D, Pavani F.
doi:10.64898/2026.10.01.26364332.abstract: Bilateral cochlear implantation (BCI) can improve spatial hearing in adults with bilateral hearing loss, but the early development of spatial hearing following sequential BCI remains poorly understood. This prospective longitudinal study investigated changes in spatial hearing experience in 23 adults undergoing sequential BCI, assessed before and at ∼1, 3, and 8 months after bilateral implantation under two conditions: spontaneous and restrained head movements. Using a motion-tracking system combined with virtual reality, sound localization was assessed through absolute and signed errors, along with self-reported localization confidence and listening effort. Subjective spatial hearing was also assessed using the Speech, Spatial and Qualities of Hearing Scale (SSQ). Localization performance improved by 1 month after bilateral implantation, as evidenced by a reduction of absolute error and in the bias toward the first-implanted ear. Participants reported greater localization confidence and lower listening effort at 1 month, although these changes were not consistently maintained at later follow-ups. SSQ scores showed improved spatial hearing at 1 month, speech perception at 3 months, and sound clarity and discriminability at 8 months. Compared with head-restrained condition, accuracy and confidence improved when spontaneous head rotations were allowed. The temporal trajectories of localization bias, confidence, and effort were modulated by the duration of experience with the first CI. These findings indicate that changes in spatial hearing can emerge soon after second CI activation. They further highlight the contribution of spontaneous head movements and previous CI experience, and support the use of complementary measures to monitor the early development of bilateral listening.

doi:10.1016/j.bandc.2026.106487.title: Recall of overlearned speech in noise: Developmental ERP findings and an episodic buffer frame for culturally situated brain activity.
doi:10.1016/j.bandc.2026.106487.authors: D'Angiulli A, Sheculski M, Morrow A.
doi:10.1016/j.bandc.2026.106487.abstract: How does extensively practiced speech memory remain dependent on momentary sensory input, and how does this interaction shape brain activity during development? This perspective integrates exploratory behavioral and event-related potential (ERP) findings from a culturally situated spoken-sequence recognition paradigm with a working memory episodic-buffer account. We reanalyzed data from children and young adults who had memorized Quranic passages despite limited Arabic comprehension. Participants heard incomplete passages with or without static noise and selected the missing final word from phonologically plausible alternatives. Noise reduced recognition accuracy, and children generally responded more slowly. Descriptive ERP patterns revealed larger, more spatially distributed responses in children, spanning early auditory processing, mid-latency positivity, and later negative activity. We propose that recognition requires temporary binding of acoustic input, serial and rhythmic expectations, visual response cues, and consolidated sequence knowledge within an episodic buffer under executive control. Noise may impair perceptual fidelity and matching between transient input and stored representations. Developmental ERP differences may reflect representational coordination rather than neural efficiency. These preliminary findings motivate testable predictions concerning cross-modal congruence, familiarity, comprehension, and independently measured expertise. Culturally embedded learning practices provide informative contexts for examining interactions among working memory, long-term knowledge, and developing neural systems supporting cognition.

doi:10.31234/osf.io/sdg6x_v1.title: Dynamic Semantic–Prosodic Integration in Emotional Speech Perception: From Channel Dominance to Precision-Weighted Predictive Coding
doi:10.31234/osf.io/sdg6x_v1.abstract: Emotional speech is an important carrier of affective information in spoken communication. Its perception depends on the joint processing of emotional semantics and prosody, yet the relative contribution of these two information sources varies across individuals and contexts. However, a unified account is still lacking of why their processing weights change and how the brain dynamically adjusts them according to the reliability of incoming information. This review synthesizes evidence on emotional semantics and prosody, from relatively independent processing to interactive integration, and argues that their relationship is best understood in terms of dynamic weight allocation. On this basis, we propose a Precision-Weighted Predictive Coding Model (PW-PC), which integrates Bayesian inference, cue precision, and prediction error within a unified framework. The model assumes that semantic and prosodic information are continuously reweighted according to current evidence and its estimated precision, while incorporating sensory reliability, experience-based expectations, contextual diagnosticity, and reweighting flexibility. This framework shifts the focus of emotional speech research from identifying which channel dominates to explaining when, why, and how the brain dynamically reallocates weight across multiple affective information sources, thereby providing a unified theoretical perspective linking behavioral performance, neural dynamics, and computational mechanisms.

doi:10.1088/1741-2552/ae9eec.title: In silico framework for benchmarking optogenetic hearing restoration.
doi:10.1088/1741-2552/ae9eec.authors: Khurana L, Nejedly P, Zhang Y, Jagger DJ, Nogueira W, Moser T, Jablonski L.
doi:10.1088/1741-2552/ae9eec.abstract: Objective . Cochlear implants (CI) partially restore hearing in profoundly hearing-impaired or deaf individuals by electrically stimulating the auditory nerve. A primary bottleneck in electrical CIs is the broad spread of electrical current from each electrode that limits the transfer of spectral information, which might be overcome by future spatially confined optogenetic stimulation. Here we established an in silico framework, FraSCO, to model sound encoding in the human cochlea by an optical CI (oCI) for testing the potential of optogenetic hearing restoration. Approach . The biophysical modelling framework combined an optical ray tracing model implementing a human cochlea implanted with a waveguide-based oCI with a single compartment model of optogenetically modified spiral ganglion neurons (SGNs). The input was an optogenetic sound coding strategy and the quality of the neural representation was evaluated based on comparison of neurograms evoked by optogenetic and electrical stimulation to the spectrogram of the sound applied. The model incorporated technologically feasible properties of the oCIs with 64 stimulation channels. Main results . The biophysical modelling framework successfully captured essential physiological features of optogenetic SGN stimulation with a minimal set of ion channel types expressed in the SGN soma. Working with a sample of 1000 SGNs distributed along the tonotopic axis to represent sound encoding, we found that improved spectral selectivity achieves comparable information encoding to electrical implants despite lower stimulation rates in current implementations of optogenetic stimulation. We also found that potential oCI users are predicted to be less impacted by noisy backgrounds. Significance . The established computational framework enables an in silico investigation and benchmarking of sound encoding in the cochlea by future oCI and state-of-the-art electrical CI. The results of the exemplary application indicate that optogenetic sound encoding has potential to improve speech understanding in noisy environments for CI users.

doi:10.31234/osf.io/qr9zt_v3.title: Weak Links between Speech Perception and Speech Production at the Subphonemic Level
doi:10.31234/osf.io/qr9zt_v3.authors: Wong BWL, Samuel AG, Kapnoula EC.
doi:10.31234/osf.io/qr9zt_v3.abstract: Recent research has shown individual differences in gradiency, defined as sensitivity to fine-grained acoustic differences at the subphonemic level. Consistency also varies, with some listeners providing more stable responses than others to repeated presentations of the same stimuli. However, it remains unclear whether gradiency and consistency are linked between perception and production. Across two experiments, 160 Spanish speakers completed a Visual Analogue Scale (VAS) task measuring perceptual gradiency and consistency along a Spanish /ba/–/pa/ continuum manipulated in 7–8 ms steps of voice onset time (VOT). The same participants also performed an explicit imitation task using the same stimuli. Results revealed only weak relationships between perceptual gradiency and imitation accuracy, as well as between perceptual consistency and imitation consistency, even after accounting for other factors related to speech perception and imitation. These findings suggest that models proposing strong perception–production coupling may not extend to the subphonemic level.

doi:10.7554/elife.109901.title: Infants at high and low likelihood for autism show different EEG developmental trajectories in speech tracking and statistical learning.
doi:10.7554/elife.109901.authors: Godel M, Fló A, Benjamin L, Dehaene-Lambertz G, Schaer M.
doi:10.7554/elife.109901.abstract: Delayed onset of canonical babbling and first words is often reported in infants later diagnosed with autism spectrum disorder. Identifying the neural mechanisms underlying language acquisition in autism is therefore critical to inform early diagnosis, prognosis, and intervention strategies. In this study, we investigated two speech processing mechanisms previously identified as atypical in children and adults with autism: the neural ability to track syllables, and statistical learning, the capacity to detect speech regularities beneath surface variability. We recorded 83 longitudinal high-density electroencephalograms from 44 infants (2.5-22.6 months) at high (HL) and low (LL) likelihood for autism and assessed their verbal outcomes at 20 months. Neural entrainment was measured at syllable and word frequencies during exposure to a multi-speaker stream of concatenated tri-syllabic words, followed by a word recognition test using evoked response potential (ERP) recording. Our findings revealed reduced tracking abilities at the syllabic level in HL infants, a measure that correlated with verbal outcomes. While HL infants did not exhibit deficits in statistical learning itself, they displayed reduced novelty orientation during the word recognition test, indicated by a reduced late ERP. By contrast, multi-talker variability temporarily disrupted word segmentation around 12 months in LL infants, but not in HL infants, potentially reflecting decreased sensitivity to human voices variability in the HL group. These results emphasize the importance of longitudinal protocols employing online, implicit measures to track the hierarchical stages of speech processing in both HL and LL infants.

doi:10.3758/s13423-026-03020-4.title: Musical expectations modulate declarative memory formation.
doi:10.3758/s13423-026-03020-4.authors: Benes N, Panitz DY, Gabay S, Mendelsohn A.
doi:10.3758/s13423-026-03020-4.abstract: Music elicits powerful engagement through the generation and resolution of expectations, yet its effects on declarative memory formation remain unclear. Using predictive processing frameworks, we examined whether harmonic expectancy and prediction error modulate memory formation for concurrently presented visual stimuli. Participants listened to Bach chorales in which musical instruments probabilistically predicted consonant or dissonant endings, generating distinct expectations of outcomes. Neutral images were presented both before and after the critical musical period, and memory was tested 24 h later. At the period where the music either changed to dissonant or remained consonant, participants were prompted to rate whether the music was pleasant or unpleasant at that time. Participants showed robust sensitivity to harmonic structure, rating consonant endings as pleasant and responding faster to dissonant endings. Critically, unsigned prediction error magnitude positively predicted subsequent recognition accuracy and confidence. Whereas the relationship between prediction error and recognition accuracy did not reliably differ across temporal periods, its relationship with confidence was significantly stronger for images encoded in the anticipatory period preceding the musical transition. These findings indicate that musical expectations modulate declarative memory, with temporal specificity evident for subjective confidence, suggesting that prediction-related processes gate episodic encoding in a graded, time-dependent manner.

doi:10.64898/2026.09.17.751377.title: Chemogenetic activation of hypothalamic oxytocin neurons reorients face exploration toward the eyes in macaques
doi:10.64898/2026.09.17.751377.authors: Ameloot A, Disarbois E, Elseedy H, Duperron C, Grinevich V, Sirigu A, Duhamel J.
doi:10.64898/2026.09.17.751377.abstract: ABSTRACT Oxytocin (OT) shapes social behavior across species. However, in humans and non-human primates, its effects have been studied mainly through exogenous administration, despite uncertainty about the extent to which peripherally administered OT reaches the brain and limited control over the neural pathways it engages. To overcome these limitations, we developed a chemogenetic approach targeting the endogenous OT system by selectively activating OT neurons in the paraventricular nucleus (PVN) and supraoptic nucleus (SON) of macaques using excitatory DREADDs. We combined this approach with digit-tracking, a non-invasive, calibration-free assay of face exploration in freely moving animals. In this task, subjects explored blurred face images through a finger-controlled viewing window, providing a proxy for gaze exploration and enabling behavioral assessment of OT neuron activation. DREADD-mediated activation redirected ongoing face exploration toward the eyes at the expense of non-face regions, increasing the consistency of eye-directed exploration and the time spent inspecting the eyes once reached. Immunohistochemical analysis confirmed selective DREADD expression in OT neurons of the PVN and SON. These findings provide the first causal evidence in primates that hypothalamic OT neurons regulate social visual orienting by increasing exploration of the eyes, thereby linking a hallmark effect of intranasal OT administration to defined central OT pathways and establishing chemogenetic access to this system in freely behaving macaques.

doi:10.1016/j.neuropsychologia.2026.1096.title: A systematic review of the maturation of selected cortical auditory event-related potentials in passive paradigms: Developmental changes from infancy to early adulthood.
doi:10.1016/j.neuropsychologia.2026.1096.authors: Martin I, Arora J, Hamill L, Cho E, Scanavini G, Radanovic A, Shaukat L, Hill NJ, Shah SA, Alkhoury L.
doi:10.1016/j.neuropsychologia.2026.1096.abstract: Electroencephalography (EEG) offers a unique window into the neural dynamics of cognition, particularly through event-related potentials (ERPs) that index sensory, attentional, and cognitive processes. EEG and ERP measures are widely used to study atypical neurodevelopment in children due to their sensitivity to disruptions caused by genetic and acquired brain disorders. We conducted a systematic review of the literature on the typical presentation of four core cortical auditory and language-related ERP components, extracted during passive paradigms, from infancy to early adulthood. These components reflect neural responses to the passive perception of discrete stimuli (N100), the automatic detection of deviant stimuli (Mismatch Negativity (MMN), sometimes in children referred to as the Mismatch Response (MMR)), the allocation of attention to deviant stimuli (P3a), and language processing of discrete stimuli (N400). Drawing from 61 studies, many of which reported on a single component within a specific age range, we chart developmental trajectories of ERP latencies, amplitudes, and scalp topographies. Across all components, latency tended to decrease with increasing age. Amplitude trajectories varied: N100 amplitude tended to decrease; MMN amplitude remained relatively stable or showed a slight decline; P3a amplitude typically increased during early childhood before decreasing in early school age; N400 amplitude consistently declined. Scalp topographical reports, among all components, revealed a shift toward increased focal activation with increasing age. Together, these findings provide a normative foundation for acoustic and auditory language processing in the context of the selected components in typical development, serving as a necessary reference point for understanding and assessing atypical development.

doi:10.3758/s13423-026-03013-3.title: How auditory rhythm perception shapes speech production: The influence of neural synchronization and rhythmic patterns.
doi:10.3758/s13423-026-03013-3.authors: Tan C, Yan Q, Zhang Q.
doi:10.3758/s13423-026-03013-3.abstract: Auditory rhythm perception facilitates language processing, yet it remains unclear how neural synchronization to external rhythms contributes to speech production. The present study examined whether individual differences in neural synchronization modulate rhythmic priming effects during speech production and whether such effects depend on the rhythmic structure of the target utterance. Eighty-six native Mandarin speakers performed a speech production task involving two four-syllable rhythmic patterns as targets: the dominant [2+2] pattern (boundary after the second syllable) and the less common [1+3] pattern (boundary after the first syllable). Each target was preceded by a rhythmically congruent or incongruent pure-tone prime. Neural synchronization to the primes was quantified using cerebral-acoustic coherence (CACoh) between EEG activity and the temporal envelope of the auditory rhythms, and rhythmic priming was assessed using response latencies. K-means clustering of CACoh measures identified two participant groups characterized by relatively high and low levels of neural synchronization. Behavioral analyses revealed a significant Group × Target Type interaction. For the less common [1+3] pattern, low synchronizers exhibited reliable rhythmic priming, whereas high synchronizers showed little or no priming benefit. In contrast, priming effects for the dominant [2+2] pattern were modest and comparable across groups. Furthermore, higher theta-band CACoh was associated with smaller priming effects for [1+3] targets, indicating that stronger neural synchronization predicted reduced behavioral facilitation. These findings suggest that the influence of auditory rhythm on speech production depends jointly on individual neural synchronization capacity and the rhythmic structure of the planned utterance. The results provide new evidence that auditory-motor interactions in speech production are shaped by both listener-specific and utterance-specific factors.

doi:10.64898/2026.10.09.758064.title: What EEG doesn’t see: a whole-brain MEG map of sleep spindles and slow oscillations
doi:10.64898/2026.10.09.758064.authors: Calvel A, Greenlaw K, Steele CJ, Coffey EB.
doi:10.64898/2026.10.09.758064.abstract: ABSTRACT Sleep spindles and slow oscillations (SOs) are hallmarks of non-rapid eye movement (NREM) sleep, linked to memory consolidation and restorative functions. They are usually detected in one or a few scalp electroencephalography (EEG) channels with parameters that vary across studies, and serve as the reference even in magnetoencephalography (MEG), fMRI and intracranial studies. We argue that these choices filter which neural activity is captured. Nineteen young adults took a daytime nap during simultaneous MEG and EEG. Using MEG source imaging across 416 cortical, subcortical and cerebellar regions, we mapped the amplitude and density of SOs (0.5–4 Hz, and 0.5–2 and 2–4 Hz separately) and of spindles (9–18 Hz, and slow, 9–12.9 Hz, and fast, 13–18 Hz, separately), and related each region’s activity to a single scalp derivation (Cz–M1). Both rhythms were detected throughout the brain, including the thalamus, hippocampus, amygdala, basal ganglia and cerebellum. The balance between bands varied across regions: fast spindles predominated over slow spindles along the dorsal midline, around the central sulcus and in the thalamus, slow spindles predominated in occipital cortex and the cerebellar hemispheres, and 2–4 Hz SOs were relatively most prominent in occipital cortex. Amplitude and density formed reliable but distinct maps: regions with larger fast spindles also had more of them, whereas SOs, and slow spindles once source depth was controlled, were larger where they were less frequent. More SOs were detected in every region than at Cz–M1, whereas more fast spindles were detected at Cz–M1 than in any single region. Around the SO, slow-spindle activity had the same timing at the scalp and in the sources, but the up-state increase in fast-spindle activity seen at the scalp was absent from local sources. Slow spindles were the most strongly shared events, and sensorimotor sources the most scalp-like. Thus, a single scalp derivation offers a selective and partly composite view of sleep oscillations, with implications for interpreting their functional roles and for targeting them with closed-loop auditory stimulation. Highlights Whole-brain MEG source maps of NREM slow oscillations and sleep spindles Amplitude and density maps align for fast spindles but diverge for slower events More slow oscillations are detected in every region than at the scalp More fast spindles are detected at the scalp than in any single region Fast spindles in sensorimotor cortex are the most scalp-like Scalp up-state fast-spindle activity is absent from local sources

doi:10.31234/osf.io/52mvr_v2.title: Multiple neural signatures of serial order access in verbal working memory
doi:10.31234/osf.io/52mvr_v2.authors: Cristoforetti G, Xu Y, Viganò S, van Dijck JP, Bottini R, Fias W.
doi:10.31234/osf.io/52mvr_v2.abstract: Serial order working memory allows information to be maintained as structured sequences, yet the neural formats supporting access to serial position remain unclear. Behavioral evidence suggests that temporal order can be recoded into spatial representations, but serial order may also rely on representations that generalize beyond the spatial configuration of encoding. Here, participants memorized digit sequences presented either left-to-right or right-to-left, thereby reversing the mapping between ordinal position and external space while keeping retrieval cues centrally presented during fMRI. Behaviorally, spatial coding during retrieval was modulated by encoding direction. Multivoxel pattern analysis revealed direction-specific decoding in lateral parietal cortex: left inferior parietal cortex encoded serial position after left-to-right encoding, whereas right inferior parietal cortex did so after right-to-left encoding. In contrast, cross-direction decoding revealed direction-invariant effects in left supramarginal and precentral regions, suggesting serial-position information that generalized across spatial layouts. Finally, univariate parametric modulation revealed activity scaling with serial position in bilateral posterior parietal cortex, left anterior hippocampus, and action-control regions. Together, these findings indicate that serial order access in working memory relies on multiple neural signatures, including spatially context-dependent representations, direction-invariant ordinal codes, and graded process-related activity.

doi:10.1093/cercor/bhag160.title: Neural signatures of serial order access in verbal working memory.
doi:10.1093/cercor/bhag160.authors: Cristoforetti G, Xu Y, Viganò S, van Dijck JP, Bottini R, Fias W.
doi:10.1093/cercor/bhag160.abstract: Serial order working memory allows information to be maintained as structured sequences, yet the neural formats supporting access to serial position remain unclear. doi:10.1162/jocn.a.2727.title: Neural Representations of Perceptual Reorganization in the Musical Scale Illusion.
doi:10.1162/jocn.a.2727.authors: Choi A, Ham J, Lee K, Choi I.
doi:10.1162/jocn.a.2727.abstract: The auditory system organizes complex acoustic input into coherent perceptual streams, yet how neural responses relate to physical stimulus structure and reported perception when the two diverge remains unclear. We investigated perceptual reorganization using the scale illusion, in which interleaved tone sequences presented separately to the two ears are typically heard as continuous melodic streams.Thirty participants listened to illusory, zigzag, and continuous sequences during EEG recording and reported whether each sequence sounded continuous or zigzag. Temporal response function models characterized neural encoding and reconstruction of amplitude-envelope (envelope) and pitch-change magnitude features. We tested whether neural responses during illusory listening corresponded more closely to reference patterns associated with the physical zigzag structure or reported continuous organization. Illusory sequences were predominantly categorized as Continuous and elicited longer RTs than non-illusory sequences. Encoding models revealed delayed pitch-change magnitude responses in the illusory condition, whereas envelope latencies remained comparatively stable. For pitch-change magnitude, reconstruction correlations computed over the full sequence exceeded chance levels estimated separately for each reference, with higher correlations for the continuous reference. Envelope correlations exceeded neither chance level, despite a small relative preference for the zigzag reference. These findings show that neural response timing and relative correspondence with the tested reference patterns depend on the modeled feature during the scale illusion. The reconstruction result concerns correlations across complete sequences and does not establish continuous tracking of the perceived melody.

doi:10.64898/2026.10.07.756537.title: Modulation of the speed of Intrinsic Alpha Frequency (IAF) with tACS modulates variability of illusory speech perception
doi:10.64898/2026.10.07.756537.authors: Deb S, Bhunia D, Singh VAV, Muralidharan V, Roy D.
doi:10.64898/2026.10.07.756537.abstract: Navigating the world requires our brains to constantly process a massive influx of information from the environment. One of the most remarkable yet complex feats the human brain performs daily is speech perception. It is a multifaceted, hierarchical process that relies heavily on the integration of auditory and visual cues, particularly in noisy environments. Neural integration of these streams is hypothesized to depend on temporal mechanisms governed by individual alpha frequency (IAF, 8-12 Hz), which serves as a key neural correlate of the temporal binding window (TBW). While IAF has been linked to multisensory integration, its role in shaping multisensory illusions remains largely unexplored. Here, we tested this directly using transcranial alternating current stimulation (tACS) to modulate occipital activity during multisensory conflict. In a two-day protocol involving 27 healthy participants, resting-state EEG was recorded to determine IAF. On Day 2, participants then performed a multisensory speech task involving congruent (pa/, /ta/, /ka/) and incongruent McGurk stimuli (auditory /pa/, visual /ka/), both at baseline and during tACS applied at IAF and offset frequencies (IAF +/- 2 Hz) over occipital electrodes. While accuracy for congruent syllables remained high across conditions, results revealed that tACS significantly reduced the perception of illusory /ta/ percepts during McGurk trials. Finally, using a phenomenological model based on Kuramoto oscillators, we provided a mechanistic explanation for the percentage of illusory responses observed across participants under the influence of tACS at IAF and offsets. This study highlights the potential for targeted neuromodulatory interventions to influence multisensory processing in clinical or professional settings.

doi:10.1093/cercor/bhag091.title: Cortico-striatal network architecture shapes rhythmic biases in music.
doi:10.1093/cercor/bhag091.authors: Lumaca M, van der Werff J, Keller PE, Kotz SA, Baggio G, Rosso M, Kakihara M, Martin M, Vuust P, Ravignani A.
doi:10.1093/cercor/bhag091.abstract: Why is human music rhythmically structured the way it is? One hypothesis is that the human brain is intrinsically wired to favor specific rhythmic organizations. To test this, we collected diffusion and resting-state functional MRI (fMRI) data from musically untrained participants and, weeks later, asked them to imitate randomly generated drumming sequences using finger taps. These imitations exhibited systematic biases toward temporal structures widespread in human music: predictable patterns characterized by isochronous organization (1:1) and other small integer ratios (2:1 and 3:1). Functional connectome analyses linked the increased rhythmic predictability of reproduced rhythms to intrinsic interactions between networks implicated in auditory timing (auditory basal ganglia) and executive control (task-positive and task-negative networks). Notably, the tendency toward isochrony-a feature highly conserved across species-was selectively associated with increased fiber density within a cortico-basal ganglia-thalamo-cortical network previously implicated in the perception and production of a metronomic pulse from music (the "beat"). Our findings reveal how stable neural architecture predisposes humans to produce rhythmically structured patterns. This evidence links intrinsic brain circuitry to individual cultural expressions, supporting the account of human symbolic systems, including music, as biocultural hybrids.

doi:10.64898/2026.10.05.755932.title: Identifying neural correlates of auditory perceptual awareness and deviance using a no-report inattentional deafness paradigm
doi:10.64898/2026.10.05.755932.authors: Ellinghorst A, Dellert T, Zhu Y, Straube T, Dykstra AR, Schlossmacher I.
doi:10.64898/2026.10.05.755932.abstract: The relationship between neural processes supporting perception, deviance processing, and post-perceptual task demands during auditory processing is not well understood. We used multitone masking and a no-report inattentional deafness paradigm to dissociate neural correlates of auditory perceptual awareness, deviance processing, and task demands. Evoked responses to physically identical target-tone pairs were recorded across three phases differing only in task instructions. In Phase A, human participants remained naïve to (and thus unaware of) the target tones. In Phase B, participants were informed about (and thus aware of) the target tones. In Phase C, participants remained aware of the target tones and judged the duration of the silent gap between them, rendering them task-relevant. When participants were aware of them, target tones elicited an auditory awareness negativity and an increased positivity in the P3 window), with larger responses when target tones were additionally task-relevant. Furthermore, though largest in Phase C, deviant stimuli elicited a mismatch negativity across all task conditions, while a significant P3 to deviants was only observed in Phase C. Thus, early and late responses can be independently modulated by awareness, deviance, and task-relevance, indicating that they do not necessarily rely on shared neural mechanisms despite overlapping spatiotemporal profiles.

doi:10.64898/2026.10.09.758111.title: A touch that lingers: synchronized patting strengthens neural tracking of auditory rhythm in newborns
doi:10.64898/2026.10.09.758111.authors: Hegde M, Edalati M, Kösem A, Foulon A, Lefebvre S, Wallois F, Trainor L, Tillmann B, Moghimi S.
doi:10.64898/2026.10.09.758111.abstract: Rhythmic auditory stimulation in early life rarely occurs in isolation. Caregivers naturally combine singing and speech with rhythmic touch, rocking, and visual cues. Newborns are sensitive to auditory rhythm from birth, yet little is known about how temporally aligned information across sensory modalities shapes the neural encoding of auditory rhythmic structure. Here, we tested whether rhythmic touch can alter how the newborn brain tracks an ongoing auditory signal beyond the period of tactile stimulation. We recorded high-density electroencephalography from full-term newborns (N = 40), 1-3 days after birth, while they were exposed to recorded French lullabies presented either alone or accompanied by gentle patting synchronized with the metrically strong beat. Patting was delivered intermittently, allowing us to compare neural responses to lullabies across conditions, notably during periods without concurrent tactile stimulation. We quantified neural tracking of the lullabies using brain-stimulus coherence and temporal response function modeling. Newborns’ neural activity synchronized with the rhythmic structure of the lullabies at frequencies corresponding to both the beat and the metrically accented strong beat. Critically, neural tracking was stronger when the lullabies had been accompanied by synchronized touch than when they were presented alone, and this enhancement persisted during subsequent periods in which no touch was delivered. Although rhythmic touch enhanced tracking in newborns with both weaker and stronger auditory-only tracking, there was a larger gain in those who initially showed weaker auditory tracking. Together, our findings reveal that the newborn brain exploits rhythmic touch to strengthen its encoding of auditory rhythm, and that this benefit outlasts the touch itself. This provides neural evidence that patting an infant in time with a song, a caregiving practice shared across cultures, does more than simply provide a tactile stimulation. It shapes how the newborn brain encodes the song’s rhythm.

doi:10.64898/2026.10.12.757951.title: The ovarian cycle and estradiol modulate cortical network state and auditory entrainment in mice and women
doi:10.64898/2026.10.12.757951.authors: Carreno Munoz MI, Chehrazi P, Ciancone Chama A, Knoth I, Fernandes do Nascimento SA, Campbell B, Csicsvari J, Chattopadhyaya B, Lippe S, Di Cristo G.
