doi:10.1111/psyp.70407.title: Delivery and Attitude Modulate Shared Neural Processing of Speech Through Distinct Frequency Channels.
doi:10.1111/psyp.70407.authors: Atia B, Berson Y, Goldstein A.
doi:10.1111/psyp.70407.abstract: Listeners' brains align when they attend to the same speech, but what determines how strongly they align is not well understood. We asked whether that alignment tracks the communicative relation between a listener and a message, manipulating it from the speaker's side and from the listener's, and bounding the account with a manipulation that alters the social setting while leaving the relation intact. In two magnetoencephalography experiments, we measured inter-subject correlation of band-limited envelopes, which resolves shared processing by frequency rather than treating it as a single quantity. In Study 1, 40 listeners watched the same actor deliver the same speech charismatically and non-charismatically, so that content and identity were held constant. Charismatic delivery raised correlation most strongly in the beta band, and after regression of the acoustic and visual features, the surviving effect was concentrated in right perisylvian cortex. In Study 2, listeners read a favorable or unfavorable description of a speaker they had never encountered and watched a second speaker either with or without a minimal cue that an audience was present. A newly formed attitude raised correlation in alpha and theta within the same right perisylvian region, whereas the audience cue, which left both the message and the listener's disposition unchanged, produced no detectable change in any band. Correlation also proved partly dispositional: how strongly a listener synchronized on one task predicted their synchrony on the other, specifically in alpha and independently of personality. Delivery and attitude thus converge on a common substrate for the speaker's expressive signal, reaching it through separate frequency channels.

doi:10.1111/psyp.70412.title: Sound Flexibly Interacts With Dual-Format Templates to Optimize Visual Search.
doi:10.1111/psyp.70412.authors: Zhai M, Zhao S, Chen Z, Feng C, Feng W.
doi:10.1111/psyp.70412.abstract: Previous studies indicate that the dual formats of templates recursively operate in tandem during visual search tasks. The guiding template with coarse features supports target localization, whereas the target template with precise features supports target identification. However, whether a sound that provides target-consistent identity information would flexibly interact with these two templates to optimize search behavior remains unclear. Across two experiments, event-related potentials (ERPs) were recorded while participants searched for and identified a visual target letter ("V" or "K"). In Experiment 1, visual targets were presented in isolation (V) or synchronously with a speech sound that was congruent (AVcon) or incongruent (AVincon) with the target; Experiment 2 additionally paired the target with a sound unrelated to both potential targets and distractors (AVun). Behaviorally, converging findings across experiments indicated that relative to AVun and V conditions, congruent sounds improved accuracy and shortened response times, whereas incongruent sounds prolonged response times. ERP results revealed early cross-modal interactions, reflected in amplitude modulations of the occipital P195 and centroparietal N270 components in the AVcon and AVincon conditions relative to summed unimodal ERPs (Exp. 1); these interactions were reduced in the AVun condition, in which the sound was uninformative about potential targets (Exp. 2). Cross-condition multivariate pattern analysis (MVPA) showed higher target-presence decoding accuracy in the AVcon condition than in the AVincon, AVun, and V conditions. Peak-to-peak improvements in the AVcon-AVincon and AVcon-V comparisons, but not the AVcon-AVun comparison, were positively correlated with corresponding improvements in behavioral accuracy. These findings suggest that the interaction between sounds and the dual formats of templates is contingent on the usefulness of available information. When the guiding template is relatively efficient, task-irrelevant sounds may generally interact with the entire visual search array. Subsequently, congruent sounds selectively enhance target-template processing, potentially contributing to improved target identification.

doi:10.1016/j.cognition.2026.106731.title: Aversive learning retroactively modulates neutral episodic memories structured by prior knowledge of predictive sequences.
doi:10.1016/j.cognition.2026.106731.abstract: Linking memories of temporally separated neutral and threatening experiences can support later recognition of early warning signals. Yet it remains unclear what cognitive processes might allow the seemingly inconsequential neutral events - encoded in safe contexts and thus prone to forgetting - to nevertheless be preserved in memory well enough to inform future threat predictions. Here, we tested whether Pavlovian threat conditioning retroactively strengthens long-term episodic memory for previously encoded neutral events by leveraging prior knowledge of their predictive relations. Young adults first learned to anticipate the order of semantic categories in two deterministic sequences (A → B → C and D → E → F) through repeated presentation of images depicting category exemplars. They then incidentally encoded trial-unique exemplars from each category during sequence viewing. In a next phase, exemplars from the third-position categories were repeated such that one (C) predicted mild electric shocks, whereas the other (F) was never reinforced, creating a category-level threat association through conditioning. After 24 h, recognition memory for exemplars of categories encoded before conditioning depended on sequence and position: when a sequence ended with a shock-predictive category, memory favored the starting category (A) over the following category (B) - an effect absent in the control categories (D and E). These results suggest that aversive learning can retroactively reshape episodic memories of neutral events when they are scaffolded by prior sequence knowledge, bridging temporal gaps and thereby potentially promoting early threat anticipation.

doi:10.64898/2026.10.10.758219.title: Acoustic Context Shapes Cortical Encoding of Spectral Discrimination in Normal and Impaired Hearing
doi:10.64898/2026.10.10.758219.authors: Undurraga JA, Stefancu I, Rekswinkel M, Simonsen LB, Van Eeckhoutte M.
doi:10.64898/2026.10.10.758219.abstract: The auditory change complex (ACC) provides a cortical measure of acoustic discrimination, yet the mechanisms shaping responses to spectrotemporally complex sounds remain poorly understood. We investigated how acoustic context and temporal-envelope variability influence cortical encoding of spectral contrast in normal-hearing (NH) and hearing-impaired (HI) listeners. Electroencephalography (EEG) was used to record ACCs and auditory steady-state responses (ASSRs) evoked by spectrotemporally modulated stimuli. We compared conventional spectro-temporal modulations (STMs) with a novel discrete spectro-temporal modulation (DSTM) paradigm, examined temporal roving, and evaluated cortical responses to spectral contrast in NH and HI listeners. ACCs elicited by DSTM stimuli were larger and more symmetrical across transition directions than those elicited by conventional STMs. Temporal roving markedly reduced responses to intensity changes while largely preserving responses to spectral changes, indicating a partial dissociation between intensity-driven and spectrally driven cortical discrimination. ACC responses decreased systematically with spectral contrast and were weaker and delayed in HI listeners. By contrast, ASSRs remained highly detectable and showed no systematic dependence on spectral contrast, supporting a distinction between contrast-sensitive cortical discrimination and ongoing envelope encoding. Temporal roving further enhanced separation between NH and HI listeners. ACC response strength was significantly associated with behavioural STM discrimination thresholds and explained variance beyond age and audiometric thresholds. These findings demonstrate that cortical representations of spectral discrimination are shaped by acoustic context and temporal-envelope statistics. Temporal roving attenuates intensity-driven responses while preserving spectrally driven discrimination, providing insight into cortical encoding of spectrotemporal contrast and its relationship to perceptual performance.

doi:10.64898/2026.10.16.759621.title: Neural categorisation of rhythm in human newborns
doi:10.64898/2026.10.16.759621.authors: Barbero, F. M.; Lenc, T.; Gallard, A.; Jacoby, N.; Polak, R.; Varlet, M.; Foulon, A.; Moghimi, S.; Nozaradan, S.
doi:10.64898/2026.10.16.759621.abstract: Music is ubiquitous across cultures, and humans engage in social interactions through music from early in life. A cornerstone of these interactions is rhythm categorisation, allowing the sheer diversity of rhythmic inputs to be mapped onto internal rhythm categories. The pervasiveness of certain rhythm categories across cultures suggests that rhythm categorisation may be partially rooted in neurobiological predispositions constraining the internal representations of rhythm. However, this view appears to conflict with the diversity of music practices across cultures, which points to a role of experience in rhythm categorisation. To assess the relative contributions of neurobiological predispositions and experience, we tested 0- to 3-day-old newborns, capitalising on their minimal postnatal experience with music. Using electroencephalography (EEG), we recorded, in newborns and adults, brain responses to drum sounds whose pattern of relative interval duration ranged from isochronous to long-short rhythms (1:1 - 2:1 interval ratio). Results indicate significant categorisation in newborns's neural responses, with a representational structure that correlate with those of adults, yet with a greater degree of differentiation across rhythms. These findings reveal neurobiological predispositions enabling rhythm categorisation to be present at birth and further shaped across the lifespan, highlighting the evolutionary roots and plasticity supporting this human cultural practice.

doi:10.1016/j.bbr.2026.116504.title: Rapid inter-individual vocal interactions in freely behaving rats revealed by acoustic source localization.
doi:10.1016/j.bbr.2026.116504.authors: Kamatani M, Hakataya S, Toya G, Yamamoto S, Okanoya K.
doi:10.1016/j.bbr.2026.116504.abstract: Ultrasonic vocalizations (USVs) in rodents have been widely used as indicators of affective states; however, their role in rapid temporal exchange between individuals remains largely unexplored, primarily due to technical limitations in identifying vocalizing individuals during free social interactions. Here, we combined acoustic source localization (USVCAM) with markerless multi-animal tracking to examine the temporal structure of vocal interactions in freely behaving rat dyads. In three dyads with sufficient vocal output, inter-individual vocalization intervals exhibited a clear peak at approximately 50-250 ms, indicating fast temporal exchanges of vocalizations between individuals. To test whether this pattern could arise from independent vocal production, we performed Monte Carlo randomized simulations based on empirically observed intra-individual intervals. The simulated distributions failed to reproduce the empirical peak and instead showed a concentration at shorter intervals, resulting in a significant distributional difference. These results reject the null hypothesis of independent vocal generation and suggest that the observed temporal structure reflects the influence of one individual's vocalizations on those of the other individual. Together, these findings extend the potential applications of rodent USVs, in addition to their established use as affective indicators, by providing a proof-of-principle demonstration of rapid inter-individual vocal exchanges and a tractable experimental framework for investigating the temporal dynamics of social vocal communication.

doi:10.3389/fnins.2026.1919376.title: Neural signatures of auditory distraction and cognitive demand during working memory performance.
doi:10.3389/fnins.2026.1919376.abstract: Cognitive performance in real-world environments often requires maintaining working memory under simultaneous cognitive demand and environmental distraction. Although both factors have independently been associated with alterations in attention and executive control, their combined neural effects remain insufficiently understood. The present study investigated the influence of auditory distraction, time pressure, and their combination on working memory performance using a multidimensional electroencephalography (EEG) framework. Thirty healthy participants completed a working memory task under baseline, distraction, time-pressure, and combined conditions while EEG was recorded from 32 channels. Neural activity was characterized using oscillatory bandpower, topographical statistical mapping, hemispheric asymmetry, and weighted Phase Lag Index functional connectivity. Behavioral performance was complemented by subjective workload and stress assessments. Distraction was primarily characterized by widespread alpha-band suppression, significant frontal and parietal delta-band increases, and decreased frontal alpha asymmetry, whereas time pressure elicited frontal and parietal theta-band power increases. Rather than representing an additive superposition of both manipulations, the combined condition exhibited a distinct spatial pattern of oscillatory changes. Hemispheric asymmetry analyses revealed condition-dependent lateralization patterns that complemented conventional bandpower analyses. While alpha asymmetry primarily differentiated distraction, beta asymmetry emerged as the most consistent hemispheric marker across the experimental conditions showing regional beta-bandpower changes, highlighting the additional value of lateralized EEG measures for characterizing cognitive demands. Functional connectivity analyses did not reveal significant condition-dependent effects. These findings demonstrate distinct oscillatory signatures of distraction, time pressure, and their combination, highlighting the value of a multidimensional EEG framework for investigating concurrent cognitive demands.

doi:10.31234/osf.io/7fsgv_v1.title: Shared Early Language Access Predicts Adult Fluid Cognition in Deaf and Hard-of-Hearing Individuals
doi:10.31234/osf.io/7fsgv_v1.authors: Dye MWG, Kartheiser G, Contreras J.
doi:10.31234/osf.io/7fsgv_v1.abstract: Early language experience has been proposed to play a central role in the development of higher cognition, but evidence from deaf and hard-of-hearing (DHH) individuals remains difficult to interpret because language ability, auditory access, and family language environment are often confounded. The present study examined fluid cognition in 208 DHH young adults with diverse histories of deafness onset, cochlear implantation, family background, and American Sign Language (ASL) acquisition. Participants completed objective measures of ASL proficiency and the NIH Toolbox Fluid Cognition Battery. Confirmatory factor analysis indicated that NIH Toolbox performance was better characterized by two latent factors, Executive Control and Memory, than by a single factor. Latent profile analysis identified four cognitive profiles reflecting dissociable patterns of performance across these domains. Traditional hearing-history and language ability variables, including age of cochlear implantation, age of deafness onset, age of ASL acquisition, and ASL comprehension and production measures did not individually predict latent cognitive factor scores. In contrast, a derived measure of early shared linguistic modality – indicating likely access to a common language modality between child and caregiver by age 3 years – significantly predicted both Executive Control and Memory scores. Early shared linguistic modality also predicted latent profile membership: participants with early shared language access had substantially lower odds of belonging to the lowest-performing cognitive profile. These findings suggest that adult cognitive outcomes among DHH individuals are associated less with auditory access per se than with early access to a shared, accessible language environment.

doi:10.31234/osf.io/k5f7d_v1.title: PRELIMINARY FRAMEWORK FOR A DYNAMIC SOCIO-ACOUSTIC MODEL OF SPEECH PERCEPTION
doi:10.31234/osf.io/k5f7d_v1.abstract: Listeners store detailed acoustic information and access social information cued by variation fast and early. Yet, how we understand all we understand remains an open question. I propose a Dynamic Socio-Acoustic Model that frames perception as a continuous, multidimensional tracking system where speech variation functions as primary cognitive information. This listener-driven model includes the fluid topological stretching of cognitive space, an acoustic exemplar space that is untethered to linguistic units and allows for multidimensional cross-context categorization. Listeners maintain a sub-lexical, macro-exemplar landscape where incoming acoustic-kinematic trajectories drive real-time resonance. Rather than matching signals to static templates, listeners construct ad-hoc categories on the fly, dynamically scaling an active grid in response to immediate environmental contrasts. By uniting continuous sensory tracking with fluid, experience-dependent spatial restructuring, this framework offers an ecological account of perception and memory that rethinks structural variation from a hurdle into a pathway to social meaning.

doi:10.64898/2026.09.19.26363478.title: Automated Assessment of Hypernasality in Motor Speech Disorders Using Nasal Cognate Distinctiveness and Nasal Posterior Probability
doi:10.64898/2026.09.19.26363478.authors: Wang F, Utianski RL, Barnard LR, Duffy JR, Botha H.
doi:10.64898/2026.09.19.26363478.abstract: Purpose To evaluate whether two automated measures of nasality, Nasal Cognate Distinctiveness (NCD) and nasal posterior probability (NPP), provide clinically meaningful markers of hypernasality in speakers with motor speech disorders (MSDs) and to determine whether hypernasality-related information extends beyond stop consonants, which are typically targeted in cognate-based approaches. Method Sentence-level speech recordings were obtained from 561 patients, including 374 neurologically typical controls and 187 individuals with MSDs. NCD was computed for voiceless stops (/p/, /t/, /k/) using likelihood ratios between stops and their nasal cognates. NPP was extracted using a phonological feature-based neural network model and analyzed for stops, consonants, and vowels. Hypernasality severity was rated by speech-language pathologists. Group differences and associations with hypernasality severity were evaluated using linear mixed-effects models and Spearman correlations, and receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analyses were used to evaluate discrimination of absent versus present hypernasality. An additional 20 controls with repeat recordings were used to evaluate test-retest reliability and minimal detectable change (MDC). Results NCD generally decreased and NPP increased with increasing hypernasality severity, with phoneme-specific severity effects observed for NCD. Across stops, NCD and NPP were strongly inversely correlated and showed comparable discrimination of absent versus present hypernasality (AUCs = 0.796 and 0.730, respectively). Consonant and vowel NPP measures were both positively associated with hypernasality severity and demonstrated identical classification performance (AUC = 0.853). No significant differences in ROC performance were observed between NCD and NPP or between consonant and vowel NPP measures. Test-retest change exceeded the MDC threshold in 2 of 20 controls for NCD and 1 of 20 for NPP. Conclusions Both NCD and NPP provide objective markers of hypernasality in speakers with MSDs. The measures capture related aspects of nasalization and demonstrate comparable ability to identify clinically meaningful hypernasality. NPP captures hypernasality-related acoustic information across both consonants and vowels, with similar relationships to severity and classification performance across sound classes. Test-retest findings provide preliminary MDC benchmarks for interpreting longitudinal change.

doi:10.64898/2026.09.23.753568.title: A nonlinear time-domain finite-element model of the human middle ear subjected to intense sound waves
doi:10.64898/2026.09.23.753568.authors: Mohammadi H, Tubelli A, Puria S, Cheng JT.
doi:10.64898/2026.09.23.753568.abstract: Computational models of the middle ear are typically developed within the linear range of the middle ear’s response, which corresponds to typical sounds in daily life. Understanding middle-ear biomechanics under high-intensity sounds is also important for assessing potential auditory damage under adverse conditions. In this study, a finite-element (FE) model of the human middle ear plus the external ear canal is presented, employing a first-order Ogden hyperelastic material formulation and time-domain nonlinear analysis to capture nonlinear deformation of soft tissues and the resulting middle-ear response. The model was analyzed using pure-tone pressure excitations applied at the ear canal entrance over the 80 Hz to 8 kHz frequency range and 110 to 180 dB sound pressure levels (SPL). The ear canal pressure near the tympanic membrane (TM) and full-field three-dimensional response of the middle ear structures were examined. Across the investigated frequency range, the simulated middle-ear motion exhibited a transition from predominantly piston-like behavior at low frequencies, up to 1 kHz, to increasingly intricate multi-modal and multi-directional vibration patterns at higher frequencies. Nonlinear behaviors became increasingly significant at high frequencies and high stimulus levels, including compressive/expansive pressure-displacement relationships, waveform distortions, and the emergence of non-harmonic spectral components. The model developed in this study provides a computational framework for studying nonlinear sound transmission through the middle ear and its implications for high-intensity acoustic exposure. The findings contribute to a better understanding of middle-ear mechanics under adverse conditions and support future investigations of acoustic trauma and hearing protection strategies.

doi:10.64898/2026.09.20.753042.title: Beyond the session: delayed effects of prefrontal theta-burst stimulation onthe liking of newly learned melodies
doi:10.64898/2026.09.20.753042.authors: Simonetto-Rizk, S.; Liu, Y.; Ginzburg, J.; Zatorre, R.; Coffey, E. B.
doi:10.64898/2026.09.20.753042.abstract: Reward operates as a cycle in which a stimulus produces a pleasure response, and the degree of pleasure experienced reinforces the behaviours that lead back to it. Music provides a useful model for examining this cycle because it is intrinsically pleasurable, can be learned, and engages reward-related frontostriatal circuitry that overlaps with circuitry involved in primary and secondary rewards, such as food, sex, and money. Transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS), a non-invasive stimulation method, has been shown to produce bidirectional effects on music-evoked pleasure by increasing or decreasing activity in cortical regions, such as the left dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (DLPFC), that are functionally connected to subcortical regions, including the striatum. Here, we further characterize the reward cycle by incorporating TMS into a paradigm that combines musical pleasure ratings with an early musical skill acquisition task. In a within-subjects, counterbalanced crossover design, 23 participants with 2-10 years of musical experience received intermittent TBS (iTBS; excitatory) and continuous TBS (cTBS; inhibitory) over the left DLPFC in separate sessions. Participants rated the pleasantness of short piano melodies before stimulation (T0), immediately afterwards (T1), and 24 hours later (T2). After stimulation, they learned to play the melodies, and pitch and rhythm accuracy were assessed during three performance phases, namely acquisition, immediately after acquisition, and 24 hours later. Liking did not differ between conditions at T1; however, the increase in liking from baseline (T0) to T2 was significantly larger following iTBS than cTBS, a divergence that emerged across the 24-hour interval spanning both learning and sleep. Pitch and rhythm accuracy did not differ between conditions at any phase, despite improvement across trials in both. These results indicate that TMS to the left DLPFC can produce delayed, condition-dependent shifts in musical liking without a parallel change in early skill acquisition.

doi:10.64898/2026.09.25.754382.title: Change-point oddball elicits pupil-linked signatures of Bayesian belief updating
doi:10.64898/2026.09.25.754382.authors: Kopel L, Hoomans J, van Gastel E, Tijhuis J, van de Graaf M, Shafik M, Matthijsse S, Murphy P, van Gaal S, Suzuki M, de Gee J.
doi:10.64898/2026.09.25.754382.abstract: The auditory oddball protocol is widely used to study neural responses to unexpected events. In conventional designs, however, stimulus statistics are stationary: deviants do not indicate environmental change and therefore should not drive learning. Here, we introduce “change-point oddball”, a passive, no-report protocol in which the standard-oddball mapping reverses at unpredictable change points, requiring inference over latent environmental states. We measured pupil-linked arousal in three human cohorts. Pupil responses were larger for state-specific oddballs than standards, decayed across newly established standards after state changes, and scaled with model-derived change-point probability. A many-standards control experiment implicated a prediction-based rather than repetition-based mechanism. Finally, within participants, stronger pupil encoding of change-point probability during the passive task was associated with greater change-point-sensitive belief updating in a separate active navigation task. Thus, passive change-point oddball preserves core signatures of adaptive belief updating, enabling cross-species and clinical investigations.

doi:10.64898/2026.10.05.756754.title: Multiscale Network Disruption of Auditory-Language Circuits Underlying Auditory Hallucinations in Schizophrenia
doi:10.64898/2026.10.05.756754.authors: Murphy AC, Martinez A, Chen Y, Avissar M, Yalçınkaya BH, Sanchez-Pena J, Patel GH, Javitt DC.
doi:10.64898/2026.10.05.756754.abstract: Background: Auditory verbal hallucinations (AVH) are among the most disabling symptoms of schizophrenia, yet the network-level mechanisms linking auditory dysfunction to hallucination severity remain poorly characterized, limiting targeted therapeutic development. Methods: Using resting-state fMRI and high-resolution surface-based parcellation (HCP-MMP), we examined auditory-language functional connectivity and mesoscale network organization in 56 patients with schizophrenia and 22 healthy controls (primary dataset, N=78). Pairwise auditory-language connectivity associations with hallucination severity (PANSS P3) were examined alongside auditory network community structure, assortativity, hub organization, and routing efficiency. To further characterize these parcel-level findings at the vertex level, we applied a region-growing approach to identify auditory-frontal connectivity patterns maximally associated with severity. In silico perturbation analyses tested the causal role of belt cortex connectivity. Key findings were independently replicated in 93 patients from the Human Connectome Project for Early Psychosis (HCP-EP), for a combined total of 171 participants. Results: Auditory-language connectivity disruptions were concentrated in belt cortex and specifically implicated ventral what-stream connections, with a vertex-wise analysis converging on the same anatomy. Auditory network segregation scaled with hallucination severity, with belt cortex emerging as the primary integrative hub governing auditory-to-language routing efficiency. Perturbation analyses showed that strengthening earlier hierarchy auditory regions reduced network segregation more than strengthening later-hierarchy regions. Reduced belt cortex coupling and elevated network segregation replicated independently in the HCP-EP sample. Conclusions: Auditory network disorganization scales with hallucination severity and replicates across independent samples, with belt cortex as the critical locus of connectivity disruption and network integration failure, identifying it as a candidate neuromodulatory target.

doi:10.1523/jneurosci.0510-26.2026.title: Enhanced pitch perception in early blind individuals and musicians is due to reduced internal noise.
doi:10.1523/jneurosci.0510-26.2026.authors: Park WJ, Awad J, Fine I.
doi:10.1523/jneurosci.0510-26.2026.abstract: Although it is commonly assumed that early blind individuals have enhanced pitch perception, the literature to date has been contradictory. We measured performance on two tasks known to recruit early versus late stages of auditory frequency tuning in early blind and sighted human adults of both sexes with matched years of musical training. The two groups showed equivalent performance on a tone detection in notched-noise task that assesses cochlear frequency selectivity. In contrast, early blind individuals showed enhanced performance in a pitch discrimination task thought to be mediated by cortical mechanisms. Computational modeling revealed that this enhancement was best explained by reduced internal noise rather than narrower frequency tuning, with both blindness and years of musical training predicting a reduction in internal noise. These findings identify internal noise as a key factor in experience-driven auditory plasticity as a result of both musical experience and early blindness. Significance Statement For centuries, early blindness has been associated with superior auditory abilities. Here we find that the enhanced pitch perception in early blind individuals is best explained by reduced internal noise at higher levels of auditory processing, rather than sharper frequency tuning. Years of musical training similarly resulted in lower internal noise, suggesting a shared mechanism through which experience improves auditory perception. These findings identify internal noise reduction as a key component of experience-dependent auditory plasticity.

doi:10.64898/2026.10.13.758910.title: Modulating Sleep Oscillations Through Targeted Memory Reactivation: Linking Functional Dynamics to Brain Microstructure
doi:10.64898/2026.10.13.758910.authors: Stee W, Foti M, Legouhy A, Guerreri M, Zhang H, Lina J, Peigneux P.
doi:10.64898/2026.10.13.758910.abstract: Background: Sleep-dependent memory consolidation reputedly rely on the coordinated activity of sleep oscillations, which may facilitate the reactivation and redistribution of newly acquired memories. Targeted memory reactivation (TMR) during sleep can experimentally modulate these processes, although effects remain variable. Moreover, how learning-related microstructural plasticity relates to sleep oscillatory activity and spindle-related network dynamics remains poorly understood. We investigated whether auditory TMR modulates sleep spindles, slow oscillations (SOs) and their co-occurrence, whether these changes relate to motor memory consolidation and diffusion MRI (dMRI) measures of brain microstructure, and whether learning and TMR alter the evolution of cortico-cortical connectivity during spindle development. Methods: Sixty healthy young adults underwent five dMRI sessions before and after motor sequence learning (Day 1), after a post-training night of regular sleep (RS) or TMR (Day 2), and before and after relearning (Day 5). Baseline and experimental nights were recorded with 256-channel high-density EEG. Oscillation densities were analyzed using mixed-design ANOVAs and related to behavioral and dMRI changes using Pearson or Spearman correlations. Intra-spindle connectivity between 148 source-reconstructed cortical regions was compared between spindle onset and end, across nights and between groups using Network-Based Statistics. Results: Spindle density, SO density and SO-spindle co-occurrence remained stable across nights in the RS group but decreased after TMR. Higher spindle density and co-occurrence were associated with greater overnight performance gains, and all oscillatory measures were associated with learning-related dMRI changes in subcortical regions, notably striatum and thalamus. Connectivity increased from the beginning to the end of the spindle duration during the baseline night in both groups, but during the experimental night only in the RS group. Conclusions: Motor learning is associated with coordinated changes in sleep oscillatory activity, within-spindle cortical connectivity and brain microstructure, supporting a dynamic interaction between learning-induced plasticity and sleep-dependent network reorganization. Under the present stimulation conditions, TMR did not enhance these processes but instead reduced sleep oscillatory activity and attenuated spindle-related connectivity dynamics, underscoring the importance of precisely targeting endogenous sleep rhythms when using TMR.

doi:10.1523/jneurosci.1323-25.2026.title: Hyperpolarization-Activated Cation Channels Confer Tonotopic Specialization for Temporal Encoding of Sound Frequency in the Cochlear Nucleus.
doi:10.1523/jneurosci.1323-25.2026.authors: Owusu-Nyantakyi K, Hamlette LS, Ashida G, Weimann S, Oline SN, Burger RM.
doi:10.1523/jneurosci.1323-25.2026.abstract: Sensory neurons are endowed with physiological characteristics that facilitate accurate signal extraction from stimuli. The functional importance of such properties is exemplified in auditory neurons where intrinsic excitability is optimized to detect frequency-specific features. In birds, the neurons of nucleus magnocellularis (NM) receive primary auditory inputs that are spatially arranged according to best frequency, or "tonotopically." Several physiological properties vary systematically along NM's tonotopic axis. Gradients of voltage-gated channels shape temporal response selectivity, enabling precise encoding of sound features. We identified a previously undescribed expression pattern of hyperpolarization-activated cation (HCN) channels in the domestic chick Gallus gallus domesticus of both sexes. Electrophysiological and immunohistochemical analyses demonstrated a tonotopic gradient of HCN1 but not HCN2 subunits that underlie I H currents along NM's tonotopic axis. To measure the effect of I H on membrane excitability along the tonotopy, we applied depolarizing current ramps prior to and during pharmacological I H block. We show I H exerts a strong influence on temporal integration properties of NM membranes. Next, we investigated whether this response modulation facilitates encoding of temporally patterned inputs by injecting depolarizing current pulse trains to simulate synaptic excitatory drive. During I H block, spike entrainment failed at high input rates, suggesting HCN channels contribute strongly to NM's temporal selectivity. Computational modeling extended these results to show a contribution of I H to high-frequency neuron responses in the presence of noise. This work establishes a tonotopic distribution of HCN channels in NM and demonstrates its contributions to temporal response selectivity, particularly at high frequencies.

doi:10.1016/j.celrep.2026.118151.title: Anterior cingulate feedback facilitates rapid global context modulation in primary visual cortex.
doi:10.1016/j.celrep.2026.118151.authors: Peterka DS, Imai F, Ross JM, Bastos G, Hornick MA, Rachmany L, Gallimore CG, Hockley A, Hamm JP.
doi:10.1016/j.celrep.2026.118151.abstract: Context modulates sensory processing. Recent proposals claim early areas like primary visual cortex (V1) are only influenced by "local" context (e.g., recent stimulus history), while "global" context (e.g., learned patterns and probabilities) modulates only higher areas. We tested this using a global/local oddball paradigm: mice viewed repeating five-item sequences (AAAA-B), where B is deviant from local context but typical in global context. Using two-photon imaging and local field potential (LFP) recording in mouse V1, we found that global predictability normalized responses to B stimuli. This effect emerged after fewer than 10 sequence repetitions, demonstrating rapid learning. When a globally deviant "C" stimulus replaced B or when B occurred at unpredictable intervals (i.e., standard oddball), V1 showed strong response enhancement. This global context modulation in V1 required top-down feedback from anterior cingulate area. However, when B was replaced by an A (AAAA-A), responses were mixed, suggesting that stimulus-specific adaptation can constrain prediction-error signals in V1.

doi:10.64898/2026.10.11.758333.title: Modeling Paralinguistic Features for Speech Neuroprostheses: A Systematic Review
doi:10.64898/2026.10.11.758333.authors: Yenikapati, M. S.; Deshpande, S.; Desai, S. P.; Santine, D. D.; Roghani, A. K.
doi:10.64898/2026.10.11.758333.abstract: Recent advances in brain-computer interface (BCI) technology have brought speech neuroprostheses closer to restoring naturalistic communication for individuals with severe motor or speech impairments. Although current systems can decode phonemic and lexical information from cortical activity, they often fail to capture paralinguistic dimensions such as intonation, prosody, loudness, and affect that are essential for conveying emotion and intent. This review synthesizes emerging research on modeling and incorporating paralinguistic features into speech neuroprosthetic design. Foundational studies have mapped the cortical organization of speech production, identifying articulatory somatotopy within the sensorimotor cortex and functional subdivisions across planning, phonological, and semantic representations. More recent work has characterized expressive encoding within the ventral precentral and supplementary motor areas, while peripheral and multimodal sensing approaches have demonstrated promising accuracy in decoding emotional states. Collectively, these findings signal a shift toward closed-loop neuroprosthetic systems that integrate affective modulation with linguistic decoding, enabling restoration of speech that is not only intelligible but expressively human. Keywords: Speech neuroprosthesis, paralinguistics, BCI, naturalistic communication

doi:10.1016/j.neuroscience.2026.09.024.title: Structural connectivity of auditory-linguistic brain networks predicts success in speech categorization and listening in noise.
doi:10.1016/j.neuroscience.2026.09.024.authors: Rizzi R, Stirn JR, Eisenhut Z, Bidelman GM.
doi:10.1016/j.neuroscience.2026.09.024.abstract: Successful speech perception requires listeners to bin continuous acoustic information into discrete phonetic categories. However, some people maintain within-category acoustic information (gradient listening) while others discard category-irrelevant information (discrete listening) during perception. Listeners also vary in how consistently they label speech sounds and more gradient/consistent labeling has been linked with better speech-in-noise (SIN) perception. Here, we test how neuroanatomical properties of the brain's major speech-language and auditory pathways relate to individual differences in speech categorization and SIN processing. We measured phonetic categorization and SIN comprehension via phoneme labeling and QuickSIN tasks. Diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI) with probabilistic tractography estimated axonal density within the bilateral arcuate fasciculi and brainstem-cortical auditory projections. Anatomical morphology (surface area, gray matter volume, thickness) was also quantified in the adjacent frontotemporal cortical areas and midbrain. Behaviorally, we found more perceptually consistent categorizers had better performance on the QuickSIN. DWI showed that more gradient listeners had greater white matter density in the left arcuate fasciculus and brainstem-cortical auditory pathways, while better SIN performance was predicted by denser white matter in the brainstem-cortical auditory pathways. Morphometric results revealed more consistent listening was associated with greater cortical thickness in right superior temporal gyrus and more gradient listening was associated with greater surface area in right pars opercularis. We infer that individual differences in phonetic categorization relate to SIN comprehension and are at least partially explained by neuroanatomical properties of the auditory-linguistic brain.

doi:10.31234/osf.io/bz56v_v1.title: Subgroup Relationships and Individual Differences in Musical Synchronization
doi:10.31234/osf.io/bz56v_v1.authors: Van Kerrebroeck B, Honda C, Lionetti D, Maes P, Wanderley M, Palmer C.
doi:10.31234/osf.io/bz56v_v1.abstract: Musicians demonstrate strong auditory-motor synchronization abilities during group performance, although most empirical studies have examined only solo or dyadic performance. We investigated musical synchronization in four-person groups performing simple and complex rhythms. Each musician's spontaneous production rate for familiar melodies provided individual difference measures of intrinsic rhythms. Participants were randomly assigned to quartets and synchronized their drumming while they performing rhythms based on Binary or Ternary Meters in Simple (1:1 isochronous) and Complex (2:3 polyrhythmic) Rhythm conditions. An unexpected perturbation cue instructed members to switch to the opposite meter, from Ternary to Binary or vice versa. Simple rhythms yielded greater synchrony and shorter relaxation times for returning to stable synchronization following perturbations than Complex polyrhythms. History-dependent effects, reflecting carryover from previous states, were observed when musicians switched between Ternary and Binary rhythms. Quartets with larger individual differences in spontaneous production rates had longer relaxation times to achieve stable coordination. Social interaction ratings indicated greater perceived relationship toward the dyadic partner than toward the four-person group in the Complex Rhythm condition, but not in the Simple Rhythm condition, consistent with in-group (partner) and out-group (group) roles. These findings were largely consistent across North American and European testing sites, suggesting that group and subgroup relationships generalize across sites.

doi:10.21203/rs.3.rs-10731927/v1.title: Photobiomodulation Therapy (PBMT) for Preventing Noise-Induced Hearing Loss
doi:10.21203/rs.3.rs-10731927/v1.authors: Griffith OC, Jarrouj G, Kessler L, Tan X, Fiebig T, Basta D, Esmailie F, Richter C.
doi:10.21203/rs.3.rs-10731927/v1.abstract: Abstract Background. The safety and efficacy of Photobiomodulation Therapy (PBMT) must be established in a pre-clinical animal study before it can be used in humans as a protective treatment for noise-induced hearing loss. Method. Twenty male mice were chronically implanted with light-emitting diodes (LEDs) in the left outer ear canal on day 0. Two days after implantation surgery (day 2), baseline hearing was assessed using auditory brainstem responses (ABRs). On days 3 & 4, PBMT was administered once daily in the implanted left ear. PBMT consisted of delivering continuous light at 24.5 mW for 0, 60, or 120 minutes. One hour after PBMT on day 5 (third day of treatment), the mice were exposed to band-limited noise (8–16 kHz) at 120 dB SPL for 2 hours. PBMT continued for four days after noise exposure. On day 10, the hearing was re-assessed. Results . Following noise exposure, ABR thresholds were drastically elevated in mice that did not receive PBMT, with more than 50% of the animals having no response at the highest sound level delivered. In mice that received 60 minutes of PBMT, ABR threshold elevations were 20 dB lower than in noise-exposed untreated animals. Mice that received 60 minutes of PBMT showed a 20 dB “rescue” effect, whereas those that received 120 minutes did not. Discussion. This study demonstrates that PBMT rescue from noise-induced hearing loss is dose-dependent: low doses can rescue hearing function, whereas high doses confer no benefit and additional cochlear damage must be considered.

doi:10.3389/fnins.2026.1915543.title: Application of electrically evoked auditory brainstem responses in cochlear reimplantation.
doi:10.3389/fnins.2026.1915543.authors: Jin Y, Bi Q, Lv Y, Chen Z, Liu Y, Liu J, Li Y, Yang W, Xu X, Li Y, Wang Z.
doi:10.3389/fnins.2026.1915543.abstract: Objectives To evaluate the role of electrically evoked auditory brainstem responses (EABRs) in assessing auditory pathway integrity and predicting auditory and speech outcomes in patients undergoing cochlear reimplantation (CRI), especially those with cochlear ossification or complex anatomy. Methods A retrospective analysis was conducted of 40 CRI patients (12 ossification, 28 non-ossification) from 2019 to 2024. Intraoperative and postoperative EABR assessments were performed to evaluate neural responses and guide cochleostomy. Parameters included the elicitation rate, V-wave amplitude, threshold, and Gibson score. Auditory-speech performance was measured by the Categories of Auditory Performance and Speech Intelligibility Rating scales, and word-recognition scores. Regression analyses identified predictors of postoperative outcomes. Results The EABR elicitation rate was 100% in non-ossification cases and 80% in ossification cases. Gibson scores were higher, and V-wave thresholds lower, in non-ossification ears ( p 2 = 0.406, p = 0.0007). Conclusions EABRs reliably assess auditory pathway integrity, inform surgical guidance, and predict postoperative auditory-speech outcomes in CRI, especially in ossified or anatomically complex cochleae. Significance The findings support the use of EABRs as a clinical adjunct to improve surgical precision and functional outcomes in challenging CRI cases.

doi:10.1016/j.neuroimage.2026.122255.title: Automated MRI-based parcellation of a putative core auditory region in individual human Heschl's gyrus.
doi:10.1016/j.neuroimage.2026.122255.authors: Namgung JY, Byeon K, Poeppel D, Park H, Lee HS, Park BY.
doi:10.1016/j.neuroimage.2026.122255.abstract: The human auditory cortex exhibits substantial anatomical variability, making precise individual-level delineation challenging. Although recent advances in imaging and machine learning techniques have enabled the delineation of approximate boundaries of the human primary auditory cortex, existing approaches often fail to adequately capture individual anatomical variability. Here, we propose an openly accessible, fully automated MRI-based pipeline for identifying a putative core auditory region within Heschl's gyrus by integrating intracortical myelin estimates with cortical curvature. A data-driven clustering algorithm was used to identify highly myelinated regions, and curvature-based constraints were subsequently applied to refine their anatomical boundaries. The resulting parcellations exhibited high myelin-related contrast and accommodated duplicated Heschl's gyri in the examined examples, illustrating their application to complex individual anatomical configurations. Comparative analyses of myelin-only and curvature-constrained definitions demonstrated that the curvature-constrained parcellation showed greater overlap with atlas-defined A1 and TE1.0 and stronger structural connectivity with the medial geniculate body of the thalamus as well as medial and lateral belt areas. Seed-based functional connectivity analyses further revealed connectivity patterns associated with auditory and multisensory functions that were consistent with previous literature. These findings support the parcellated region as an anatomically informed, MRI-based operational definition of a putative core auditory region. Although tonotopic validation remains necessary to establish the correspondence between parcellated boundaries and functionally defined auditory core areas, the proposed approach provides a reproducible framework for investigating the structural and functional organization of Heschl's gyrus at the individual level.

doi:10.21203/rs.3.rs-10149311/v1.title: Hearing impairment is associated with impaired glymphatic function in middle- and older-aged adults: evidence from DTI-ALPS imaging
doi:10.21203/rs.3.rs-10149311/v1.authors: Huang C, Yang C, Wu M, Wu B, Shi T, Qin Z, Luo Y, An Y, Zhang J, Jiang P, Long M, Yang J, Kuang G, Wang L.
doi:10.21203/rs.3.rs-10149311/v1.abstract: Abstract Hearing impairment is a common age-related sensory disorder and has been increasingly linked to central nervous system changes beyond peripheral auditory dysfunction. This study aimed to investigate the relationship between hearing impairment and glymphatic system function using the diffusion tensor imaging along the perivascular space (DTI-ALPS) index, and to explore its potential as an imaging biomarker in middle- and older-aged adults. A total of 131 participants aged 45–80 years were enrolled, including 71 individuals with normal hearing and 60 with hearing impairment defined by pure-tone average thresholds ≥ 25 dB HL. All participants underwent brain MRI with diffusion tensor imaging, and glymphatic function was evaluated using the DTI-ALPS index. Cognitive function was assessed using the Mini-Mental State Examination and Montreal Cognitive Assessment. Associations between pure-tone average and DTI-ALPS indices were examined using Spearman correlation analysis. Logistic regression models were applied to identify independent factors associated with hearing impairment, and receiver operating characteristic analysis was used to evaluate diagnostic performance. Participants with hearing impairment were older, more frequently male, and exhibited lower MoCA scores compared with controls. Global and regional DTI-ALPS indices were significantly reduced in the hearing impairment group and were inversely correlated with hearing thresholds. In multivariate analysis, both older age and lower DTI-ALPS index remained independently associated with hearing impairment. The combined model incorporating age and DTI-ALPS achieved the best discriminative performance. These findings suggest that hearing impairment is independently associated with reduced glymphatic system function, and that the DTI-ALPS index, particularly when combined with age, may serve as a promising imaging biomarker for age-related hearing decline.

doi:10.64898/2026.09.18.751660.title: Classical music in cognitive rehabilitation: Three case studies of spatial neglect
doi:10.64898/2026.09.18.751660.authors: Zeineldin, R.; Takamura, Y.; Chea, M.; Naccache, L.; Bayen, E.; Toba, M. N.; Bartolomeo, P.
doi:10.64898/2026.09.18.751660.abstract: Chronic spatial neglect after right-hemisphere stroke reflects network dysfunction, with recovery influenced by structural connectivity. Music recruits coordinated bi-hemispheric activity and may promote interhemispheric communication after stroke. Following our pilot study in post-stroke aphasia, we asked whether classical music modulates connectivity and behavior in chronic neglect. Three patients completed a crossover protocol comparing two weeks of daily audiovisual classical music with an audiobook control, with neglect, mood, quality-of-life, diffusion MRI, and resting-state high-density EEG measures. All showed right superior longitudinal fasciculus II disconnection with preserved callosal pathways. In N2, line bisection shifted leftward across all five lines after music, together with increased posterior interhemispheric theta-band weighted symbolic mutual information (wSMI), then deteriorated into the pathological range after the audiobook, without mood improvement. N1 showed mixed behavioral effects, with mood and quality of life improving after music. N3 showed no significant spatial improvement and worsened mood after music. These heterogeneous responses motivate larger studies of connectional predictors. The findings support the feasibility of classical music as an adjunct to neglect rehabilitation and suggest that cognitive changes may occur independently of mood, while the audiobook cannot be considered an inert control.

doi:10.31234/osf.io/2p7ex_v3.title: Credible Signaling through Sound – the Role of Timbre in Music Recognition in Young BaYaka Foragers
doi:10.31234/osf.io/2p7ex_v3.authors: van der Vlist MMC, Li J, van Schaik FTM, Mundry R, Honing H, Janmaat KRL.
doi:10.31234/osf.io/2p7ex_v3.abstract: This study explored perceptual sensitivity to spectral and temporal acoustic features in music recognition among BaYaka hunter-gatherer children. Using an interactive, non-competitive game (Move to Match), we tested song recognition under various forms of audio degradation to identify which musical dimensions are crucial for recognizing familiar songs. BaYaka children demonstrated robust recognition of songs across unaltered, spectrally degraded, and temporally degraded versions, highlighting sensitivity to multiple acoustic dimensions. We suggest that songs may be recognized despite degradations because of spectral contour processing, rather than pitch and rhythm cues alone. Moreover, recognition performance decreased for duration-degraded songs (“plinks”), as the brevity constrains the cues available to listeners. However, song identification of (spectrally degraded) plinks far exceeded chance levels and outperformed Western adults performing similar tasks. This suggests that onset-transients and spectral shape, contributing to timbre perception, might serve as reliable markers for identifying musical sounds. We discuss the possibility that music cognition evolved for reasons beyond social bonding to support identification of personal contributions within musical exchanges through timbre, which may hold importance in cooperative contexts. As one of the first experimental studies of music perception in hunter-gatherers, this work demonstrates the potential of culturally adapted methods for future cross-cultural research.

doi:10.31234/osf.io/5e2yr_v2.title: Infants’ learning of tones and VOT contrasts in the lab
doi:10.31234/osf.io/5e2yr_v2.abstract: Infants likely home in on the speech categories in the ambient language(s) by attending to the acoustic cue distributions present in the input, but direct experimental evidence for this remains scarce. Young infants’ discrimination of /d-t/ and Mandarin Chinese tones T2-T4 was assessed over the course of a repeated exposure-test pro- cedure. In addition to being the first to document the emergence of perceptual categories through repeated testing of the same infants, this study suggests that perceptual learning through acoustic cue distributions could also account for the development of lexical tone perception.

doi:10.64898/2026.09.21.753073.title: Auditory brainstem response amplitude predicts age-related forward masking temporal-processing deficits in normal-hearing listeners
doi:10.64898/2026.09.21.753073.authors: Huang CG, Costantino M, Soleimanpour R, Beinke T, Anderson S, Goupell MJ.
doi:10.64898/2026.09.21.753073.abstract: Aging has profound effects on sensory systems, such that older adults can report problems in hearing despite having normal audiometric thresholds. While it is known that older listeners have poorer temporal processing than younger listeners, there is limited understanding of how these deficits interact with effects of sound level, in particular when they are above conversational level (e.g., > 65 dB SPL). Here we wanted to investigate the link between temporal processing and sound level as a function of age in normal-hearing listeners. Using a forward-masking paradigm, auditory brainstem responses (ABRs) and behavioral detection thresholds were measured at different masker levels. It was found that with increasing age and masker sound level, the Wave V amplitudes of older listeners decreased and directly correlated with behavioral detection thresholds of the probe stimulus in the forward-masking paradigm. These results elucidate the fundamental effects of aging on temporal processing and its interactions with sound level in the central auditory system. The results of this study have clinical implications for the concept of normal hearing in the aging population and how older listeners may struggle in different listening environments that are not captured by simple audiometry. Further delineating the important effects of aging will pave the way for earlier clinical diagnosis of hearing disorders and personalized treatments for different forms of age-related hearing loss.

doi:10.64898/2026.09.24.26363901.title: Visualising large audiological data beyond the audiogram for auditory phenotyping
doi:10.64898/2026.09.24.26363901.authors: Encina-Llamas G, Kjærbøl E, Kressner AA.
doi:10.64898/2026.09.24.26363901.abstract: The pure-tone audiogram remains the cornerstone of hearing assessment, yet it captures only part of the functional consequences of cochlear damage. Most phenotyping schemes rely solely on the audiogram, which cannot detect hidden suprathreshold dysfunction when thresholds are normal. How best to represent audiological data — as discrete phenotypes or as a continuous space — remains unresolved. Using a retrospective database from the Copenhagen Hearing and Balance Centre, Rigshospitalet (Denmark; 1995–2022; 251,986 ear-session units from 81,883 adults with normal or sensorineural audiograms), we compared linear (PCA) and non-linear (UMAP) embeddings of the audiogram alone and with word recognition in quiet (WRS max -Q). Here we show that a linear embedding suffices for the audiogram, but a non-linear one becomes advantageous once suprathreshold measures are added. PCA compressed the audiogram onto two interpretable axes, overall level and slope, explaining 91.5% of the variance, with ears forming a continuous cloud that published reference schemes tiled into overlapping regions. For the audiogram alone, UMAP recovered the same organisation. WRS max -Q varied widely among ears with similar audiograms; adding it left the PCA unchanged but reorganised the UMAP. A synthetic experiment illustrated this: ears with identical audiograms but different WRS max -Q separated under UMAP, not PCA. Combining thresholds with WRS max -Q, UMAP yielded a continuous representation — a prototype Hearing Loss Map — where each ear’s position reflects threshold and suprathreshold measures. Representing hearing loss as a location in a continuous space rather than as discrete categories may better reflect its graded nature, with clinical relevance for individual patients.

doi:10.64898/2026.09.24.754009.title: Vestibular signals enhance the temporal precision of predictive movements to musical rhythms
doi:10.64898/2026.09.24.754009.abstract: Humans exhibit head movements synchronized with musical rhythms, frequently observed during instrument playing or dancing (e.g., hip hop). We conjectured that vestibular input from head movements could aid motor execution anticipatory of musical rhythms, known as sensorimotor synchronization (SMS). To examine this, we applied subthreshold galvanic vestibular stimulation (GVS) simultaneously with musical beats while healthy adults performed SMS to those beats. We designed a GVS waveform where the current rose steeply before each beat onset, which was expected to trigger intense vestibular afferent firing before the beats (as actual head movements would). Participants flexed their index finger in synchrony with the beats of syncopated auditory rhythms. In GVS trials, the SMS timing variability was significantly lower than in trials without GVS, suggesting that vestibular input stabilizes SMS to musical beats. Additionally, a control experiment using a waveform with a gradually increasing current revealed no significant difference in SMS variability between trials with and without GVS. This study provides causal evidence that the vestibular system is involved in synchronized movement to music. In addition, the results suggest that a specific parameter of the GVS waveform could influence predictive motor execution anticipatory of upcoming auditory events.

doi:10.31234/osf.io/jatxy_v1.title: Effect of an online music program on behavioral co-regulation in mothers and children with cochlear implants and with normal hearing
doi:10.31234/osf.io/jatxy_v1.authors: Santangelo M, Barachetti C, Lense MD, Guerzoni L, Cuda D, Majorano M.
doi:10.31234/osf.io/jatxy_v1.abstract: Children with cochlear implants (CIs) could show disruptions of contingency in early interactions. Music and rhythmic activities could improve co-regulation in mother-child dyads with CIs. This study explores i) the impact of an online music program on behavioral co-regulation of dyads with children with CIs (CI-T; N = 15; M = 17.70 months, SD = 6.60) who participated in the program, a CI control group (CI-C; N = 16; M = 19.39 months, SD = 6.50), and dyads with normal hearing children (NH-T; N = 14; M = 16.14 months, SD = 3.55) who participated in the program; ii) the associations in the CI-groups between practices of music at home and behavioral co-regulation. The CI-groups were assessed at three (T1) and six (T2) months after CIs’ activation. The NH-T group was assessed before (T1) and after (T2) the program. Analyses of video-recordings revealed significant increases at T2 in the duration of mother-child contingent and affective behaviors in the CI-T group, compared to the CI-C group. In the CI-groups, correlational analyses show positive associations between maternal reports of music at home and mother-child contingent and affective responses. The potential of music activities for auditory rehabilitation after CIs activation is discussed.

doi:10.64898/2026.09.24.754199.title: A rapid, machine-learning readout of cochlear neural degeneration that transfers from animals to humans
doi:10.64898/2026.09.24.754199.authors: Andrino LS, Gall R, Klara J, Akcakaya M, Bartlett EL, Parthasarathy A.
doi:10.64898/2026.09.24.754199.abstract: Standard hearing tests miss cochlear neural degeneration (CND), the loss of synapses between inner hair cells and auditory nerve fibers that may underlie unexplained hearing difficulty in roughly one in ten adults. Envelope following responses (EFRs) can index this neural loss noninvasively, but conventional protocols are too slow for clinical use. We tested a dynamic amplitude-modulated (dAM) EFR that sweeps the full modulation spectrum in a single brief stimulus. In Mongolian gerbils with histologically verified CND, dAM EFRs revealed selective deficits at fast modulation rates without threshold elevation. A machine-learning classifier distinguished young from middle-aged animals with high accuracy; additionally, its most informative feature, power near 400-500 Hz, tracked synapse counts, indicating a readout of cochlear neural health rather than age. Applied without retraining to 56 human listeners, the gerbil-trained classifier separated age groups above chance. dAM EFRs thus offer a rapid, objective and clinically viable marker of CND.

doi:10.1523/jneurosci.0476-26.2026.title: Normal Audiogram Does Not Confirm Intact Cochlear Amplification: Compressive Nonlinearity Reveals Incipient Cochlear Changes.
doi:10.1523/jneurosci.0476-26.2026.abstract: The cochlear amplifier, mediated by outer hair cell-driven nonlinear mechanics, enables the remarkable sensitivity and dynamic range of human hearing. Cochlear compression is a defining feature of this active process and is known to deteriorate with hearing loss. Among individuals with normal audiograms, cochlear compression is generally presumed to be invariant, an assumption that has not been systematically examined. If incipient cochlear changes precede measurable threshold shifts, variability in compressive nonlinearity may represent an early peripheral correlate of emerging dysfunction and a potential mechanistic contributor to auditory processing differences. Whether cochlear compression varies meaningfully among individuals with normal audiograms, and what such variability reveals about the earliest stages of cochlear dysfunction, remains unknown. Here, we quantified compressive nonlinearity using distortion-product otoacoustic emission (DPOAE) input/output (i/o) functions with stringent signal-to-noise criteria, applying covariate-controlled mixed-effects models within a dimensional framework that treated compression as a continuous outcome to isolate structured individual differences ( n = 144 ears; male, 46). Compression metrics demonstrated substantial interindividual variability despite normal-hearing thresholds. Subtle differences in standard-frequency thresholds were associated with variations in cochlear gain. Extended high-frequency sensitivity, an index of basal cochlear integrity, showed additional associations with DPOAE i/o function, implicating basal vulnerability in shaping cochlear nonlinearity. Age-related effects were detectable even within a restricted young-adult cohort, indicating that cochlear operating characteristics may begin to diverge early in adulthood. These findings challenge the assumption of invariant compression in normal hearing and suggest that alterations in cochlear nonlinear processing may reflect incipient cochlear dysfunction that precedes overt hearing loss.
journal_names: The Journal of neuroscience : the official journal of the Society for Neuroscience

doi:10.31234/osf.io/be2ft_v1.title: Eye-gaze dynamics reveal the adaptive nature of real-time noisy-channel inference in speech comprehension
doi:10.31234/osf.io/be2ft_v1.abstract: To understand spoken language, listeners must extract meaning from acoustic input that is variable and noisy. The noisy-channel framework posits that listeners overcome this uncertainty by rationally inferring the speaker's intent, combining prior expectations with a model of how the message may have been corrupted during transmission. However, the exact nature of this noise model and its sensitivity to context (e.g., speaker or acoustic environment) remain unknown. Here, I use eye-tracking to measure human speech processing as it unfolds on the millisecond timescale, and I use the representational geometry of a self-supervised speech model (HuBERT) to estimate the noise model. I show that spoken word comprehension is well captured as real-time Bayesian belief updating. Further, listeners flexibly tune their expectation of noise to the specific acoustic environment. These results extend the noisy-channel framework to the moment-by-moment comprehension of speech. More broadly, these findings demonstrate that the human language system continuously adapts its internal model to the statistical structure of the communicative environment. By linking noisy-channel inference with real-time perceptual dynamics, this work highlights the remarkable flexibility of human cognition in navigating uncertainty and opens the door to investigating internal representations in human and artificial speech recognition systems through their fine-grained temporal dynamics.

doi:10.20944/preprints202610.0146.v1.title: Sirtuin Activation in the Cochlea During Honokiol-Mediated Protection Against Cisplatin Ototoxicity
doi:10.20944/preprints202610.0146.v1.authors: Thomas D, Zhou Y, Koo C, Kessler L, Pandya P, Fuentes RJ, Robinson A, Sriram S, Guntupalli P, Richter C, Tan X.
doi:10.20944/preprints202610.0146.v1.abstract: Background: /Objectives: Cisplatin induced hearing loss (CIHL) is a major global health sequela of chemotherapy, affecting over half a million cancer patients annually. We previously reported that honokiol, a multifunctional molecule compatible with cisplatin, protects against CIHL and upregulates sirtuin 3. Sirtuin family is composed of seven highly conserved while differentially expressed members which are critical enzymes for oxidative stress regulation in different cellular compartments. Therefore, this study aims to further verify the expression and upregulation of the entire sirtuin family during honokiol-mediated hearing protection against CIHL in a tumor-bearing mouse model. Methods: Adult female mice carrying mouse mammary tumor virus polyomavirus middle T agent oncogene were used. These mice developed palpable tumors automatically at the age of 70.8±10.3 days. CIHL was induced using a three-cycle (14 days/cycle) low-dose (4 mg/kg/day for 4 days per cycle, intraperitoneal injection) cisplatin treatment mimicking chemotherapy regimens. Honokiol (5-20 mg/kg) was administered one hour before cisplatin. Cochlear function was evaluated by auditory brainstem response threshold shifts and synaptic changes. Immunostaining and RT-qPCR were performed to verify the upregulation of sirtuin family members (1, 2, 3, 5, and 7) during these processes. Results: CIHL was observed at high-frequency range (24-32 kHz), which was mitigated by honokiol treatment. The optimal dose of honokiol for oto-protection and animal survival was 10 mg/kg. Fluorescence signals of sirtuins 1, 2, 3, 5, and 7 increased in cochleae from honokiol-treated mice. RT-qPCR confirmed a significant upregulation of sirtuin 3 mRNA with honokiol treatment. Conclusions: Sirtuin family upregulation was involved in honokiol-mediated hearing protection against CIHL. The dose-response curve of honokiol lays the foundation for potential translational applications for human studies.

doi:10.31234/osf.io/qhc5a_v1.title: Measuring musicality at home: Preliminary validation of the Music@Home questionnaires in a Greek population
doi:10.31234/osf.io/qhc5a_v1.authors: Drakoulaki K, Anagnostopoulou C, Triantafyllaki A, Bairaktari O, Polytimou AN.
doi:10.31234/osf.io/qhc5a_v1.abstract: Music@Home was developed in the United Kingdom as a systematic instrument for the assessment of informal musical interactions in the home environments of children under the age of 5. It has been successfully adapted and validated in German, and widely used in research with typically developing children, children with neurodevelopmental disabilities, and adults reporting their early music exposure retrospectively. In the present study, we adapted and conducted a preliminary validation of the Music@Home Infant and Preschool questionnaires for a Greek-speaking population. A total of 238 Greek-speaking primary caregivers completed either version, along with measures of cognitive stimulation at home and child language and communication development. Both Greek questionnaires demonstrated acceptable to good confirmatory fit, strong internal reliability, and evidence for divergent validity, with test-retest reliability established for the Preschool version, indicating that musical engagement represents a distinct aspect of the home environment rather than general cognitive stimulation. Exploratory analyses revealed modest positive associations between Infant scores and parent-reported language outcomes, consistent with previous research linking early musical experiences and language development. These findings provide initial evidence that the Greek Music@Home is a psychometrically sound tool for assessing the home musical environment in Greek-speaking populations and highlight the value of cross-cultural adaptations for research on music cognition, language, and broader developmental outcomes.

doi:10.21203/rs.3.rs-10460435/v1.title: Diffusion Tensor Imaging of Auditory Pathway Fiber Bundles in Children with Hearing Impairment from Bilirubin Encephalopathy: Alterations in Fractional Anisotropy and Diffusion Coefficient

doi:10.21203/rs.3.rs-10460435/v1.abstract: Abstract Objective To investigate changes in diffusion tensor imaging (DTI) parameters of auditory pathway fiber bundles in children with hearing impairment caused by bilirubin encephalopathy. Methods A total of 36 children with bilirubin encephalopathy and 36 control children were examined using a 3.0T superconducting magnetic resonance scanner (Siemens 3.0T Skyra, Siemens, Germany). DTI parameters, including fractional anisotropy (FA) and radial diffusivity (RD), were measured in the lateral lemniscus and inferior colliculus along the auditory pathway. These data were analyzed using independent samples t-test, and linear regression.
