doi:10.1016/j.celrep.2026.118107.title: Mitochondrial transfer protects against cisplatin-induced hearing loss by fumarate-mediated activation of mitophagy.
doi:10.1016/j.celrep.2026.118107.authors: Wu Y, Gu Y, Wang Y, Li R, Shi W, Liu J, Lai C, Wang X, Tang J, Pan D, Zhang Y, Wei N, Zheng Y, Wang J, Yang M, Fu X, Chai R, Wang G, Shan Y.
doi:10.1016/j.celrep.2026.118107.abstract: Sensorineural hearing loss (SNHL) affects millions of individuals worldwide, with platinum-based chemotherapeutics identified as a significant cause. In this study, we elucidate the mechanism by which mitochondrial transfer from mesenchymal stem/stromal cells (MSCs) protects against cisplatin-induced cochlear injury in a mouse model. Systemically administered MSCs home to the cochlea and transfer mitochondria to damaged spiral ganglion neurons (SGNs) via tunneling nanotubes, leading to elevated intracellular levels of the Krebs cycle intermediate fumarate, which activates mitophagy to eliminate dysfunctional mitochondria. Mechanistically, dimethyl fumarate (DMF)-a clinically available fumarate derivative-covalently modifies the phosphatase PPP1CB at cysteine 126, thereby blocking PPP1CB-mediated dephosphorylation of mitofusin 2 (MFN2), which in turn enhances mitophagy and ultimately preserves auditory function. These findings reveal that MSCs orchestrate mitochondrial replacement in damaged SGNs by delivering healthy mitochondria and facilitating the removal of impaired ones, underscoring the therapeutic potential of this strategy for treating SNHL related to mitochondrial dysfunction.

doi:10.1016/j.bbr.2026.116529.title: A dual behavioral and electrophysiological evaluation of the sodium salicylate induced tinnitus model in rats: Comparing click and chirp stimuli in auditory brainstem responses.
doi:10.1016/j.bbr.2026.116529.authors: Aydemir BE, Yiğit AA, Güneşer Ö.
doi:10.1016/j.bbr.2026.116529.abstract: Animal models are essential for investigating tinnitus physiology and therapeutic interventions. This study aimed to evaluate a salicylate-induced tinnitus rat model using a dual behavioral-electrophysiological approach and to compare the sensitivity of click and chirp stimuli in auditory brainstem responses (ABRs). Following sound-silence conditioning in a water T-maze (WTM), the salicylate group received sodium salicylate (300 mg/kg, i.p.) for six days, while the sham group received 0.9% saline. Tinnitus presence was behaviorally assessed via the water T maze swimming test, followed by ABR recordings under anesthesia using click and chirp stimuli at 80 dB SPL (waves I-V) and 20 dB SPL (wave II for hearing loss evaluation). Twenty-four male Sprague-Dawley rats with normal hearing were analyzed to sham (n = 13) and salicylate (n = 11) groups. Behaviorally, rats in the salicylate group spent significantly more time in the sound-associated arm during silence, demonstrating tinnitus-like behavior. Electrophysiologically, salicylate administration induced significant amplitude increases in waves III exclusively in click-evoked ABRs. Conversely, chirp-evoked ABR amplitudes showed no alterations post-salicylate exposure. In the latency analyses, while the three-way interaction was not significant. The stimulus x time two-way interaction was found to be statistically significant only for wave V. In conclusion, combining Water T-Maze testing with ABR recordings offers a time-efficient and animal-welfare-oriented approach to evaluate experimental tinnitus. Under the present recording conditions, click-evoked ABRs captured amplitude alterations more responsively than chirp stimuli in this specific acute model, though further research is required before click stimuli can be established as a generally superior marker for tinnitus assessment.

doi:10.64898/2026.10.09.757851.title: KDM6A Haploinsufficiency Is Insufficient to Disrupt Cochlear Structure and Auditory Function in Mouse Models of Kabuki Syndrome Type 2
doi:10.64898/2026.10.09.757851.authors: Shimizu Y, Wakamori S, Smith L, Behnammanesh G, Honkura Y, Suzuki J, Bird J, Katori Y, Someya S.
doi:10.64898/2026.10.09.757851.abstract: Objective Kabuki syndrome type 2 (KS2) is a rare X-linked disorder caused by pathogenic variants in KDM6A and is frequently associated with hearing impairment. Because auditory phenotypes include sensorineural, conductive, and mixed hearing loss, we examined whether Kdm6a deficiency directly impairs cochlear morphology or auditory function in mice. Methods We generated Nestin-Cre; Kdm6a conditional mutants and a germline-derived global Kdm6a deletion model using Sox2-Cre -mediated germline recombination. Auditory function and cochlear morphology were assessed by auditory brainstem responses (ABRs), distortion product otoacoustic emissions (DPOAEs), and histological analyses. Results Whole-body hemizygous or homozygous Kdm6a deletion resulted in embryonic lethality. Analyses therefore focused on Nestin-Cre; Kdm6a flox/Y males and females carrying a germline-derived heterozygous Kdm6a deletion. In Nestin-Cre mutants, ABR thresholds, wave I amplitudes and latencies, and DPOAE measures at 8, 16, and 32 kHz were comparable with littermate controls at 4 and 8 weeks. In heterozygous deletion females, ABR thresholds, wave I amplitudes and latencies at 4–64 kHz and DPOAE measures at 8, 16, and 32 kHz were comparable with male and female wild-type controls. No overt cochlear pathology was observed in either model. Conclusion Kdm6a deficiency in the viable mouse models examined did not produce overt cochlear pathology or baseline auditory dysfunction. These findings suggest that partial Kdm6a loss alone is insufficient to produce a robust primary cochlear phenotype in young mice and highlight the potential contributions of non-cochlear, developmental, central, and later-onset mechanisms to hearing impairment in KS2. Clinically, these findings support careful evaluation for potentially treatable middle-ear disease.

doi:10.64898/2026.10.15.759497.title: Kilohertz electrical stimulation drives widespread neuronal activation and temporal interference imposes focal rhythmic modulation
doi:10.64898/2026.10.15.759497.authors: Yoshimoto, R.; Stern, M. A.; Eggers, T.; Acerbo, E.; Laxpati, N. G.; Berglund, K.; Gutekunst, C.-A.
doi:10.64898/2026.10.15.759497.abstract: Temporal interference (TI) stimulation has attracted attention as a non-invasive approach that can target deep brain structures through interacting kilohertz-frequency electric fields. Its basic premise is that TI stimulation evokes neuronal responses through low-frequency amplitude modulation (AM), while the underlying kilohertz-frequency stimulation is ineffective to induce activity, the latter of which has not been tested rigorously at the cellular level. Here, we combined two-photon imaging in mouse models with immunohistochemistry and computational modeling to characterize spatiotemporal patterns of neuronal responses during TI stimulation. We found that kilohertz-frequency stimulation was sufficient to evoke activity without AM. In contrast, AM organized neuronal activity into rhythmic responses at AM frequency, with the strongest entrainment near the center of interference. Thus, kilohertz-frequency stimulation can drive widespread neuronal activation, upon which TI imposes focal rhythmic modulation. Our results provide a framework for refining TI stimulation and highlight the potential of kilohertz-frequency stimulation for brain stimulation.

doi:10.64898/2026.10.17.759861.title: Spatiotemporal transcriptomic dynamic across the auditory pathway from young to old age in 5xFAD Alzheimer disease mice
doi:10.64898/2026.10.17.759861.authors: Kong Y, Zhai T, Zhao H.
doi:10.64898/2026.10.17.759861.abstract: Auditory dysfunction can precede clinical dementia, but the molecular progression of Alzheimer disease (AD) pathology from the sensory periphery to auditory cortex remains poorly resolved. We performed bulk RNA sequencing of auditory cortex (AC), inferior colliculus (IC), cochlear nucleus (CN), and cochlea from 5xFAD and wild-type mice at postnatal day 50 (P50), 8 months, 11 months, and 16 months. Age-specific genotype effects and Genotype x Age interactions were evaluated using DESeq2, followed by Hallmark, KEGG, and Gene Ontology gene-set enrichment analyses and a cross-region synthesis of interaction trajectories. At P50, AC, IC, and cochlea showed coordinated suppression of mitochondrial metabolism, translation, RNA processing, and proteostasis, whereas CN displayed the opposite metabolic and biosynthetic profile together with reduced synaptic and adhesion programs. At 8 months, inflammatory interactions converged across all four regions, including interferon, complement, IL6-JAK-STAT3, and broader immune-response pathways. This coordination fractured at 11 months: AC and IC retained inflammatory and negative synaptic shifts, whereas CN and cochlea frequently changed in the opposite direction, including transient positive shifts in synaptic programs. By 16 months, immune interactions converged again, while metabolic, proteostatic, and synaptic trajectories remained region dependent; CN opposed AC, IC, and cochlea in several major metabolic programs. These findings define a distributed, asynchronous response rather than a monotonic bottom-up or top-down progression. The resulting spatiotemporal map links early metabolic stress, intermediate central-peripheral decoupling, and late inflammatory convergence, providing a molecular framework for evaluating peripheral to central auditory gain and temporal-processing measures as candidate indicators of AD progression.

doi:10.22541/authorea.15010124/v1.title: Incidental Sounds of Locomotion as Information: From Collective Flight to Active Sensing
doi:10.22541/authorea.15010124/v1.abstract: What can evolution do with information that movement already provides? Locomotion inevitably generates incidental sounds of locomotion (ISOL), which may provide a bidirectional flow of information within moving groups: individuals can obtain information from the locomotor sounds of neighbours while simultaneously generating information about their own movements. Such reciprocal information could facilitate mutual adjustment of movement, while ISOL may also produce auditory masking. Synchronization of group movements has therefore been suggested as one possible means of reducing such masking. Here, I examine the hypothesis that ISOL may provide spatial and temporal information during collective flight and consider how movement-generated acoustic information may be integrated with visual and other sensory information within individuals while simultaneously providing information to neighbouring individuals. Acoustic information may complement vision, particularly when visual information is reduced or unreliable. Locomotion, respiration and sound production are closely coupled in flying animals, and in bats biosonar production is integrated with respiratory and locomotor activity while retaining considerable temporal flexibility. Together with independently evolved echolocation systems in birds, these relationships suggest a broader evolutionary possibility: capacities for extracting spatial information from sounds already associated with movement could provide a substrate upon which more active forms of acoustic sensing develop. This represents a possible functional continuum rather than an evolutionary sequence; each incremental change would need to provide an advantage within its own behavioural context. The hypothesis generates testable predictions spanning sensory physiology, biomechanics and collective behaviour.

doi:10.64898/2026.09.18.752626.title: Predictive coding networks capture human neural representations missing in supervised DNNs
doi:10.64898/2026.09.18.752626.authors: Gütlin D, Kittelmann D, Auksztulewicz R.
doi:10.64898/2026.09.18.752626.abstract: Neuroscientific learning theories propose that the brain acquires knowledge by constructing internal world models. Supervised learning, the dominant approach in deep neural networks (DNN), relies on external category labels, making it difficult to reconcile with biological learning. There is an increasing trend towards more biologically valid approaches, such as predictive (minimize future surprise) or contrastive (minimize response to expected, maximize to unexpected inputs) objectives, but these approaches typically rely on pretrained DNN models that vary widely in architecture, size, and hyperparameters, making direct comparisons difficult. Here, we isolate the effect of learning by comparing small, identical networks trained with predictive, contrastive, and supervised learning objectives, as well as local (layer-restricted) vs. global (full backpropagation) learning. We show that brain representations after statistical learning are better modeled by a predictive local target than a supervised or contrastive target, and that during learning, the brain attenuates category-specific representations while retaining predictive ones. We additionally show that predictive objectives explain brain variance that standard supervised DNNs do not, and that this variance is tied to predictive rather than stimulus or mismatch processing. These findings demonstrate a controlled approach for testing the algorithmic basis of learning and identify prediction as a core learning mechanism.

doi:10.64898/2026.10.12.758475.title: Expecting the unexpected: Great apes anticipate surprise in others
doi:10.64898/2026.10.12.758475.authors: Laumer, I. B.; Lewis, L. S.; Eckert, J.; Winkler, S.; Koester, M.; Mundry, R.; Haun, D.; Krupenye, C.; Cartmill, E. A.
doi:10.64898/2026.10.12.758475.abstract: Humans adeptly navigate complex social environments by attempting to anticipate the actions and emotional responses of others. Although our closest ape relatives have sophisticated social cognitive abilities, we do not know whether they have a cognitive understanding of others' emotions. For the epistemic emotion surprise, a cognitive understanding would require sensitivity to an agent's belief, to reality, and to any misalignment between the two, allowing one to model the mental conditions that drive surprise. In a non-invasive eye tracking study with 31 chimpanzees and bonobos, apes showed evidence of a cognitive understanding of surprise: they detected the misalignment between an agent's belief and reality, exhibiting greater pupil dilation right before an agent encountered an unexpected outcome relative to an expected one. This suggests that apes and humans share a more complex understanding of others' mental lives than previously thought, capacities that likely evolved millions of years ago in a common ancestor.
doi:10.64898/2026.10.12.758475.institution: Max Planck Institute of Animal Behavior, Department of Anthropology, University of California Los Angeles, USA

doi:10.64898/2026.10.08.757608.title: Human Hippocampal Theta-Gamma Phase-Amplitude Coupling Signals the Distance to Remembered Goals
doi:10.64898/2026.10.08.757608.authors: Huang, Z.; Goumas, P.; Bisby, J. A.; Rodionov, R.; Diehl, B.; McEvoy, A. W.; Walker, M. C.; Vivekananda, U.; Burgess, N.; Bush, D.
doi:10.64898/2026.10.08.757608.abstract: In mammals, flexible navigation is believed to rely on a cognitive map of known locations supported by the hippocampus and surrounding medial temporal lobe structures. Hippocampal place cells typically exhibit spatial firing fields within a given environment. Moreover, their firing is modulated by the movement-related theta rhythm such that "theta sweeps" of place cell activity encode the trajectory towards a hidden reward location during goal-directed navigation. Here, we attempted to detect signatures of theta sweeps in the human hippocampal local field potential (LFP) recorded with intracranial EEG. Specifically, we hypothesised that sequences of locations along a planned trajectory encoded by distinct cell assemblies are associated with gamma activity at successive theta phases. To test this hypothesis, we asked N=9 patients with epilepsy to perform a spatial navigation task in desktop virtual reality while we recorded LFP signals from depth electrode contacts implanted across the medial temporal lobe. Consistent with our predictions, we found an increase in hippocampal theta-gamma phase-amplitude coupling, a decrease in gamma power, and theta phase precession of gamma activity as hidden goal locations were approached and the sequence of locations remaining to be traversed became shorter. This suggests that goal-directed hippocampal theta sweeps during navigation are reflected in LFP theta-gamma phase-amplitude coupling, and that these neural mechanisms of model-based planning are conserved across species.
doi:10.64898/2026.10.08.757608.institution: UCL Department of Neuroscience, Physiology, and Pharmacology

doi:10.1162/jocn.a.2628.title: Working Memory Facilitates Event Segmentation Via Boundary-triggered Reactivation and Partial Accumulation during Events.
doi:10.1162/jocn.a.2628.authors: Güler B, Karahamza S, Şentürk YD, Bein O, Clewett D, Günseli E.
doi:10.1162/jocn.a.2628.abstract: Event segmentation is the cognitive process of dividing continuous experiences into meaningful units. Although working memory (WM) is believed to play an instrumental role in event segmentation, its specific contribution remains under debate. Here, we used two electroencephalography indices of WM load, alpha-band suppression and contralateral delay activity amplitude, to test the extent to which WM representations reflect gradually accumulating information during unfolding events, boundary-triggered reactivation at event transitions, or both. Participants viewed object images paired with sounds that both remained in the same category for six consecutive items to form a stable event, followed by two items from another category, creating an event boundary. Temporal order and sequential memory were used to assess event segmentation. We found increased alpha-band suppression following event transitions, supporting the reactivation account. Evidence for the accumulation was mixed, with no evidence for increased alpha-band suppression and moderate evidence for increased contralateral delay activity during events. These results indicate that WM contributes to event segmentation primarily through boundary-triggered reactivation, with only limited evidence for within-event accumulation.

doi:10.64898/2026.10.12.758444.title: Neurite Complexity and Plasticity Markers Track Synaptic Vesicle Density in the Living Human Brain: A Multimodal PET-MRI-EEG Study
doi:10.64898/2026.10.12.758444.authors: Agnorelli C, Peill J, Kurtin DL, Mallon O, Sawicka G, Shatalina E, Godfrey K, Murphy R, Ahmad K, Oestreich LKL, Sumner R, Alberti M, Wall M, Ertl N, Searle G, Clarke M, Zhou K, Osugo M, Sarem U, Weiss B, Greenway K, Jauhar S, Fagiolini A, Carhart-Harris R, Matthews PM, Rabiner E, Nutt D, Erritzoe D.
doi:10.64898/2026.10.12.758444.abstract: Neuroplasticity, the brain's capacity to reorganise its structure and function, is a transdiagnostic feature across psychiatric and neurodegenerative diseases and a putative mechanism of action for pharmacological interventions. [11C]-UCBJ positron emission tomography (PET), which quantifies synaptic vesicle glycoprotein 2A (SV2A) density, offers the most direct in vivo measure of human synaptic density, but its relationship to complementary, more scalable neuroimaging measures of structural and functional plasticity remains uncharacterised. We combined [11C]-UCBJ PET, diffusion weighted imaging (DWI/NODDI), resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging (rs-fMRI), and electroencephalography (EEG)-based sensory tasks (roving mismatch negativity, MMN; visual long-term potentiation, vLTP) in 18 healthy volunteers to test the relationship between synaptic terminal SV2A density and complementary structural and functional neuroplasticity measures, and whether these relationships were reproducible following pharmacological challenge with ketamine (n = 11) or N,N-dimethyltryptamine (DMT; n = 7). There were no statistically significant differences in PET-derived SV2A binding potential (BPND), DWI-derived neurite orientation dispersion (ODI) and structural weighted degree (SWD), EEG-derived MMN repetition suppression, and late-phase vLTP P2 potentiation, 1 to 8 days following DMT and ketamine exposure compared to baseline. BPND was coupled with ODI across cortical regions before and after pharmacological challenge, and this relationship was tighter within visual, attentional, and frontoparietal control brain networks. SWD showed a weaker, more spatially restricted association with BPND, primarily in regions belonging to the limbic and visual brain networks, but was not replicated post-drug. No consistent association was found between BPND and functional weighted degree (FWD), derived from rs-fMRI, at baseline or after pharmacological challenge. Frontotemporal BPND was positively associated with MMN repetition suppression (r = 0.61), and occipital BPND with late-phase vLTP P2 potentiation (r = 0.54), with the MMN-BPND association replicating after pharmacological challenge (r = 0.49). These findings link synaptic terminal SV2A density in the living human brain to neurite architecture and the capacity for short-term and Hebbian-like long-term synaptic plasticity, while dissociating these relationships from generic functional connectivity and magnitude of sensory-evoked responses. These data provide cross-modal validation for DWI- and EEG-derived measures as biological indices and surrogate measures of human synaptic plasticity.

doi:10.21203/rs.3.rs-11314841/v1.title: Rhythms of the Mind: The Physics of Sound, Neural Entrainment, and Sensorimotor Learning in Music—Implications for Cognitive Function, Psychological Well-Being, and Inner Peace
doi:10.21203/rs.3.rs-11314841/v1.abstract: Abstract Music brings together physical sound, auditory perception, cognitive processing, motor coordination, emotional regulation, and subjective experience. Learning and practising music require the continuous integration of acoustic information, attention, memory, temporal prediction, movement, and feedback. This conceptual integrative review examines how the physics of sound and the neuroscience of rhythmic processing can inform the study of musical learning, sensorimotor integration, psychological well-being, and inner peace. It discusses acoustic frequency, period, wavelength, superposition, rhythm, and timing accuracy alongside auditory–motor coupling, neural entrainment, executive functions, and emotional regulation. Published evidence suggests that musical training can benefit selected auditory and closely related processing skills, while findings concerning far transfer to general cognition and stress recovery are more variable. The article distinguishes active musical learning from passive listening and professionally guided music therapy, and it avoids treating mechanical resonance as equivalent to neural entrainment or assuming that particular frequencies automatically produce healing. A physics-informed conceptual framework is proposed in which measurable acoustic features and structured practice may influence task-specific perceptual and motor learning, while emotional and well-being outcomes are shaped by personal preference, social context, and individual differences. Because no original participant data were collected, the results represent a qualitative synthesis of published evidence rather than new experimental findings. The article concludes that music offers a valuable interdisciplinary context for investigating the connections between physical sound, learning, coordinated action, and subjective well-being, while emphasizing the need for transparent methods and empirical testing.

doi:10.1016/j.celrep.2026.118123.title: Inhibiting the right dorsolateral prefrontal cortex selectively enhances unsupervised statistical learning.
doi:10.1016/j.celrep.2026.118123.authors: Pesthy O, Pesthy ZV, Vékony T, Janacsek K, Fabó D, Nemeth D.
doi:10.1016/j.celrep.2026.118123.abstract: The brain must balance the automatic extraction of regularities with top-down cognitive control, yet the hemispheric contributions of the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (DLPFC) remain unresolved. Here, we applied inhibitory repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation to the left, right, or bilateral DLPFC in 95 adults during a probabilistic sequence learning task. We found that inhibiting the right and bilateral DLPFC enhanced statistical learning compared to sham stimulation. Contrary to the hypothesis that interference from existing knowledge would mediate this effect, episodic memory performance was unaffected. As an alternative, we propose that right DLPFC inhibition shifts cognitive processing toward an exploratory information-sampling strategy, supported by our finding of greater reaction time variability in the right and bilateral stimulation groups. Our results provide causal evidence for a right-lateralized suppressive influence of the DLPFC on unsupervised learning and suggest that its role is linked to information-processing style rather than direct competition with episodic memory systems.

doi:10.64898/2026.09.25.754226.title: A comparison of female competitive traits: Female aggression peaks at nest building but female song spans multiple contexts in a temperate songbird
doi:10.64898/2026.09.25.754226.authors: Gleason, M.; Krieg, C.; Ododm, K.
doi:10.64898/2026.09.25.754226.abstract: Female-female competition is increasingly recognized as a key driver of female ornamentation, including birdsong, which often functions in intrasexual competition. However, the specific resources females use elaborate traits to compete for remain unclear. In addition, few studies have simultaneously investigated the use of multiple competitive traits in females, despite growing independent interest in these traits (e.g., female song and aggression). We investigated the competitive contexts of female song, aggression and calling behavior in northern house wrens (Troglodytes aedon) to determine which resources females compete for across the breeding season. We simulated conspecific territorial intrusions using female song at three breeding stages representing different contexts: arrival (mate and territory acquisition), nest building (nest site and breeding status defense), and egg laying (brood defense). We tested whether female song and physical aggression varied as reproductive resources shifted across the breeding cycle. Females were significantly more aggressive during nest building, showing 5.8 times greater odds of a higher-intensity aggressive response during nest building compared to arrival. Female song output was similar across early stages but declined during egg laying, though this was not statistically significant after correction for multiple comparisons and individuals varied substantially in overall singing propensity. Non-song vocalizations varied by call type and breeding stage. Calls associated with aggression occurred most frequently during nest building, consistent with peak physical aggression responses. Together, these results identify nest building as the stage of highest female aggression, consistent with heightened competition over nest cavities and associated breeding status in this cavity-nesting species. In contrast, female song occurred across all stages and appears to function in multiple competitive contexts. This study provides evidence for context and mode-specific female signaling in a temperate songbird and highlights that females strategically use aggression, calls, and song to mediate social conflict across breeding contexts.

doi:10.64898/2026.10.15.758668.title: Division of vocal signaling in cooperating marmoset dyads
doi:10.64898/2026.10.15.758668.authors: Nandy, G.; Meisner, O. C.; Shi, W.; Nandy, A. S.; Jadi, M. P.; Chang, S. W. C.
doi:10.64898/2026.10.15.758668.abstract: Communication enables partners to coordinate actions toward shared goals, but how vocal communication is organized during cooperation remains poorly understood. We recorded vocalizations from three common marmoset (Callithrix jacchus) dyads as they learned a mutual cooperation task requiring coordinated lever pulls for reward. Vocal behavior was divided by social hierarchy: dominants produced t-peeps, whereas subordinates produced chirps. Interestingly, dominant t-peeps followed failed cooperative pulls, peaked when cooperative bouts broke down, and declined after learning. By contrast, subordinate chirps followed successful pulls, accumulated during sustained cooperation, and persisted after learning. Each call was linked to the task role of the caller: dominant animals t-peeped more in sessions they led, and subordinates chirped mainly after cooperations they initiated, associations that sharpened with learning. Thus, social rank determined which vocal signal a partner used, whereas task role and the state of cooperation determined when to communicate. These complementary vocal signals of failure and success reveal how hierarchy, task role and task phase organize communication during joint action in cooperating marmosets.

doi:10.21203/rs.3.rs-11132963/v1.title: Cognitive Load, Writing Anxiety, and Syntactic Complexity in Teaching Turkish as a Foreign Language: An Experimental Intervention Study
doi:10.21203/rs.3.rs-11132963/v1.authors: Köçeri K, Akçay A, Aydıntürk A, Arslan A.
doi:10.21203/rs.3.rs-11132963/v1.abstract: Abstract Writing in a foreign language ranks among the most cognitively demanding tasks confronting language learners, requiring the simultaneous management of linguistic form, affective states, and limited working memory capacity. Although growing evidence demonstrates that cognitive load (CL) and foreign language writing anxiety (FLWA) each independently suppress syntactic complexity (SC) in learner writing, no intervention study has yet systematically targeted both mechanisms within the Teaching Turkish as a Foreign Language (TaFL) context. This study employed a quasi-experimental pretest–posttest non-equivalent control group design with 300 international students across four universities in Türkiye. The 14-week Cognitive-Affective Writing Enhancement Programme (CAWEP) combined structured task design scaffolding, syntactic schema-building activities, and evidence-based anxiety regulation workshops. ANCOVA results revealed large, significant post-test advantages for the experimental group in extraneous CL (η²p = .27), writing anxiety (η²p = .25), and SC (η²p = .30). Bootstrapped mediation analyses confirmed that FLWA partially mediates the extraneous CL–SC relationship, and concurrent think-aloud protocols provided convergent process-level evidence. Findings support integrating CL-informed task design and anxiety reduction into TaFL writing instruction.

doi:10.64898/2026.09.25.754219.title: Parents’ neural dynamics in response to their children’s speech
doi:10.64898/2026.09.25.754219.authors: Elmlinger SL, Rosenberg E, Jaffe-Dax S, Nencheva ML, Lee C, Kosie JE, Lew-Williams C.
doi:10.64898/2026.09.25.754219.abstract: ABSTRACT The development of speech in human children is a protracted process that depends on social experience. From early life, young children produce vocalizations in the presence of others, which affords unique opportunities for feedback about how to communicate successfully. However, for feedback to happen, young children’s speech needs to effect change in the brains of their caregivers. Using dual-brain functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) to measure real-time communication between caregivers and their 2-to 3-year-old children ( n = 56), we found that children’s vocalizations selectively modulated caregivers’ brain activity. Parents’ brains showed a rapid response to children’s production of speech that was communicatively advanced (multiword utterances) vs. less advanced (babble). The findings imply that if part of learning to talk is figuring out how to get your communication partner to listen, then early conversations likely present continuous opportunities for feedback that guide children toward advances in spoken language.

doi:10.31234/osf.io/s5wbt_v1.title: Phoneme overlap analysis of the visual benefit for speech-in-noise perception
doi:10.31234/osf.io/s5wbt_v1.authors: Magnotti J, Zhang Y, Zhu L, Yu Y, Beauchamp M.
doi:10.31234/osf.io/s5wbt_v1.abstract: Seeing the face of the talker improves the intelligibility of speech-in-noise, termed the visualbenefit. The visual benefit is usually measured at the whole-word level, with responses classifiedas "correct" or "incorrect". An alternative method measures visual benefit using the phonemeoverlap between stimulus and response. In 55 participants presented with auditory andaudiovisual words, phoneme-overlap analysis estimated 289 different visual benefit values,compared with only three different values for whole-word analysis. Phoneme-overlap detected apositive visual benefit in 67% of word-participant pairs, in contrast to 32% for whole-wordanalysis. Individual words varied greatly in their phoneme-overlap visual benefit, from 1% to72%. Variability across words was accurately predicted (r = 0.78) by the phoneme compositionof the word and the visual benefit for untested words could be predicted with a median error of9%. Measuring the visual benefit for individual phonemes revealed similarly high variability(1% to 70%) with six phonemes (W, F, V, TH, P, AW) exhibiting visual benefit more than onestandard deviation above the mean. The increased sensitivity of phoneme-overlap analysisrelative to conventional whole-word analysis may provide a useful tool for investigatingaudiovisual speech perception in clinical, neuroscience and computer science contexts.

doi:10.31234/osf.io/c6834_v1.title: Crossmodal Congruency Affects Sensitivity but not Speed in Auditory–Tactile Go/NoGo Tasks
doi:10.31234/osf.io/c6834_v1.abstract: Crossmodal congruency and interference influence perception and action depending on modality, congruency, and task constraints. This study investigated auditory–tactile interactions using a Go/NoGo paradigm to dissociate effects on response speed (reaction time, RT) and perceptual sensitivity (d’). Participants performed a frequency discrimination task in which high- and low-frequency auditory tones (1000 vs. 500 Hz) and tactile vibrations (100 vs. 70 Hz) served as Go and NoGo signals across five conditions: unimodal auditory (A0), unimodal tactile (T0), auditory targets with tactile distractors (At), tactile targets with auditory distractors (Ta), and a combined condition (AT). In the crossmodal conditions, participants attended one modality while ignoring the other, and distractors were either response-congruent (both stimuli signaled the same response) or response-incongruent (the two modalities signaled different responses). Modality significantly affected performance, yielding particularly slow RTs and reduced d’ in the tactile-target condition containing auditory distractors (Ta). Crossmodal congruency robustly altered sensitivity, showing higher d’ for congruent than incongruent trials, particularly for tactile targets, but did not reliably influence RT. No evidence for multisensory facilitation emerged in the combined condition. These findings reveal a dissociation between speed and sensitivity in auditory–tactile processing, consistent with accounts where crossmodal congruency primarily limits or enhances the quality of perceptual evidence.

doi:10.64898/2026.09.24.753595.title: Memory-based and surround-based pattern completion show distinct laminar profiles in human V1
doi:10.64898/2026.09.24.753595.authors: Zhang, Z.; Abbatecola, C.; Huang, Y.; Lazarova, Y. Y.; Paton, A.; Wimber, M.; Levelt, C. N.; Larkum, M. E.; Muckli, L. F.; Petro, L. S.
doi:10.64898/2026.09.24.753595.abstract: Visual input is often incomplete, requiring the brain to infer missing information from prior experience or contextual cues. Establishing whether memory-derived and context-derived information shape pattern completion through shared or distinct top-down pathways is central to understanding how perception emerges from the integration of sensory input and prior knowledge. Across two experiments, we used 7T layer fMRI to measure activity in an occluded region of human V1 while participants viewed natural scenes. Memory-based completion was enabled by varying the level of exposure to full scene images before scanning, while surround-based completion was implemented via two scenes that were repeatedly presented in partially occluded form but never seen intact. In both fMRI experiments, category decoding in the occluded V1 region only emerged after multiple prior exposures, whereas novel scenes did not show reliable decoding. Repeated partially occluded scenes also supported decoding, despite the hidden region never being shown, consistent with surround-based pattern completion. Critically, mnemonic and surround-based pattern completion showed opposite laminar decoding profiles across V1 depths, with mnemonic feedback dominating deep layers, and surround-based feedback dominating superficial layers. Together, these findings suggest that completion in the early visual cortex depends on the sources of inferred information, revealing dissociable feedback pathways for memory- and context-driven inference.

doi:10.64898/2026.09.29.755540.title: MR-ARFI and Beyond: Characterizing the Temporal Dynamics of Acoustic Radiation Force in Human Brain
doi:10.64898/2026.09.29.755540.authors: Mohammadjavadi M, Pauly KB, Glover GH.
doi:10.64898/2026.09.29.755540.abstract: Purpose Magnetic Resonance Acoustic Radiation Force Imaging (MR-ARFI) encodes focused ultrasound (FUS)-induced tissue displacements to MR phase shifts. Because these phase shifts are small, optimizing displacement sensitivity and minimizing motion artifacts requires characterization of the temporal dynamics of acoustic radiation force (ARF). Beyond sequence design, such characterization enables MR-ARFI to serve as a probe of brain viscoelastic behavior and can inform the design of therapeutic ultrasound pulsing schemes by quantifying how rapidly tissue deforms and relaxes. Methods We developed a dynamic model assuming a gamma-variate impulse response for ARF(t), with time constant (τ) to be estimated. A single-shot spin echo ARFI acquisition with a bipolar motion encoding gradient (MEG) was implemented, incorporating retrospective corrections for head motion and physiological noise. A 500 kHz FUS pulse was applied in on/off blocks while systematically varying the timing between the MEG and sonication. The resulting phase time series were fit to the model to estimate τ in five human participants. To assess sensitivity to tissue stiffness, τ was additionally measured in two customized gelatin phantoms of differing stiffness, characterized independently by MR elastography (MRE). Results The average measured time constant in human participants was τ= 3.7 ± 0.27 ms. Comparing the two phantoms, the stiffer phantom exhibited a shorter τ (3.0–3.5 ms) than the softer phantom (4.0–4.5 ms), which tracked the MRE-derived Kelvin-Voigt viscoelastic time constants. In addition, the peak ARFI displacement was lower in the stiffer phantom (0.17 vs 0.74 μm for the less stiff phantom), and a broader displacement focal spot size (FWHM 22 mm vs 15 mm). Conclusion This time-series approach with motion and physiological noise corrections validates an MR-based technique capable of characterizing the brain’s temporal response to sonication-induced mechanical forces, providing a foundation for optimizing the design of ultrasound pulsing schemes for ARFI, as well as for future studies of brain biomechanics.

doi:10.64898/2026.09.29.26364278.title: An explainable multimodal framework for exploring depression-associated speech representations in Alzheimer’s disease
doi:10.64898/2026.09.29.26364278.authors: Hassan H, Patel D, Aagela H, Johnson A.
doi:10.64898/2026.09.29.26364278.abstract: Depression in Alzheimer’s disease (AD) is clinically challenging to characterise because affective and cognitive manifestations frequently overlap with the underlying neurodegenerative condition. This study investigates depression-related speech patterns in AD using an explainable multimodal framework that integrates linguistic and acoustic features from elicited picture-description speech. To address the absence of directly observed depression labels in the target AD cohort, we employ a source-informed cross-dataset transfer strategy. Unsupervised clustering identified two distinct speech sub-phenotypes within the AD cohort. By comparing these unsupervised representations to a depression-labelled source corpus, one cluster demonstrated mathematical proximity (measured via cosine similarity in a shared latent space) to the source depression centroid. We explicitly acknowledge that this proximity reflects geometric similarity in a shared latent space, which may encapsulate overlapping domain characteristics alongside affective variance. To validate the structural integrity and separability of these discovered clusters, a proxy supervised classification task was employed. The retained multimodal artificial neural network (ANN) integrated information from both modalities and achieved 92.73% cluster separability accuracy. This demonstrates that the representation-derived two-cluster partition was highly learnable on the independent internal hold-out test set; it does not establish clinical validity, longitudinal stability, or diagnostic validity of the identified sub-phenotypes. For interpretability, Shapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) analysis was utilised to extract feature attributions and organise influential acoustic and linguistic features into a multimodal taxonomy. Furthermore, a Multimodal SHAP Attribution Magnitude (MSAM) score was derived as an exploratory model-based attribution score rather than a clinically validated severity measure. Ultimately, this study provides an interpretable computational baseline for characterising depression-related speech variance in AD, establishing a structural foundation for future prospective validation using independently labelled clinical cohorts. Author Summary Depression can be difficult to recognise in people with Alzheimer’s disease because changes in mood, motivation, language, and behaviour may overlap with symptoms of cognitive impairment. Speech analysis offers a possible way of studying these changes, but datasets containing both Alzheimer’s disease and independently verified depression labels are limited. We therefore explored whether speech representations from an Alzheimer’s disease cohort could be compared with a separate depression-labelled speech dataset. We used acoustic and linguistic features to identify groups of participants with similar speech characteristics and then examined whether these groups could be reliably reproduced by supervised machine-learning models. The best multimodal model reproduced the representation-derived grouping with 92.73% accuracy on an independent participant-level test set. Importantly, this result does not demonstrate that the participants had depression, because depression was not independently assessed in the Alzheimer’s disease cohort. Instead, the study provides an exploratory computational framework for studying cross-corpus speech similarities and identifies features that contributed to the learned speech representations. Prospective studies with clinically assessed depression status are needed before such methods can be considered for clinical use. Such studies should also examine whether the observed speech patterns remain informative after accounting for cognitive impairment, age, medication, speaking task, and recording conditions. This work therefore represents a hypothesis-generating computational step rather than a diagnostic tool.

doi:10.1523/eneuro.0092-26.2026.title: Population-genetic and evolutionary context of a CRIP3 variant associated with age-related hearing loss.
doi:10.1523/eneuro.0092-26.2026.authors: Brongo SE, Aqil A, Xu-Friedman MA, Gokcumen O.
doi:10.1523/eneuro.0092-26.2026.abstract: Age-related hearing loss is a widespread sensory impairment affecting one third of the elderly population, yet the genetic underpinnings of this condition remain incompletely understood. In this study, we investigate the evolutionary context of a non-synonymous variant (rs2242416) in the CRIP3 gene, which is expressed in auditory hair cells, and previously associated with hearing loss. We first confirm that rs2242416 shows strong and consistent association with hearing loss across multiple genome-wide association studies. Notably, rs2242416 is also associated with reduced risk of heart related phenotypes, suggesting potential pleiotropic effects. The variant substitutes the nonpolar isoleucine for the polar threonine at an amino acid site that is otherwise highly conserved across placental mammals. By causing the amino acid change, the variant is predicted to subtly alter the structure of the CRIP3 protein. Moreover, the population genetics of the CRIP3 locus reveals an increased frequency of the derived threonine allele of rs2242416 in Eurasian populations following the out-of-Africa migration of humans more than 50,000 years ago. Nevertheless, the role of natural selection in generating this increased allele frequency in Eurasians remains inconclusive. Together, these results provide phenotypic, evolutionary, and molecular context for CRIP3 variation and highlight rs2242416 as a promising candidate for functional studies. Significance Statement Age-related hearing loss is highly prevalent, yet the specific genetic variants that contribute to disease risk remain poorly understood. Here, we investigate a variant (rs2242416) that causes an amino acid change in the CRIP3 gene. While this variant is associated with hearing loss in multiple genome-wide association studies (GWAS), virtually no focused attention has been given to it. By integrating GWAS findings with evolutionary and population genetic analyses, we provide broader context for interpreting this variant. Our results support rs2242416 as a candidate functional variant increasing hearing loss risk in humans. Overall, this study demonstrates the value of combining population genetics with human GWAS to prioritize variants for functional validation.

doi:10.64898/2026.10.07.756069.title: Vibrotactile transcutaneous auricular vagus nerve stimulation (taVNS) during working memory: convergent electrophysiological evidence for cortical efficiency
doi:10.64898/2026.10.07.756069.authors: Tan G, Demarest P, Kardashina T, Adams J, Willie JT, Roland J, Gorlewicz JL, Brunner P, Leuthardt EC.
doi:10.64898/2026.10.07.756069.abstract: Background Working memory, the cognitive ability to maintain and manipulate a finite amount of information, is fundamental in reasoning, learning, and decision-making. Working memory erodes in conditions from Alzheimer’s disease to stroke to healthy aging. Transcutaneous auricular vagus nerve stimulation (taVNS) is a promising neuromodulation method for improving working memory. By stimulating the auricular branch of the vagus nerve, taVNS is thought to engage ascending arousal systems such as the locus coeruleus-norepinephrine (LC-NE) system. However, the physiological link between LC-NE system modulation via taVNS and improved working memory remains largely unknown. This mechanistic gap limits the rational optimization of the stimulation protocol and the identification of the cognitive functions and patient populations that are likely to benefit. Objective We test two competing hypotheses for how taVNS may improve working memory: sensory amplification or enhancement of cortical efficiency. The sensory-amplification hypothesis predicts increased cortical responses to stimuli, whereas the cortical-efficiency hypothesis predicts reduced cortical responses. Methods Twenty healthy adults completed N-back working memory tasks during three counterbalanced sessions: baseline, active vibrotactile taVNS (vtaVNS), and sham stimulation, while we simultaneously recorded electroencephalography, electrocardiography, eye-tracking, and behavioral responses. To study the effect of vtaVNS on neuronal activity, we also recruited 20 patients with epilepsy undergoing invasive monitoring. Of these, 19 fully completed the spatial working-memory task. We quantified cortical responses to visual stimuli using event-related potentials (ERPs) in scalp EEG and high-gamma activity in intracranial local field potentials. To examine prediction of the cortical-efficiency hypothesis, we further explored the effect of vtaVNS on distance to criticality and heartbeat-evoked potentials. Results Active vtaVNS reduced both scalp-recorded visual ERP and high-gamma response in temporal cortices, relative to sham stimulation. Moreover, smaller visual event-related potentials were associated with successful encoding during the most demanding working-memory condition (i.e., 4-back task). Exploratory analyses showed that vtaVNS shifted cortical dynamics closer to criticality. Conclusion Our results converge on the conclusion that vtaVNS does not uniformly amplify cortical responses to external stimuli. Instead, vtaVNS enhances cortical efficiency, supporting more effective allocation of cognitive resources between exteroceptive and mnemonic processes. These findings provide a framework for predicting when taVNS will be most beneficial and for optimizing stimulation protocols across cognitive and clinical applications. Highlights Consistent visual event-related potential in human subjects during an N-back working memory task Vibrotactile taVNS reduced stimulus-evoked cortical responses in both scalp EEG and intracranial high-gamma activity (70-150 Hz). Reduced visual event-related potentials are associated with successful encoding in the 4-back task. Vibrotactile taVNS shifted cortical dynamics toward a near-critical regime.

doi:10.21203/rs.3.rs-10388644/v1.title: Designing a motion-controlled game framework to develop bodily–kinesthetic intelligence in deaf and hard-of-hearing children
doi:10.21203/rs.3.rs-10388644/v1.authors: Sun J, Jiang X, Gao Z, Li Y, Zheng X, Zhou W, Gao Z, Fung A.
doi:10.21203/rs.3.rs-10388644/v1.abstract: Abstract Purpose Motion-controlled games offer a promising pathway for embodied learning, yet there remains limited evidence-based guidance on how to design and evaluate such games to foster bodily–kinesthetic intelligence (BKI) for deaf and hard-of-hearing (DHH) learners. This study develops and instantiates a design framework, grounded in universal and inclusive design principles, for motion-controlled learning games targeting BKI in DHH children. Methods Following a design-based research process, we operationalized BKI into six subdimensions and instantiated these constructs in a motion-controlled role-playing game, My Super Power, implemented with Kinect-based full-body interaction and augmented with vibrotactile cues to support rhythm perception. A school-based pre–post mixed-methods intervention was conducted with 35 DHH (aged 8–10). Learning outcomes were triangulated through (i) performance tasks scored using Kinect system logs and third-party observation, (ii) a self-report questionnaire, and (iii) semi-structured interviews. Results Paired-samples t-tests indicated significant pre-post changes in in-system task performance across BKI subdimensions, while self-reports suggested substantial perceived gains. Qualitative findings further explained how scaffolded spatial exploration, haptic-supported rhythm tasks, decomposed movement rehearsal, and fail-forward feedback mechanisms sustained engagement and practice. Conclusion The study contributes (1) a mapping from motion-game mechanics to BKI subskills, and (2) the Motion-controlled games for Bodily-kinesthetic intelligence in DHH children (MBD) framework as a transferable, universal-design-informed guide for motion-controlled educational games that supports equitable participation and digital inclusion of DHH children in inclusive and special education contexts.

doi:10.64898/2026.10.02.756363.title: Using the aperiodic slope across learning to predict sleep-based memory consolidation
doi:10.64898/2026.10.02.756363.authors: Anesbury A, Caldwell HB, Lushington K, Al Safadi M, Chatburn A.
doi:10.64898/2026.10.02.756363.abstract: Homeostatic mechanisms adjust synaptic strengths to regulate neuronal activity across wake-sleep cycles. Although sleep supports memory consolidation, limited research has explored how sleep-induced homeostatic changes influence memory outcomes in humans. The EEG-derived aperiodic slope (1/f) could be a candidate measure of homeostatic memory processes through its reflection of neural excitation-inhibition balance. In this study, 27 participants learned object-word pairs, and completed an immediate recognition test before either a nap or equivalent wakeful period. Resting-state EEG was recorded, both before and after learning and the interval, to derive changes in aperiodic slope values. A delayed recognition test then assessed whether changes in the aperiodic slope (i.e., homeostatic activity) across learning and the interval predicted memory accuracy and N400 amplitude, an index of stimulus expectancy and recognition. Our study found evidence to suggest homeostatic renormalisation, for the nap condition only, indicated by a shift towards inhibition across sleep which was inversely related to the slope change across learning. Although the aperiodic slope change across the nap and wake intervals did not predict delayed memory accuracy, a shift towards inhibition during learning was beneficial for memory accuracy, only in the nap condition. Similarly, a shift towards inhibition across learning, followed by a shift towards excitation in the nap condition, predicted reduced N400 amplitudes. This suggests that homeostatic renormalisation across the nap influenced model updating and stimulus expectancy. This study provides evidence for a link between synaptic homeostatic processes and memory consolidation, emphasising the importance of encoding-related aperiodic activity in this relationship.

doi:10.12688/f1000research.191423.1.title: Diagnostic Accuracy of Pure-Tone Audiometry and Otoacoustic Emissions for School-Based Hearing Screening in Children: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
doi:10.12688/f1000research.191423.1.authors: Abo Hussin AY, Elnaseeh WM, Majzoub RA, Al Jabr IK, Babekr NBA, Almaghnam TF.
doi:10.12688/f1000research.191423.1.abstract: Background: School-based hearing screening can identify hearing loss that develops after birth or becomes apparent later in childhood. Pure-tone audiometry (PTA) and otoacoustic emissions (OAE) are widely used, but diagnostic performance varies across thresholds, technologies, populations and reference standards. Methods We searched PubMed, Scopus, the Cochrane Library and Google Scholar from database inception to 19 September 2026, with supplementary discovery using Elicit, OpenAlex and ASTA. A single reviewer conducted screening, extraction and risk-of-bias assessment, with structured second-pass verification. Eligible studies evaluated PTA or OAE in school-based or school-entry settings against an appropriate audiological reference standard and reported interpretable diagnostic-accuracy data. Risk of bias was assessed using QUADAS-2. PTA studies with reconstructable 2 × 2 data were synthesised using a Reitsma-type bivariate random-effects model fitted by restricted maximum likelihood; OAE evidence was synthesised narratively. Results The search identified 2,198 records; 262 duplicates were removed and 1,936 unique records were screened. Fifty-five reports were sought, 26 were not retrieved and 29 full texts were assessed. Fifteen reports representing 14 unique studies were included. Six independent PTA datasets were included in the primary meta-analysis. Pooled sensitivity was 77.2% (95% CI 58.3–89.1%) and pooled specificity was 92.5% (95% CI 74.8–98.1%). Replacing the 15-dB Robler threshold with the 20-dB threshold yielded sensitivity of 75.3% and specificity of 93.2%. Prediction ranges were wide, indicating substantial between-study heterogeneity. Eight studies were classified as having high overall QUADAS-2 concern. OAE evidence was too heterogeneous and sparse for a defensible pooled estimate. Conclusions PTA shows relatively high specificity but variable sensitivity for school-based hearing screening. Performance depends on screening threshold, implementation, population and reference standard. Current OAE evidence is insufficient for a reliable pooled estimate. Future studies should use standardised thresholds, complete verification, clearly defined reference standards and full 2 × 2 reporting.

doi:10.1073/pnas.2611415123.title: Pregnancy damps thermoregulatory rhythms across timescales through neural estrogen signaling in mice.
doi:10.1073/pnas.2611415123.authors: Cortes LR, Xiong L, Vree AR, Reis FMCV, Kim N, Feng B, Hansen MR, Rashid S, Sandoval NP, Lopez JI, He Y, Adhikari A, van Veen JE, Garfinkel A, Deeds EJ, Colwell CS, Correa SM.
doi:10.1073/pnas.2611415123.abstract: Pregnancy induces widespread physiological adaptations, including changes to core temperature (T c ), that may reduce fetal heat stress and enhance metabolic stability. Despite the potential importance of maternal thermoregulatory changes, the neural mechanisms organizing homeostatic rhythms during pregnancy remain poorly understood. Here, we demonstrate that pregnancy profoundly reshapes thermoregulatory dynamics across diurnal and ultradian timescales and that these changes are partially orchestrated by estrogen receptor alpha (ERα) signaling in neurons of the medial preoptic area (MPO ERɑ ). Using in vivo calcium recordings of MPO ERɑ neurons, we show that MPO ERɑ neural activity is synchronized with T c oscillations in nonpregnant mice. Notably, this synchronization is lost during pregnancy and reemerges after parturition, indicating that MPO ERɑ activity and T c are synchronized in a manner that is dependent on reproductive state. Using chemogenetic inhibition, we show that MPO ERɑ neurons are required for the lowering of T c in late pregnancy. Using a genomic estrogen signaling reporter, we demonstrate that MPO ERɑ neurons exhibit enhanced estrogen signaling in late pregnancy. This estrogen signaling helps coordinate maternal T c changes, as selectively ablating ERα expression in the MPO increased T c and its circadian and ultradian rhythmicity. Finally, we show that manipulating MPO ERɑ cell activity and MPO Esr1 expression affected neonates: Silencing MPO ERɑ neurons led to premature birth, while both silencing and gene ablation led to sex-specific changes to offspring body mass. In summary, these findings reveal a global suppression of T c circadian and ultradian rhythmicity during pregnancy and identify ERα as a central modulator of these rhythms with consequences for fetal development.

doi:10.3758/s13423-026-03015-1.title: Why are pictures remembered better than sounds? The roles of subjective vividness of mental imagery and semantic labels.
doi:10.3758/s13423-026-03015-1.authors: Ahmad FN, Tremblay S, Alvi M, Karkuszewski MD, Kan Z, Ruso I, Hockley WE.
doi:10.3758/s13423-026-03015-1.abstract: Pictures are recognized more accurately than environmental sounds, possibly because pictures provide enhanced conceptual and perceptual representations than sounds. Conceptual-perceptual distinctiveness (CPD) theory proposes that pictures benefit from stronger semantic organization and more diagnostic perceptual detail. It remains unclear whether the picture superiority effect reflects differences in the subjective vividness of retrieved memories and whether increasing category-level semantic support can enhance vividness for environmental sounds, thereby reducing picture superiority in recognition memory. Vividness was assessed independently of recognition by having participants generate a mental image from a written label and rate its vividness before old/new judgment of the recognition probe. Experiment 1 replicated the picture superiority effect, with pictures producing higher vividness and recognition accuracy than sounds. In Experiments 2A and 2B, written labels strengthened category-level semantic support for sounds, increasing vividness and target recognition and eliminating modality differences for targets. However, pictures continued to show superior lure (i.e., exemplar foil) discrimination and higher vividness preceding accurate lure rejection. Generalized linear mixed-effects (GLMM) analyses showed that vividness selectively predicted correct target recognition for pictures, whereas for sounds, greater vividness also increased false recognition of lures. Together, these findings suggest that semantic support enhances vividness of mental imagery and target recognition for sounds, whereas the picture superiority effect for lure recognition reflects stronger item-specific retrieval information.

doi:10.1016/j.neubiorev.2026.107007.title: Disrupted metabolic support of intrinsic brain rhythms as a driver of spatiotemporal fragmentation in schizophrenia.
doi:10.1016/j.neubiorev.2026.107007.abstract: Schizophrenia can involve disturbances of lived time, lived space, and pre-reflective selfhood. This Perspective examines whether impaired adaptation of cerebral energy metabolism to changing neural demand could provide a physiological constraint on the temporal and spatial organization of neural activity relevant to these experiences. Evidence from cellular models, magnetic resonance spectroscopy, metabolic imaging, electrophysiology, and functional neuroimaging is synthesized, with emphasis on oxidative capacity, respiratory reserve, high-energy phosphate transfer, glycolytic regulation, and metabolic-neural relationships. Across these levels, bioenergetic abnormalities are documented in schizophrenia, but the available evidence does not establish a uniform metabolic deficit or a causal chain from cellular metabolism to psychopathology. A testable hypothesis is therefore proposed: impaired metabolic adaptation may limit neural reconfiguration across functional states, including oscillatory synchronization, intrinsic neural timescale flexibility, and large-scale network differentiation. A staged multimodal assay is outlined, combining functional [18 F] FDG positron emission tomography and electroencephalography during graded 40-Hz auditory stimulation. Primary analyses test metabolic and neural demand-response functions and their relative scaling; secondary analyses address within-condition coupling, recruitment and recovery kinetics, and dimension-matched associations with lived time, lived space, and self-experience. The framework extends spatiotemporal psychopathology by specifying a candidate physiological mechanism while preserving the distinction between neural and experiential levels. It generates falsifiable predictions for mechanistic, longitudinal, and therapeutic studies in schizophrenia.

doi:10.64898/2026.09.30.755465.title: Distinct population dimensions separate sensory adaptation and expectation-related signals in visual cortex
doi:10.64898/2026.09.30.755465.authors: Kim S, Vazquez A, Batista-Brito R, Sjulson L.
doi:10.64898/2026.09.30.755465.abstract: Mismatch negativity is conventionally quantified as a scalar response-amplitude difference between rare deviant and repeated standard stimuli, leaving its organization at the neuronal population level unresolved. We recorded population activity in mouse primary visual cortex (V1) during visual odd-ball and control paradigms while testing contributions from anterior cingulate cortex (ACC) input using optogenetic inhibition. Mismatch modulated firing rates bidirectionally, and these changes largely canceled out on average, yet produced robustly separable population activity patterns. On the stimulus-encoding manifold, repeated standard exposure produced standard-specific response attenuation and a shared rotation of standard and deviant representations, revealing a component not isolated by conventional stimulus-specific adaptation and deviance-detection contrasts. Off the manifold, standards and deviants occupied opposing positions along an ACC-modulated axis consistent with expectation confirmation and violation. Thus, visual mismatch responses engage separable transformations of stimulus representations and expectation-related population activity, with ACC input selectively contributing to the latter while not significantly affecting stimulus encoding or on-manifold adaptation.

doi:10.1162/jocn.a.2630.title: Sensorimotor Adaptation of Vocal Pitch Is Impaired in Cerebellar Ataxia.
doi:10.1162/jocn.a.2630.abstract: Sensory errors, mismatches between predicted sensory outcomes of movement and reafferent sensory feedback, drive changes in the feedforward control of future motor behavior that correct for those errors. Across a wide variety of motor behaviors, individuals with cerebellar damage show impairments in these corrections, strongly suggesting a key role of the cerebellum in sensorimotor adaptation. However, the extent to which the cerebellum is involved in controlling vocal pitch is currently unknown. Crucially, vocal pitch differs in several ways from other systems that suggest it relies more on feedback than feedforward control. Adaptation itself also differs in vocal pitch: Rather than the gradual buildup/decay of learning seen in other systems, pitch adaptation and deadaptation are almost immediate. Together, this questions whether adaptation in vocal pitch relies on the same mechanism as other motor domains. Here, we test the hypothesis that the cerebellum underlies sensorimotor adaptation in vocal pitch, testing the domain generality of this neurocomputational process. In both sustained vocalization and a more natural word production task, individuals with cerebellar ataxia fail to adapt to external auditory perturbation of vocal pitch. The lack of adaptation observed, compared to the impaired but present adaptation seen in other systems, suggests that the cerebellum plays an especially critical role in maintaining accurate control of vocal pitch. Conversely, we failed to detect a previously observed increase in online compensation to vocal pitch errors in ataxia, potentially suggesting this may be an idiosyncratic change in control rather than a common trait in this population.

doi:10.1038/s41386-026-02568-y.title: ICER-Controlled inhibitory plasticity of amygdala engram neurons regulates fear memory precision.
doi:10.1038/s41386-026-02568-y.authors: Lee H, Lee S, Yoo T, Nghi TD, Truong L, Ryu GY, Park J, Park SK, Kim JH.
doi:10.1038/s41386-026-02568-y.abstract: Fear discrimination-the ability to distinguish threatening stimuli from non-threatening ones-is an essential adaptive behavior, yet the neural mechanisms underlying individual differences in discrimination precision remain unclear. Here, we show that parvalbumin-positive interneuron (PV-IN)-mediated feedforward inhibition to fear engram neurons (ENs) in the lateral amygdala is selectively enhanced following auditory fear conditioning, driven by increased postsynaptic expression of α1 subunit (Gabra1)-containing GABA A receptors. Disruption of PV-IN activity during fear retrieval-via optogenetic or chemogenetic inhibition-or selective induction of inhibitory long-term depression at PV → EN synapses impaired fear discrimination, increasing freezing to novel tones while sparing responses to the conditioned stimulus. Mechanistically, we identify inducible cAMP early repressor (ICER) as a transcriptional regulator that limits inhibitory plasticity by downregulating Gabra1 expression, thereby promoting fear generalization. These findings establish a previously unrecognized form of inhibitory synaptic plasticity that governs the precision of fear memory and suggest potential therapeutic targets for maladaptive fear overgeneralization in disorders such as post-traumatic stress disorder.

doi:10.1016/j.bbr.2026.116485.title: Structure, function, and mechanism of Rodentia vocalizations across the lifespan.
doi:10.1016/j.bbr.2026.116485.abstract: Vocalizations are an integral way that rodents and many other mammals communicate. Historically, research on rodent vocalizations focused on laboratory-derived strains of two species, house mice (Mus musculus), and brown rats (Rattus norvegicus). However, with over 2,000 species, Rodentia is one of the largest vertebrate orders with many other species available for communication research. In this review, we synthesize recent findings on lesser-studied species spanning five Rodentia families: Muridae, Caviidae, Cricetidae, Bathyergidae (includes Heterocephalidae), and Sciuridae. First, we take an evolutionary perspective to compare adult vocalizations within and across these five Rodentia families. Then, we take a developmental perspective to characterize immature vocalizations and how they transition to mature vocalizations. Next, we survey the potential functions of rodent by examining the behavioural contexts in which they occur. Finally, we summarize findings on the physiological mechanisms that underpin rodent vocalizations, from biomechanics to neuromodulator systems and neural circuits. Together, this research shows that Rodentia is an excellent taxonomic group for exploring the diversity and evolution of vertebrate acoustic communication.

doi:10.1162/jocn.a.2723.title: The Effect of Perceptually Challenging Conditions on Speech and Sign Language Perception.
doi:10.1162/jocn.a.2723.authors: Figuerola CT, Signoret C, Holmer E, Andin J.
doi:10.1162/jocn.a.2723.abstract: Language is often processed in perceptually challenging conditions. Although the neural correlates of speech processing in such conditions have been well studied, this is not the case for sign language. Thus, it is unknown whether the neural mechanisms involved in this process are comparable across language modalities. One reason for the lack of studies in sign language might be attributed to the difficulties in adapting perceptual manipulations from the context of speech to sign language. In the present study, we aim to address the gap in the literature by investigating whether the neural correlates for processing language presented in perceptually challenging conditions are similar across the visual and auditory modalities, using manipulations of background noise and spectral degradation that are comparable between languages and a within-subject design. We recruited 22 hearing signers who did a perceptual attention task while in an MRI scanner, in which the signal is either clear, presented in background noise, or spectrally degraded. Overall, our results suggest that language processing in perceptually challenging conditions relies primarily on modality-specific mechanisms rather than a shared, modality-independent neural system. Whereas speech processing appeared relatively robust to perceptual degradation, sign language recruited additional visual indicating modality-dependent compensatory strategies. These findings refine current neurobiological models of language by demonstrating that perceptual challenge interacts fundamentally with language modality.

doi:10.64898/2026.09.26.754418.title: Auditory timing precision is determined by spectro-temporal continuity across sounds, not individual sound acoustics
doi:10.64898/2026.09.26.754418.authors: Mock CM, Ilge L, Oganian Y.
doi:10.64898/2026.09.26.754418.abstract: Predicting when an event will occur is key to perceiving and evaluating dynamic sensory inputs, such as speech. The utility of temporal predictions hinges on perceptual timing precision (PTP), the sensitivity to deviations between actual and predicted sound onset times. Past work suggests that PTP is primarily determined by acoustic properties of target sounds, regardless of the acoustics of preceding sound cues. In contrast, in four experiments, we discover that PTP is best when context and target sound spectra and temporal envelopes match, with only minor effects of individual sound acoustics. This ability to utilize contextual continuity improved with musical aptitude. Theoretical modeling showed that spectrally tuned oscillatory entrainment to sound onsets and offsets is necessary to account for our results. In sum, the precision of temporal predictions is defined not by the acoustics of individual sounds but by the continuity of spectral and temporal content within a sound stream.

doi:10.1002/cne.70207.title: The Nucleus of the Brachium of the Inferior Colliculus Contains Thalamic-Like and Midbrain-Like Subregions.
doi:10.1002/cne.70207.authors: Ito T, Takahashi K, Yamamoto M, Okamoto S, Takahashi M, Hioki H, Saqib KA.
doi:10.1002/cne.70207.abstract: The ventral division of the medial geniculate body (MGV) is the core auditory thalamic nucleus and is bordered dorsally, medially, and ventrally by shell nuclei; a caudal shell counterpart has not been identified. The nucleus of the brachium of the inferior colliculus (nBIC), long viewed as a rostral extension of the midbrain IC, contains neurons that project to auditory and adjacent cortex, blurring the thalamus-midbrain boundary. We hypothesized that the nBIC contains both thalamic-like and midbrain-like neurons. We combined cytoarchitectural, neuroanatomical, and molecular approaches to test the hypothesis: Viral tracing to differentially tag thalamocortical and tectothalamic populations, retrograde cortical labeling, in situ hybridization for VGLUT2 and VGAT, and immunohistochemistry for GAD67, calretinin, and parvalbumin. The nBIC segregated into two zones: a rostrolateral region virtually devoid of GABAergic cells and enriched for glutamatergic neurons, and a caudomedial region containing intermingled GABAergic and glutamatergic neurons. Thalamocortical nBIC neurons were confined to the rostrolateral zone, whereas tectothalamic neurons were concentrated caudomedially; spatial analyses confirmed segregation. Cortically projecting nBIC neurons expressed VGLUT2 mRNA and lacked collaterals in the medial geniculate or superior colliculus, instead arborizing in the striatum and auditory cortex. Calcium-binding markers further differentiated the zones, with calretinin enriched rostrally and parvalbumin increasing caudally. These data indicate that, although indistinct by Nissl cytoarchitecture, the nBIC is a chimeric structure composed of a thalamus-like, thalamocortical rostrolateral zone and a midbrain-like caudomedial zone, suggesting a caudal shell-type complement to the MGV.

doi:10.31234/osf.io/utnkx_v1.title: Synchrony under uncertainty. The effects of auditory context on the perception of the temporal location of quasi-musical sounds
doi:10.31234/osf.io/utnkx_v1.authors: Danielsen A, Leske S, London J.
doi:10.31234/osf.io/utnkx_v1.abstract: Auditory perception and sensorimotor synchronization always occur within a specific auditory context, a fact that is often overlooked when they are studied in the laboratory. Here we address the question of how our perception of a given sound's temporal characteristics is modulated by the sounds surrounding it. Previous research has highlighted the importance of acoustic factors like attack and duration in defining both a sound's perceived temporal position ("P-center") and the temporal range in which it is heard as synchronized with another sound ("beat bin"). Our experiment investigated whether the same probe/target pair is perceived differently when situated in contexts of sounds with different acoustic features, from contexts of mostly clear, sharply defined sounds to contexts of mostly “muddy,” noisy ones. Our findings reveal that the P-center of the target sound shifts progressively later as the context becomes dominated by sounds with softer onsets, and the variability of P-center location—indicative of the width of the beat bin—also increases under such conditions. These results significantly advance our understanding of how sonic environments influence the perception of a sound's temporal characteristics, and shed light on its underlying neural mechanisms. The study offers new insights into the intricate nature of temporal perception in complex auditory environments and sets the stage for further exploration of the mechanisms underlying auditory processing and synchronization.

doi:10.31234/osf.io/2mfzk_v1.title: Music-Based Interventions for Cognition and Brain Health: the ARM framework
doi:10.31234/osf.io/2mfzk_v1.authors: Loui P, Peelle JE, Grahn JA.
doi:10.31234/osf.io/2mfzk_v1.abstract: Music-based interventions (MBIs) have shown promise in addressing cognitive, motor, and language impairments across neurological and neurodevelopmental conditions. Despite an increasing number of controlled studies that have assessed the potential rehabilitative effects of music, neural mechanisms underlying therapeutic benefits remain poorly understood. Here we present the ARM framework: a neurobiologically-informed model integrating three key systems: Auditory processing networks that encode temporal and spectral features; Reward circuitry activated by musical pleasure and prediction, and Motor systems engaged through auditory-motor coupling and rhythmic entrainment. We examine how specific MBIs leverage these systems to varying degrees and show how understanding these mechanisms is essential for predicting individual treatment response, personalizing interventions, and developing next-generation therapeutic approaches that optimize engagement of specific neural systems.

doi:10.64898/2026.10.06.756750.title: Newborns modulate and synchronise their Non-Nutritive Sucking behaviour to the temporal structure of sound
doi:10.64898/2026.10.06.756750.authors: Arioli M, Federici A, Silvestri V, Santini M, Colombo L, Giannì ML, Bottari D, Macchi Cassia V.
doi:10.64898/2026.10.06.756750.abstract: Sensorimotor synchronization, the ability to align motor behaviour with the temporal structure of external stimuli, is thought to emerge gradually during development, but its origins remain unclear. Here, we investigated whether newborns can adapt their sucking behaviour and synchronise it to the temporal structure of auditory stimuli within the first days of life. Forty-one healthy full-term newborns (24-72 hours old) were exposed to two three-minute auditory streams differing in temporal structure: a highly structured stream with a stable temporal pattern and a highly variant stream with greater temporal variability, while their non-nutritive sucking (NNS) was continuously recorded. We assessed changes in NNS frequency and pressure and quantified NNS-sound coupling using magnitude-squared coherence at frequencies distinctive to each auditory stream. Structured stimulation promoted a more organised NNS, with more suck bursts than the variant stream, and increased sucking vigour, with a transiently higher suck peak rate during the first minute relative to the variant stream and greater suck pressure relative to silence. Coherence analyses revealed that coherence was selectively higher at the frequencies distinctive to each auditory stream, both for the structured and the highly variant stimulus. These findings show that, within hours of birth, NNS behaviour can selectively align with stimulus-specific temporal regularities, even when these are weakly predictable and lack a dominant periodicity.
