doi:10.21203/rs.3.rs-11134147/v1.title: Brain-inspired cascaded EEG speech decoding with conformal calibration and adaptive exit: simulation validation and five-stage real-data assessment
doi:10.21203/rs.3.rs-11134147/v1.abstract: Abstract Background Online EEG-based speech decoding faces dual challenges: limited computational resources for real-time deployment, and unreliable early-exit decisions when models underestimate their own errors (silent dropping of speech segments). Existing deep decoding models lack statistically rigorous uncertainty quantification, and the exchangeability assumption of conformal prediction— commonly used for calibration—is questionable for strongly auto-correlated neural signals. Systematic evidence on when and why conformal guarantees fail on real EEG, and whether online repair is feasible, remains scarce. New method We propose a brain-inspired three-tier cascaded decoding architecture (linear baseline → MLP residual corrections), equipped with pinball quantile error heads (τ = 0.75) for conservative error estimation, split-conformal temperature calibration with a block-wise variant to mitigate exchangeability violation, and an adaptive exit controller that decouples computational budget (ρ- quantile) from precision safety (κ· ˆe ≤ ϵ). For online distribution shifts, we implement Gibbs–Candès adaptive conformal inference (ACI) to dynamically adjust κ without relying on error-head quality. The framework is validated through simulation and a five-stage real-data assessment on OpenNeuro ds004279 (3 subjects, speech-perception EEG), plus an extended three-method cross-validation (temporal TRF, CCA lag scan, word-onset ERP permutation) to adjudicate millisecond-scale speech tracking. Results Simulation confirms conformal coverage at 84.5% (target 85%), exit rate anchored at 39.5%±0.6%, and 18 non-dominated Pareto solutions all outperforming the full-run baseline. On square-wave event labels, coverage remains 85.0% across four scenarios, and adaptive exit beats both full-run and baseline in 3/3 subjects. Switching to real audio envelopes increases label information 3.4-fold (|r| 0.057→0.194) but collapses coverage to 7–29%. Block-conformal root-cause analysis identifies six-fold κ drift across subjects, strongly coupled to error-head calibration failure. ACI repairs coverage to ∼99% in 2/3 subjects (including one with negative calibration correlation), while the remaining case is diagnosed as “uncalibratable” due to test-segment error-structure collapse, necessitating data-quality gating. Extended experiment shows that crude pipelines yield all-negative results from dual technical failures (drift artifact, ERD normalization failure); after official preprocessing alignment, word-boundary β/γ ERD emerges (group p = 0.028, 3/9 individual significant) and temporal CCA shows group significance (t = 5.24, p = 0.0004) despite individual r Comparison with existing methods Unlike conventional deep decoders (CNNs, LSTMs) and recent attention-based models that provide only point estimates without uncertainty bounds, our framework delivers distribution-free coverage guarantees via conformal calibration. The adaptive exit mechanism offers flexible speed-accuracy trade-offs absent in fixed-architecture models. Critically, ACI maintains validity even when error-head ranking fails—a property not achievable by static conformal approaches. Our five-stage negative-result trajectory (including coverage collapse and rootcause diagnosis) provides an applicability boundary map for conformal prediction on real neural data, which prior studies have not systematically documented. The extended three-method cross-validation further reveals that band-power CCA, commonly used in the literature, can produce false positives due to segment-level coupling, whereas temporal CCA and word-onset ERP provide more reliable group-level speech-tracking signals. Conclusions The proposed cascaded framework with conformal calibration and adaptive exit is validated both in simulation and real-EEG scenarios, with ACI effectively repairing coverage under distribution shifts. The deployable profile defaults to TRF linear regression + ACI + quality gating, with cascaded MLP reserved for high-signal-to-noise conditions. The extended experiment establishes a methodological baseline requiring full preprocessing-chain alignment, temporal features, and threemethod cross-validation for speech-tracking studies. All code and results are released open-source for reproducible research.

doi:10.64898/2026.09.17.752025.title: The activation function of CA3 pyramidal neurons is optimal for the stable recall of memory patterns
doi:10.64898/2026.09.17.752025.authors: Cohen, U.; Picher, M. M.; Navas-Olive, A.; Lengyel, M.
doi:10.64898/2026.09.17.752025.abstract: Hippocampal area CA3 is widely believed to serve a core memory function: retrieving distributed patterns of neural activity that were previously stored in the recurrent connections between neurons. However, it remains unknown how the physiological properties of individual neurons contribute to this function. Here, we present a mathematical analysis of a canonical recurrent neural network model of CA3. Our analysis provides three main, experimentally testable predictions for recurrent circuits performing stable memory recall. Two of these predictions, that pyramidal cells should be characterized by elevated intrinsic excitability and by inhibition-dominated recurrent connections, are consistent with previous experimental findings. We thus focused on testing the third prediction: that neuronal activation functions have an exponent slightly above $1$. For this, we performed \textit{in vivo} intracellular recordings of 49 pyramidal neurons from the CA3 area of behaving mice. Fitting a range of parametric models to these voltage traces and performing statistical model comparison revealed an average neural activation exponent slightly above $1$, confirming our theoretical predictions, with substantial heterogeneity across cells, which remains to be accounted for by the theory. An analysis of 133 further cells from two other previous studies provided neural activation exponent estimates highly consistent with those we found in our data. Our results suggest that the properties of hippocampal CA3 area are tuned to support reliable memory recall even at the level of single neurons.

doi:10.64898/2026.09.28.755085.title: Oxytocin and Vasopressin Immunoreactivity Differs Across Auditory Brainstem Nuclei in Rodents with Distinct Social Systems
doi:10.64898/2026.09.28.755085.authors: Joseph L, Boren L, Ingram G, McCullagh EA.
doi:10.64898/2026.09.28.755085.abstract: ABSTRACT Oxytocin (OT) and vasopressin (AVP) are neuropeptide hormones involved in regulating animal social behavior and a broad spectrum of physiological processes. Although their distributions are well documented in neuroendocrine regions of the forebrain and midbrain, their expression in the hindbrain remains poorly understood. Here, we used immunohistochemistry to quantify OT and AVP immunoreactive puncta within three auditory brainstem nuclei, the lateral superior olive (LSO), the medial superior olive (MSO), and the medial nucleus of the trapezoid body (MNTB) in six wild-caught rodent species differing in sociality. We also quantified the volume of these nuclei and examined variation in total brain volume across species and sociality. OT and AVP puncta count differed among species and social groups. Group-living species exhibited higher OT and AVP puncta counts than monogamous and solitary species in the LSO and MNTB. In the MSO, OT puncta counts did not differ among social groups, whereas AVP puncta counts were higher in group-living than in monogamous and solitary species. Total brain volume and the volumes of the MNTB and MSO differed among species, but not across social groups, whereas LSO volume did not differ among species or sociality. These findings revealed sociality-related variation in OT and AVP immunoreactive puncta within auditory brainstem circuits and suggest that neuropeptide signaling within early auditory brainstem pathways may contribute to the neural integration of social and auditory information.

doi:10.64898/2026.09.27.754842.title: Viral Strategies for In Vivo Optogenetic Stimulation of Purkinje Cell Terminals and Electrophysiological Characterization of Downstream Cerebellar Nuclear Activity in Mice
doi:10.64898/2026.09.27.754842.authors: Merino E, Jung SJ, Antzoulatos EG, Fioravante D.
doi:10.64898/2026.09.27.754842.abstract: ABSTRACT The cerebellar cortex regulates motor and cognitive function through its sole output neurons, the Purkinje cells (PCs), which inhibit downstream targets, yet precise manipulation of PC activity in vivo remains technically challenging. Here, we describe two viral strategies with differing cell-type specificities for in vivo optogenetic control of PCs and functional assessment of neural activity in downstream target regions. Specifically, we detail strategies for expression of the fast channelrhodopsin ChETA in PCs that enable light-evoked activation of PC axonal terminals in medial deep cerebellar nuclei (mDCN), and demonstrate light-evoked modulation of mDCN neural activity using in vivo extracellular electrophysiology. This protocol provides a reproducible and adaptable framework for cell-type-specific manipulation and functional characterization of cerebellar circuits, with broad applicability to studies of cerebellar physiology, motor and nonmotor behavior, learning and disease. SUMMARY This protocol describes viral strategies for in vivo optogenetic tagging of cerebellar Purkinje cells and extracellular electrophysiological recording of opsin-evoked responses in the medial deep cerebellar nucleus, providing a reproducible approach to investigate cerebellar circuit connectivity and functional interactions with cell-type specificity.

doi:10.1016/j.neuroimage.2026.122266.title: Functional organization of the perirhinal cortex in natural scene processing and memory.
doi:10.1016/j.neuroimage.2026.122266.abstract: The perirhinal cortex (PRC) has long been implicated in object perception and recognition memory; however, its role in processing complex natural scenes and its internal functional organization are not well understood. In the current study, we investigated the relationship between object- and scene-related visual feature (faces, bodies, and place) representations in PRC and the visual cortex, and the spatial pattern within PRC for visual processing and memory. Utilizing fMRI data from a continuous recognition task involving natural scenes (from the Natural Scenes Dataset), we first quantified the trial-by-trial decoding accuracy for visual features across distributed visual cortical regions and within the PRC. Our results demonstrate that multivariate pattern feature decodability in the PRC increase significantly when visual features are broadly represented across distributed regions in visual cortex. The PRC exhibited a robust subsequent memory effect, though the memory outcome was not directly predicted by the level of distributed visual feature representation. Critically, left PRC showed a posterior bias for the multivariate decoding of the place feature. Vertex-level univariate analyses uncovered a posterior bias for face-feature-driven vertices and an anterior bias for memory-driven vertices, which is more consistent in the right PRC. Together, these findings suggest that the PRC may play a flexible role in scene processing that extends beyond object representation and highlights an anterior-posterior functional gradient within the human PRC that supports perceptual or mnemonic processes.

doi:10.1111/ejn.70709.title: Towards a Brain-Computer Interface (BCI) for Improving Phonological Processing in Developmental Dyslexia: An Exploratory Study.
doi:10.1111/ejn.70709.authors: Zheng X, Araújo J, Busson Q, Goswami U.
doi:10.1111/ejn.70709.abstract: Brain-computer interfaces (BCIs) have immense potential regarding the provision of therapies for disorders of development, but to date have typically been created for non-linguistic disorders such as ADHD (attention deficit hyperactivity disorder). Here, we present a BCI designed to improve linguistic phonological processing during natural speech listening, aimed at participants with developmental dyslexia. Phonological 'deficits' are considered a core feature of dyslexia across languages and are present from infancy in those later diagnosed with dyslexia. Here, a non-invasive EEG-BCI relying on auditory inputs and visual feedback was developed to optimise brain patterns related to phonological development in infants and children. The BCI focused on neural patterns identified using Temporal Sampling theory, which has found the theta/delta ratio during natural speech listening to be a key neural associate of impaired phonology. As a first step, the BCI was tested with adults. Adults with and without dyslexia played the BCI for 16 sessions and received pre- and post-testing regarding phonological awareness and single word and non-word reading skills. Learning was assessed both online, as in most BCI studies, and offline, enabling removal of a greater number of potential EEG artefacts. Significant associations between offline BCI scores (a measure of BCI learning) and improvements in non-word reading were found for all participants who learned the BCI, both dyslexic and control. BCI learning also showed significant associations with improvements in real word reading and amplitude rise time discrimination. The data are interpreted with respect to Temporal Sampling theory.

doi:10.64898/2026.09.28.755199.title: Respiration and individual differences shape behavioral and inter-brain synchronization
doi:10.64898/2026.09.28.755199.abstract: Humans coordinate their actions while their bodies and brains synchronize in social interactions, yet how behavioral, physiological, and neural dynamics interact during interpersonal coordination remains largely unknown. We investigated how respiration and individual differences influence behavioral and inter-brain synchrony in a musical synchronization task, which requires precise temporal alignment. Eighty-eight individuals first produced a familiar melody at their most comfortable rate to measure their spontaneous production rate (SPR). They then synchronized the melody with a randomly assigned unfamiliar partner under natural (unpaced), instructed in-phase, and instructed anti-phase breathing conditions, while hyperscanning 64-channel electroencephalography (EEG), respiration, auditory-motor timing, and perceived social connectedness were recorded. Relative to natural respiration, both in-phase and anti-phase breathing increased inter-brain phase-locking and perceived social closeness but reduced behavioral synchrony; the instructed respiratory phase relationship was mirrored in their inter-brain relative phase. Differences in phase of respiratory cycles (inhalation and exhalation) also influenced coordination: Inhalation was associated with stronger inter-brain synchronization but less precise and stable behavioral coordination than was exhalation. Moreover, Individual differences influenced coordination: Partners with the faster SPR consistently preceded the slower partners and exhibited an alpha-band inter-brain phase advance in synchronization, whereas dyads with similar SPR showed greater behavioral synchrony and smaller inter-brain phase difference. Our findings identify respiration as a previously overlooked factor that organizes behavioral and neural synchronization, while individual intrinsic rhythms constrain how interacting partners align in time. Together, these findings reveal a dynamic interplay between the rhythms of the body and brain during human social interactions. Significance statement Respiration is a fundamental physiological process that shapes human cognition, yet its role in social interaction is unknown. We studied randomly paired dyads who synchronized music together, a human social behavior that requires fine temporal coordination. We found that respiratory rate, respiratory phase, and the inhale-exhale cycle shaped both behavioral and inter-brain dynamics. Moreover, people varied substantially in the natural rate at which they spontaneously produced music. Individual differences in this intrinsic frequency predicted both behavioral and inter-brain coordination in the dyads’ performances. These findings highlight the active role of the body-brain connection in human social interaction, and establish causal evidence disentangling behavioral, physiological, and neural processes in joint action through respiration.

doi:10.64898/2026.10.16.759637.title: Supramodal Coding of Detection and Confidence in the Human Cortex
doi:10.64898/2026.10.16.759637.authors: Porte P, Robin A, Boscher F, Dezier C, Goueytes D, Mahdian S, Hoffmann D, Kahane P, Minotti L, Pereira M, Caron-Guyon J, Goupil L, Faivre N.
doi:10.64898/2026.10.16.759637.abstract: Perception is inherently multisensory, yet it remains unclear whether the brain detects stimuli and evaluates confidence in these detections using circuits shared across senses or circuits specific to each modality. Prior evidence is limited: scalp electrophysiology cannot localize where a shared code operates, whereas functional imaging cannot resolve its timing. We recorded intracranial activity (stereoelectroencephalography) in eight patients with epilepsy who performed a near-threshold audiovisual detection task in which they reported, on each trial, whether a visual, auditory, or audiovisual stimulus was present and rated their confidence, both overall and separately for each modality. Analyzing high-gamma activity at the single-channel and region-of-interest levels, we found that stimulus detection involved a broadly distributed, largely supramodal set of cortical regions responding regardless of modality, including the insula, dorsomedial prefrontal cortex, and superior temporal gyrus. Multivariate decoders trained to distinguish detected from undetected stimuli in one modality generalized to the other modality, indicating a shared detection code within these regions. Confidence relied on a more mixed architecture but was also substantially supramodal. Finally, the auditory cortex encoded confidence information about its non-preferred (visual) modality, with a similar effect in the visual cortex for auditory confidence, suggesting that the involvement of sensory cortices in confidence is not confined to its preferred input.

doi:10.1016/j.neuron.2026.09.017.title: A cross-species AAV platform for precise microglial interrogation.
doi:10.1016/j.neuron.2026.09.017.authors: Yu F, Wang R, Di R, Xu K, Gao J, Shang H, Yuan Z, Dai R, Wu W, Weng D, Gao X, Li H, Yu T, Zhang Y, Wang X, Luan G, Zhao F, Luo M.
doi:10.1016/j.neuron.2026.09.017.abstract: Targeting microglia with adeno-associated viruses (AAVs) remains challenging because of inefficient transduction, off-target expression, and inconsistent payload performance. Here, we develop an integrated, Cre-independent AAV platform that combines a compact 446-bp microglia-specific regulatory element (MSRE), a high-yield AAV2/9.m capsid, microRNA-mediated neuronal de-targeting, and a microglia-tailored codon-optimization strategy. Following direct intracranial delivery, the optimized vector achieves robust, long-lasting transgene expression with greater than 90% microglial specificity across multiple mouse brain regions, including in an Alzheimer's disease model. With doxorubicin-assisted delivery, the platform also enables efficient and selective microglial targeting in rats, rhesus macaques, and human ex vivo brain slices. Codon optimization supports the expression of otherwise challenging functional payloads, enabling calcium imaging, chemogenetic manipulation, and CRISPR-Cas9-mediated genome editing. This cross-species toolkit provides a versatile resource for investigating microglial biology and developing microglia-directed therapeutic strategies.

doi:10.64898/2026.10.05.755780.title: Astrocytes in the Dentate Gyrus Shift the Equilibrium from Pattern Separation to Pattern Completion and Inhibit Fear Extinction
doi:10.64898/2026.10.05.755780.authors: Wang, M.; Kambali, M.; Nagarajan, R.; Lyu, J.; Kuan, H.-Y.; Yu, X.; Rudolph, U.
doi:10.64898/2026.10.05.755780.abstract: Pattern separation and pattern completion are core hippocampal computations linked to memory interference and overgeneralization in many neuropsychiatric disorders and to mnemonic discrimination deficits in neurodegenerative conditions. Astrocytes are increasingly recognized as important integrators and modulators of neuronal activity as many studies have shown changes in animal behavior and neural circuits induced by manipulation of astrocytic activity. The role of astrocytes in the dentate gyrus for learning and memory is, however, largely unknown. To investigate the functional significance of astrocytic activity in the dentate gyrus, we expressed the calcium extruding pump hPMCA2w/b (CalEx), resulting in inhibition of astrocytic calcium activity, the Gq-coupled receptor hM3Dq, or the Gi-coupled receptor hM4Di, allowing chronic activation of Gq- and Gi-dependent pathways by a designer drug, in dentate gyrus astrocytes. Our main finding is that inhibition of astrocytic calcium activity by CalEx resulted in improved pattern separation and impaired pattern completion. In -vivo calcium imaging revealed that CalEx expression in astrocytes altered the neuronal activity pattern in dentate gyrus neurons with an overall inhibitory effect. This suggests that in the dentate gyrus astrocytes promote the activity of these neurons. Furthermore, chronic activation of hM4Di resulted in impaired between-session fear extinction while chronic activation of hM3Dq resulted in impaired within-session fear extinction and improved pattern separation learning over multiple days, suggesting that activation of astrocytic activity enhances mechanistically separable forms of fear extinction in a Gq- or Gi-pathway-specific manner. Our findings reveal that dentate gyrus astrocytic calcium shifts the balance between pattern separation and pattern completion towards pattern completion and thus modulates an essential neuronal functional output of the dentate gyrus. Chronic activation of astrocytes inhibits fear extinction, and thus also affects management of memory interference. Our findings imply that astrocytic modulation may be beneficial to treat cognitive deficits in disorders in which overgeneralization is a problem.

doi:10.64898/2026.09.19.752867.title: Stable Network Motifs with Divergent Engagement Across Memory Outcomes
doi:10.64898/2026.09.19.752867.authors: Kumar A, Tyner K, Moseley R, Svalina M, Geller AS, Rutishauser U, Kramer DR, Thompson JA.
doi:10.64898/2026.09.19.752867.abstract: Visual recognition memory depends on coordinated interactions across distributed medial temporal, prefrontal, and limbic networks, yet the sub-second large-scale network dynamics distinguishing successful from unsuccessful recognition remain poorly understood. Here we used intracranial EEG recordings from seven patients (4 female, 3 male) with medically refractory epilepsy performing a new–old visual recognition memory task to characterize time-resolved directed functional connectivity and dynamic network organization. Directed effective connectivity was estimated using bivariate Granger causality in a sliding-window framework, and dynamic community structure was identified using the Louvain modularity algorithm. Successful recognition (Hits) was associated with a qualitatively distinct network configuration: low modularity (Q = 0.05 vs. 0.09–0.15 in other conditions), a cross-hemispheric community structure integrating left medial temporal lobe (MTL) with right prefrontal cortex, and sustained network integration throughout the post-stimulus period. Right-hemisphere nodes within this cross-hemispheric community showed stronger within-community directed connectivity than left-hemisphere nodes (mean asymmetry index = 0.33, p Significance Statement How does the brain recognize something it has seen before? This study used direct intracranial brain recordings in epilepsy patients to examine how networks of brain regions communicate during successful and unsuccessful recognition memory. We found that successful recognition is not simply a matter of greater connectivity strength. It requires a qualitatively different pattern of large-scale network organization in which left-hemisphere memory regions and right-hemisphere evaluation regions form a unified, cross-hemispheric network. Unsuccessful rejection of novel images, by contrast, was characterized by early, segregated right-hemisphere activity. These findings therefore present a potential, specific, circuit-level mechanism supporting recognition memory, with implications for understanding memory dysfunction in neurological disorders such as epilepsy and Alzheimer’s disease.

doi:10.21203/rs.3.rs-10833317/v1.title: Effects of Short-Term Keyboard Training on Anticipatory Beta Dynamics and Cognitive-Motor Sets in Beginners: An Electroencephalography Study
doi:10.21203/rs.3.rs-10833317/v1.authors: Akimoto Y, Ochiai J, Nakahira KT.
doi:10.21203/rs.3.rs-10833317/v1.abstract: Abstract Playing keyboard instruments poses significant challenges for beginners. Nevertheless, the rapid neurophysiological adaptations shaping proactive readiness during early training remain poorly understood. To address this, we investigated how three days of keyboard practice alters anticipatory neural activity in 23 complete beginners. We hypothesized that short-term keyboard training would establish anticipatory cognitive and motor sets prior to visual score presentation, with increased beta-band event-related synchronization serving as a neural index of this process. Participants listened to five-tone auditory sequences that were either repeated across the three practice days or generated randomly, viewed the corresponding visual scores, and then performed the sequences. Anticipatory oscillatory activity was recorded using a wireless electroencephalography system immediately preceding the score presentation. Linear mixed-effects modeling revealed a significant Day × Stimulus interaction in anterior frontal beta power (13–30 Hz), characterized by increased beta synchronization in the random condition by Day 3. Single-trial analyses further revealed that trial-by-trial fluctuations in beta synchronization were associated with slower reaction times, specifically on Day 2. These findings demonstrate that early skill acquisition induces rapid and structured modifications in proactive neural systems, establishing a neurophysiological foundation for how the novice brain builds anticipatory cognitive and motor sets during initial musical training.

doi:10.1523/jneurosci.0242-26.2026.title: Late Cross-Modal Biases in Neural Spatial Representations Revealed by EEG Decoding.
doi:10.1523/jneurosci.0242-26.2026.authors: Buhmann Z, Robinson AK, Mattingley JB, Rideaux R.
doi:10.1523/jneurosci.0242-26.2026.abstract: During audiovisual perception, spatial information from vision and audition is combined, often producing biases such as the ventriloquist effect. While these interactions are well documented behaviorally, it remains unclear when cross-modal information begins to alter modality-specific spatial representations in the brain. Here we used cross-generalized inverted encoding modeling of electroencephalography (EEG) data to track the temporal evolution of spatial representations during a spatial ventriloquist task. Human participants (both sexes) localized audiovisual stimuli with horizontally offset auditory and visual components. Decoders trained on unisensory EEG responses were applied to audiovisual trials to estimate whether and when spatial representations of one modality were biased toward the other. Behaviorally, participants integrated cues but showed slight visual overweighting. Neural decoding revealed robust spatial representations for both modalities, with early unisensory encoding remaining unaffected by cross-modal input. Cross-modal biases emerged only later (from ∼200 ms onward), within a generalized representational window, and occurred sequentially: auditory representations were biased earlier than visual. These findings indicate that multisensory spatial integration arises via recurrent feedback during later processing stages, while early sensory-specific representations remain independent, providing a neural basis for the temporal dynamics underlying the ventriloquist effect.

doi:10.64898/2026.09.28.754986.title: Sequential maturation of supramammillary glutamatergic/GABAergic co-transmission onto adult-born dentate granule cells
doi:10.64898/2026.09.28.754986.authors: Hashimotodani Y, Konno K, Yamasaki M, Sakaba T.
doi:10.64898/2026.09.28.754986.abstract: Hypothalamic supramammillary nucleus (SuM) neurons project to the dentate gyrus and co-release glutamate and GABA, thereby regulating hippocampal information processing. However, how synapses mediating glutamate/GABA co-transmission are established during development remains unclear. Here, we investigated the functional and structural maturation of SuM inputs onto adult-born granule cells (GCs). We found that most newborn GCs received GABAergic responses without detectable glutamatergic responses, whereas a smaller population exhibited glutamate/GABA co-transmission. Newborn GCs with glutamate/GABA co-transmission showed more mature anatomical and physiological properties than GABA-only neurons, with greater dendritic complexity, longer dendritic length, lower input resistance, and stronger medial perforant path inputs. Postsynaptic depolarization failed to induce synapse unsilencing in GABA-only neurons but induced robust long-term potentiation in newborn GCs with glutamatergic transmission, indicating that plasticity at SuM inputs emerges after functional glutamatergic transmission is established. Morphological analysis showed that SuM terminals apposed to newborn GCs contained both VGluT2 and VIAAT, whereas postsynaptic receptor organization remained immature. Moreover, environmental enrichment and chemogenetic activation of SuM neurons increased the proportion of newborn GCs receiving glutamate/GABA co-transmission, suggesting that SuM activity promotes the emergence of glutamatergic transmission. Together, these results suggest that SuM inputs onto newborn GCs undergo sequential maturation from initial GABAergic transmission to glutamate/GABA co-transmission, a process likely supported by SuM activity-dependent postsynaptic maturation. Significance Synaptic transmission is generally thought to be mediated by a single neurotransmitter, yet some synapses use more than one neurotransmitter. How these dual-transmitter synapses are formed during neuronal development remains poorly understood. We studied inputs from the supramammillary nucleus to adult-born dentate granule cells, a model in which synapses mature as newborn neurons integrate into hippocampal circuits. We found that these inputs first provide GABAergic transmission and later acquire functional glutamatergic transmission as newborn granule cells mature, leading to glutamate/GABA co-transmission. This transition was promoted by activity of supramammillary neurons. These findings reveal a sequential mechanism for establishing dual-transmitter synapses and provide insight into how circuit activity shapes the functional integration of newborn neurons in the adult brain.

doi:10.64898/2026.10.01.755966.title: Translating functional brain activity between humans and monkeys
doi:10.64898/2026.10.01.755966.authors: Braunlich, K.; Duyck, M.; Duffield, S.; Behel, K.; Baker, C. I.; Conway, B. R.
doi:10.64898/2026.10.01.755966.abstract: Comparing brain responses across species is essential for identifying models of human cognition and testing theories of brain evolution, but differences in brain size, measurement techniques, and signal dynamics make it challenging. Here we collected dense fMRI data in macaques and humans using the same movies, static-image sequences, and tasks, and developed a multivariate analysis method that aligns neural representations temporally and spatially. The resulting data-driven framework provides a quantitative translation of brain responses among individuals and between species. Using this framework, we uncovered a broadly conserved cross-species hierarchy of retinotopic visual areas and whole-brain correspondence. Yet within this structure, we found that higher-order macaque areas shared more information with lower-order human areas, particularly during movies, providing evidence of species differences. We also identified potential macaque precursors to human regions involved in high-level cognition, including theory-of-mind and reading. These results offer a blueprint for common representational principles across species.

doi:10.21203/rs.3.rs-10781456/v1.title: Effects of Alpha-Band Binaural Beat Entrainment on Anxiety and Aggression in Men With Opioid Use Disorder: A Randomized Sham-Controlled Trial Running Title: Binaural Beat Entrainment in Opioid Use Disorder
doi:10.21203/rs.3.rs-10781456/v1.abstract: Abstract Background: Opioid use disorder (OUD) is frequently accompanied by anxiety and aggression, both of which adversely affect treatment adherence, relapse risk, and long-term rehabilitation outcomes. Non-pharmacological neuromodulation approaches, including binaural beat stimulation, have attracted increasing attention as potential adjunctive interventions for improving emotional regulation. However, evidence regarding the efficacy of alpha-band binaural beat entrainment in individuals with OUD remains limited. Objective: To evaluate the efficacy of alpha-band binaural beat entrainment, compared with sham auditory stimulation, in reducing anxiety and aggression among men undergoing residential treatment for opioid use disorder. Methods: A two-arm randomized, sham-controlled, pretest–posttest clinical trial was conducted among 30 men with opioid use disorder recruited from a residential addiction treatment center. Participants were randomly allocated (1:1) to either an alpha-band binaural beat intervention group (n = 15) or a sham stimulation group (n = 15). The intervention consisted of ten 30-minute sessions of alpha-band binaural beat stimulation administered over three weeks, while the control group received an acoustically comparable sham intervention without binaural beat frequencies. Anxiety and aggression were assessed before and after the intervention using the Beck Anxiety Inventory (BAI) and the Buss–Perry Aggression Questionnaire (BPAQ), respectively. Between-group differences in post-intervention outcomes were analyzed using analysis of covariance (ANCOVA), adjusting for baseline scores. Statistical significance was established at P Results: After adjustment for baseline scores, the intervention group showed significantly lower post-intervention anxiety than the sham group (P Conclusions: Alpha-band binaural beat entrainment was associated with significant improvements in anxiety and aggression among men undergoing treatment for opioid use disorder compared with sham auditory stimulation. These findings suggest that alpha-band binaural beat stimulation may represent a promising, non-invasive adjunctive intervention that warrants further clinical evaluation for enhancing emotional regulation during addiction rehabilitation. Larger multicenter randomized trials with longer follow-up periods and neurophysiological outcome measures are warranted to confirm these preliminary findings Trial registration Iranian Registry of Clinical Trials (IRCT), IRCT20251206068230N1, retrospectively registered on 31 January 2026.

doi:10.31234/osf.io/cj2wm_v1.title: Tone Timing: An Eye-Tracking Study of Dynamic F0 Integration in Spoken Word Recognition
doi:10.31234/osf.io/cj2wm_v1.abstract: To recognize words, listeners must map a temporally unfolding auditory input to representations at multiple levels. Typical accounts argue for immediate and incremental integration of asynchronous acoustic cues, such that each cue is used to partially update phonemic or lexical representations as soon as it arrives, with later cues further modulating those decisions. However, recent studies suggest that incrementality is not universal and fricatives follow a different principle in which early cues are stored in a memory buffer and listeners wait to identify the phoneme until all cues have arrived. It is unknown why different speech sounds show these differences. Here, we extend this paradigm to lexical tone, an acoustic/phonetic dimension which extends over a syllable and tracks the dynamics of F0. In a visual world experiment, we index the relative activation of minimal pairs only differing in Mandarin tones as they change over time to ask whether lexical tone is incrementally integrated or processed in a buffered manner. Our findings first show lexical activation patterns are closely coupled to the timing of pitch contours, supporting the immediate integration of lexical tone. Therefore, with respect to temporal integration of asynchronous cues, tone is like most segments, though different from fricatives.

doi:10.64898/2026.09.24.754075.title: Seizure control via astrocyte targeted optogenetic extracellular potassium modulation: computational analysis of K + vs non-selective cation conducting opsins
doi:10.64898/2026.09.24.754075.authors: Weyn L, Tarnaud T, Joseph W, Raedt R, Tanghe E.
doi:10.64898/2026.09.24.754075.abstract: ABSTRACT Aims Seizure generation has been strongly linked to the accumulation of extracellular potassium. As astrocytes play a key role in potassium homeostasis, astrocyte targeted optogenetic modulation of extracellular potassium has been proposed as a novel strategy for seizure control. The effectiveness of such modulation is expected to depend strongly on the ion selectivity of the employed opsin. This study aims to mechanistically compare potassium-selective (WiChR) and cation-conducting (ChR2-like, ChR2 ∗ ) opsins for astrocyte targeted modulation of extracellular potassium, and to determine how astrocytic properties and stimulation parameters influence modulation efficacy. Methods A conductance-based computational framework was used to model astrocyte extracellular space interactions, incorporating ion-specific photocurrents, Na + / K + -ATPase activity, and gap junction-mediated coupling within the astrocytic syncytium. Systematic parameter sweeps were performed to evaluate the influence of ion selectivity, astrocytic parameters, and stimulation paradigms on potassium dynamics. Results WiChR-based modulation consistently produced more effective and robust reductions in [K + ] e than ChR2 * , via direct K + inward currents and reduced dependence on pump activity. In contrast, ChR2 * primarily limited potassium accumulation rather than reversing it and exhibited greater sensitivity to parameter variations, particularly Na + / K + -ATPase activity. The effectiveness of astrocyte targeted modulation was strongly dependent on syncytial integrity, with reduced gap junction coupling impairing potassium clearance. Optimal stimulation performance for WiChR was observed for a pulse repetition period of 20 ms , with outcomes determined by the interaction between opsin kinetics and stimulation parameters. Conclusions These results demonstrate that activation of WiChR opsins in astrocytes can reduce extracellular potassium levels and thereby modulate neuronal excitability. Ion selectivity emerges as a key determinant of modulation efficacy at the astrocytic level, with potassium-selective opsins providing a more direct and reliable approach than non-selective cation-conducting alternatives. Together, these findings establish a mechanistic basis for optogenetic activation of astrocytic potassium buffering as a potential strategy for seizure suppression and other neurological disorders associated with potassium dysregulation. AUTHOR SUMMARY Excessive accumulation of potassium in the extracellular space is thought to contribute to seizures by increasing neuronal excitability. Astrocytes play a central role in regulating extracellular potassium levels and have therefore emerged as promising targets for therapeutic intervention. Optogenetic tools enable light-controlled ion currents to be introduced into astrocytes, potentially enabling direct modulation of potassium homeostasis. Previous experimental work has shown that astrocytic modulation via non-selective cation channels can reduce seizure activity, but the recent development of potassium-selective opsins raises the possibility of directly controlling astrocyte-mediated potassium currents. However, it remains unclear how the ion selectivity of these currents influences their ability to regulate extracellular potassium. Using a computational model of astrocyte potassium homeostasis, we compared the effects of activating a potassium-selective opsin (WiChR) with a non-selective cation-conducting opsin (ChR2-like). We found that potassium-selective modulation produces a larger and more robust reduction in extracellular potassium because potassium currents directly contribute to potassium clearance. In contrast, ChR2-like modulation relies more strongly on indirect mechanisms, including sodium accumulation and enhanced pump activity, making its effectiveness more sensitive to cellular properties and network conditions. We also identified astrocytic gap-junction coupling as a key determinant of successful potassium regulation. These findings identify potassium-selective opsins as a promising tool for controlling extracellular potassium dynamics. More broadly, this study provides mechanistic insight into how astrocytes regulate brain excitability and offers guidance for the development of future optogenetic strategies targeting disorders associated with disrupted potassium homeostasis.

doi:10.64898/2026.09.25.754065.title: Task-specific preferences guide forward planning in sequential decision-making
doi:10.64898/2026.09.25.754065.authors: Lepauvre, A.; Ott, F.; Kiebel, S. J.
doi:10.64898/2026.09.25.754065.abstract: Everyday problems often require choosing among actions with different future consequences, even though fully evaluating those consequences is often computationally infeasible. The human brain is remarkable in its ability to solve such complex problems efficiently. In this paper, we hypothesize that this capacity arises from a principle inspired by Bayesian accounts of perception and sensorimotor control: evidence derived from effortful forward planning is integrated with task-specific preferences akin to priors, weighted by the uncertainty of these preferences. To test this hypothesis, we used a sequential decision-making task with a relatively large state space. Model comparison showed that participants' deviations from optimal forward planning are best captured by task-specific preferences, rather than by unsystematic errors, recent action-history effects, or offer-context biases. Moreover, the influence of forward planning on participants' responses depended on preference uncertainty, as evidenced by both choice behavior and reaction times, and preferences were not arbitrary but instead supported above-stochastic performance even in the absence of forward planning. Together, these results are consistent with a Bayesian-inspired interpretation of decision making, in which costly forward planning is integrated with state-dependent priors or preferences. These preferences may provide an inexpensive, quickly available first-pass solution, which is complemented by forward planning when preference-based guidance is uncertain.

doi:10.1109/tbme.2026.3654558.title: A Dual Classifier-Regressor Architecture for Heart Sound Onset/Offset Detection.
doi:10.1109/tbme.2026.3654558.authors: Somarathne P, Herath S, Gargiulo G, Breen P, Anderson N, Yao Y, Liu T, Withana A.
doi:10.1109/tbme.2026.3654558.abstract: Objective Identifying the first and second heart sounds (S1 and S2) from phonocardiogram (PCG) signals is an essential step in automating the diagnosis of cardiac conditions such as irregular heartbeat, valve misfunctions, and heart failure. Recent research inspired by image segmentation has shown promise in utilising deep neural networks for point-wise PCG segmentation with the support of synchronised electrocardiogram (ECG). This paper shifts the focus from point-wise segmentation to identifying the onset/offset of S1 and S2 heart sounds in the PCG signal. Methods We incorporate the ECG signal and its keypoints to improve the detection of the heart sounds. Our proposed method employs a joint classifier-regressor architecture for predicting the probability and the location of transitions in the PCG signal. Results When evaluated on the largest publicly available PhysioNet/CinC 2016 dataset, the proposed approach outperforms the existing state-of-the-art methods, achieving a sensitivity of 0.98 and a positive predictive value of 0.98 in identifying midpoints of S1 and S2 segments. It also identifies the onset/offset locations with an 11.11 ms error. Conclusion It is evident that identifying the transitions simplifies, leading to better training and inference. Significance In addition to achieving state-of-the-art results, this proposed approach could also be adapted to other physiological signals, such as respiration, blood pressure, or muscle activity, for locating regions of activity/interest.

doi:10.21203/rs.3.rs-10316519/v1.title: Speech and Voice Biomarkers for Parkinson’s disease Detection: A Systematic Review of Machine Learning and Deep Learning Models
doi:10.21203/rs.3.rs-10316519/v1.abstract: Abstract Parkinson's disease (PD) is a progressive disease that impacts movement and other functions. Voice disorders can present early in the disease process and voice analysis is an appealing non-invasive means of detection and monitoring of PD. The aim of the present review is to explore the application of machine learning (ML) and deep learning (DL) techniques to the diagnosis and prognosis of PD using voice signals. We applied the PRISMA 2020 guidelines to search ScienceDirect, IEEE Xplore, and ACM Digital Library for studies from the last eight years (2017–2025) with specific set criteria. A large number of public datasets, such as UCI Parkinson's data set and PC-GITA corpus, are included in this review. It briefly reviews some of the important acoustic characteristics, including jitter, shimmer, harmonic-to-noise ratio (HNR), mel-frequency cepstral coefficients (MFCCs), nonlinear dynamic measures, spectrogram features, and wavelet features. The review also covers the selection of features, reduction of data, and optimization of models. It provides a comparison of traditional ML models such as Support Vector Machine (SVM), Random Forest (RF), k-Nearest Neighbors (k-NN), Logistic Regression with advanced DL models including Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs), recurrent neural networks, transformers and hybrid models that incorporate handcrafted and learned features. Last but not least, it shows how explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) can facilitate easier clinical interpretation of results. The results of most studies indicate over an 80% accuracy for PD detection using voice, indicating that the methods work. At the same time, there are issues including imbalanced data sets, scarcity of long-term studies, variations in study methodology, and a lack of generalizability between the data sets. The review proposes a standard and consistent approach along with several areas that could be explored in the future, such as integrating multiple types of data, conducting long-term studies, implementing federated learning, and building privacy-preserving AI systems for real-world clinical applications.

doi:10.64898/2026.10.06.756964.title: Expert and Novice Visuomotor Strategies in a Sequential Football Task Reflect Distinct Generative Models
doi:10.64898/2026.10.06.756964.authors: Hacques, G.; Iodice, P.; Dehorne, A.; Chaigneau, A.; Pezzulo, G.
doi:10.64898/2026.10.06.756964.abstract: In visuomotor sequential tasks, chaining actions smoothly requires tight coordination between sensory and motor systems to deal with competing demands, such as reducing uncertainty about future opportunities for action while controlling ongoing ones. In a football-based decision-making task, experts and novices used different strategies to overcome these competing demands, demonstrating a proactive and a sequential visuomotor strategy, respectively. We propose a computational explanation of expertise-related difference in policy selection, grounded in the active inference framework. We simulated the selection of sequence of actions using a partially observable Markov decision process (POMDP) model, and we manipulated three parameters: the reward structure, the prior beliefs about state transition, and the sensory precision. Simulations showed that selection of the proactive strategy relied on strong prior beliefs, high sensory precision and high valuation of fast passing. Conversely, the sequential policy was selected when rapid performance was not highly valued, or under noisy prior beliefs, or lower level of sensory precision. Decreasing sensory precision and adding noise in prior beliefs also decreased decision accuracy. These results suggest that policy selection leading to novice or expert visuomotor strategy reflects differences in the underlying generative model, particularly in how agents value different aspects of the task.

doi:10.20944/preprints202610.1079.v1.title: Evaluating Camouflaged Object Detection Priors for Weakly Supervised Localization of Respiratory Sound Events
doi:10.20944/preprints202610.1079.v1.abstract: No public respiratory sound dataset provides event-level time-frequency mask annotation, so the localization of crackles and wheezes must be learned under weak supervision. This study evaluates whether two architectural priors from camouflaged object detection, frequency attention and reverse attention, transfer to this task. They are implemented as optional modules on a U-Net and tested in two studies: a synthetic benchmark with exact masks and controlled camouflage, and the SPRSound database with full-band annotations over ten patient-disjoint splits. The benchmark shows that the broadband signal-to-noise ratio does not measure camouflage: at the same nominal value, a wheeze sits 26 dB above a crackle within its own mask. Frequency attention improves event-based F1 by 0.053 over a capacity-matched control, with a positive sign in 9 of 10 splits. Reverse attention does not replicate on new seeds. The advantage attenuates on the independent test set, the drop lies in precision, and a conventional convolutional recurrent neural network is numerically superior. Five hypotheses about the mechanism are evaluated and none is confirmed. This work does not propose a competitive method: it measures what transfers and what does not.

doi:10.1038/s41386-026-02577-x.title: Multiple-context extinction strengthens fear suppression through hippocampal dopamine D2R-dependent memory updating.
doi:10.1038/s41386-026-02577-x.authors: Hammerman EA, Penna SR, Gonzalez SE, Patel S, Roebuck C, Lock EK, Desmond C, Fukunaga Y, Maloy GC, Cazares VA.
doi:10.1038/s41386-026-02577-x.abstract: Extinction learning, which underlies exposure therapy, generates safety memories that are often context-dependent, limiting their persistence and generalization. Although varying contextual cues during extinction has been proposed to strengthen safety learning, the neural mechanisms remain unknown. Here, we compared fear extinction conducted in a single context (SCFE) or multiple contexts (MCFE) in 129S1 and C57BL/6J mice. MCFE enhanced extinction learning and generalized extinction recall in novel contexts at 2-d, with this advantage persisting at 30-d when intervening testing occurred in the trained extinction context. This enhancement required exposure to distinct, but not novel, contexts and did not prevent spontaneous recovery or US-induced reinstatement. Dual Fos-TRAP activity mapping revealed differential recruitment of the fear conditioning-tagged cells following MCFE and identified the hippocampus as a key node supporting MCFE. Consistent with this, chemogenetic silencing of dorsal, but not ventral, hippocampus selectively impaired extinction acquisition during MCFE and abolished its behavioral advantage. Likewise, local blockade of dopamine D2-, but not D1-like, receptors in the dorsal hippocampus eliminated the enhancement in extinction acquisition produced by MCFE. Together, these findings demonstrate that contextual variation strengthens and generalizes extinction learning through dorsal hippocampal dopamine D2-like receptor-dependent memory updating, identifying a neural mechanism through which behavioral modifications of exposure therapy can improve fear suppression.

doi:10.1523/eneuro.0394-25.2026.title: ACORN: Adaptive Consensus of Repeated Clusterings identifies pyramidal neurons and interneurons in the primate motor cortex based on extracellular spike waveforms.
doi:10.1523/eneuro.0394-25.2026.authors: Soltesz Z, Tenorio VS, Tohyama T, Baker AM, Baker SN, Kraskov A.
doi:10.1523/eneuro.0394-25.2026.abstract: Understanding how neural circuits generate behaviour requires knowledge of both neural activity patterns and the cell types they originate from. While the scale of neuronal recordings has dramatically increased since the advent of dense multicontact probes, accurate identification of cell types remains elusive. Traditional approaches have used spike width to attempt a classification, with narrow spikes assumed to be inhibitory interneurons. However, fast pyramidal tract neurons (PTNs, known to be excitatory) with thin spikes and interneurons with wide spikes challenge these assumptions. Here we accomplish three related objectives. First, we produce a ground truth dataset of extracellular spike shapes from electrophysiologically identified pyramidal neurons from primary (M1) and supplementary motor areas (SMA) and optogenetically identified interneurons in M1 in female macaque monkeys. Next, we show that spike width correlates with antidromic latency not only in M1 but also in the SMA, suggesting that it is a physiologically meaningful measure across the motor cortex. Finally, we introduce our unsupervised ensemble clustering method, "ACORN", and characterise its performance on our neocortical macaque dataset, the C4 cerebellar database, and a juxtacellularly recorded mouse dataset, demonstrating strong out-of-the-box performance across species, brain areas, and recording techniques. ACORN can cluster neuronal waveforms without training or tuning, and provides data-derived confidence values for its predictions. Our ground truth data can be used as a reference to help identify or verify clusters in novel datasets. Together, our method and database provide a streamlined foundation for electrophysiological cell classification without necessitating changes to recording paradigms. Significance Statement High-density extracellular recordings are increasingly the norm in neuroscience, but accurate and non-invasive identification of cells remains a challenge. Here we provide a database of action potential spike shapes from pyramidal tract neurons and interneurons of the macaque supplementary motor area, whose identities we verified using nerve stimulation and optogenetics, respectively. We introduce the neuron clustering method "ACORN", and showcase its robustness by evaluating its performance on a variety of distinct datasets. Our training-free clustering technique is designed to support experimentalists, while our ground truth database can enhance and validate future datasets and method development.

doi:10.1016/j.brainres.2026.150558.title: Anticipated relevance prepares visual processing for efficient memory-guided selection.
doi:10.1016/j.brainres.2026.150558.authors: Dietz L, Strauch C, Arora K, Van der Stigchel S, Chota S, Gayet S.
doi:10.1016/j.brainres.2026.150558.abstract: Finding an object typically involves using working memory to select relevant visual information at the right time. Using EEG, we investigated how predictable changes in stimulus relevance influence top-down visual selection. Participants memorized an oriented grating, followed by a cue indicating which of two sequentially presented probes was relevant for a memory-match/-mismatch judgment. Consistent with earlier work, relevant probes evoked stronger univariate responses than irrelevant probes. Furthermore, responses to (memory-matching and memory-mismatching) probes were more distinct when they were relevant compared to irrelevant. Crucially, using rapid invisible frequency tagging (RIFT), we found that visual responses to the (empty) probe location were enhanced even before the presentation of relevant (compared to irrelevant) probes. Predictable changes in stimulus relevance, therefore, induce both pro-active and re-active changes in visual processing. We conclude that anticipating the (ir)relevance of upcoming visual events enables the visual system to prepare for efficient memory-guided visual selection.

doi:10.64898/2026.10.09.757930.title: How Social Value Guides Curiosity, Information Search, and Memory in Younger and Older Adults
doi:10.64898/2026.10.09.757930.authors: Vaziri M, Tanberg P, Yeung RC, Spaniol J.
doi:10.64898/2026.10.09.757930.abstract: Epistemic curiosity, or the desire for new knowledge, benefits emotional, physical, and cognitive health across the lifespan. Initially believed to be solely intrinsically motivated, recent work has found that extrinsic motivators can also drive epistemic curiosity. One example of the latter is the perceived social value of information, such as popularity metrics on social media platforms (e.g., upvotes on Reddit.com). However, it remains unclear whether the influence of social value cues extends to curiosity-related behaviors, such as information search and memory, and whether these effects vary with age. The current study was designed to fill these knowledge gaps. In two experiments, younger and older adults (total N = 367) rated their curiosity for user-generated trivia questions that varied in social value (high or low upvote counts on Reddit.com). Upvote counts were either visible (upvote visible condition) or not visible (upvote invisible condition). In Experiment 1, participants had the opportunity to reveal the answer to each trivia question, a measure of information seeking. Although social value increased curiosity, it did not influence information seeking. In Experiment 2, answer reveal was mandatory, and participants received a surprise recall test for the answers. Social value again increased curiosity, particularly for younger adults, but had no influence on memory. Overall, these findings replicate social-value effects on curiosity in younger and older adults, but they provide no evidence that social value motivates information search or episodic memory. These findings highlight the limits of extrinsic influences on epistemic behaviors across the adult lifespan.

doi:10.1371/journal.pcbi.1014820.title: Granger sensori-behavioral functional taxonomy of neuronal ensemble activity from two-photon calcium imaging data.
doi:10.1371/journal.pcbi.1014820.authors: Khosravi S, Francis NA, Kanold PO, Babadi B.
doi:10.1371/journal.pcbi.1014820.abstract: Understanding how neuronal populations interact to encode and transform sensory information is a fundamental challenge in computational neuroscience. Most existing studies, however, study neural encoding, behavioral readout, and functional connectivity as disjoint problems. Two-photon calcium imaging enables simultaneous recording of large neuronal ensembles in vivo, driven by diverse stimuli and eliciting distinct behaviors. However, extracting directional functional connectivity metrics as well as encoding and readout properties of neurons from such data remains difficult due to indirect and noisy observations of spiking activity, slow temporal dynamics, and the latent interplay between external stimuli and endogenous neural processes. Here, we introduce a unified conceptual and operational modeling and inference framework for directly extracting functional Granger causal (GC) effects between neurons, from external stimuli to neurons, and from neurons to behavior, from two-photon imaging data, in the sense of Granger's temporal predictability. Inspired by the intersection information framework, we also identify neurons that encode features of sensory stimuli that inform behavioral readout. The resulting GC networks together with the taxonomy of functional sensori-behavioral relevance, which we call G-taxonomy, provides a powerful statistical analysis framework, enabled by the integration of several techniques including state-space modeling and inference, variational inference, and point processes. We applied the proposed framework to simulated and experimentally-recorded two-photon imaging from the mouse auditory cortex (A1) during both passive listening and active tone discrimination. Our simulation studies reveal significant improvement of our proposed methodology over existing techniques. Analysis of experimental data from the mouse A1 identifies distinct groups of cells with diverse sensori-behavioral relevance, as well as changes in functional connectivity associated with correct vs. incorrect behavior. In summary, this work provides a principled and data-driven methodology for uncovering directional interactions among the neurons, sensory stimuli, and behavior, all within the same statistical framework, offering new insights into how distributed cortical populations transform sensory inputs into behaviorally relevant representations.

doi:10.64898/2026.10.13.758762.title: Independently tunable subcortical oscillators enable prefrontal control of cortical coupling
doi:10.64898/2026.10.13.758762.authors: Mozaffarilegha, M.; Kolaxi, A.; Nikoletopoulou, V.; Ito, H. T.
doi:10.64898/2026.10.13.758762.abstract: Oscillatory coherence between brain regions varies flexibly with behavioral demands, yet the circuit mechanism underlying this control remains unclear. Theta rhythm, which coordinates prefrontal-hippocampal activity, is classically attributed to a pacemaker in the medial septum (MS), with the supramammillary nucleus (SuM) as its modulator. Here we show that SuM instead operates as an independently tunable theta oscillator. In rats performing a spatial alternation task, SuM theta frequency decreased before the choice point while MS theta frequency remained stable, reducing the SuM-MS frequency mismatch in both population spiking and local field potentials. The size of this mismatch predicted theta-rhythm coordination between the medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC) and hippocampal CA1 in both the alternation task and open-field foraging. Inhibiting direct mPFC input to SuM abolished the behavior-dependent modulation of SuM frequency and disrupted mPFC-CA1 coupling. These findings place a subcortical theta oscillator under top-down prefrontal control and identify the SuM-MS frequency mismatch as a control variable for interregional coordination.

doi:10.64898/2026.10.14.759228.title: Delayed maturation of hippocampal trisynaptic circuitry underlies the protracted development of episodic-like memory
doi:10.64898/2026.10.14.759228.authors: McKenzie, C.; Ramsaran, A. I.; Saderi, M.; Haar, S.; Josselyn, S. A.; Frankland, P. W.
doi:10.64898/2026.10.14.759228.abstract: The ability to form high-resolution episodic memories emerges relatively late in development, but the circuit mechanisms underlying this transition are unknown. CA1 receives entorhinal input through a direct monosynaptic pathway and an indirect trisynaptic pathway via the dentate gyrus and CA3. In mice, CA3[->]CA1 innervation matured later than MEC[->]CA1 innervation, with pronounced maturation between P20 and P24. Trisynaptic pathway maturation was necessary for high-resolution memory and was shaped by neuronal activity and early-life experience. Mechanistically, trisynaptic activity promoted perineuronal net assembly around downstream parvalbumin-expressing interneurons, facilitating their maturation and subsequent recruitment during learning to constrain CA1 encoding ensembles. Thus, activity-dependent maturation of trisynaptic circuitry provides a unified circuit and cellular account of a sensitive period for the emergence of episodic-like memory.

doi:10.64898/2026.09.29.755342.title: Neocortical Feedback Biases Hippocampal Reactivation Toward Unconsolidated Memories in a Predictive-Coding Model of Systems Consolidation
doi:10.64898/2026.09.29.755342.abstract: During sleep and quiet wakefulness, the brain spontaneously revisits neural activity patterns associated with previous experience, a phenomenon known as reactivation, or replay. Reactivation is thought to support systems consolidation, the process by which memory retrieval becomes progressively more dependent on neocortical circuits and less dependent on the hippocampus. Importantly, reactivation is not indiscriminate: it preferentially targets specific memories, such as new or weakly learned ones. These observations have motivated the development of computational models accounting for the spontaneous reactivation of memories, their prioritisation for replay, and their transfer between the hippocampus and neocortex. In parallel, predictive-coding (PC) models have shown how computations attributed to hippocampal and neocortical circuits can arise from local prediction-error dynamics. Here, we connect these two lines of work by showing how autonomous intrinsic dynamics in coupled PC networks can transfer stored memory content between neural systems. The hippocampus and neocortex are modelled as two coupled PC associative memory networks, with asymmetric coupling motivated by reported interactions between hippocampal area CA1 and the prefrontal cortex. This coupling establishes a closed-loop dialogue in which hippocampal activity drives neocortical learning, while neocortical feedback biases subsequent hippocampal activity toward content for which neocortical support remains weak. We prove that this feedback steers hippocampal activity toward states of higher neocortical free energy, so that prioritisation emerges from the dynamics rather than from an explicit scheduler. In our model, neocortical learning relies exclusively on spontaneous hippocampal activity, without access to the initial training corpus. Nevertheless, we show that the neocortical network acquires correlated memory content faster than direct training on randomly sampled memories. This advantage appeared for sufficiently correlated memories, grew with their correlation, and persisted when new memories were incrementally added during transfer. Together, these results provide a PC account in which neocortical feedback organises hippocampal reactivation to support efficient memory transfer during systems consolidation.

doi:10.64898/2026.10.11.758396.title: The effect of dominance rank on behavioural response to playback calls in ring-tailed lemurs (Lemur catta)
doi:10.64898/2026.10.11.758396.authors: Gerner, N.; Mundry, R.; Gold, O.; Wierucka, K.
doi:10.64898/2026.10.11.758396.abstract: In group-living species, dominance hierarchies play a central role in shaping social dynamics, influencing both agonistic and affiliative interactions. Being able to recognise an individual's dominance rank at a distance, can reduce direct conflicts, facilitating group coordination, and mediating social cohesion. While the role of dominance in relation to aggressive or reproductive vocalizations has been well documented, its influence on affiliative contact calls, particularly in mediating group movement and social integration, remains underexplored. We conducted playback experiments with free-ranging adult ringtailed lemurs (Lemur catta) at the Affenwald Wildlife Park to investigate how dominance rank of the caller and rank differences between caller and listener affect behavioral responses. Using Generalized Linear Mixed Models (GLMMs), we analysed three response variables: vocal response, number of visual scans, and occurrence of movement. Our results revealed sex-specific effects: females exhibited increased movement following contact calls from high-ranking individuals, and tended to refrain from moving when their own rank exceeded that of the caller. In contrast, no significant effects of dominance rank were observed in males. These findings suggest that high-ranking females may play an important role in initiating group movement. This study provides insights into the role of dominance rank in mediating social coordination through contact calls and provides a foundation for further research into the role of vocal communication in maintaining group cohesion in primates.

doi:10.64898/2026.09.24.754261.title: Toward A Whole-Brain Interface Enabled by High-Resolution Surface Electrophysiology
doi:10.64898/2026.09.24.754261.authors: Ho E, Barth K, Dister J, Srivastava A, Poole AJ, Claudi F, Lucas MV, Miller JS, Hettick M, Byun YW, Anushiravani R, Murphy M, Konrad P, Bhatia S, Adams G, Carte S, Ottonello D, Bederson J, Saez I, Kellner C, Tostaeva G, Kopell BH, Cummins DD, Ulkatan S, Ghatan S, Cajigas I, Pesaran B, Borges PG, Qureshi Q, Haggerty J, Wang Z, Crone N, Bettegowda C, Lehner K, Luo S, Angrick M, Greene R, Comair Y, Aronson JP, Lawton M, Prakash P, Lei T, Lee JH, Slutzky MW, Tate M, Paulk A, Dunn G, Grannan B, Serruya MD, Hines K, Wu C, Rosenwasser R, Berger A, Levy EI, Siddiqui AH, Riley J, Davies JM, Strauss J, Mager MJ, Mermel CH, Rapoport BI.
doi:10.64898/2026.09.24.754261.abstract: The goal of building a whole-brain interface - capable of generating a real-time digital representation of the state of the entire central nervous system - has long been framed as a hardware challenge of recording simultaneously from ever-larger numbers of microelectrodes. Advances in high-resolution neural interfaces now enable electrophysiologic interaction with the human nervous system at spatial and temporal resolutions previously unattainable without disrupting tissue architecture or physiology. These capabilities create new opportunities for mechanistic neuroscience, neuroprosthetics, and precision-guided neurosurgery. With the advent of modern microelectrode array technology, however, the whole-brain interface has also become a data challenge. Rather than pursuing large-scale human brain recording purely through a single device placed in a single patient, we demonstrate here that systematic multi-subject aggregation, across brain regions and behavioral paradigms, in a common anatomical framework, can achieve something functionally similar to a whole-brain interface. Here we present an approach to a functional atlas of the human central nervous system derived from high-resolution surface electrophysiology recordings obtained in the first 70 patients implanted with an anatomically conformal, thin-film neural interface positioned in more than 100 locations. The atlas comprises >100,000 electrode deployments and catalogs placement across a broad range of neuroanatomic targets spanning the motor, sensory, language, auditory, and associative domains, as well as brainstem and spinal cord structures that have historically been difficult to access at high electrophysiologic resolution. Across participants, aggregated recordings reveal somatotopic organization, including digit representations that follow a lateral-to-medial ordering consistent with classical homuncular maps, with transitions between adjacent representations occurring over spatial scales of approximately 0.8 - 2.0 mm; canonical frequency-band signatures, such as movement-related beta-band suppression and focal high-gamma (70 - 200 Hz) increases during motor and speech behaviors; and task-modulated population dynamics in both evoked and spontaneous activity across cortical, brainstem, and spinal cord regions. These findings yield insight into patterns of mesoscale electrophysiological dynamics conserved across the entire human central nervous system, suggesting that fine-scale functional organization is preserved across individuals when aligned to common anatomical landmarks. We further demonstrate several applications of these high-resolution recordings, including real-time neural decoding from upper extremity motor cortex to enable real-time neuroprosthetic control, and from ventrolateral cortex to decode cortical correlates of spoken language, facial movements, and complex facial expressions of emotion, supporting initial feasibility of combined verbal and nonverbal communication interfaces. Together, these results establish a paradigm for approaching large-scale interfaces with the human brain, as well as a starting point for a scalable, extensible atlas of human electrophysiologic function designed to accelerate discovery across basic neuroscience, translational research, and clinical neurotechnology.

doi:10.1162/jocn.a.2634.title: Stimulation of Right Temporal Cortex Enhances Talker Typicality Judgments.
doi:10.1162/jocn.a.2634.authors: Luthra S, Mechtenberg H, Olson HE, Zaharchuk HA, Myers EB.
doi:10.1162/jocn.a.2634.abstract: Listeners are exquisitely sensitive to the ways that different talkers produce speech sounds, and such sensitivity may allow listeners to condition speech perception on talker information. A growing body of neuroimaging data suggests that although phonetic processing is largely supported by the brain's left hemisphere, the integration of talker information during speech perception recruits the right hemisphere, especially right temporal cortex. However, an open question is whether recruitment of the right hemisphere is strictly necessary for integrating talker information and phonetic detail or simply incidental. Here, we leverage TMS to test for a causal role of the right middle temporal gyrus (RMTG) in accessing a listener's beliefs about a talker's phonetic signature. During an initial exposure phase, participants heard pairs of talkers, one of whom produced voiceless stop consonants (e.g., /k/) with a relatively short voice onset time (VOT) and one who employed relatively long VOTs; listeners learned what variation was typical of each talker without disruption from TMS. During a subsequent test, TMS was administered to the RMTG, left middle temporal gyrus (LMTG), or a control site (scalp vertex) before listeners judged whether VOT variants were typical of a learned talker. We found that listeners were best able to determine what phonetic variation was typical of a talker following RMTG stimulation; stimulation of the LMTG did not influence performance relative to vertex stimulation. Overall, results indicate that the balance of activation across the two hemispheres is critical for accessing talker-specific phonetic detail.

doi:10.64898/2026.10.01.755588.title: Traveling brain waves support flexible storage of human working memory
doi:10.64898/2026.10.01.755588.authors: Zeng Y, Hilla Y, Peylo C, Taylor P, Imbach L, Sarnthein J, Alamia A, Sauseng P.
doi:10.64898/2026.10.01.755588.abstract: Human working memory enables us to temporarily store and flexibly utilize information. It is thought that there are two distinct neural mechanisms by which information is retained in working memory: persistent firing of working memory-relevant neurons 1 , or short-term synaptic plasticity in the absence of ongoing neuronal firing 2 . However, both these mechanisms can lead to strong neural interference when working memory contents are updated with novel information. As an alternative, here we propose that information can be flexibly held in working memory in the form of traveling waves - spatiotemporal patterns of neural activity that propagate across brain tissue. In an artificial neural network, we simulated wave propagation by passing transient neural firing patterns representative of single-item information across different network layers. In comparison to sustained neural firing, we demonstrate that these transient traveling waves result in minimal synaptic plasticity, thereby facilitating working memory updating without significant neural interference. We then identified such traveling waves in intracranial recordings from the human temporal lobe. Traveling waves precisely when information was being encoded and persisted uniformly throughout maintenance and recall, aligning with the activation pattern seen in the artificial neural network. In trials where participants committed memory errors, no such continuous traveling wave activity in the temporal lobe was observed. Our data from artificial neural networks and human intracranial brain recordings converge to indicate that neural traveling waves support information processing in working memory while minimizing interference during updating. This here reported mechanism, together with the classical working memory models, serves as a mutually complementary, multi-mechanistic framework for working memory storage.

doi:10.31234/osf.io/d3c9t_v2.title: Memory precision fluctuates with theta rhythmicity in humans
doi:10.31234/osf.io/d3c9t_v2.authors: Houser T, Acker R, Zeithamova D.
doi:10.31234/osf.io/d3c9t_v2.abstract: Rodent research indicates that the hippocampus naturally oscillates between memory encoding and retrieval phases at theta rhythm, indicating that the timing of when information reaches the hippocampus can determine encoding success. However, non-invasively probing such oscillations is challenging in humans. Here, we employed a recently developed dense sampling approach to construct a time course of memory encoding success. Using an attention-grabbing cue expected to reset theta phase, we varied the delay between the cue and to-be-remembered stimulus. Experiment 1 replicated recent finding that human associative memory performance fluctuates with theta rhythmicity, with the best fitting frequency at 8 Hz. Experiment 2 tested and confirmed a new prediction that memory precision also fluctuates with theta rhythmicity, consistent with hippocampal models postulating oscillations in the relative engagement of alternative processing pathways. Together, these findings suggest that the rapid neural fluctuations underpinning memory processes are robust enough to be observed using the dense behavioral sampling approach. Moreover, this work substantiates models of episodic memory and provides new avenues to study models of hippocampal function in humas noninvasively, providing evidence from a purely behavioral approach that human mnemonic discrimination fluctuates with theta rhythm.

doi:10.31234/osf.io/83wc5_v1.title: Irregular Natural Environments Are Associated with Better Context-Supported Recall
doi:10.31234/osf.io/83wc5_v1.authors: Huynh DC, Hussein AK, Fich LB, Djebbara Z.
doi:10.31234/osf.io/83wc5_v1.abstract: Natural environments are often treated as a relatively uniform category in cognitive research despite substantial variation in their spatial organization and regularity. This study examined whether episodic memory depends not only on environmental type but also on the internal structure of the environment.
