Sixty participants experienced four immersive virtual environments in a 2 × 2 within-subject design crossing environmental type (natural vs. urban) with structural regularity (rhythmic vs. irregular). Memory was assessed using free, cued, and delayed recall and analyzed using linear mixed-effects models controlling for presentation order. Immediate recall showed little evidence of environmental effects. In contrast, Cued Recall 1 showed a significant Environment × Regularity interaction, with the irregular natural environment producing the highest performance. Follow-up contrasts showed higher recall in irregular nature than in all three comparison conditions for Cued Recall 1 and Delayed Recall, with a more selective advantage during Cued Recall 2. Retention proportions did not differ across conditions, indicating that delayed differences reflected earlier memory advantages rather than differential forgetting. These findings suggest that episodic memory effects associated with natural environments cannot be understood through a nature–urban distinction alone. Instead, the internal organization of an environment may shape memory, with irregular natural environments potentially providing more distinctive contextual information that becomes particularly useful during context-supported retrieval.

doi:10.1162/imag.a.1389.title: The late positive component in recognition memory is linked to mnemonic evidence accumulation.
doi:10.1162/imag.a.1389.authors: Sun J, Feuerriegel D, Nightingale M, Osth AF.
doi:10.1162/imag.a.1389.abstract: Recognising objects from memory requires an integration of sensory and mnemonic information. This process has been theorised to occur via a stochastic evidence accumulation process implemented within the parietal cortex. Recent electroencephalographic (EEG) evidence indicates that the widely studied parietal Late Positive Component (LPC) shows characteristics of such a mnemonic accumulation signal. Here, we formally investigated this hypothesis using generative computational modelling that links a trial-level memory strength variable in the Diffusion Decision Model (DDM) with LPC amplitudes prior to the time of the decision. We recorded EEG from 24 participants making recognition judgements based on either studied or novel words. Each participant completed up to three testing sessions. We replicated recent findings that the LPC ramps up and peaks around the time of the decision and corresponding motor response. LPC amplitudes also covaried with accuracy and response time, as expected of a neural correlate of memory strength. By fitting DDMs to LPC amplitudes and behavioural data using specialised neural network tools, we demonstrate that LPC amplitudes are selectively associated with the rate of evidence accumulation, signifying memory strength. This association was stronger for previously studied words compared to novel words, and strongest at the time window immediately prior to the recognition decision. Our findings, therefore, recast the LPC as a neural signature of mnemonic strength linked to the rate of evidence accumulation during recognition memory decisions.

doi:10.64898/2026.10.17.759806.title: Learned Audiovisual Predictability Modulates Depth-Resolved Hippocampal-Cortical Functional Coupling
doi:10.64898/2026.10.17.759806.authors: Sozzi, S.; Enan, M.; Auksztulewicz, R.; Schwiedrzik, C.; Melloni, L.; Esposito, F.; Vanello, N.; De Martino, F.
doi:10.64898/2026.10.17.759806.abstract: Perception reflects the dynamic integration of prior expectations, uncertainty, and incoming sensory evidence, but the neural circuitry supporting these computations remains debated. Current theories implicate coordinated interactions between the hippocampus and neocortex, potentially at the level of hippocampal subfields and cortical layers. Evidence in humans has come primarily from the visual domain, while less is known about how these interactions support learned auditory predictions. Using submillimetre 7T fMRI, we investigated depth-resolved functional coupling between hippocampal subfields and temporal and frontal cortical regions during audiovisual associative prediction. Participants learned deterministic associations between visual cues and auditory syllables, allowing us to compare auditory processing in predictable and unpredictable contexts. Predictability-related connectivity changes showed a spatially structured pattern involving DG/CA3-pSTG and CA1-inferior frontal regions, with significant edge-wise effects resolved across cortical depths. These findings provide fine-grained evidence that learned auditory predictability modulates hippocampal-cortical functional interactions across temporo-frontal systems.

doi:10.64898/2026.09.28.755157.title: Cellular Determinants of CA1 Pyramidal Cell Recruitment during Sharp-Wave Ripples
doi:10.64898/2026.09.28.755157.authors: Angerbauer R, Lim TH, Jonas P, Helmchen F, Zhang X.
doi:10.64898/2026.09.28.755157.abstract: Hippocampal ripples, accompanied by highly synchronous neuronal firing, are critical for immediate offline memory consolidation, learning, and planning. However, the cellular mechanisms that determine which individual neurons are recruited to participate in action potential (AP) firing during ripples remain unclear. We investigated the membrane potential (V m ) dynamics of CA1 pyramidal cells during ripples using whole-cell recordings in awake, head-fixed mice. We found that ripple participation was strongly associated with concurrent membrane-potential depolarization on an event-to-event basis, whereas between-cell differences in overall participation propensity were jointly explained by ripple-associated depolarization and intrinsic excitability. Applying this framework across CA1 cell populations revealed that differences in recruitment between superficial and deep pyramidal cells were primarily driven by ripple-associated depolarization, counteracted by excitability. Differences between place and non-place cells were similarly driven by ripple-associated depolarization, though this effect acted in the same direction as excitability. Finally, we identified the post-ripple LFP rebound as a prominent marker of ripple diversity linked to post-ripple membrane-potential hyperpolarization at the single-neuron level. Together, these findings provide a mechanistic understanding of how CA1 pyramidal cells are selectively recruited during hippocampal ripples.

doi:10.1126/sciadv.aeh8870.title: Noninvasive ultrashort wave neuromodulation enhances glymphatic clearance to alleviate traumatic brain edema and Alzheimer's pathology.
doi:10.1126/sciadv.aeh8870.authors: Liu J, Xu C, Ruan H, Zhang K, Wang F, Qin Q, Li X, Chen Y, Tan Y, Qiu Y, Chen H, Wang Y, Yang Z, Zhang Y, Zhu Y, Chang C, Jiang X, Peng N.
doi:10.1126/sciadv.aeh8870.abstract: The glymphatic system clears cerebral waste, yet strategies to enhance its function remain elusive. Here, we show that 40.68 MHz ultrashort wave (USW) rapidly enhances glymphatic bulk flow in healthy mice within 10 minutes. USW potentiates both glymphatic influx and efflux, concomitant with increased Delta wave neuronal synchronization, as confirmed by local field potentials and electroencephalograms. Chemogenetic silencing confirms that USW-driven glymphatic enhancement depends on neuronal activity, while pharmacological blockade of aquaporin-4 (AQP4) abolishes the effects, revealing dual reliance on neural dynamics and astrocytic water channels. Mechanistically, USW-induced Delta oscillations promote AQP4 polarization, coupling synchronized firing to perivascular AQP4 redistribution. Moreover, USW ameliorates traumatic brain injury-induced cerebral edema and improves cognitive deficits in Alzheimer's mice by restoring glymphatic function. Our findings establish USW as a non-invasive neuromodulatory strategy for enhancing glymphatic clearance, offering therapeutic potential for neurological disorders characterized by glymphatic dysfunction.

doi:10.64898/2026.09.17.751718.title: Priors for perceived speed combine supramodally for visual-tactile motion but not for audio-visual motion
doi:10.64898/2026.09.17.751718.authors: Tonelli A, Phan CK, Alais D.
doi:10.64898/2026.09.17.751718.abstract: Perception combines incoming sensory evidence with priors learned from preceding input. One example is the central tendency effect in which stimulus estimates regress towards a prior based on the mean of the stimulus distribution. Whether such priors are specific to each modality or shared across modalities remains unresolved. Here, we examined this question using speed perception in the visual, auditory and tactile modalities and used central tendency as a behavioral probe. By giving each modality its own speed range, clear predictions emerge when modalities are interleaved: if priors are modality specific, each modality should maintain its own central-tendency bias whereas a supramodal prior would exhibit a different mean based on the pooled set of speeds. Moreover, a supra-modal prior should exhibit precision weighting, with the more reliable cue receiving more weight. For vision and touch, speed estimates converged when interleaved: both modalities shifted but the less reliable one shifted more, consistent with a precision-weighted supramodal prior. For vision and audition, the priors remained largely distinct: audition (the less reliable modality) showed a partial shift but did not converge on the precision-weighted, supramodal mean. This was not explained by the large audio–visual reliability difference: it persisted when visual precision was reduced. These results show that in the motion domain, visual and tactile signals can combine crossmodally, but auditory and visual signals do not. Supramodal processing of motion therefore depends on which senses are involved and is likely explained by the lack of an early spatial mapping in audition.

doi:10.64898/2026.09.17.752172.title: Hunger reconfigures a reward learning circuit into a memory competent mode
doi:10.64898/2026.09.17.752172.authors: Park A, Senapati B, Mancini N, Zhang Y, Choi J, Cone I, Treiber CD, Costa RP, Fenk L, Bidaye S, Waddell S.
doi:10.64898/2026.09.17.752172.abstract: Internal states such as hunger dynamically reshape activity across circuits to support resource seeking. Neuromodulation provides a means of controlling such physiological properties of neurons, but how this flexibility regulates memory networks remains unclear. Here, we describe how hunger reconfigures a dopaminergic food-reward circuit between two physiological modes that support memory formation, in Drosophila . Starvation suppresses baseline dopaminergic activity through peptidergic signalling, enabling reward-evoked, large-amplitude dopamine neuron spikes to reinforce learning. This spiking mode can be engaged by sugar consumption and persists beyond feeding, reflecting the fly’s satiety state. Persistent dopaminergic large-amplitude spiking reinforces learning and transitions the memory network into a mode that prioritizes consolidation of recently acquired memories. The transition from hunger to satiation is also reflected in the activity of postsynaptic output neurons that shift from a tonic, decorrelated mode that is responsive to dopamine into a bursting, correlated mode in which further dopaminergic modulation is occluded. Therefore, nutrient deprivation reconfigures the memory circuit into a learning competent dopamine-receptive mode, which persistent reinforcing dopamine then switches into a satiated mode driving memory consolidation. Together these processes mechanistically intertwine state-dependent reward-signalling with subsequent memory stabilization through transitions in physiological mode.

doi:10.1126/sciadv.aed2474.title: An inspiration-off attractor supports the robust and flexible control of breathing.
doi:10.1126/sciadv.aed2474.authors: Bush NE, Oliveira LM, Glovak ZT, Ramirez JM.
doi:10.1126/sciadv.aed2474.abstract: Breathing is a fundamental motor rhythm necessary to sustain life. The rhythm and pattern of breathing arises from the coordination of a rostrocaudally extended ventral respiratory column (VRC) in the medulla. Although recurrent excitation is sufficient for rhythmic bursting in reduced in vitro preparations, comparatively less is understood about how inhibition and excitation interact with feedback circuits to generate the breathing rhythm in vivo. Here, we expand on the classical "inspiratory-off switch" model that inhibitory signaling from lung stretch afferent pathways plays a critical role in generating the breathing rhythm in vivo. We perform high-density extracellular recordings along the length of the VRC during optogenetic and physiological manipulations and apply computational analyses to characterize how these perturbations govern low-dimensional neural dynamics. We show that stimulation of GABAergic afferents of the nucleus of the solitary tract advance or delay breathing in a manner similar to, but quantitatively distinct from, inhibition local to the VRC. We use generative dynamical models to show that inhibitory activity controls respiratory activity through transient stabilization of an attractive region of the low-dimensional manifold corresponding to expiration. Together, these results propose an "inspiratory-off attractor" model that underlies network level control of breathing in vivo.

doi:10.64898/2026.09.14.751437.title: Connectivity allometry is a robust organizing principle of the human functional connectome
doi:10.64898/2026.09.14.751437.authors: Wu C, Qiu X, Li J, Jin S, Jiang X, Wang J.
doi:10.64898/2026.09.14.751437.abstract: A defining feature of the human brain is its multiscale organization, in which regional processes are integrated into coherent whole-brain network architecture. How local functional organization adapts to variation in this global architecture, however, remains largely unknown. Here, we addressed this question by applying an allometric scaling framework to resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging data from four large-scale datasets spanning different cultures, cognitive states, developmental stages, and clinical conditions. We found that human functional networks were organized according to a robust and spatially heterogeneous connectivity allometry, whereby regional functional connectivity scales nonlinearly with whole-brain connectivity strength. This scaling architecture closely followed the cortical sensorimotor–association hierarchy, with lower-order systems exhibiting supralinear scaling and higher-order systems exhibiting sublinear scaling. Connectivity allometry was further associated with multiscale neurobiological organization, including regional metabolic properties, neurotransmitter receptor distributions, and transcriptomic landscapes, indicating that local–global functional scaling is embedded within fundamental biological gradients of cortical organization. Moreover, the scaling pattern and its biological associations were highly reproducible across independent cross-cultural cohorts. Importantly, connectivity allometry remained remarkably stable across working memory conditions regardless of cognitive load, emerged by late childhood, and was broadly preserved in children and adolescents with autism spectrum disorder despite region-specific alterations. Together, these findings establish connectivity allometry as a previously unrecognized organizational principle of the human functional connectome and provide a quantitative framework linking regional functional organization to whole-brain network architecture in health and disease.

doi:10.64898/2026.09.14.751602.title: CA1 reinstatement and novelty response independently support recognition memory
doi:10.64898/2026.09.14.751602.authors: Quent JA, Zhang M, Vatansever D.
doi:10.64898/2026.09.14.751602.abstract: One of the central tensions in memory research is whether consistency or differentiation across events is beneficial for remembering. While theoretical models posit that the hippocampal subfield CA1 subserves both types of computations, it remains unclear how it can simultaneously express both in service of recognition memory. Here, we contrasted the two prominent functions of CA1: reinstatement (consistency) and novelty processing (differentiation) to address this gap. To this end, we analysed the Natural Scenes Dataset featuring eight participants who completed a continuous recognition memory task spanning 41 separate days with 213,000 trials in total. We calculated reinstatement and novelty indices for each image and then examined the degree to which these reflected successful memory encoding. We found that CA1 showed evidence for encoding-related reinstatement as well as for novelty processing even after controlling for each other. Reinstatement was specific to retrieving the initial representation during the first retrieval attempt and did not extend to other forms of reinstatement. Exploratory analyses additionally identified reinstatement in CA3, which exhibited different response profiles compared to CA1. Our work thus highlights that computations of consistency as well as differentiation can be orthogonal signals contributing independently to memory success and can simultaneously co-exist within the same region of the hippocampus. Significance statement One of the central tensions in memory research is whether consistency, measured by reinstatement or differentiation, measured by activation difference across repeated events benefits remembering. While both have been associated with the hippocampal subfield CA1, it remains unclear how they can simultaneously support recognition memory. Here, we leveraged 7T precision fMRI in a densely-sampled continuous recognition task and demonstrated that reinstatement of the first representation and the novelty response co-exist in CA1. Critically, both independently predict subsequent memory success, suggesting computations of consistency and differentiation are orthogonal signals. We additionally identified subfield CA3 in which reinstatement, but not novelty, is predictive of memory, further highlighting the unique role of CA1 as a convergent hub of multiple hippocampal functions.

doi:10.1016/j.cognition.2026.106727.title: The objecthood of visual working memory representations influences their interaction with attention.
doi:10.1016/j.cognition.2026.106727.authors: Chen L, Zheng J, Xu M, Zhu P, Fu Y, Shen M, Chen H.
doi:10.1016/j.cognition.2026.106727.abstract: Visual working memory (VWM) guides attentional selection toward memory-matching information in the environment. However, in the classical VWM-driven attentional capture paradigm, this effect is substantially reduced when multiple representations are simultaneously maintained. Although this capacity limitation has been attributed to a limited number of active VWM representations, it remains unclear what constitutes the functional unit underlying this limitation. Here, we examined whether objecthood enables multiple features to function as a single unit for attentional guidance. Across five experiments, participants memorized multiple features that either belonged to the same object or to separate objects before performing a visual search task containing memory-matching distractors. Replicating previous findings, multiple features failed to produce VWM-driven attentional capture when they belonged to separate objects. Critically, when the same features were integrated into a single object, they reliably guided attention. This objecthood effect generalized from two to three colors, extended to features from different dimensions (color and orientation) and different modalities (visual and verbal color representations), and could not be explained by differences in memory fidelity. These findings suggest that the capacity limitation in VWM-driven attentional capture operates over integrated representational units rather than individual features, with objecthood serving as an effective organizational principle that integrates multiple features into a single unit for attentional guidance.

doi:10.64898/2026.09.23.753700.title: Frontoparietal effective connectivity supports working memory in early childhood
doi:10.64898/2026.09.23.753700.authors: Guedj C, Bollinger L, Marie D, Laera G, Ceresetti R, Comparini A, Richiardi J, Kliegel M, James CE.
doi:10.64898/2026.09.23.753700.abstract: Working memory (WM), a core executive function that supports learning and reasoning, undergoes rapid development during early childhood years. Neural activation patterns underlying WM have been extensively studied in both adults and children, revealing increasing involvement of the frontoparietal network (FPN) with age and coordinated interactions with the default mode network (DMN). However, relatively little is known about how these network interactions develop in children, particularly within the visuospatial domain. The present study investigated the influence of age and task performance on effective connectivity within the FPN and its interactions with DMN hubs during a visuospatial WM task in early childhood. Functional MRI data were collected during a visual n-back task with two WM load levels (0-back and 2-back) in 120 typically developing children aged 5-8 years. Dynamic Causal Modeling (DCM) with parametric empirical Bayes was used to estimate effective connectivity among eight regions of interest spanning the FPN and DMN. Behaviorally, age-related gains were steepest under high-load for accuracy, and under low-load for reaction time, suggesting WM capacity is a demand-sensitive marker of development at this age. At the network level, high-load robustly engaged the FPN, whereas low-load was associated with relatively greater engagement of DMN and episodic memory-related regions. Baseline effective connectivity was dominated by parietal-to-frontal drive and strong self-inhibition in the anterior cingulate cortex. Age-related effects on this architecture were sparse, involving asymmetric interhemispheric frontal coupling and reduced parieto-cingulate coupling, whereas accuracy-related effects were larger in magnitude, particularly at self-connections. More accurate children showed greater excitability in frontal and parietal FPN nodes alongside increased self-inhibition in the precuneus, a DMN hub, consistent with a neural efficiency account in which better performance reflects more selective, rather than more global, network engagement. Task load further shaped connectivity in distinct ways: low-load elicited widespread inter-regional modulation, whereas high-load predominantly modulated self-connections, with age and accuracy effects on this modulation dissociating by load. These findings suggest that, in primary school children, current task performance was associated with more pronounced differences in frontoparietal effective connectivity than was age, and that WM-related network engagement becomes increasingly selective and load-dependent across this developmental window.

doi:10.64898/2026.09.28.755061.title: Acoustic Monitoring of Tropical Bats: Saccopteryx bilineata’s response to habitat and time across a restoration gradient using a 2D-CNN
doi:10.64898/2026.09.28.755061.authors: Secord I, Zhang X, Preston-Allen R, Banks-Leite C.
doi:10.64898/2026.09.28.755061.abstract: Global biodiversity loss is a consequence of habitat degradation and fragmentation caused by the expansion of the Anthropocene and the overexploitation of natural resources. Passive acoustic monitoring enables longitudinal assessment of biodiversity but generates massive datasets. Advancements in machine learning have enabled the development of convolutional neural networks capable of automating this process. We developed a lightweight 2D convolutional neural network capable of detecting echolocation calls of the greater sac-winged bat, Saccopteryx bilineata , an insectivorous aerial edge-foraging bat, across a tropical restoration gradient in Pará, Brazil. The 2D-CNN model achieved a 97.84% accuracy and 100% precision. Deploying this model across 157,335 field recordings across 29 sampling points resampled over 3 years (2023-2025) yielded 2,098 positive detections of S. bilineata . Generalised linear mixed models revealed that time since reforestation significantly increased the odds of detecting S. bilineata (β = 0.22, p < 0.001), and that detection probability was 2.14 times higher in restoration plots than in forest habitats (β = 0.76, p = 0.0701). Acoustic hardware had a significant covariate influence in both fitted models (β = 0.52, β = 0.72, both p < 0.001). These findings demonstrate the practical applications of deep learning and bioacoustics to quantify habitat recovery and the value of restoration in regenerating functional ecological niches for aerial insectivores during early successional stages.

doi:10.1111/ejn.70706.title: Emergence of Deviance Detection in Cortical Cultures Through Maturation, Criticality, and Early Experience.
doi:10.1111/ejn.70706.authors: Zhang ZD, Yaron A, Akita D, Shiramatsu TI, Chao ZC, Takahashi H.
doi:10.1111/ejn.70706.abstract: Mismatch negativity (MMN) in humans is widely interpreted as reflecting deviance detection (DD) within predictive processing frameworks. However, the developmental processes by which DD emerges and matures during early cortical development remain incompletely understood. Here, we longitudinally tracked the development of DD in dissociated cortical cultures grown on high-density CMOS microelectrode arrays from Day In Vitro (DIV) 10 to DIV30 (Study 1) and compared cultures with and without early structured stimulation at DIV31-35 (Study 2). Cultures were stimulated with oddball and many-standards control paradigms while spontaneous and evoked activity were recorded. In Study 1, stimulus-evoked responses at early stages were largely confined to fast components corresponding to direct stimulation effects. From DIV15 onward, robust late responses emerged, and deviant stimuli evoked stronger responses than frequent and control stimuli, marking the emergence of DD as defined in this study. By DIV30, responses became stronger, faster, and more temporally precise. Neuronal avalanche analysis revealed a transition from subcritical to near-critical dynamics across development. Cultures exhibiting power-law-like statistics showed larger DD indices, although DD was also observed in non-critical networks. These findings indicate that critical dynamics are not required for DD, but critical-like states are associated with more robust and differentiated DD responses as networks mature. In Study 2, both groups shifted toward power-law-like avalanche distributions, with no significant difference in their developmental trajectories. At DIV31-35, stimulated cultures had earlier peak responses and lower DD indices than controls, but these group differences were not significant. Together, these findings indicate that dissociated cortical cultures can exhibit DD under simplified in vitro conditions and that its developmental trajectory is associated with network maturation and self-organization toward critical-like dynamics.

doi:10.64898/2026.09.30.755824.title: Multi-modal ion-transport function of potassium channelrhodopsins
doi:10.64898/2026.09.30.755824.authors: Shimamura R, Kikuchi M, Nakamura T, Tajima S, Fujimoto KJ, Sugiura M, Tabe J, Minamisawa K, Abe-Yoshizumi R, Nishikino T, Hososhima S, Yanai T, Furutani Y, Tsunoda SP, Kandori H.
doi:10.64898/2026.09.30.755824.abstract: Light-gated K+ channelrhodopsins (KCRs) are recognized as an ideal neuronal silencing tool in optogenetics. KCRs contain functionally important residues for a light-driven H+ pump bacteriorhodopsin, but their roles have been unclear. Utilizing electrophysiological methods, we demonstrate that KCRs function as a light-driven H+ pump in the absence of K+. Transport experiments using pH electrodes further elucidated the function of the H+-pump, which operates even in the presence of K+. The hypothesis that the H+ pump exerts a blocking effect on K+ transport in KCRs has been postulated. Furthermore, we ascertained that there was conversion of KCRs from the H+ pump into the H+ channel by light, yet this conversion was never reversed. However, the addition of K+ resulted in the formation of the K+ channel. KCRs exhibit three distinct functional states, H+ pump, H+ channel, and K+ channel. These multifaceted functions are modulated by environmental ions and light.

doi:10.64898/2026.10.02.755939.title: Motivational incentives improve working memory performance by enhancing memory-based representations rather than altering response strategies
doi:10.64898/2026.10.02.755939.authors: Nair V, Agnel O, Mızrak E, Manohar SG.
doi:10.64898/2026.10.02.755939.abstract: Motivational incentives are known to improve working memory (WM) when items differ in value, but whether they enhance performance when all items are equally valued, and if so, by what mechanism, remains unclear. Improvements could reflect enhanced memory-based representations or speed-accuracy trade-offs, whereby incentives promote slower, more cautious responding without improving memory itself. Here, we tested these alternatives across two experiments using an auditory WM task in which incentives varied across trials, but all items on a trial were equally incentivised. In Experiment 1,we allowed participants to resubmit their responses if desired. Reward-related improvements in WM performance were selectively observed when memory load was high, and only at serial positions associated with greater interference. These improvements were also dissociated from systematic response slowing and resubmission behaviour. This indicated that the benefits of incentives were unlikely to be attributable to response caution. Critically, in Experiment 2, motivational benefits persisted under strict response deadlines, where speed cannot be traded for accuracy. Computational modelling showed that reward selectively improved the precision of memory-based responses without reducing guessing. Together, these findings indicate that motivational incentives improve WM by enhancing the quality of memory-based representations, rather than by strategic slowing or altering response strategies.

doi:10.64898/2026.10.09.757763.title: The anterior insular cortex mediates higher-order threat learning and memory
doi:10.64898/2026.10.09.757763.authors: Namkung, H.; Mukherjee, B.; de Chabot, J.; Lockhart, S.; Guttman, L.; Isehak, I.; Clark, A.; Saito, A.; Miura, I.; Ishizuka, K.; Kwon, H.; Sawa, A.
doi:10.64898/2026.10.09.757763.abstract: Learning about potential threats is indispensable for survival, and its deficits underlie numerous neuropsychiatric disorders. Human brain imaging suggests the anterior insular cortex (AIC) as a key neural correlate of threat learning, yet its mechanistic role remains unclear. Leveraging multimodal systems neuroscience approaches, we demonstrate that AIC excitatory neurons, specifically layer 5 pyramidal neurons projecting to the basolateral amygdala, are essential for higher-order threat learning/memory. They are specifically required when a predictor is temporally separated from an aversive event or when the predictive information is embedded within a diffuse context. In contrast, the AIC is dispensable for elementary, temporally contiguous threat learning. Surprisingly, while the AIC promotes memory formation, it also constrains the level of fear expression during retrieval in a context-dependent manner. This bidirectional control is mediated by the recruitment of distinct AIC neuronal ensembles. Together, we identify a novel circuit mechanism for bidirectional regulation of higher-order threat learning/memory.

doi:10.31234/osf.io/rsq7g_v1.title: The Same Memory Retrieved Differently: Competition Enables Flexible Generalization in Hippocampus-like Networks
doi:10.31234/osf.io/rsq7g_v1.authors: Ralston R, Turner B, Sloutsky V.
doi:10.31234/osf.io/rsq7g_v1.abstract: Hippocampus supports the retrieval of richly detailed episodic memories from sparse cues. However, an event can be detailed and also lead to generalization. To explain both phenomena, researchers have proposed multiple memory systems or distinct memory traces for specific and general content. In contrast, we argue that a single system can support both specificity and generalization. To do this, we present ATHENA, a formal framework that reinterprets cognitive memory models as recurrent neural networks. We show that many episodic memory models are single-step approximations of dynamic networks with competitive retrieval mechanisms, similar to Modern Hopfield Networks. Notably, under a cognitive interpretation, the intensity of the competitive process is a psychologically-meaningful parameter that shapes generalization in the network. Through simulations, we demonstrate that modulating this parameter during retrieval leads the same traces to produce qualitatively different forms of generalization over the same memory traces. We then extend our analysis to sequential memory, and show how the same competitive retrieval process can be combined with known hippocampal circuits to achieve more sophisticated forms of generalization. These results demonstrate the flexibility of single-system memory retrieval and highlight the interplay of specific and general mnemonic content.

doi:10.64898/2026.10.08.26365030.title: Retinal arteriolar tortuosity as a candidate genetic window to inner-ear microvasculature: distributed sharing with blood pressure at CSK and PAWR and a roadmap for larger hearing GWAS
doi:10.64898/2026.10.08.26365030.abstract: Background The inner ear is supplied by the labyrinthine artery, which is functionally close to an end artery with limited collateral reserve. Microvascular abnormalities have been implicated in sudden sensorineural hearing loss (SSNHL) and age-related hearing loss, yet inner-ear microvasculature cannot be assessed in vivo and current hearing genome-wide association studies (GWAS) are underpowered. We evaluated the shared genetic architecture of retinal arteriolar tortuosity (retina_AT) with blood pressure, cerebral small vessel disease (cSVD) and hearing phenotypes, and examined whether retinal microvasculature could serve as a candidate genetic window to inner-ear microvasculature. Methods We used linkage-disequilibrium score regression (LDSC) to estimate SNP heritability for 19 phenotypes and genome-wide genetic correlations (rg) for 11 prespecified pairs. We ran approximate Bayes-factor colocalization (coloc.abf) between 19 independent retinal loci and systolic blood pressure (SBP), together with 95% credible-set fine-mapping, UCSC gene annotation, colocalization with GTEx aortic and tibial-artery expression QTL (eQTL) data and with white-matter hyperintensities (WMH), hearing-GWAS power calculations, and univariable and multivariable Mendelian randomization (MR) of blood pressure and heart rate on hearing. Results Only retina_AT with SBP was significant genome-wide (rg = 0.10, P = 4.2×10⁻⁵, FDR q = 0.00042). The strongest retinal locus, 13q34, did not colocalize (PP.H3 = 0.996; peaks about 267 kb apart; allelic heterogeneity), whereas two secondary loci colocalized strongly—CSK at 15q24 (PP.H4 = 0.98; 3/3 credible variants within CSK) and PAWR at 12q21 (PP.H4 = 0.99; 3/5 within PAWR)— supported by tissue-matched, moderate eQTL evidence (PP.H4 = 0.71–0.75). At 13q34, retina_AT with WMH was an adequately powered null (PP.H4 = 0.019; only this region and phenotype were tested). On the hearing side, sharing of the blood-pressure magnitude (rg ≈ 0.10) was a near-powered null (about 1.5-fold larger sample needed for 80% power under that assumption, versus about 15-fold for weak rg ≈ 0.03 sharing), and rg ≥ 0.12 was excluded; MR found no robust causal effect. Conclusions Retinal arteriolar tortuosity shows limited, distributed genetic sharing with blood pressure at the vascular-tone genes CSK and PAWR; no sharing with WMH was observed at 13q34 (only this region was tested). Retinal microvasculature may serve as a candidate genetic window to inner-ear microvasculature, but this analogy awaits direct testing by larger, vessel-oriented hearing GWAS and inner-ear tissue functional studies.

doi:10.64898/2026.10.05.756834.title: Not all memory declines with age: Neural correlates of implicit associative memory in younger and older adults.
doi:10.64898/2026.10.05.756834.authors: Davis, E. E.; Davis, S. W.; Olsen, R. K.; Campbell, K. L.
doi:10.64898/2026.10.05.756834.abstract: While explicit associative memory declines with age, implicit associative memory remains preserved. Few studies have examined the neural basis of implicit associative memory in aging, and it remains unclear whether the hippocampus is required as it is more often associated with explicit associative memory. While undergoing functional magnetic resonance imaging, young and old adults completed a speeded object categorization task in which they viewed pictured objects with superimposed words. Implicit memory was tested by presenting intact (original pairs) and rearranged pairs (items previously presented, but not together) from encoding while participants did the same categorization task. Associative priming was defined as faster reaction times (behavioural associative priming) and less activation for intact than rearranged pairs at retrieval (neural associative priming). Whole-brain analyses revealed neural associative priming in occipitotemporal and frontal regions that did not differ by age. A region of interest analysis (using subject-specific masks of medial temporal lobe regions) showed that only older adults had greater posterior hippocampal activation to intact than rearranged items at test, though activation in the hippocampus did not relate to behavioural associative priming. In contrast, greater behavioural associative priming was related to greater neural associative priming in the perirhinal cortex in both age groups. Together, these findings suggest that implicit associative priming remains intact with age, possibly because it relies on additional processes outside the hippocampus such as perirhinal-dependent unitization.

doi:10.31234/osf.io/54jba_v2.title: Psychological therapy for auditory verbal hallucinations: A qualitative assessment of voice-hearers’ experiences and preferences
doi:10.31234/osf.io/54jba_v2.authors: Brederoo S, van Ittersum G, Goedhart F, Tewelde-Kampert I, Veling W, Geraets C.
doi:10.31234/osf.io/54jba_v2.abstract: BackgroundPsychological therapy for voice-hearing is increasingly recognized as an important component of care for people who hear voices. However, relatively little is known about voice-hearers’ experiences and preferences regarding psychological interventions for voice-hearing. The present study aimed to examine this in a transdiagnostic sample of voice-hearers.MethodsAn online survey was completed by 178 voice-hearers, who were recruited through multiple community-based and clinical channels. The survey assessed experiences with psychological therapy and discussing voices with therapists, asked about treatment preferences and goals, and experiences and wishes with regard to peer support.ResultsThree-quarters of respondents had previously sought help for voice-hearing, and about half reported having been offered psychological therapy. Among those who had followed therapy, overall satisfaction was moderate to high and respondents generally reported a positive relation with their therapist. With regard to treatment goals, out of eight options respondents prioritized reducing negative consequences and distress from voice-hearing over reducing voice frequency. Understanding voices and developing coping strategies were the most highly prioritized treatment foci out of nine options. Among reasons to decline psychological therapy were having no confidence it would be helpful, it not being the right time, and not trusting the therapist. Relatively few respondents had received peer support, but a larger proportion reported a current or past need for such support.ConclusionsRespondents emphasized the importance of individualized care, a trusting therapeutic relationship, and shared-decision making. Incorporating questionnaires similar to the present survey at the start of psychological therapy may help facilitate shared decision-making and strengthen the therapeutic alliance.

doi:10.21203/rs.3.rs-11384026/v1.title: Large Language Models in Hearing Care
doi:10.21203/rs.3.rs-11384026/v1.authors: Wang S, Mo C, Wu J, Siu AKY, Zhao F, Wasmann JA, Swanepoel DW, Manchaiah V.
doi:10.21203/rs.3.rs-11384026/v1.abstract: Abstract Large language models (LLMs) may support hearing care, but evidence of clinical benefit remains unclear. We conducted a scoping review across eight databases, with searches updated in September 2026. Among 110 included reports, 95 empirical analysis units comprised 62 model-centered benchmarks, 31 application-oriented investigations, and two adoption surveys. Applications addressed assessment scoring, clinical documentation, rehabilitation content, biomedical evidence processing, psychosocial support, and research. Fourteen empirical units evaluated prototypes or target users; none tested prospective service deployment or comparative clinical impact. Privacy evaluation concerned attitudes or perceived confidentiality; no included study tested technical privacy safeguards. Current evidence supports selected task-specific capabilities, not established improvements in care. Future research should prioritize applications addressing defined hearing-care needs and compare them with usual care or simpler alternatives. Evaluation should measure patient and professional benefit, safety, privacy, accessibility, and workload rather than response accuracy alone.

doi:10.64898/2026.09.27.754757.title: The development of slow and fast theta oscillations in the human brain
doi:10.64898/2026.09.27.754757.authors: Cross, Z. R.; Gray, S. M.; Dede, A. J. O.; Rivera, Y. M.; Yin, Q.; Vahidi, P.; Rau, E. M. B.; Cyr, C.; Holubecki, A. M.; Asano, E.; McManus, O. K.; Sattar, S.; Saez, I.; Girgis, F.; King-Stephens, D.; Weber, P. B.; Laxer, K. D.; Schuele, S. U.; Wu, J. Y.; Kam, S. K.; Raskin, J. S.; Shaikhouni, A.; Brunner, P.; Roland, J. L.; Braga, R. M.; Knight, R. T.; Ofen, N.; Johnson, E. L.
doi:10.64898/2026.09.27.754757.abstract: Theta oscillations are pivotal for attention and memory, with developmental shifts in theta activity and connectivity tracking memory ability across the lifespan. Building on initial evidence that the theta band separates into slow and fast sub-bands across development within the medial temporal lobe (MTL) and the prefrontal cortex (PFC), this preregistered study (https://osf.io/gsru7) characterized the frequencies of slow (~1.5-4.5 Hz) and fast (~4.5-9.0 Hz) theta oscillations across the brain in a large developmental cohort. We analyzed intracranial EEG (iEEG) recordings from widespread brain regions in 101 children and adults (5.93-54.00 years, 63 males; n electrodes = 5691) using task-based (attention to to-be-remembered visual stimuli) and task-free (resting-state) data. We reveal distinct slow and fast theta oscillations in all regions and identify a spatial gradient in both frequency ranges, with slow theta oscillations speeding up and fast theta oscillations slowing down from posterior to anterior regions. The dissociation between slow and fast theta frequencies peaks during young adulthood, mirroring the developmental trajectory of attention and memory. In the hippocampus and PFC, attentional state (task-based, task-free) modulated age effects, and individual differences in task-based slow theta frequencies predicted individual differences in memory performance, linking the development of slow theta oscillations to the development of memory. Gray matter volume was not associated with age- or task-related differences in theta frequencies, suggesting that the development of theta oscillations is independent of regional brain structure. This study establishes developmental trajectories of slow and fast theta oscillations in localized brain regions and links the maturation of hippocampal and PFC slow theta oscillations to the development of attention and memory.

doi:10.64898/2026.09.23.753025.title: Auricular vagus nerve stimulation facilitates contextual fear extinction via insular–mPFC pathway without affecting reconsolidation
doi:10.64898/2026.09.23.753025.authors: Kuniishi H, Takeuchi E, Hashimoto O, Yamada M, Sekiguchi M, Matsuzaki H.
doi:10.64898/2026.09.23.753025.abstract: Cervical vagus nerve stimulation (VNS) suppresses conditioned fear in rodents and may serve as an adjunct to exposure-based therapy for anxiety disorders. Non-invasive auricular VNS also reduces conditioned fear in humans, although the underlying mechanisms remain unclear. Using a contextual fear conditioning paradigm, in which brief re-exposure induces reconsolidation and prolonged re-exposure promotes extinction learning in mice, we examined whether auricular VNS modulates these distinct memory processes. Auricular VNS during prolonged, but not brief, re-exposure reduced subsequent freezing, indicating facilitation of extinction learning without affecting reconsolidation. Stimulation restricted to the latter half of prolonged re-exposure, when extinction learning was underway, was sufficient to reduce subsequent fear responses. As a potential neural circuit mechanism, we focused on projections from the posterior insular cortex (pIC) to the medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC). The pIC receives interoceptive signals, including vagal input, whereas the mPFC plays a key role in fear regulation. Auricular VNS during extinction learning increased c-Fos expression in pIC neurons projecting to the infralimbic and dorsal peduncular cortex (IL/DP) within the mPFC. Optogenetic activation of the pIC– IL/DP pathway mimicked the extinction-facilitating effect of auricular VNS, whereas inhibition blocked it. These results demonstrate that auricular VNS promotes extinction learning of contextual fear memory by activating the pIC–IL/DP circuit, providing insight into how vagal afferent stimulation engages insular–prefrontal networks to modulate fear.

doi:10.64898/2026.09.30.755786.title: Spontaneous slow waves index multiple dimensions of recovery in Disorders of Consciousness
doi:10.64898/2026.09.30.755786.authors: Ruyant Belabbas A, Boullet A, Manasova D, Le Coz A, Valente M, Lejeune F, Sitt JD, Naccache L, Rohaut B, Andrillon T.
doi:10.64898/2026.09.30.755786.abstract: ABSTRACT Whether and how residual awareness is expressed in patients with Disorders of Consciousness (DoC) depends on the severity of brain damage and the transient functional state of the cortex at assessment. Classically, DoC are associated with electroencephalographic (EEG) slowing, marked by high-amplitude slow waves, even during the day. Yet, slow waves are also a hallmark of healthy sleep, where they are thought to serve restorative functions and to help maintain network homeostasis. Here, we asked whether slow waves in DoC can provide insights into the severity of cortical dysfunction or, conversely, into the preservation of residual awareness and recovery potential, by characterizing their spatial, temporal and morphological properties. We analyzed 256-channel EEG recorded during the ‘Local-Global’ auditory paradigm in 236 DoC patients, including 123 in Unresponsive Wakefulness Syndrome (UWS), 62 in a Minimally Conscious State minus (MCS-) and 29 in MCS plus (MCS+). High-amplitude slow waves were detected as local events, and their density, amplitude and slopes were quantified scalp-wide and channel-wise, by mean level and temporal variability across the recording. Slow-wave features were related to concurrent (Coma Recovery Scale-Revised - CRS-R, ‘Local-Global’ paradigm) and follow-up (one-year Glasgow Outcome Scale-Extended - GOS-E) assessments of consciousness and functional recovery. Associations with MRI-derived measures of cortical integrity and structural connectivity, and differences between anoxic and traumatic etiologies, were also examined. Slow waves were more frequent in less severe DoC patients (i.e., MCS) compared to UWS. Slow-wave slopes were also steeper frontally and increased at a faster rate in patients exhibiting higher levels of consciousness and/or markers of conscious access during the ‘Local-Global’ paradigm. More frequent and steeper slow waves at baseline further predicted recovery of consciousness and of functional independence at one year. At the individual level, slow-wave features classified states of consciousness above chance (AUC = 0.62 and 0.71 for MCS- and MCS+ versus UWS), whereas outcome prediction remained modest (0.56-0.58). These clinical associations had a structural basis: slow-wave occurrence was greater after traumatic than anoxic injury and scaled with the integrity of subcortico-cortical projection fibers and consciousness-related cortical networks. Contrary to the classical view of delta activity as a non-specific marker of impaired consciousness, prominent spontaneous slow waves indexed behavioral and neurophysiological signs of awareness and better recovery. Beyond reflecting a propensity for pathological bistability, they may also signal the integrity of the networks required to generate them, together with their residual capacity for dynamic regulation. Highlights Spontaneous slow waves were detected as discrete local events in 236 DoC patients, moving beyond time-averaged spectral measures of cortical slowing. Slow-wave properties carried diagnostic information about the state of consciousness, whether defined behaviorally (CRS-R) or neurophysiologically (conscious access to auditory information in ‘Local-Global’ ERP paradigm). Slow wave frequency and slope during the acute phase in the ICU predicted improvement of consciousness state and recovery of functional independence at one year. Within-session ‘fatigue-like’ temporal modulation of slow waves increased with the level of consciousness recovery, being more pronounced in MCS+ than in UWS and MCS-patients. Slow-wave expression scaled with subcortico-cortical fibers and cortical network integrity, and was greater after traumatic than anoxic injury, suggesting they signal preserved network integrity rather than damage alone.

doi:10.64898/2026.10.05.756590.title: Moving object generates topographic responses in the majority of entorhinal neurons
doi:10.64898/2026.10.05.756590.authors: Purandare, C. S.; Durand, S.; Hardcastle, B.; Gillis, R.; Carlson, M.; Belski, H.; Peene, C.; Bawany, A.; Jha, S.; Amaya, A.; Ha, V.; Han, W.; Ouellette, B.; Johnson, T.; Naidoo, R.; Nguyen, K.; Suarez, L.; Wilkes, J.; Young, A.; Caldejon, S.; Swapp, J.; Williford, A.; Groblewski, P.; Lecoq, J.; Mehta, M. R.
doi:10.64898/2026.10.05.756590.abstract: Vision is crucial in generating a complex array of responses in rodents during spatial exploration and in humans during memory tasks. These tasks involve other variables too, e.g. multisensory cues in rodents and complex memories in humans. Further, there are major differences between the medial and lateral entorhinal cortical (MEC and LEC) functional cell types. To understand the contribution of purely visual information to entorhinal responses, we presented a simple, moving vertical bar of light to head-fixed mice, without any task or reward. Surprisingly, 66% (2391/3601) of the MEC broad spiking neurons were significantly modulated by the bar position on the screen. Visual tuning in MEC had a pronounced dorsoventral topography --the tuning strength dropped from 79% in the dorsal most quartile to 40% in the ventral most quartile. Unlike major differences in spatial and other codes between MEC and LEC during free foraging experiments, LEC cells showed very similar visual tuning (392/606, 65%), including the dorso-ventral gradient in LEC5. Additionally, the majority of putative interneurons, from MEC as well as LEC, showed similar, widespread visual tuning, unlike spatial tasks. Neurons also encoded the object motion direction (naso-temporal vs. temporo-nasal visual motion) with changes in mean rate, tuning strength and/or tuning location. Such directional nature of visual tuning indicates significant history-dependence or sequence encoding. Consistently, replacing the continuous motion by randomly flashing bar of light abolished bar-tuning in two-thirds of continuous bar-tuned cells and substantially altered tuning in the rest. These results reveal the contribution of purely visual inputs in generating anatomically organized responses in the majority of entorhinal neurons. The prevalence and similarity of visual tuning across all layers of MEC as well as LEC exceeds that of other known functional cell types (like grid cells in MEC or egocentric object tuning/time-cells in LEC) during spatial navigation tasks and could be foundational in understanding entorhinal complexity.

doi:10.7554/elife.106148.title: Individual dopaminergic neurons induce unique, yet overlapping combinations of behavioural modulations, including safety learning, memory retrieval, and acute locomotion.
doi:10.7554/elife.106148.authors: Toshima N, Behrad A, Behnke F, Kaushik G, Weiglein A, Strauch M, Thoener J, Kobler O, Wang MLM, Fukushima A, Dörr M, Schleyer M.
doi:10.7554/elife.106148.abstract: Two evolutionary highly conserved functions of dopamine are to carry 'teaching' signals during associative learning and to control movement. In mammals and humans, these functions are generally thought to be produced by different populations of neurons. Here, we investigated in the larva of Drosophila melanogaster whether both these functions can be induced by the same individual dopaminergic neurons in the central brain. Focusing on the dopaminergic neurons of the DL1 cluster, we asked whether the optogenetic activation of individual neurons established associative punishment and/or safety memories, controlled the retrieval of the established memories, and acutely modulated locomotion. We found that each neuron had a unique yet overlapping set of behavioural effects. Several individual neurons both established a memory and modulated acute locomotion by increasing the animals' bending and decreasing their velocity. Our results demonstrate that individual dopaminergic neurons can fulfil a surprisingly broad range of functions in different behavioural contexts. Given the highly conserved roles of the dopaminergic system across the animal kingdom, this study raises the question whether a similarly diverse functionality can be found also in other animals, including humans.

doi:10.64898/2026.10.13.758866.title: Comparing re-referencing methods for human intracranial EEG
doi:10.64898/2026.10.13.758866.authors: Kolibius, L. D.; Parish, G.; van der Plas, M.; Ter Wal, M.; Rollings, D.; Gollwitzer, S.; Walther, K.; Hopfengärtner, R.; Hamer, H.; Wimber, M.; Hanslmayr, S.
doi:10.64898/2026.10.13.758866.abstract: Stereo-electroencephalography (SEEG) involves the implantation of depth electrodes in the brain to monitor epileptic seizures for surgical feasibility. As the electrodes advance into deeper limbic structures, the macro contacts distributed along the shaft record electrical activity from more lateral sites, while a bundled array of microwires simultaneously captures highly localised signals from the tip of the electrode. In a clinical setting these electrical signals are recorded relative to a reference signal, which may be sub-optimal for subsequent analyses that are unrelated to clinical objectives. Therefore, a secondary re-referencing operation is often undertaken to transform the signal in relation to a specific hypothesis. Despite a recent surge in SEEG studies, comparative studies on the much-understudied issue of re-referencing are sparse. Here, we analyse data collected from 16 human patients during an episodic memory task and comparatively apply a range of re-referencing methods to both macro contact and micro-wire data. We find that the choice of method changes the proportion of trials that survive artefact rejection, low frequency power, and the aperiodic background against which that power is read. In the hippocampal recordings, however, no method differed from any other in the size of a memory effect in power or spike-field coherence. This early transformative decision therefore bears on how the signal is described. We found no evidence that it changes the detectability of the behavioural effects tested here, and no method reversed the direction of a memory effect.

doi:10.1016/j.brainres.2026.150574.title: Neural processing of facial expressions: An ERP study in athletes and non-athletes.
doi:10.1016/j.brainres.2026.150574.authors: Wu C, Li X, Astikainen P.
doi:10.1016/j.brainres.2026.150574.abstract: Facial expressions are important cues for conveying social-emotional information, and their processing unfolds across multiple neural stages. The study employed event-related potentials to examine the neural dynamics of facial-expression change detection while testing the role of sports expertise. It further examined whether N170 responses showed prediction-error-related enhancement. Non-athletes, team-sport athletes, and individual-sport athletes completed ignore- and attend-oddball tasks, with angry and happy faces presented as rare stimulus types (deviants) and neutral faces as the frequent stimulus type (standard). An ignore-equiprobable task provided physically identical, probability-matched control stimuli for angry and happy deviants. For P1 in both oddball conditions, amplitudes were smaller for happy than for angry and neutral faces, suggesting expression-related modulation during early sensory encoding. For N170, amplitudes showed a robust graded pattern (angry > happy > neutral, more negative) in each task condition, indicating sensitivity to expression category during perceptual face representation. For P3b in the attend-oddball condition, amplitudes were larger for angry and happy faces than for neutral faces, and larger for angry than for happy faces, consistent with greater resource allocation to rare emotional targets, particularly angry faces, during task-relevant target detection and stimulus evaluation. Separately, comparison of N170 responses to probability-matched deviant and control stimuli provided no evidence for prediction-error-related N170 enhancement for either angry or happy faces. No reliable modulation by sports expertise was observed in the present sample and task conditions. Overall, multistage neural responses were strongly shaped by expression category, highlighting expression-related effects on early sensory, perceptual, and later evaluative processing.

doi:10.64898/2026.09.14.751605.title: T2 relaxometry for myelin water fraction: an ex vivo brain imaging study
doi:10.64898/2026.09.14.751605.authors: Sanches, L.; Taghizadehsalehabad, N.; Moqadam, R.; Adame-Gonzalez, W.; Alasmar, Z.; Mirault, D.; Piredda, G. F.; Turecki, G.; Maranzano, J.; Mechawar, N.; The CIMA-Q group, ; Chakravarty, M.; Dadar, M.; Zeighami, Y.
doi:10.64898/2026.09.14.751605.abstract: Abstract Introduction: Myelin water imaging provides a non-invasive approach for indirectly investigating myelin content of the brain by magnetic resonance Imaging (MRI). Myelin water fraction (MWF) reflects the fraction of water signal associated with water trapped between myelin layers. Postmortem imaging provides a unique opportunity to validate MWF metrics against gold-standard postmortem neuropathology. However, there is a need for validated sequences that would be applicable in postmortem settings. In this study, we validated and compared the applicability of turbo spin echo (TSE) and gradient-and-spin-echo (GRASE) techniques for myelin water imaging in formaldehyde fixed postmortem human brains. Methods: 40 postmortem human brain hemispheres were scanned with TSE and GRASE sequences. Acquired data were reconstructed using a non-parametric multicomponent T2 relaxometry approach using a consistent framework to support comparison between GRASE- and TSE-derived measures. Agreement between derived measures was quantified at both voxel and regional level. Maps derived from the full 32-echo GRASE reconstruction were compared against a truncated 14-echo reconstruction to examine the contribution of the longer echoes to the derived maps. Finally, a random forest regression model was trained based on TSE data to predict the GRASE-derived MWF maps. Results: Both sequences provided robust multicomponent T2 characterization across the brain, and the derived measures showed anatomical patterns consistent with expected differences across tissue types. TSE and GRASE derived maps had moderate to strong agreement at voxel (0.41 0.98, pFDR < 0.001). The nonlinear random forest regression model trained on TSE maps was able to accurately reproduce the MWF maps derived from GRASE (r = 0.91, RMSE = 8.87). Discussion: TSE and GRASE32 capture strongly related multicomponent T2 information in fixed postmortem human brain tissue, but with systematic and tissue-dependent quantitative differences across derived measures. These differences suggest that direct interchangeability should not be assumed and that cross-sequence mapping or calibration is required when quantitative equivalence is desired.

doi:10.31234/osf.io/acwsy_v1.title: A modality-general bias towards meaning, not enhanced prior knowledge, is linked to hallucination-proneness in the general population
doi:10.31234/osf.io/acwsy_v1.authors: Hammers F, Wu X, Alderson-Day B, Clarke C, Blake E, Evans S.
doi:10.31234/osf.io/acwsy_v1.abstract: Predictive processing theories propose that hallucinations arise from excessive influence of prior expectations on perception. Although these theories implicitly generalise across modalities, previous findings suggest potentially different mechanisms in vision and audition. In this study, we tested predictive processing accounts in the visual and auditory modalities in 177 healthy adults using well-matched prior knowledge tasks. Participants discriminated degraded meaningful targets from control stimuli before and after exposure to clear template stimuli, providing explicit prior knowledge. Signal detection analyses quantified pre-exposure response bias (criterion, C) and improvements in discrimination sensitivity (d′) following exposure. Hallucination-proneness was measured using the Cardiff Anomalous Perceptions Scale (CAPS). Prior knowledge improved discrimination equally across modalities, but individual differences in this benefit were unrelated to hallucination-proneness, with Bayesian analyses supporting the null hypothesis. Instead, hallucination-proneness was associated with a more liberal pre-exposure response bias in both modalities. When entered together in regression models, response bias was a stronger predictor of hallucination-proneness than prior knowledge benefit in both modalities. These findings suggest that hallucination-proneness is characterised by a modality-general bias towards meaningful interpretations of ambiguous sensory input, rather than enhanced directed use of prior knowledge.

doi:10.64898/2026.09.25.754337.title: Goals Drive Adaptive Analysis of Linguistic Features During Reading
doi:10.64898/2026.09.25.754337.authors: Alex P, Schwarz J, Tatler BW, Konopka A, Klimovich-Gray A.
doi:10.64898/2026.09.25.754337.abstract: Reading behaviour is sensitive to contextual demands. For example, when reading to study or answer questions, readers strategically allocate more attention to goal-relevant sections, read slower, and regress more frequently to extract specific information based on task demands. This suggests that readers flexibly adapt their strategies according to goals and situational constraints. However, the neurocognitive mechanisms supporting this flexibility remain unclear. To test this, we combined eye-tracking with EEG during naturalistic reading and examined how short-term reading goals modulated the neural tracking of hierarchical linguistic features at the orthographic (orthographic neighbourhood size), lexical (word frequency), and contextual-semantic (Surprisal) levels. Forty native English speakers read narratives in three goal conditions: Baseline (no goal), Proofreading (detect spelling errors), and Comprehension (attend to content). Fixation-aligned word-level EEG activity was modelled using multivariate temporal response function to estimate the strength of feature-specific neural tracking. Orthographic tracking was significantly enhanced during Proofreading relative to Baseline, and predicted better Proofreading accuracy. Conversely, stronger frequency tracking predicted better Comprehension accuracy. Contextual-semantic tracking was not modulated by task goal. These findings suggest that reading goals selectively bias neural processing towards linguistic features (sublexical vs. lexical) that support successful task performance, providing evidence for short-term functional plasticity in linguistic processing and supporting a flexible predictive processing account of goal-directed reading.

doi:10.64898/2026.09.21.753134.title: O -mannosylation of fibrocystin and fibrocystin-L expands TMEM260 sequon selectivity and provides a potential link to the renal and auditory phenotypes of SHDRA
doi:10.64898/2026.09.21.753134.authors: Kaynert J, Hopf C, Brand-Merseburger S, Garbers C, Pich A, Buettner FFR.
doi:10.64898/2026.09.21.753134.abstract: Protein O- mannosylation in the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) regulates the maturation and function of extracellular proteins, yet the substrate spectrum and biological functions of individual O- mannosyltransferases remain incompletely understood. TMEM260 is an ER-resident O- mannosyltransferase that modifies immunoglobulin-like, plexins, transcription factors (IPT) domains. Here, we identify fibrocystin and fibrocystin-L, encoded by PKHD1 and PKHD1L1 , respectively, as novel TMEM260-mediated O- mannosylated proteins. By combining screening of human proteomic datasets with mass spectrometry-based analysis of IPT domains expressed in TMEM260-deficient HEK293 cells, we demonstrate that multiple IPT domains of fibrocystin and fibrocystin-L are modified by TMEM260. Our findings expand the known substrate requirements of TMEM260 by revealing tolerance of substantial sequon variation and demonstrating serine as an alternative acceptor residue within IPT domains. In humans, loss-of-function variants in TMEM260 cause structural heart defects and renal anomalies (SHDRA) syndrome, whereas pathogenic variants in fibrocystin cause autosomal recessive polycystic kidney disease (ARPKD). Notably, patients with SHDRA and ARPKD share overlapping renal phenotypes, suggesting that impaired TMEM260 function may phenocopy aspects of fibrocystin-associated diseases. Given that fibrocystin is a substrate protein for TMEM260-mediated O- mannosylation, these findings raise the possibility that functional impairment of TMEM260 causes aberrant O- mannosylation of fibrocystin. Thereby fibrocystin function might be compromised leading to the renal phenotype observed in patients with TMEM260 mutations. To directly assess the functional relevance of this modification, we expressed recombinant fibrocystin fragments in TMEM260-deficient cells complemented with either wild-type TMEM260 or a catalytically inactive TMEM260 mutant. Further, we investigate the O- mannosylation of the threonine residue directly C- terminal to the ARPKD-associated patient mutation L1407R. Strikingly, substitution of leucine L1407 by the patient-associated arginine residue, completely abolished O- mannosylation of the adjacent threonine, demonstrating that this disease-associated mutation directly disrupts a TMEM260-dependent O- mannosylation site. Together, our findings establish fibrocystin and fibrocystin-L as TMEM260-dependent O- mannosylated proteins and reveal a potential molecular mechanism linking defective TMEM260-mediated O- mannosylation to the renal phenotype of SHDRA, which overlaps with PKHD1 -associated ARPKD.

doi:10.64898/2026.09.17.752300.title: Beyond the glass: testing visitor effects on the behavior of captive teleost fish in public aquaria
doi:10.64898/2026.09.17.752300.authors: Vincent L, Turco T, Mourin J, Attia J, Tribot AS.
doi:10.64898/2026.09.17.752300.abstract: ABSTRACT Zoos and public aquariums serve as essential hubs for wildlife conservation, public education, and scientific research; however, the success of these missions depends upon maintaining high animal welfare standards despite constant human presence. A primary concern is the ‘visitor effect’: the alteration of animal behavior due to human presence. While this phenomenon is well-documented in captive mammals and has been explored in chondrichthyes, it remains largely unexamined in teleost fish, despite evidence of their sensitivity to human stimuli in natural environments. This study addresses this knowledge gap by investigating the behavioral responses of 13 teleost species to varying levels of crowd density, direct human solicitation, and ambient noise. Our multivariate analysis reveals that visitor density and visitor-induced disturbances are significant drivers of behavioral change, with species identity acting as the primary source of variance. We observed high inter-taxonomic variability: while several species (including Euxiphipops sextriatus, Dascyllus aruanus , and Zebrasoma flavescens ) showed marked sensitivity through significant alterations in stress-coping, exploration, and aggression, others remained behaviorally stable. Furthermore, acoustic analysis indicates a complex soundscape where visitor density correlates with increased sound amplitude, particularly in the 100 Hz to 400 Hz range—a critical band for teleost hearing—suggesting that visitor-induced noise is distinct from the aquarium’s technical background noise. These findings underscore that the ‘visitor effect’ is not a uniform phenomenon but a complex interaction shaped by species-specific sensitivity and distinct anthropogenic stressors. Our results highlight the necessity of incorporating species-specific behavioral data and acoustic monitoring into welfare management protocols to better mitigate the impact of human presence on captive fish populations.

doi:10.1016/j.brainres.2026.150557.title: Retraction notice to "Increased hemispheric functional connectivity compensates speech perception in older adults with hearing loss" [Brain Res. 1876 (2026) 150201].
doi:10.1016/j.brainres.2026.150557.authors: Liu Y, Ding J, Wang S, Kou N, Wang S.

doi:10.31234/osf.io/hjfzq_v3.title: Orthography Shapes L2 Stress PerceptionAcross Development: Evidence from L1 Mandarin Learners of Portuguese
doi:10.31234/osf.io/hjfzq_v3.abstract: Despite growing evidence that written input shapes second-language speech learning, its role in suprasegmental acquisition remains underexplored. This study examines whether orthography facilitates lexical stress identification through syllable weight. Portuguese is well suited for this question because stress placement is strongly conditioned by syllable weight, which is transparently encoded in the writing system. A total of 186 L1 Mandarin speakers identified stress location in Portuguese pseudowords presented either auditorily or with accompanying written forms. Naïve listeners used syllable weight as a stress cue only when orthographic information was available, whereas experienced learners showed weight sensitivity from auditory input alone. For experienced learners, however, orthography did not further enhance weight sensitivity; instead, it biased responses toward the default penultimate- stress pattern. These findings suggest that orthographic effects change over L2 development, interacting with auditory cue weighting and distributional regularities in L2 stress perception.

doi:10.1523/jneurosci.0492-26.2026.title: Prioritization in Working Memory Reduces Interference via Beta Band-Linked Stimulus Transformations.
doi:10.1523/jneurosci.0492-26.2026.abstract: We studied the effects of prioritization in a two-step retrocuing task in which male and female humans hold two items in working memory, and the item not cued by the first cue cannot be dropped because it may be prioritized by the second cue. In Experiment 1, using a dense sampling procedure, recall performance oscillated at 15 Hz ("low-beta") in the prioritization task, in comparison with 20 Hz ("higher-beta") in a matched neutral-cue task. Furthermore, the prioritized item was shielded from bias exerted by the uncued item, as well as by items from the previous trial. In Experiment 2, we sought EEG correlates of these effects while participants performed variants of the two tasks. The prioritization cue uniquely triggered a phase reset at 15 Hz and an increase in oscillatory peaks at the "low-beta" frequency. Burst analysis ruled out bursting as a possible underlying factor. Self-correlation analysis of the EEG time series revealed that the prioritization cue triggered greater reorganization of the whole-topography EEG pattern than the neutral cue and for the uncued item than for the cued item. These results provide evidence that the shielding effects of prioritization may arise from the transformation of the not-prioritized item into an "unprioritized" state that is implemented and maintained by a mechanism that cycles in the "low-beta" frequency range (centered on roughly 15 Hz).
journal_names: The Journal of neuroscience : the official journal of the Society for Neuroscience

doi:10.64898/2026.09.28.755184.title: Distinct EEG microstate signatures across different pain types
doi:10.64898/2026.09.28.755184.authors: Rabiei P, Champagne A, Barrette L, Fakhry N, Massé-Alarie H, Coll M.
doi:10.64898/2026.09.28.755184.abstract: Pain is associated with dynamic brain reorganization. Electroencephalographic microstates can characterize transient large-scale brain states, yet findings across pain studies are inconsistent. Two features may contribute: conditions have been studied in isolation, and analytical pipelines vary widely. We applied a harmonized analysis pipeline across three pain conditions: capsaicin-induced pain, assessed within participants against a pain-free baseline, and non-chronic and chronic back pain, each compared with matched controls. Using a five-minute resting-state electroencephalographic recordings we examined microstate topography, temporal expression and transition probabilities, and directly compared pain-related differences across pain states. We identified five microstates (A-E), corresponding to auditory, visual, salience, and attentional networks. Capsaicin pain showed increased expression of microstate C and reduced expression of microstates A, D and E. Transitions were redistributed towards microstate C, indicating a shift toward salience-related processing at the expense of sensory and attentional dynamics. In clinical back pain, effects were smaller and diverged by pain type: non-chronic back pain showed lower microstate C occurrence, opposite in direction to the capsaicin effect, whereas chronic back pain showed lower microstate D global explained variance, suggesting salience and attentional differences in clinical pain. Direct comparisons showed weaker pain-related increases in microstate C expression in both clinical back pain groups than capsaicin pain, with additional differences involving microstates A, D and E. These findings argue against a unitary EEG microstate signature of pain and instead reveal pain-type-specific patterns of large-scale brain dynamics, with microstate C providing the clearest distinction between experimental and clinical pain.

doi:10.64898/2026.10.05.756655.title: The RNA-binding protein TRIM71 Promotes Supporting Cell Reprogramming and Hair Cell Regeneration by Activating Sall4
doi:10.64898/2026.10.05.756655.authors: Li L, Huang H, Meng S, Liu X, Wang Y, Qiao R, Xuan Y, Hu Q, Ma X, Ma H, Dong S, Wang Y, Zhang Y, Sun B, Li J, Kolanus W, Doetzlhofer A, Li X.
doi:10.64898/2026.10.05.756655.abstract: Hair cell (HC) loss in the auditory organ (cochlea) is irreversible and represents the leading cause of deafness in humans. The absence of HC regeneration is primarily due to the limited plasticity of cochlear supporting cells (SCs). Using a novel doxycycline-inducible TRIM71 transgenic mouse model, this study demonstrates that overexpression of the RNA-binding protein TRIM71 promotes spontaneous cochlear HC regeneration in neonatal mice. Experiments in cochlear organoids indicate that TRIM71 reprograms SCs into progenitor-like cells and that this reprogramming is further enhanced by coactivation of follistatin (FST). FST augments TRIM71-induced increases in chromatin accessibility at progenitor and HC-specific gene loci, facilitating their transcriptional activation in SCs. Notably, FST also enhances TRIM71-induced reactivation of Sall4, which, like Trim71, is highly expressed in early otic progenitors. Using cochlear organoids and explants, we show that the early otic transcription factor SALL4 is required for TRIM71-induced HC formation. By contrast, SALL4 overexpression inhibits HC formation by maintaining reprogrammed SCs in an undifferentiated, proliferative state. These findings establish TRIM71 as an activator of HC regeneration in vivo, provide mechanistic insights into TRIM71’s role in SC reprogramming, and identify SALL4 as its essential effector. Significance Statement The mammalian cochlea lacks intrinsic capacity for hair cell (HC) regeneration, a deficiency that underlies the permanent nature of hearing loss. Using a novel inducible transgenic mouse model, we demonstrate that reactivation of Trim71, an otic progenitor gene, promotes HC regeneration in perinatal mice. TRIM71 induces an otic progenitor-like transcriptional program in supporting cells (SCs) through Sall4 activation, while concurrently initiating mesenchymal gene expression. This conflicting transcriptional state is resolved by co-activating follistatin, which suppresses mesenchymal conversion genes and increases chromatin accessibility at progenitor- and HC-specific gene loci. Collectively, our findings establish a mechanistic framework wherein TRIM71 functions as a key regulator of SC plasticity and identify the transcription factor SALL4 as a critical downstream effector in HC regeneration.

doi:10.64898/2026.10.01.755866.title: cyto7: an open, vertex-level cortical type atlas of the human cortex
doi:10.64898/2026.10.01.755866.authors: Salvador, R.; Mercadal, B.; Castaldo, F.; Garcia-Cabezas, M. A.; Ruffini, G.
doi:10.64898/2026.10.01.755866.abstract: The cerebral cortex is organized along a gradient of laminar complexity, indexed principally by the emergence and granularity of layer IV and by the size of layer III neuron somata, and cortical types are the ordered categories along it. The Structural Model builds on that gradient to predict laminar connectivity, plasticity and disease vulnerability (Barbas and Rempel-Clower, 1997; Garcia-Cabezas et al., 2019). Existing digital cortical-type maps are area-level: they assign one type per classical area and cannot represent a type boundary that runs through an area. We release cyto7, an open, vertex-level, seven-type cortical-type atlas delineated on the fsaverage surface following the Garcia-Cabezas protocol and revised by the protocol's authors. We distribute the atlas with a reusable quality-control and support framework.
