A topological audit reports the map against four spatial rules that follow from cortical type analysis and the dual origin of the neocortex theory: neighbouring vertices differ by at most one type, the least complex cortex forms one continuous limbic belt, eulaminate II forms a single matrix enclosing a few holes, and eulaminate III and koniocortex form isolated islands. These were imposed during construction rather than tested, and the audit reports what imposing them cost. A vertex-wise benchmark against the existing area-level map, one type per von Economo-Koskinas area, shows exact agreement at 52.5% of vertices, with disagreement almost always a single level and concentrated inside the large, heterogeneous areas that a single areal label cannot resolve. Where the two maps disagree, cyto7's label better matches the independent multimodal profile in 60.1% of pooled feature-by-vertex comparisons, against 46% under a rotation null and 54% under granularity-matched alternative partitions (p = 0.020), the harder of the two. A per-vertex anatomical support score, computed from anatomy alone, states how strongly each hand-drawn label is backed by the anatomical evidence, and is deliberately not a calibrated error probability. We then validate cyto7 against independent brain measures not used to define it, under a spatial-autocorrelation (spin) null with FDR control. Intracortical myelin (T1w/T2w) increases, cortical thickness decreases, and the principal functional-connectivity gradient reverses along the type axis (all q of about 0.006 or less). Source-reconstructed resting-state MEG dynamics also track the axis: the intrinsic timescale shortens toward koniocortex (rho of about -0.46) and survives the null, as do the spectral centroid and the slow/fast band-power ratio, whereas the aperiodic 1/f exponent does not. The laminar marker genes are where cyto7 differs most from a quantisation of a continuous map: it shows a larger absolute correlation with the layer-IV marker RORB (rho = +0.78) and the layer-V marker FEZF2 (-0.59) than seven-level septiles of myelin, of the functional gradient or of a histological gradient, on four of five markers, while tying or losing to those septiles on the macroscale proxies. These are larger observed associations against three tested quantisations, not a test that the differences between maps are reliable, and they do not establish the accuracy of any individual boundary. Defined from anatomy alone, cyto7 recovers the sensorimotor-to-association hierarchy and, on these markers, some of the laminar signal underlying it. It is released with its full pipeline and an uncalibrated anatomical support score as a reusable substrate for structure-function and modelling studies.
doi:10.64898/2026.10.01.755866.institution: Neuroelectrics Barcelona SLU (Spain); Barcelona Computational Foundation, Barcelona, Spain.

doi:10.31234/osf.io/n2sfm_v1.title: srifm: Role of lexical information for perceptual learning
doi:10.31234/osf.io/n2sfm_v1.authors: Cristia A, Hultén A, Mitterer H.
doi:10.31234/osf.io/n2sfm_v1.abstract: Linguistic representations continue to be updated, probably implicitly, as a side effect of normal language use. In particular, a large body of work shows that we learn novel pronunciations of well-established phonemic categories rapidly (Norris, McQueen, & Cutler, 2003). This learning is thought to be automatic, such that it operates quickly once there is sufficient information to disambiguate the identity of that novel pronunciation: Effects are seen after encountering 10 instances of the ambiguous sound within unambiguous lexical items. Here, we uses perceptual learning to test predictions from two types of theories of speech perception, lexical feedback models (e.g., TRACE, McClelland & Elman, 1986; Magnuson et al., 2003) and autonomous models (e.g., Shortlist, Norris, 1994; Merge, McQueen & Cutler, 2010). According to TRACE, phonemes, and words are tracked in the input in parallel, and decisions at both of these levels are influenced online by the other levels. In this model, disambiguation is driven by the lexical level. In contrast, Merge postulates that listeners accumulate knowledge of sublexical representations, such as diphone probabilities, in addition to lexical knowledge.

doi:10.64898/2026.10.08.757623.title: Domain-specific and domain-general signatures of dyscalculia in computational models of behavior and parietal cortex
doi:10.64898/2026.10.08.757623.authors: Renkert, M. F.; de Hollander, G.; Biegel, C.; Valk, S.; Kucian, K.; Ruff, C. C.
doi:10.64898/2026.10.08.757623.abstract: Developmental dyscalculia is a learning disorder characterized by marked difficulties in numerical cognition, yet its cognitive and neural underpinnings remain debated. Competing accounts attribute dyscalculia either to domain-specific imprecise representations of number or to domain-general deficits in the maintenance and integration of numerical information. Here, we test both accounts in 33 adolescents and young adults with dyscalculia and 33 age- and gender-matched controls (15-23 years) who performed a sequential numerosity comparison task during fMRI. Joint computational modeling of choices and response times allowed us to dissociate perceptual and memory noise from decision variables governing the speed-accuracy tradeoff, while complementary neuroimaging analyses characterized neural number representations and their network embedding. Specifically, we quantified the precision of parietal numerosity tuning with numerical population receptive field (nPRF) modeling and derived individualized functional network maps of the same region using community detection algorithms applied to connectivity patterns. Dyscalculic participants showed greater perceptual and memory noise but also a more cautious response criterion, trading speed for accuracy to compensate for representational imprecision. Neurally, the numerosity model explained less variance in parietal cortex, suggesting less precise numerical representations, and individualized network maps assigned less of this cortex to the dorsal attention network and more to a visual network. Rather than supporting a dichotomy between the two accounts, our findings suggest that dyscalculia reflects both less precise numerical representations in parietal cortex and an altered allocation of this cortex to distributed functional systems.

doi:10.31234/osf.io/fnrdy_v1.title: Valence Automatically Elicits Vowel Articulation
doi:10.31234/osf.io/fnrdy_v1.authors: Parajuli S, Löffler CS, Rummer R, Körner A.
doi:10.31234/osf.io/fnrdy_v1.abstract: The association between vowels and valence is known as valence sound symbolism. For example, the vowel /i/ (as in English "meet") is associated with more positive valence than the vowel /o/ (as in German “Boot”). The present experiment employs an implicit paradigm to determine whether valence sound symbolism, like size and shape sound symbolism, operates automatically. Participants (N = 47) classified valenced facial expressions by articulating the target vowels /i/ or /o/. Specifically, in the congruent blocks, participants were instructed to say /i/ for happy and /o/ for angry faces, and in the incongruent blocks, to say /i/ for angry and /o/ for happy faces. Response initiation times were faster in congruent compared to incongruent blocks. An additional analysis of acoustic parameters revealed a significant interaction between congruency and vowel type for pitch (f0). Specifically, /i/ was produced with higher pitch in the congruent blocks (happy faces) than in the incongruent blocks (angry faces), whereas /o/ was produced with higher pitch in the incongruent blocks (happy faces) than in the congruent blocks (angry faces). In sum, the present results indicate that the association between vowels and valence operates automatically, thereby contributing to our knowledge of cognitive processing during valence sound symbolism.

doi:10.1016/j.neuroimage.2026.122292.title: Decoding Spatial Attention in the Cocktail Party Problem Using Whole-head High-Density fNIRS.
doi:10.1016/j.neuroimage.2026.122292.authors: Duwadi S, Rogers D, Boyd AD, Carlton LB, Zhang Y, Gaona AK, Pathiyaparambath AD, Chaudhury R, Magee G, Zimmermann BB, O'Brien WJ, von Lühmann A, Boas DA, Yücel MA, Sen K.
doi:10.1016/j.neuroimage.2026.122292.abstract: Spatial attention is critical for solving the cocktail party problem, a longstanding problem in neuroscience and artificial speech recognition. The ability to decode where humans are attending in a cocktail party like scene would empower applications in brain computer interfaces and assistive devices such as hearing aids. Here we demonstrate that, in an overt attention task, the attended spatial location can be decoded robustly from single trial hemodynamic responses, using a whole head high density fNIRS system. We also identify critical brain regions that make the highest contribution to decoding accuracy. Specifically, we find that decoding based on a small fraction of channels located within the left and right inferior parietal lobule (IPL) achieves maximal decoding accuracy comparable to all channels. Decoding fell close to chance in a covert auditory condition in which participants held central fixation while attending to the same talkers, indicating that auditory attention alone without orientation is not sufficient for decoding. Finally, control experiments suggest that overt-condition decoding is influenced by sustained eye position/gaze direction, not eye movement. These results support the development of fNIRS-integrated BCIs and assistive devices controlled by overt spatial attention.

doi:10.1111/ejn.70700.title: Altered Timing of Self-Voice Processing in Parkinson's Disease.
doi:10.1111/ejn.70700.authors: Contreras-Ruston F, Criscuolo A, Callén A, Cucurell D, Navarra J, Kotz SA.
doi:10.1111/ejn.70700.abstract: Parkinson's disease (PD) affects voice and speech production, often resulting in reduced vocal intensity and monotonous speech. Recent studies suggest that these changes can be partially explained by altered sensory feedback processing in speech production: individuals with PD (IwPD) may fail to monitor and adapt sensory feedback when producing speech. We investigated PD voice production using a voice playback paradigm and focused on the sensory attenuation typically observed in event-related responses (ERPs) to the self-generated voice. When sensory feedback is intact, the P50, N100, and P200 responses to a self-generated voice are attenuated compared to an externally generated voice. Twenty-three IwPD and 23 matched healthy controls (HCs) completed the voice playback study with three conditions: self-generated voice (auditory-motor [AMC]), externally generated voice (auditory-only [AOC]), and motor-only. Linear mixed models assessed group differences in ERP morphology. Groups differed in the N100 latency response: IwPD showed a greater shift in latency between AMC and AOC than healthy controls. Regarding the P200, a significant group-by-condition interaction indicated that IwPD, unlike healthy controls, produced larger amplitudes for the self-generated than the passively listened to voice. Taken together, these findings suggest that the processing of one's own voice in IwPD is altered in terms of temporal precision rather than in the N100 suppression effect per se. This effect was accompanied by an enhanced P200 attentional response. These response patterns in IwPD are indicative of likely progressing difficulties in regulating one's own voice, characteristic of Parkinson's disease.

doi:10.64898/2026.10.16.759765.title: Intelligent systems distribute memory across internal and embodied resources
doi:10.64898/2026.10.16.759765.authors: Zhang, R.; Pitkow, X.; Angelaki, D.
doi:10.64898/2026.10.16.759765.abstract: Intelligent systems do not operate in isolation from the body, yet how bodily actions support internal computation remains unclear. Here we show that primates and artificial agents recruit eye movements to maintain beliefs about hidden goals when internal computation is constrained. In a naturalistic navigation task, both systems spontaneously tracked goals with their eyes after they disappeared from view. This strategy emerged in artificial agents only when internal memory was constrained, identifying resource constraints as a driver of memory externalization. Restricting gaze impaired performance in both systems, while natural behavioral variability and causal perturbations in agents established a direct influence of oculomotor state on internal beliefs about hidden goals. Across agents, varying the reliability of internal memory and gaze redistributed goal information between internal and embodied states. The same resource-allocation principle predicted the distribution of goal information in macaque parietal cortex, where greater reliance on gaze was accompanied by weaker gaze-independent neural representations. Together, these findings identify eye movements as embodied memory and reveal a convergent principle across intelligent systems: memory is allocated across internal and embodied resources according to their reliability.

doi:10.21203/rs.3.rs-11072309/v1.title: Gna14-Associated Gq–IP₃R Signaling Contributes to the Transition to Sustained Calcium Dysregulation in Cisplatin Ototoxicity
doi:10.21203/rs.3.rs-11072309/v1.authors: Lai S, Yu H, Sun Y, Tong Q, He Y, Yu H.
doi:10.21203/rs.3.rs-11072309/v1.abstract: Abstract Cisplatin ototoxicity is generally viewed as the progressive accumulation of cellular damage, but whether cochlear cells pass through a definable transition before irreversible injury remains unclear. Here, calcium imaging at defined time points over 72 h revealed a biphasic response in mouse cochlear explants. Early fluctuations in the calcium signal were followed by sustained elevation that persisted after cisplatin withdrawal. This transition was accompanied by mitochondrial oxidative stress, consistent with a shift from an early compensated phase toward sustained calcium dysregulation. The transition was accompanied by remodeling of ER-mitochondria contacts (MERCs) and mitochondrial structural damage. Time-resolved transcriptomics identified Gna14 near the transition boundary, and Gna14 silencing reduced hair-cell injury. Pharmacological experiments further implicated Gq-IP₃R signaling in the calcium phenotype. p-Coumaric acid (p-CA) induced thermal stabilization of Gna14 and attenuated sustained calcium dysregulation, MERC remodeling, ER stress, and mitochondrial dysfunction. In a chronic mouse model, p-CA preserved auditory thresholds and cochlear cellular architecture without reducing cisplatin cytotoxicity in two tested nasopharyngeal carcinoma cell lines. These findings suggest that cisplatin ototoxicity contains a previously underappreciated transition from compensated calcium handling to a persistent organelle-stress state. Targeting this transition before overt cochlear injury may provide a temporal strategy for otoprotection. RNA-sequencing data are available in the Genome Sequence Archive under accession CRA050592.

doi:10.64898/2026.10.11.758303.title: A Control-Theoretic Account of Cognitive Effort in Working Memory
doi:10.64898/2026.10.11.758303.abstract: Cognitive effort is closely linked to prefrontal control, but the control demands imposed by working memory remain poorly understood at the level of neural circuits. We formulated frontoparietal regulation as a feedback-control problem in a conductance-based spiking network comprising an intraparietal ring attractor and a recurrent dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (dlPFC) actuator. A local data-driven task–actuator model was identified around the cue-offset mnemonic state and used to design linear-quadratic regulation. Increasing memory load produced a strong monotonic rise in realized post-cue control effort, driven primarily by sustained dlPFC recruitment. Cue-aligned selective routing supported higher mnemonic loads with substantially less control effort than spatially nonspecific routing. Mean-matched open-loop stimulation reproduced much of the nominal retention benefit, whereas state-dependent feedback provided greater robustness when mnemonic activity was perturbed. Finite-horizon analysis revealed a strongly anisotropic, effectively low-dimensional control geometry dominated by a common mnemonic direction, with much weaker access to item-differentiating directions. These results link increasing working-memory demand to greater sustained prefrontal control requirements and show how frontoparietal routing geometry shapes the efficiency and robustness of mnemonic regulation.

doi:10.64898/2026.10.07.757368.title: The Cost to Scroll: Short-form Video Use and Episodic Memory
doi:10.64898/2026.10.07.757368.authors: Chen KK, Miller DS, Nguyen KK, Wagner AD, Tran TT.
doi:10.64898/2026.10.07.757368.abstract: Short-form video platforms expose users to rapid streams of novel content; these features are posited to place heavy demands on cognitive processes. In a preregistered online study, we used device-reported screen time to examine whether short-form video use is associated with sustained attention and episodic memory in participants aged 18–24 yrs ( N = 502). During a sustained attention task, participants made indoor/outdoor decisions on scene stimuli, with 90% frequent trials and 10% infrequent trials; the subsequent surprise recognition test assessed memory for these items. Among participants with device-reported TikTok or Instagram use ( N = 398), short-form video use was not associated with attention performance. By contrast, greater short-form video use was associated with poorer episodic memory; this relationship was driven by poorer recognition of infrequent-category items. These findings connect heavier short-form video consumption with poorer episodic memory in young adults, showing how daily digital habits co-vary with memory function.

doi:10.64898/2026.09.24.754025.title: Mice adapt their learning rate to stochasticity and volatility through a simple heuristic
doi:10.64898/2026.09.24.754025.authors: Chevallier, C.; Cobos Alvarez, J.; Debos, E.; Marillat, E.; Perroy, J.; Naude, J.
doi:10.64898/2026.09.24.754025.abstract: Learning from outcomes requires weighing each surprise by how much it is likely to mean. Two properties of the environment set that weight in opposite directions: volatility, the rate at which contingencies change, and stochasticity, the noise in outcomes around a stable contingency. Whether animals separate the two is unresolved, in part because varying reward probability in a reversal task makes outcomes noisier and the two options harder to tell apart at once. We trained male and female mice on a probabilistic reversal task for intracranial self-stimulation, scaling reward magnitude with reward probability so that the expected reward of each option and the difference between them stayed constant while outcome variance varied, and crossing this with different reversal rates. Simulations show that adapting the learning rate alone and adapting the decision policy alone are near-equivalent solutions across the environments we tested. Mice adopted the first adjustment: their fitted learning rate rose with volatility and fell with stochasticity, in both directions predicted by reward maximization, while their inverse temperature stayed fixed. This joint dependence was reproduced only by a meta-learning rule that reads stochasticity from the size of prediction errors and volatility from how often recent outcomes favored switching
doi:10.64898/2026.09.24.754025.institution: IGF, Univ. Montpellier, CNRS, Inserm, Montpellier, France

doi:10.1523/jneurosci.2277-25.2026.title: Monosynaptic GABAergic projections from a subset of suprachiasmatic nucleus neuromedin S neurons suppress preoptic area kisspeptin neuron firing in female mice.
doi:10.1523/jneurosci.2277-25.2026.authors: Abdulmajeed WI, Neuman PN, Jamieson BB, Thomas SX, Rim Y, Novak AG, Lehman MN, Campbell RE, Piet R.
doi:10.1523/jneurosci.2277-25.2026.abstract: Neural control of ovulation is critical for reproductive success. In spontaneous ovulators, this is achieved through hypothalamic neural circuits relaying ovarian follicle maturity cues to gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH)-secreting neurons to drive the preovulatory luteinizing hormone (LH) surge. Within these circuits, kisspeptin-expressing neurons in the rostral periventricular region of the third ventricle (RP3V KISS1 neurons) are thought to stimulate GnRH neurons for the LH surge. In female rodents, the central circadian clock in the suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN) regulates the timing of RP3V KISS1 and GnRH neuron activation, coordinating neuroendocrine control of ovulation and behavior. However, the mechanisms thereof are not fully understood. Here, we examined the potential regulation of RP3V KISS1 neuron activity by neuromedin S (NMS)-expressing SCN neurons - a neuronal population essential for circadian rhythms - using anatomical tract-tracing, optogenetics and electrophysiology in female mice. Our observations indicate that a subset of SCN NMS neurons, likely distinct from the canonical arginine vasopressin and vasoactive intestinal peptide SCN populations, projects to RP3V KISS1 neurons. Optogenetic activation of these projections evokes monosynaptic release of GABA onto ≈ 75% of RP3V KISS1 neurons. Whereas exogenous NMS only moderately affected RP3V KISS1 neuron activity, with no effect on firing and altered intracellular calcium concentration in subsets of cells, GABA release from SCN NMS fibers in the RP3V potently suppressed KISS1 neuron action potential firing, through activation of GABA A receptors. Together, these findings reveal additional complexity in the regulation of the GnRH neuronal network by the central circadian clock. Potential implications of these observations for the timing of the LH surge are discussed. Significance statement In females of multiple species, neuroendocrine circuits in the hypothalamus, which include preoptic area kisspeptin neurons and converge on the gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH) neurons, integrate information about gonadal state with circadian cues to triggers ovulation. The mechanisms though which the central circadian clock in the suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN) relays timing cues to the GnRH neuronal network are, however, incompletely understood. Using anatomical and functional approaches, we found that a previously unsuspected subpopulation of SCN neurons projects to preoptic area kisspeptin neurons and, unexpectedly, suppresses these cells' activity through the release of the inhibitory neurotransmitter GABA. Our observations suggest that control of activity within the GnRH neuronal network for ovulation might extend beyond modulation by canonical SCN neuropeptides.

doi:10.64898/2026.09.27.754840.title: Hyperexcitable but seizure-free: hippocampal network dysfunction in a Wolfram syndrome model
doi:10.64898/2026.09.27.754840.authors: Ahmadi, S.; Pinera, J. G.; Dokholyan, S.; Sauerbeck, A. D.; Phan, H. N.; Carman, B.; Debnath, A.; Brunwasser, S.; Skinner, G.; Rensing, N.; Wong, M.; Cearlock, C.; Maloney, S. E.; Kummer, T. T.; Singamaneni, S.; Cirrito, J.; Foutz, T. J.; Urano, F.
doi:10.64898/2026.09.27.754840.abstract: Wolfram syndrome (WS) is a rare, life-limiting progressive neurodegenerative disorder caused by pathogenic variants in the WFS1 gene. It is a prototype endoplasmic reticulum (ER) stress disorder, and the mechanisms underlying neurological phenotypes in WS remain incompletely understood. Although WFS1 protein is abundant in the hippocampus, the role of this region in WS remains relatively understudied. Here we characterize hippocampal function across scales in mice carrying a patient orthologous Wfs1 variant (p.W542*) on both alleles. Male mutants lose excitatory synapses, and dissociated hippocampal neurons are markedly hyperexcitable yet generate no increase in network bursting and no shift in network criticality, indicating that their additional firing is not recruited into coordinated population activity. This finding translates in vivo wherein intracranial electroencephalogram (EEG) recordings show no epileptiform activity or seizures in either sex, with no hippocampal astrogliosis, alongside a male-specific reduction in hippocampal low-gamma power. Additionally, EEG demonstrates a sex-specific disruption of sleep, which parallels a sex-divergent synaptic phenotype. Mutant male mice show impaired hippocampus-dependent fear memory and reduced voluntary motor activity. Taken together, we propose that cellular hyperexcitability in the WS hippocampus does not translate into increased network bursting, potentially due to disproportionate loss of excitatory synapses. This dissociation may provide a functional substrate for the neurological features of WS.

doi:10.1016/j.bbr.2026.116525.title: The regulatory roles of the medial septum and hippocampus in spatial memory impairment of PTSD mice.
doi:10.1016/j.bbr.2026.116525.authors: Ren KX, Xie YL, Wu YJ, Zheng C, Xu AP, Luo H, Zha YY, Wang MY, Zhang HH.
doi:10.1016/j.bbr.2026.116525.abstract: This experiment was based on the establishment of an analogue of post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) in mice, aiming to explore the regulatory effects of the medial septum (MS) and the hippocampus (HIP) on spatial memory impairment in mice, and to establish a theoretical foundation for revealing the pathological basis of PTSD-related spatial memory impairment. The PTSD mouse model was prepared, behavioral testing, FluoroGold (FG) retrograde tracing technique, viral tracing technique, in vivo fiber photometry recording technique, chemogenetic technology and in vivo electrophysiological recording techniques were applied to observe and analyze the changes in spatial memory ability and the central regulatory mechanism. PTSD mice showed heightened anxiety, impaired spatial memory, suppressed Sch-CA1 long-term potentiation, and hyperactivity of MS-CA1 cholinergic neurons; chemogenetic inhibition of this pathway rescued both the behavioral and synaptic plasticity deficits. The regulation of spatial memory impairment in PTSD mice involves MS-resident cholinergic neurons. We found a cholinergic pathway connection between MS and CA1, and this pathway may regulate murine spatial cognition by influencing the synaptic plasticity of Sch-CA1.

doi:10.64898/2026.10.12.758574.title: Neural correlates of ketamine-induced dilation of temporal expectation
doi:10.64898/2026.10.12.758574.authors: Waters JR, Madeira B, Shadlen MN, Shushruth S.
doi:10.64898/2026.10.12.758574.abstract: Time estimation is critical to many cognitive operations, including decision-making, working memory, and action planning. Neural correlates of interval timing have been described across multiple cortical and subcortical networks, both at a single-neuron level (as ramping activity) and population level (as dynamical motifs). Low-dose ketamine, a dissociative anesthetic and potent antidepressant, is known to distort time perception, but how it affects these neural correlates is unknown. In two male macaques performing a time-anticipation task, we administered subanesthetic doses of ketamine under a pharmacokinetically guided intravenous infusion protocol. We recorded neural activity from the parietal area LIP, a region associated with interval timing. Behaviorally, ketamine caused monkeys to respond as though less time had elapsed than had actually passed under objective clock time, a dose-dependent dilation of time estimation. This behavioral change was accompanied by parallel effects on the neural representation of elapsed time. At the single-neuron level, ketamine flattened anticipatory ramping activity. At the population level, it induced a rotation of delay-period activity in neural state space, away from the pre-ketamine configuration. By linking a graded pharmacological manipulation to concurrent shifts in behavior and cortical neural activity, we show that ketamine dilates perceived time while reshaping LIP population dynamics. These findings offer a route to probe how cortical activity supports time estimation and point to a network mechanism that could contribute to ketamine's dissociative and antidepressant effects.

doi:10.64898/2026.09.22.753486.title: Diurnal rhythmicity modulates self-blaming behaviours and neural processing of autobiographical guilt memories in the trait-like and state-like manner
doi:10.64898/2026.09.22.753486.authors: Zareba, M. R.; Gonzalez-Garcia, I.; Ibanez Montolio, M.; Visser, M.
doi:10.64898/2026.09.22.753486.abstract: Increasing evidence implicates late chronotype and higher distinctness as two diurnal dimensions associated with a risk for affective dysregulation. Nonetheless, the underlying behavioural and neural mechanisms remain poorly understood. Previous works in depressive and anxious populations have demonstrated an important role of maladaptive self-blaming processes, with pivotal contributions from superior anterior temporal lobes (sATL), involved in social conceptual knowledge, and subgenual anterior cingulate cortex (sgACC), related to self-worth and social affiliative processing. In the current study, we first tested how diurnal rhythm characteristics were associated with self-blaming emotions and related coping mechanisms through hypothetical social scenarios where participants or their close friends acted towards one another against social norms. Secondly, to probe alterations in the neural correlates of self-blaming, the participants underwent functional neuroimaging during reliving of autobiographical guilt memories. On the behavioural level, late chronotypes demonstrated decreased self-distancing and contextually-maladaptive blaming patterns, i.e. increased blaming of the action recipients rather than the agents. This was paralleled by decreased self-blame-related activity in the sATL and sgACC. Distinctness was associated with altered task-dependent sATL connectivity with hippocampus, brainstem and cerebellum. Importantly, some of the neuroimaging findings reflected interactions between the diurnal rhythm characteristics and time-of-day. As such, the current work provides plausible correlates of adverse emotional outcomes in late chronotypes. Furthermore, it suggests that affective processing reflects an interplay between stable trait-like characteristics and dynamic state-like processes varying across the day, contributing to fine-grained understanding of how emotional cognition is embedded in the brain.

doi:10.64898/2026.10.01.755870.title: Individualized Gabor Flicker for Well-Tolerated Neural Entrainment During Working Memory
doi:10.64898/2026.10.01.755870.authors: Blanc C, Dehais F, Scannella S.
doi:10.64898/2026.10.01.755870.abstract: Rhythmic visual stimulation offers a non-invasive means of modulating oscillatory brain activity, but conventional flicker may induce considerable visual discomfort. We developed an individualized Gabor flicker stimulation designed to balance neural entrainment and tolerability. In Experiment 1, thirty-four participants passively viewed Plain and Gabor flickers presented at their individual alpha frequency (IAF), IAF - 2 Hz, or IAF + 2 Hz, and at threshold-adjusted or full intensity. Steady-state visual evoked potential signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) was highest at IAF and increased with intensity. Plain and Gabor flickers produced comparable overall SNR, but Gabor flicker was rated as substantially more comfortable and less mentally fatiguing, with stimulation at IAF providing the most favorable balance between neural entrainment and tolerability. In Experiment 2, the optimized stimulation parameters were applied during a retro-cue working memory task using individualized theta and alpha frequency flickers. Stimulation increased SNR and inter-trial phase coherence relative to a non rhythmic Natural condition. No behavioral benefit was observed in the full sample. However, an exploratory subgroup analysis indicated higher accuracy with theta stimulation of cued representations and alpha stimulation of uncued representations than in the Natural condition among participants who showed limited baseline retro-cue benefits. These findings show that individualized Gabor flicker can provide robust and well-tolerated neural entrainment during passive viewing and working memory retention, although its behavioral effects may vary across individuals according to their cognitive performance.

doi:10.7554/elife.107370.title: A cortical-hippocampal communication undergoes rebalancing after new learning.
doi:10.7554/elife.107370.abstract: The brain's ability to consolidate a wide range of memories while maintaining their distinctiveness across experiences remains poorly understood. Sharp-wave ripples, neural oscillations that occur predominantly within CA1 of the hippocampus during immobility and sleep, have been shown to play a critical role in the consolidation process. More recently, evidence has uncovered functional heterogeneity of pyramidal neurons within distinct sublayers of CA1 that display unique properties during ripples, potentially contributing to memory specificity. Despite this, it remains unclear exactly how ripples shift the activity of CA1 neuronal populations to accommodate the consolidation of specific memories and how sublayer differences manifest. Here, we studied interactions between the anterior cingulate cortex (ACC) and CA1 neurons during ripples and discovered a reorganization of their communication following learning. Specifically, using a generalized linear model decoder, we demonstrated the pre-existence of ACC-to-CA1 communication, which is weakened during post-training sleep following learning, suggesting that ACC activity reallocates the contribution of CA1 neurons during memory formation. Interestingly, the reorganization appeared unique for a subset of CA1 superficial (CA1sup) neurons that were task inactive, whereas communication between the ACC and CA1deep neurons remained largely stable across pre- and post-training sleep. Consistent with this sublayer-selective reorganization, we found that optogenetic stimulations of the ACC preferentially suppressed CA1sup neurons while activating a unique subset of CA1 interneurons. Overall, these findings highlight an important role of the ACC in rebalancing CA1 neuronal populations' contribution in learning and memory consolidation.

doi:10.64898/2026.10.02.756298.title: A Computational Model Captures Orexin-Dependent Modulation of Memory Consolidation
doi:10.64898/2026.10.02.756298.authors: Shakleina P, Guy AT, Trombetta EM.
doi:10.64898/2026.10.02.756298.abstract: Hippocampal sharp-wave ripple (SWR) events occur during post-experience rest and sleep and play a significant role in memory consolidation. Recent ex vivo studies have found orexin-driven neuromodulatory effects on SWR parameters and proposed that they can influence memory consolidation. Additionally, behavioral studies demonstrate contradictory results regarding orexinergic effects on memory acquisition depending on task structure and intervention time. This inconsistency, along with the diffuse spread of orexin receptors (OXR) in the CA1 and CA3 hippocampus, challenges theoretical interpretation of orexinergic effects on memory. To reconcile this problem, we propose a rate-based model linking orexinergic tone-dependent SWR statistics to memory performance. The model combines an encoding module whose gain scales with the global orexinergic tone with a consolidation module driven by OX2R-specific replay dynamics. The model is based on a plasticity rule that considers SWR events as the unit of induction. Therefore, weight change requires sufficient replay content and depolarizing drive. We observed that, depending on the task structure, encoding-dominant learning benefits discrimination as the orexin drive increases. Consolidation-dominant learning shows a non-monotonic relationship with an internal optimum level of orexinergic tone. This interaction highlights that stronger truncation at higher receptor engagement shortens memory replay and reduces the efficacy of the consolidation process. The model predicts that the optimal regime depends on task complexity reflected in sequence length. Together, these results demonstrate how task demands determine whether increased orexinergic drive enhances or impairs effective consolidation and SWR-dependent replay in the hippocampus.

doi:10.31234/osf.io/dsk5r_v1.title: The Emergent Structure of Memory Phenomenology Depends on Whether Memories Are More Episodic or Semantic
doi:10.31234/osf.io/dsk5r_v1.abstract: Phenomenological characteristics are central to theoretical distinctions among modern memory constructs. The scene construction framework proposes that episodic remembering involves the construction of coherent scenes, such that the structure of phenomenology may reflect the engagement of the hippocampus and related regions during recall. However, most phenomenology research relies on instruments with content and scoring schemes that embed theoretical assumptions into their measurements. Here, we explored whether phenomenological characteristics emerge from self-reported memory experiences as anticipated by episodic memory theory. We solicited memories from a large online sample, following each response with a novel questionnaire designed to evaluate the phenomenology of individual memories. We used folded bottom-up factor analyses to examine and validate the global latent factor structure of participants’ memory experiences. Consistent with Tulving’s declarative memory framework, our analyses produced five stable dimensions: imagery, autonoetic consciousness, mental time travel, relational memory, and semantic memory. In order, these dimensions reflect multi-modal perceptual reexperiencing, personal meaning, sense of reliving, detailed spatiotemporal context, and conscious use of semantic knowledge during recall. The semantic memory dimension has no clear predecessor, suggesting the strategic use of general knowledge during recall is a distinct and previously uncharacterized aspect of remembering. This factor structure generalized across memories elicited by recent and remote episodic prompts. However, distinct versions of mental time travel and relational memory emerged in response to the semantic prompt, suggesting these dimensions of memory are context-sensitive rather than fixed. While our findings validate the link between episodic memory and its theorized phenomenological elements, they also invite broader investigation of how phenomenology may vary across different classes of memory.

doi:10.64898/2026.10.09.758035.title: Sustained Activation of a Defensive Behavior-Related Circuit Elicits a distinct Homeostatic Sleep Response
doi:10.64898/2026.10.09.758035.authors: Yang C, Lombardi V, Uygun DS, Brown RE, McKenna JT, Basheer R.
doi:10.64898/2026.10.09.758035.abstract: Summary Animals and humans often forgo sleep in response to other physiological needs. Prolonged wakefulness leads to a compensatory homeostatic sleep response involving enhanced amounts of sleep and electroencephalographic delta (0.5-4 Hz) power, yet how the type of preceding wakefulness and brain activity affects this response is poorly understood. Here we compared the pattern of brain activity and the homeostatic sleep response following sustained wakefulness induced by either gentle handling (GH), a widely used form of sleep deprivation in rodents; or optogenetic stimulation of neurons involved in avoidance/defensive responses, basal forebrain (BF) vesicular glutamatergic transporter type 2 (vGluT2) neurons. Local infusion of ionotropic glutamate receptor antagonists partially attenuated the wake-inducing effect of vGluT2-stimulation, but not that of GH, suggesting mediation by other non-glutamatergic BF subtypes. These antagonists also tended to produce more NREM sleep and a shorter NREM latency in the recovery period following vGluT2-stimulation. Both manipulations increased high theta (7-9 Hz) during wakefulness, an effect partially blocked by local infusion of the glutamate antagonist cocktail. Enhanced NREM sleep time and NREM delta power in the recovery period were more pronounced following GH than following vGluT2 stimulation. Whole-brain cFos immunohistochemistry revealed stronger neuronal activity in brain regions involved in stress and avoidance/defensive behaviors with vGluT2 stimulation, compared to GH. Our results demonstrate that activation of a brain system involved in defensive behavior (BF vGluT2) elicits a distinct and diminished homeostatic sleep response compared to GH, potentially an evolutionary sleep adaptation which would maintain vigilance in the face of an ongoing threat.

doi:10.21203/rs.3.rs-11359503/v1.title: Clinical and neurophysiological effects of imagery rehearsal therapy and targeted memory reactivation in post-traumatic stress disorder
doi:10.21203/rs.3.rs-11359503/v1.authors: Lüthi O, Rochas V, Theux A, Clerget A, Bayer L, Perogamvros L.
doi:10.21203/rs.3.rs-11359503/v1.abstract: Abstract Post-traumatic stress disorder is frequently associated with post-traumatic nightmares, which may be related to cortical hyperarousal. Imagery Rehearsal Therapy is the first-line treatment for nightmares. Targeted Memory Reactivation, which reactivates specific memories during sleep to enhance memory consolidation, has been shown to enhance the effects of Imagery Rehearsal Therapy in idiopathic nightmares. This study investigated the efficacy of Imagery Rehearsal Therapy for traumatic nightmares and broader post-traumatic stress disorder symptoms, and whether these effects could be enhanced by Targeted Memory Reactivation. Thirty-six adults diagnosed with post-traumatic stress disorder received either Imagery Rehearsal Therapy alone (n = 17) or Imagery Rehearsal Therapy combined with Targeted Memory Reactivation (n = 19). Participants completed three weekly Imagery Rehearsal Therapy sessions and underwent polysomnographic recordings before and after the intervention. In the combined treatment group, a sensory cue associated with the positive therapy scenario was presented during sessions and reactivated nightly during rapid eye movement sleep at home using a sleep headband. Imagery Rehearsal Therapy significantly improved post-traumatic stress disorder symptoms and associated outcomes, including insomnia severity, nightmare frequency/distress, and depressive symptoms. No additional benefit of Targeted Memory Reactivation was observed. Compared to healthy individuals, trauma-exposed patients showed baseline polysomnographic alterations suggestive of cortical hyperarousal, including increased frontocentral beta activity during non-rapid eye movement sleep and reduced frontal delta activity during rapid eye movement sleep. Following treatment, beta activity decreased, while Targeted Memory Reactivation was associated with additional posterior sleep-related neural changes during rapid eye movement sleep, in regions previously implicated in dream experience.

doi:10.64898/2026.09.24.754081.title: Predictive perception via simultaneous learning and inference
doi:10.64898/2026.09.24.754081.authors: Enan M, Senden M, Janik P, Vidal Y, Auksztulewicz R, De Martino F.
doi:10.64898/2026.09.24.754081.abstract: Perception has been proposed to involve an inferential process that combines noisy sensory evidence with prior expectations to estimate the latent states of the environment. Exact Bayesian inference is intractable in the continuous, high-dimensional state spaces of the natural world. Variational schemes address this by restricting the form of the posterior, whereas sampling schemes represent the posterior with a finite set of samples. In both cases the approximation concerns the posterior rather than the state space over which it is defined. Here we place the approximation elsewhere. Rather than restricting the form of the posterior, we restrict the state space, modeling environmental states as discrete and thereby making Bayesian filtering exact. Beliefs are then unconstrained in shape and what has to be learned can be reduced to a transition matrix updated online by a local rule. The cost is that the states, rather than the distribution, must be specified in advance. The Simultaneous Learning and Inference Model (SLIM) combines this exact filtering with a gated Hebbian rule that learns transitions from inferred rather than observed states. In simulations SLIM recovers environmental dynamics under sensory noise and adapts when those dynamics change, with error growing only once the sensor becomes uninformative. A hierarchical instantiation reproduces local and global prediction error effects. Applied to two auditory decision-making experiments under noise, SLIM reproduces behavioral signatures of expectation and supplies trial-level measures of expectation and surprise. Exact inference over a small discrete state space with a single local Hebbian rule is therefore sufficient to account for these phenomena, without an explicit optimization objective and without a parametric approximation to the posterior.

doi:10.1109/tbme.2026.3653024.title: RUNet: A Zero-Calibration Framework for Cross-Domain EEG Decoding via Riemannian and Unsupervised Representation Learning.
doi:10.1109/tbme.2026.3653024.authors: Jin J, Wang C, Xu R, He X, Wu X, Li J, Chen W, Wang X, Cichocki A.
doi:10.1109/tbme.2026.3653024.abstract: Objective Inter-session and inter-subject variability in electroencephalography (EEG) signals, resulting from individual differences and environmental factors, poses a major challenge for neural decoding in brain-computer interface (BCI) applications. Methods To address this issue, we propose RUNet, a zero-calibration motor imagery EEG decoding framework based on Riemannian manifold learning and unsupervised representation learning. RUNet incorporates a multi-scale spatiotemporal convolutional module that jointly captures local-global spatial and multi-resolution temporal dynamics features. To enhance the robustness of EEG features against non-stationarity, a polysynergistic covariance optimization module is employed, which strengthens the covariance matrix representation through multiple regularizations and adaptive fusion. In addition, RUNet integrates the Riemannian Affine Log Mapping layer, based on Affine-Invariant Transformation and Log-Euclidean Mapping, in an end-to-end manner to mitigate cross-domain covariance drift and enhance domain-invariant feature learning. A transfer learning framework is further integrated into RUNet: during pre-training, an unsupervised contrastive loss is applied to resting-state EEG data to learn domain-invariant spatiotemporal features; during retraining, task-specific data are used to enhance discriminability and feature disentanglement. Conclusion Experimental results on the BCI Competition IV 2a, 2b datasets and a self-collected laboratory dataset show that RUNet achieves average cross-session accuracies of 87.19%, 88.03% and 85.45%, and cross-subject accuracies of 68.09%, 78.29% and 87.25%, respectively. On the PhysioNet dataset, a cross-subject accuracy of 78.14% is achieved. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of RUNet's unified pipeline and its robust cross-domain generalization.

doi:10.1371/journal.pcbi.1014761.title: Drift-diffusion dynamics of hippocampal replay.
doi:10.1371/journal.pcbi.1014761.abstract: Replay in the hippocampus during sharp-wave ripples is thought to play major roles in learning and memory. However, existing analysis methods often lead to inconsistent and inaccurate metrics for characterizing replay dynamics. We develop a novel computational framework that models the replay dynamics using a drift-diffusion process. Further, to capture the potentially rich population-level dynamics during sharp-wave ripples, our model allows switching between multiple well-motivated types of dynamics. Applications of our method to rat hippocampal recordings lead to a number of insights. First, our results reveal that a small fraction of SWRs are stationary, and those with drift-diffusion dynamics generally have a much higher speed than the animal's movement. Second, we find that replay dynamics are heterogeneous and inconsistent with a random walk model proposed previously. The mean-squared displacement of replay trajectories scales quadratically with time, supporting the presence of substantial drifts. Third, we find that only a tiny fraction of SWR events (less than 1%) exhibit sequential structure at the timescale of 100 ms before the animal had spatial experience in an environment. This suggests that, while neural activity in the hippocampus may be coordinated before the animal's spatial experience (i.e., preplay), the level of coordination is much weaker than that after spatial experience. Overall, our approach enables precise characterizations and unambiguous interpretations of population dynamics during sharp-wave ripples, which more broadly can provide a better understanding of the functions and underlying mechanisms of replay.

doi:10.7554/elife.111851.title: Reduced dorsal CA1 activity limits retention of the temporal component of declarative memory in the Cntnap2 knockout mouse model of autism.
doi:10.7554/elife.111851.authors: Rawlinson EC, McCullough MH, Sellami A, Marighetto A, Al-Abed AS, Dehorter N.
doi:10.7554/elife.111851.abstract: Growing evidence implicates the hippocampus in the pathophysiology of autism spectrum disorder, particularly in the domains of social interactions and cognition. Yet, the mechanisms driving the hippocampal-dependent cognitive atypicalities in autism remain poorly defined. Here, we characterized how dysfunction of the CA1 subfield of the dorsal hippocampus drives abnormalities in critical components of declarative memory. Using trace fear conditioning in the Cntnap2 knockout mouse model of autism, we found that capabilities to retain the association of temporally distant stimuli (i.e. temporal binding) were reduced relative to wildtype mice. Fiber photometry and optogenetic experiments demonstrated that reduced CA1 activity during temporal gaps underlies this impairment, linking CA1 dysfunction to a deficit in long-term memory retention in autism. Using a relational/declarative memory task, we also revealed a deficit in flexible spatial memory, and a preferential use of egocentric learning strategy. This inflexible learning strategy resulted from an imbalance between memory system activity, promoting frontostriatal-dependent procedural learning instead of dorsal CA1/hippocampus-dependent relational/declarative memory. Overall, this study establishes dorsal CA1 dysfunction as a circuit-level mechanism underlying cognitive inflexibility in autism, providing a neurobiological framework for hippocampal-dependent memory deficits in the condition.

doi:10.64898/2026.09.18.752742.title: Single neurons in the human substantia nigra encode social learning signals
doi:10.64898/2026.09.18.752742.authors: Davis, A. N.; Perl, O.; Kopell, B. H.; Heflin, M.; Fu, Q. X.; Qasim, S. E.; Imtiaz, Z.; Kato, A.; Na, S.; Mikail, N.; Mayberg, H. S.; Montague, R.; Saez, I.; Gu, X.
doi:10.64898/2026.09.18.752742.abstract: Humans are remarkable at adapting to changing norms, yet we know little about how the human brain encodes these social signals at the single neuron level. Here, we recorded the activity of single neurons in the substantia nigra and globus pallidus in neurosurgical participants as they played an iterative ultimatum game versus human and computer avatars. Using computational modeling of behavior, we found that putative dopaminergic units in the substantia nigra tracked the valence of norm prediction errors, with greater encoding during gameplay with human versus computer avatars. Analogous analyses in the globus pallidus, a nucleus adjacent to the substantia nigra, found no significant effect. Our results identify a novel role for the substantia nigra in encoding social learning signals.
doi:10.64898/2026.09.18.752742.institution: Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai

doi:10.64898/2026.10.13.758895.title: Beyond Rate: Hippocampal Phase Codes for Space and Memory
doi:10.64898/2026.10.13.758895.authors: Kolibius, L. D.; Hermiller, M. S.; ter Wal, M.; van der Plas, M.; Gollwitzer, S.; Walther, K.; Hopfengärtner, R.; Hamer, H.; Khazali, M. F.; Hanslmayr, S.; Bowman, H.; Jacobs, J.
doi:10.64898/2026.10.13.758895.abstract: Place cells and concept neurons are defined by a rise in firing rate at a particular location or for a particular person or object. Neurons without such a rise remain unlabeled, although they keep firing during the task. Such neurons could still carry information in the timing of their spikes. Hippocampal theta provides a reference for this timing. We therefore asked whether the theta phase of a neuron's spikes depends on location or on the viewed image, even when its firing rate does not. We analysed hippocampal neurons in humans navigating a virtual city, rats running on a linear track, and humans viewing images of anima ls, faces, and places. In both navigation datasets, more neurons than expected by chance fired at a consistent theta phase at particular locations. This phase tuning remained after we excluded neurons whose firing rate depended on location. In human navigation, the spike phases of these remaining neurons improved location decoding beyond the firing rates of all neurons. More phase-tuned neurons than expected by chance also fired at progressively earlier theta phases as participants passed each neuron's preferred location. This pattern resembles phase precession, which classically occurs as an animal crosses the firing-rate field of a place cell. The neurons that showed it had no firing-rate field, so their phase shift was anchored to the location defined by phase tuning alone. During image viewing, more neurons than expected by chance changed the theta phase of their spikes after a particular image appeared. This effect remained after we removed, for each neuron, the images that changed its firing rate. Spike phases alone also predicted the image category above chance. Theta-relative spike timing therefore carries in formation about location and images that firing rate alone misses. We propose that weak input changes when a neuron fires with in the theta cycle, whereas strong input also raises its firing rate.

doi:10.31234/osf.io/8ev52_v1.title: Neural representations of emotional working memory in athletes
doi:10.31234/osf.io/8ev52_v1.authors: Li L, Tang S, SunMeirong, Li Y, QiMengdi, Xie J, Li D.
doi:10.31234/osf.io/8ev52_v1.abstract: Research on athletic expertise often emphasizes performance differences, leaving less clear how athletes and non-athletes represent emotional information during working memory. We examined whether group differences involve the timing and content of neural representations as memory demands change. Two experiments used a sequential emotional working memory task with loads of two or four images. Experiment 1 compared 25 athletes (16 female, mean age: 20.16 years) and 25 non-athletes (16 female, mean age: 21.04 years) using positive and negative images; Experiment 2 used negative images and included 36 athletes (19 female, mean age: 19.92 years) and 37 non-athletes (19 female, mean age: 20.41 years) in the final electroencephalography (EEG) sample. EEG time–frequency analysis exhibited that athletes showed lower theta power during encoding and maintaining comparing to non-athletes. Representational similarity analysis (RSA) further revealed that athletes showed greater arousal representations, while non-athletes showed greater semantic representations. When memory demand increased, visual-model similarity suggested that athletes can keep the visual information precisely, but non-athletes showed a load-dependent decline of visual representations. These findings provide novel neural evidence that athlete-related differences in emotional working memory involve the timing and content of neural representations, rather than a uniform behavioral advantage.

doi:10.21203/rs.3.rs-10926709/v1.title: Comparative Analysis of Classical Machine Learning and Deep Learning Regression Models for Codon-Level k-mer Composition Analysis of the Nipah Virus Genome
doi:10.21203/rs.3.rs-10926709/v1.authors: Abid¹ A, Bilal¹ M, Khan SUR.
doi:10.21203/rs.3.rs-10926709/v1.abstract: Abstract The Nipah virus (NiV) is highly virulent zoonotic paramyxovirus, where a complete genome sequence resource is relatively limited compared to other emerging pathogens. In this study, the codon level (3-mer) k-mer composition analysis of 93 complete Nipah virus genome sequences retrieved from the NCBI Nucleotide database was presented. The genomes were encoded into a vector of 64 elements representing the number of appearances of each of the 64 three-nucleotide combinations. The feature set was subjected to descriptive statistics, covariance and Pearson correlation between each feature, which showed very high degrees of pairwise collinearity in the set of codon-count features. Using a correlation-based feature-selection procedure (|r| > 0.99), the feature space was reduced from 64 to 5 almost independent codon counts (AAA, TAG, TCG, CGC and CCG). We considered seven regression algorithms across three learning paradigms (classical models: Linear Regression, K-Nearest Neighbors, Support Vector Machine/SVR, an ensemble model: Random Forest, deep sequential models: Long Short-Term Memory network and Simple Recurrent Neural Network, and a Decision Tree baseline) and compared their performance using the number of codons CCG as a regression target and the remaining four codon counts as predictors. The 70/20/10 train/validation/test split was used to train all models, and they were compared using the coefficient of determination (R²), root mean squared error (RMSE), and mean absolute error (MAE). Decision Tree Regression achieved the best performance (R² = 0.9945), followed by Linear Regression (R² = 0.9908), Random Forest (R² = 0.9892), LSTM (R² = 0.9731), and SimpleRNN (R² = 0.9718), while KNN (R² = 0.8038) and SVM/SVR (R² = 0.1038 with feature scaling) underperformed. The results are evaluated with the knowledge of the large compositional constraints on codon usage over a set of Nipah virus genomes, the known sensitivity of instance- and margin-based regressors to unscaled, collinear small-sample data, and the limited benefit of deep sequential architectures on a pseudo-sequence of a very small tabular sample (no temporal dimension). This paper presents in a transparent manner the pipeline results, statistical results and comparative modeling results, along with the limitations of the dataset, as a baseline for future codon-composition based computational studies of Nipah virus.

doi:10.64898/2026.09.21.753217.title: Brain Mechanisms of Lexicality in Bilingual Emotion Processing
doi:10.64898/2026.09.21.753217.authors: Xiao C, Liu J, Zhang Y, Lyu W, Desai RH, Feilong M.
doi:10.64898/2026.09.21.753217.abstract: Understanding how native speakers and second language (L2) learners process language differently is fundamental to theories of language acquisition, comprehension, and use. A central debate in this literature concerns the inconsistent findings in emotional prosody processing between native speakers and L2 learners, partly attributable to stimulus lexicality: some studies use real words, whereas others use pseudowords. To resolve this discrepancy, we measured fMRI responses in 15 native speakers and 15 L2 learners while they listened to Mandarin real-word and pseudoword stimuli. Both groups engaged in overlapping auditory, cognitive, and affective regions, including the auditory cortex, inferior frontal cortex, superior temporal cortex, and the temporoparietal junction. However, the two groups showed distinct responses depending on lexicality: native speakers showed stronger recruitment of temporal regions for pseudowords, whereas L2 learners showed greater frontoparietal activation for real words. These patterns were consistent across positive and negative prosody conditions. Furthermore, among L2 learners, higher proficiency was associated with greater frontal activation for real words, but not pseudowords. Together, these findings demonstrate that the differences between native speakers and L2 learners depend critically on stimulus lexicality, highlighting the role of lexicality in bilingual emotion processing.

doi:10.64898/2026.10.03.755714.title: Dispelling the Plateau Assumption: Case-Based Evidence for Language Recovery in Chronic-Post Stroke Aphasia
doi:10.64898/2026.10.03.755714.authors: Chang EH, Laks AB, Shattuck K, DeMarco AT, Turkeltaub PE.
doi:10.64898/2026.10.03.755714.abstract: Objective: Recovery from post-stroke aphasia is traditionally thought to plateau within a year after stroke. As such, no studies have characterized long-term recovery using comprehensive behavioral assessment and longitudinal functional MRI. We sought to characterize behavioral and neuroplastic changes over nearly six years in a patient with chronic post-stroke aphasia. Methods: A patient with chronic left hemisphere stroke underwent behavioral assessment and task-based fMRI at 9, 22, 33 and 71 months after stroke. Testing assessed auditory comprehension, semantic and phonological processing, naming, reading, spelling, motor speech, and executive function. Task-related activation during an adaptive semantic matching paradigm was quantified within language and semantic regions of interest. Results: Behavior improved across multiple language domains. WAB-R Aphasia Quotient increased from 49.2 to 69.2, along with the large gains in word finding, connected speech, reading and spelling, whereas auditory comprehension remained relatively stable. fMRI demonstrated progressively increasing activation within left-hemisphere language regions, reaching normative range by the final assessment, along with increasing activation in semantic/executive regions. Discussion: Recovery of language production abilities can continue for years after stroke, supported by neuroplastic changes in the brain. Neurologists should inform stroke survivors that aphasia recovery can continue indefinitely after stroke.

doi:10.1016/j.neuroscience.2026.10.013.title: Synchronized audiovisual stimulation enhances neural entrainment: convergent evidence from complementary EEG biomarkers.
doi:10.1016/j.neuroscience.2026.10.013.abstract: Rhythmic sensory stimulation modulates oscillations via frequency-specific entrainment, but synchronized auditory contributions remain unclear, and periodic-aperiodic decomposition has not been applied to audiovisual entrainment. Forty adults received visual stimulation at 8, 20, and 40 Hz, alone (VF) or synchronized with binaural beats of identical frequencies (VF + BB). EEG was analyzed using power spectral density (PSD), topographical mapping, Sample Entropy (SampEn), Lempel-Ziv Complexity (LZC), Phase-Locking Regularity (PLR), and IRASA to separate periodic (SSVEP) from aperiodic (1/f) contributions. Visual flicker induced frequency-specific entrainment, and binaural beats modulated responses frequency-dependently. At 8 Hz, flicker elicited a periodic SSVEP; adding binaural beats enhanced this component and increased aperiodic activity. At 20 Hz, synchronized audiovisual stimulation enhanced both periodic and aperiodic components. At 40 Hz, IRASA showed no significant periodic modulation; VF + BB produced a widespread increase in aperiodic offset and exponent, absent under VF alone. VF + BB reduced SampEn across all frequencies and increased PLR at 8 and 20 Hz, whereas LZC decreased at 8 Hz and increased at 20 Hz. Synchronized audiovisual stimulation produced frequency-dependent changes in EEG spectral organization. At 8 and 20 Hz, adding binaural beats enhanced the periodic SSVEP component, with changes in the aperiodic background. At 40 Hz, conventional PSD showed increased gamma activity, but periodic-aperiodic decomposition did not reveal significant periodic enhancement; audiovisual stimulation primarily altered aperiodic offset and exponent. Complementary regularity and phase-based measures showed frequency-dependent temporal changes. Findings highlight combining conventional spectral analysis, periodic-aperiodic decomposition, and complementary EEG biomarkers to characterize synchronized audiovisual stimulation.

doi:10.64898/2026.10.08.757585.title: Agency and Embodiment Provide Dissociable Benefits to Perception, Metacognition and Neural Processing During Active Sensing
doi:10.64898/2026.10.08.757585.authors: Tang Z, Dowsett J, Taylor P, Ferreiro DN, Pecka M.
doi:10.64898/2026.10.08.757585.abstract: Metacognition, judging how reliable our own perceptual decisions are, is central to adaptive behavior. Such judgments hinge on the reliability of the sensory evidence on which that decision is based, and active sensing through self-directed exploration is known to improve perception itself. Yet, how agency, the authorship over self-initiated actions, and the processing of the sensory consequences, which is implicit to active sensing, modulate metacognition and its calibration, remains unknown. Whether physical embodiment adds to this beyond virtual exploration is similarly unclear, yet relevant both for daily life and for self-monitoring in agentic AI. Here, we combined a naturalistic auditory search paradigm with mobile electroencephalography. Twenty participants performed a target-detection task under three conditions: active embodied exploration, active screen-based exploration, and passive listening to replays of their own trials, while we obtained steady-state auditory evoked potentials (SSAEPs) to characterize stimulus-locked neural responses. We find that both agency conditions improved accuracy, metacognitive sensitivity, and overall SSAEP amplitude relative to passive listening, indicating that agency, rather than whole-body movement, drives these enhancements. Crucially, however, embodiment uniquely grounded both the target-evoked neural response and the subjects’ confidence to immediate sensory evidence. Thus, agency alone broadly enhances perceptual and neural processing, but embodiment specifically anchors confidence, neurally and behaviorally, to the present. Significance Statement How well we judge the reliability of our perception, called metacognitive sensitivity, matters more than ever, as we increasingly are presented with information passively through screens rather than gathering it actively via self-initiated exploration. Does actively seeking information sharpen self-monitoring, and does the medium (body vs. screen) matter? We show that active search enhances metacognitive sensitivity and brain responses alike, whether embodied or screen-based. Only embodied search, however, anchors self-evaluation to the present: Behaviorally, embodiment facilitates coupling of confidence tracking directly to current evidence rather than the previous trial’s outcome, while neuronally, it enhances responses in frontal brain regions during periods of heightened subjective confidence. This embodied grounding of self-monitoring may prove pivotal for building reliably agentic AI systems.

doi:10.64898/2026.10.16.759581.title: Real-time noise cancellation for EEG monitoring and brain–computer interfaces
doi:10.64898/2026.10.16.759581.authors: Makkonen M, Kahilakoski O, Metsomaa J, Lioumis P, Ilmoniemi RJ, Mutanen TP.
doi:10.64898/2026.10.16.759581.abstract: Raw electroencephalography (EEG) data suffer from a low signal-to-noise ratio (SNR). Effective real-time cleaning of EEG would improve the robustness of EEG monitoring, brain–computer interfaces, and brain-state-dependent stimulation applications in both laboratory and real-life environments. Here, we present a real-time source-estimate-utilizing noise-discarding algorithm (rtSOUND) for EEG noise suppression. We adapted the established offline SOUND algorithm for real-time use and implemented it into an open-source EEG-processing software. Instead of using conventional temporal filtering, SOUND operates the data with a spatial filter. This makes it particularly suitable for real-time applications, since each streamed data sample can be cleaned separately in near real-time. Unlike temporal filtering methods, SOUND does not make assumptions about the frequency content of noise and brain signals but assumes that the noise topographies differ from those generated by brain activity. With an EEG forward model, rtSOUND cross-validates the EEG time series and estimates the spatial distribution of noise, resulting in a data-cleaning linear spatial filter. Each streamed EEG sample is processed synchronously, and the filter is periodically updated in an asynchronous parallel process. The algorithm rapidly updates the spatial filter in response to changes in the data, ensuring that noise reduction is both immediate and accurately adapted to the current EEG state. rtSOUND was validated with transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS)–EEG and resting-state EEG datasets measured from 25 healthy subjects. SNR of both TMS-evoked potentials and resting-state data consistently improved across various metrics. rtSOUND particularly benefitted channels with poor SNR, while retaining the waveforms in high-quality channels. The algorithm was fast enough to process data streamed at 5 kHz. rtSOUND improves the SNR of EEG in real time, providing a robust method to improve signal quality for brain-state-monitoring applications.

doi:10.1093/scan/nsag079.title: Individualized Theta Transcranial Alternating Current Stimulation Modulates Mnemonic Discrimination and ERP Responses to Positive Information in Individuals With Elevated Depressive Symptoms.
doi:10.1093/scan/nsag079.authors: Huang X, Zhou M, Wang C, Huang Y, Wang W, Shao J, Mao J, Li J, Zhang L, Ye R, Zhu C, Tian Y, He K, Yu F, Wang K.
doi:10.1093/scan/nsag079.abstract: Individuals with elevated depressive symptoms often show impairments in positive memory processing. This randomized, double-blind study investigated whether individualized theta-frequency transcranial alternating current stimulation (tACS) using an OFC-oriented montage modulates mnemonic discrimination and ERP responses to positive information. Sixty-one individuals with elevated depressive symptoms received either real or sham stimulation before completing an emotional mnemonic discrimination task. Behavioral results showed that lure discrimination increased following real stimulation but not sham stimulation. EEG results showed that real stimulation modulated ERP responses during positive memory encoding and retrieval, as reflected by increased late positive potential (LPP) amplitudes during encoding and altered early retrieval-related ERP amplitudes. These findings suggest that individualized theta-tACS may influence both mnemonic discrimination performance and neural responses to positive information.

doi:10.64898/2026.10.13.758724.title: Spatial working memory enhances gamma oscillations in rodent olfactory bulb and medial prefrontal cortex
doi:10.64898/2026.10.13.758724.authors: Mooziri, M.; Samii Moghaddam, A.; Raoufy, M. R.; Mirshekar, M. A.
doi:10.64898/2026.10.13.758724.abstract: Spatial working memory (SWM), a specialized form of working memory that temporarily encodes and retains spatial information, is fundamental to guide animal behaviors, yet our current knowledge of its circuit mechanisms remains far from known. Since, olfactory bulb (OB) and medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC) are critical brain structures for a wide range of cognitive behaviors, we hypothesized that the OB-mPFC circuit gamma oscillations might support rodent SWM processing. Our results show that SWM enhances regional low (30-60 Hz), but not high (60-100 Hz), gamma oscillations in both OB and mPFC, in correlation with the animals behavioral performance. Additionally, the OB-mPFC gamma band functional connectivity is strengthened by SWM. Moreover, we find that mPFC gamma oscillatory information transfer to OB supports the animals SWM performance. We also show that OB low gamma oscillations are modulated by mPFC delta phase, which further signifies the roles of mPFC feedbacks to shape OB gamma activity during SWM. These results suggest that OB-mPFC circuit gamma rhythms underlie SWM processing, and point towards possible mechanisms for cognitive disorders.

doi:10.1523/jneurosci.0632-26.2026.title: The central melanocortin system regulates growth hormone secretion.
doi:10.1523/jneurosci.0632-26.2026.authors: Sousa LMM, do N Vicente VA, Alves GA, Metzger M, Frazao R, Donato J.
doi:10.1523/jneurosci.0632-26.2026.abstract: The central melanocortin system is crucial for controlling food intake and metabolism. It includes neurons that produce pro-opiomelanocortin (POMC), a prohormone that generates the melanocortin receptor (MCR) agonist alpha-melanocyte-stimulating hormone (α-MSH), and neurons that produce agouti-related protein (AgRP), an endogenous MCR antagonist. This system also influences neuroendocrine neurons, thereby impacting pituitary hormone secretion. However, it remains unclear whether the central melanocortin system also modulates growth hormone (GH) secretion. Here we showed that arcuate nucleus (ARH) GH-releasing hormone (GHRH) neurons receive inputs from α-MSH and AgRP axons. α-MSH activates a subset (∼25%) of ARH GHRH neurons. Serial blood GH measurements were taken before and after systemic saline or clozapine N-oxide injections in mice expressing the excitatory hM3Dq-Gq receptor in POMC-expressing cells. Activation of POMC-expressing cells elevated blood GH levels compared with baseline or saline-injected mice, in both males and females. To determine whether AgRP neurons inhibit GH secretion, mice expressing the hM3Dq-Gq receptor simultaneously in AgRP- and GHRH-expressing cells were created. While chemogenetic activation of GHRH neurons caused a strong GH secretion, co-activation of AgRP neurons inhibited this response in both sexes. Additionally, Fos expression in GHRH-activated neurons was blunted when AgRP neurons were co-stimulated. Mice expressing the hM3Dq-Gq receptor only in MC4R-expressing cells were also investigated; however, activation of MC4R neurons did not alter GH levels. In conclusion, the central melanocortin system modulates the activity of GHRH neurons and GH secretion possibly through MC4R-independent pathways. These findings highlight a critical hypothalamic neurocircuit that integrates metabolic cues to regulate the somatotropic axis. Significance Statement The central melanocortin system processes both short- and long-term nutritional signals to regulate metabolism and various neuroendocrine axes. Here, we show that growth hormone (GH) secretion is controlled by hypothalamic neurons of the central melanocortin system, including populations that express POMC and AgRP. This regulation occurs, at least in part, through modulation of GH-releasing hormone neuron activity, a key group of cells that control pituitary GH secretion. Overall, these findings reveal a hypothalamic circuit that links nutritional status to the regulation of the GH axis, providing new insights into how growth is adaptively controlled by energy availability.
journal_names: The Journal of neuroscience : the official journal of the Society for Neuroscience

doi:10.64898/2026.09.24.753809.title: Hippocampal and large-scale functional connectivity reorganization following freediving training, and relationships with episodic memory
doi:10.64898/2026.09.24.753809.authors: Micaux J, Habibi AT, Mauconduit F, Boumezbeur F, Chiron C, Noulhiane M.
doi:10.64898/2026.09.24.753809.abstract: The hippocampus is particularly vulnerable to hypoxia, yet freedivers, who repeatedly undergo voluntary breath-hold hypoxia, do not appear to show the memory impairments commonly reported after involuntary hypoxic exposure. We investigated whether freediving training is associated with functional connectivity reorganization at the whole-brain and hippocampal levels, and whether hippocampal connectivity relates to preserved episodic memory performance. Seventeen male recreational freedivers underwent fMRI before and after a 7-month standardized training period, and 20 matched aerobic-trained controls were assessed at baseline. Functional connectivity analyses examined (i) whole-brain ROI-to-ROI connectivity, (ii) seed-to-voxel connectivity from the bilateral hippocampus and selected cortical seeds, and (iii) associations between hippocampal connectivity and episodic memory. Compared with controls, freedivers showed distinct connectivity patterns during apnea and rest. After training, whole-brain analyses revealed reorganization involving salience, frontoparietal, sensorimotor, visual, and cerebellar systems. Hippocampal analyses showed reduced connectivity with sensorimotor and default mode regions, alongside increased connectivity with cerebellar and visual areas, with stronger effects after training. In freedivers, specific post-training hippocampal connectivity was associated with episodic memory performance. These findings suggest that repeated voluntary hypoxia during freediving training is associated with selective functional reorganization of hippocampal and large-scale brain networks. This pattern may reflect adaptive neuroplasticity linked to preserved episodic memory under intermittent hypoxic exposure. Key points Freedivers exhibit selective hippocampal functional connectivity differences during voluntary intermittent breath-hold hypoxia, including reduced coupling with sensorimotor and default mode regions and increased coupling with cerebellar areas. A 7-month training period is associated with large-scale network reorganization involving salience, frontoparietal, sensorimotor, visual, and cerebellar systems. Post-training hippocampal connectivity is associated with preserved episodic memory performance, consistent with adaptive functional reorganization under voluntary intermittent hypoxia.

doi:10.64898/2026.10.02.756214.title: Dietary magnesium supplement enhances memory through Hippo signaling
doi:10.64898/2026.10.02.756214.authors: Wu, Y.; Treiber, C. D.; Waddell, S.
doi:10.64898/2026.10.02.756214.abstract: Dietary magnesium (Mg2+) supplement enhances memory in mammals and Drosophila, but whether and how Mg2+ changes molecular states of neurons, remains unknown. Here we used single-cell RNA sequencing to map cell-type specific transcriptional responses to memory-enhancing dietary Mg2+. These analyses revealed changes in Hippo-pathway gene expression in memory-relevant {beta} Kenyon Cells (KCs) of the mushroom bodies. Targeted knock-down of Merlin, hippo (hpo) and warts demonstrated requirement in {beta} KCs for Mg2+-enhanced, but not baseline memory. Further study of Hippo signaling identified Yorkie (yki) transcriptional coactivator and DNA-binding partner Scalloped (sd) to be required for baseline and Mg2+-enhanced memory. Moreover, releasing Yki::Sd of inhibition from Tondu-domain containing growth inhibitor (Tgi) specifically in {beta} KCs enhanced memory, independent of diet. Analyses of Yki::Sd target genes identified several required in {beta} KCs for baseline memory, including crb and Glut1 which are also Mg2+-induced in a Hippo-dependent manner in {beta} KCs. These genes suggest that aiding the metabolic demands of long-term memory and facilitating structural neuronal plasticity are key mediators of Mg2+-induced memory enhancement.
