doi:10.64898/2026.10.04.756569.title: Thalamic Dysconnectivity and Negative Symptoms in Schizophrenia Spectrum Disorder
doi:10.64898/2026.10.04.756569.authors: Kunitoki, K.; Adhikari, B. M.; Ankeeta, A.; Gao, S.; Ma, Y.; Straub, K. T.; Dos Santos Alves Maria, G.; Pagan, A. F.; Warner, A. R.; Du, X.; Kochunov, P.; Hong, L. E.
doi:10.64898/2026.10.04.756569.abstract: Background and Hypothesis Negative symptoms in schizophrenia spectrum disorder (SSD) are associated with poor functional outcomes and reduced quality of life; however, effective treatments remain limited. A better understanding of the underlying brain mechanisms is needed to develop better treatments. Neuroimaging studies implicate multiple brain networks in negative symptoms, though findings remain heterogeneous, potentially reflecting the multidimensionality of both symptoms and brain networks. Larger, more systematic dissections are required to identify the key hub(s) underlying negative symptoms. Study Design Structural MRI data from 394 participants (210 SSD, 184 healthy controls [HC]) were analyzed to identify cortical thickness and subcortical volume demonstrating both SSD-HC differences and associations with negative symptoms measured by the Brief Negative Symptom Scale (BNSS). Regions meeting both criteria were selected as seeds for resting-state functional connectivity analyses in 143 SSD patients to examine association with negative symptoms and their subdomains. Study Results The thalamus was the only region demonstrating significant structural abnormalities both in SSD and an association with BNSS total score (p-FDR<0.05). Functional-network-defined thalamic subregions were subsequently examined. Several thalamic hypoconnectivities were significantly corresponded with negative symptoms, involving thalamic subregions associated with the cortical default mode, somatosensory, medial temporal, and dorsal attention networks (p=0.001, corrected<0.05). Blunted affect showed the most extensive thalamic connectivity alterations, involving the striatum, cerebellum, and temporoparietal junction/superior temporal sulcus (TPJ-STS). Thalamic hypoconnectivity with TPJ-STS was also associated with overall negative symptoms and anhedonia. Conclusions This study identifies the thalamus as a central hub of negative symptom-related dysfunction in SSD and highlights specific thalamic subnetworks as potential targets for circuit-based interventions.
doi:10.64898/2026.10.04.756569.institution: University of Texas Health Science Center at Houston

doi:10.64898/2026.10.06.749912.title: Shifts in neural representations, not gaze, track how people reinterpret ambiguous social scenes
doi:10.64898/2026.10.06.749912.authors: Sava-Segal CA, Benson TG, Finn ES.
doi:10.64898/2026.10.06.749912.abstract: How do we come to “see” the same thing differently after hearing someone else’s perspective? Revising an interpretation could reflect changes in how the brain represents the meaning of what we see, changes in how we visually sample the input, or both. To disentangle these mechanisms, we developed MindLibs, an adaptive fMRI and eye-tracking paradigm in which participants generate interpretations of ambiguous photographs and then view alternative interpretations chosen in real time to vary in semantic content from their own. Exposure to semantically distant alternatives revealed a strong link between reinterpretation as reported behaviorally and representational shifts in association cortex, but no systematic relationship between reinterpretation and changes in gaze. In particular, representational shifts in lateral default-mode network regions (DMN-B) predicted reinterpretation independently of shifts in frontoparietal, attention, and visual networks, and independently of whether gaze changed. In contrast, shifts in visual cortex tracked reinterpretation only when gaze also shifted, and contributed no unique variance beyond DMN-B. These findings identify higher-order conceptual reconfiguration, rather than perceptual resampling, as the primary account of how people revise the meaning of an ambiguous scene.

doi:10.64898/2026.09.28.755202.title: Age-related differences in episodic memory precision are robust across time of day, chronotype, and testing format
doi:10.64898/2026.09.28.755202.authors: Maybury, J. S.; Simons, J. S.
doi:10.64898/2026.09.28.755202.abstract: Older adults typically exhibit reduced episodic memory precision, while maintaining relatively preserved retrieval success. However, little is known about whether these age-related differences are influenced by internal biological factors (e.g., chronotype) or external testing conditions (e.g., experiment format, time of day). To address this question, younger and older adults completed an object-location memory task online, either in the morning or evening, and either with or without video-based supervision. Memory performance was assessed using mean absolute error and Bayesian hierarchical mixture modelling, which dissociated memory precision ({kappa}) from the probability of memory-based responding ({theta}). Immediate memory performance was high across age groups, irrespective of time of day. Greater encoding error predicted greater retrieval error, and participants tested in the video condition exhibited lower recall error and higher recognition performance than those tested without supervision. Consistent with prior studies, older adults exhibited reduced memory precision relative to younger adults, whereas retrieval success remained largely intact. However, Bayesian Hierarchical Modelling provided no evidence that time of day, experiment format, or their interactions with age influenced either memory precision or retrieval probability. Older adults reported stronger morning preferences than younger adults, and participants generally selected testing times that aligned with their chronotype. Nevertheless, alignment between chronotype and testing time did not modulate memory performance. The results indicate that age-related differences in episodic memory precision are robust across variations in testing context, including time of day, experiment format, and individual differences in chronotype. More broadly, the results support the feasibility of remote and unsupervised testing for memory precision research and suggest that chronotype and testing time are unlikely to be major sources of variability in immediate object-location memory performance.
doi:10.64898/2026.09.28.755202.institution: Department of Experimental Psychology, University of Cambridge, Downing Street, Cambridge UK

doi:10.64898/2026.10.06.757069.title: Language-associated brain representations covary with disruption of selfhood under psilocybin
doi:10.64898/2026.10.06.757069.authors: Cooper, G.; Stoliker, D.; Astl Delgado, S. V.; Blackburne, G.; Novelli, L.; Green, D. W.; Razi, A.; Das, R. K.; Skipper, J. I.
doi:10.64898/2026.10.06.757069.abstract: Language helps organise experience into an idiosyncratic, temporally extended sense of self. We therefore used fMRI to investigate whether greater similarity between participants in the activity of language-associated brain regions accompanied psilocybin-induced loss of selfhood. Participants heard music and viewed moving clouds at baseline and after 19 mg psilocybin. At each brain location and time point, we tested whether similarity increased with each pair's summed rank on the Ego Dissolution Inventory (EDI; N=43). We grouped independent components of these associations by time course and decoded each group's map with Neurosynth. Elementary visual imagery (SI; N=49) and baseline activity served as comparators. Under psilocybin, one group formed a distributed, left-lateralised frontotemporal network matching the Neurosynth language map (r=.382, spatial-null p<.001, q=.003), nearly twice the largest comparator estimate (SI: r=.208, p=.004, q=.028; baseline: r<.12). In exploratory analyses, resting-state connectivity of this network decreased with posterior visual cortex and increased with thalamic and frontal regions. Participants with higher EDI scores showed larger changes (Spearman's rho=.455, Bonferroni-adjusted p=.048; SI: rho=.008), most strongly for items describing loss of ego or identity (rho=.43 to .51). We propose that language-associated systems incorporate each person's semantic and autobiographical context into experience, and that disrupting them contributes to loss of ego and identity.

doi:10.64898/2026.10.08.757687.title: Tasting from memory: reconstructing taste from visual cues in the human brain
doi:10.64898/2026.10.08.757687.authors: Berman, S.; Lawen, A.; Xu, S.; Kahn, I.; Shohamy, D.
doi:10.64898/2026.10.08.757687.abstract: Taste guides us toward nourishment and away from harm. Yet when we decide what to eat, taste only exists in memory, evoked by a cue. How the brain retrieves taste memories is almost entirely unknown. If memory re-creates experience, it should reproduce the brain's activation while tasting, even in the absence of taste. We scanned participants while they formed and then retrieved associations between tastes and visual cues. The gustatory cortex was engaged during retrieval and distinguished among remembered tastes, but not using the patterns it had formed while tasting. Patterns persisted instead in lateral parietal cortex, distinguishing individual tastes, not just taste-categories. Activity in the amygdala covaried with this same parietal region and amygdala activity predicted which associations were retained. Taste memory is not simply a re-creation of sensory experience, but a distinct representation, outside the taste system, yet specific enough to guide what we choose to eat.

doi:10.31234/osf.io/asn89_v2.title: Perceptual similarity landscape differs between young and clinically unimpaired older adults and contributes to long-term memory precision
doi:10.31234/osf.io/asn89_v2.authors: Yang H, He M, Han A, Pimentel-Hurlburt DK, Glueck JAE, Jung ZK, Southward RJ, Deutsch GK, Samudra N, Purdon PL, Wandell BA, Wagner AD.
doi:10.31234/osf.io/asn89_v2.abstract: The precision of memory for event features is lower in older relative to young adults. Recent studies that examined continuous reproduction data with a mixture model –– which estimates two parameters putatively reflecting reduced fidelity/precision and outright forgetting –– suggest age-related memory decline is associated with a selective or larger reduction in mnemonic precision vs. forgetting. However, emerging evidence indicates that performance on continuous reproduction paradigms depends not just on memory, but also on the psychophysical similarity function (PSF) of the perceptual feature space, which may also change with age. Using a recently developed one-parameter statistical model of continuous reproduction memory data that mechanistically accounts for the empirically measured PSF, we examined whether age-related differences in continuous reproduction data are at least partially explained by age-related differences in perception. Young adults (age 18-25 yrs, N = 55) and clinically unimpaired older adults (age 68-86 yrs, N = 54) with normal color vision performed (a) a continuous reproduction task probing long-term memory for object color, (b) a Likert color similarity judgement task, and (c) a color matching task. We first replicated previous findings of age-related differences in memory precision for the colors of previously encountered objects and identified age-related changes in color perception on the similarity and matching tasks. We then characterized the age-group specific perceptual landscape by constructing the PSF using the similarity task data. Subsequent model comparison revealed that for both age groups, the more parsimonious one-parameter model, which accounts for the age-group specific PSF, explained continuous reproduction data better than the mixture model. Notably, the PSFs differed between age groups, and the difference was not explained by individual differences in response bias or trial-history effects. When we replaced the PSF estimated from older adults’ perceptual data with that estimated from the younger adults in the one-parameter model, it produced a worse fit to older adults’ continuous reproduction data compared to the model with the age-group appropriate PSF, further supporting a link between age-related changes in perception and the precision of episodic memory.

doi:10.64898/2026.09.22.753530.title: Retinal adaptive mechanisms confer selectivity to homogeneous objects in natural scenes
doi:10.64898/2026.09.22.753530.authors: Lorenzi, B.; Varro, D.; Baroux, R.; Virgili, S.; Marre, O.
doi:10.64898/2026.09.22.753530.abstract: Adaptive mechanisms in sensory neurons are crucial to transmit information in different contexts. In the retina, it is assumed that their role is to normalize neuronal responses to input statistics like mean and variance. However, this role has mostly been characterized with simple, artificial stimuli, and remains unclear for natural stimuli. Here we show that during their response to natural scenes, adaptive mechanisms reshape the feature selectivity of ganglion cells, the retinal output. We recorded retinal ganglion cell responses to rapid sequences of natural images in mice. Including a bio-inspired adaptive mechanism in an artificial neural network model was necessary to predict cell responses to new sequences of natural images. This adaptive mechanism tuned specific cell types to selectively respond to homogeneous regions situated within cluttered visual surrounds, a feature suited for detecting threats. Adaptive mechanisms do not merely normalize responses but actively enable new feature selectivity in the early visual system.
doi:10.64898/2026.09.22.753530.institution: Sorbonne Universite; Institut de la Vision; Inserm; CNRS, Paris, France; Rothschild Foundation Hospital, 29 rue Manin, Paris 75019, France

doi:10.64898/2026.09.29.754498.title: The Walking Brain: Mapping feature-specific cortical responses to naturally unfolding sensory experience in the real world
doi:10.64898/2026.09.29.754498.authors: Altınkaynak M, Carlton LB, Topkoç E, Boas DA, Yücel MA.
doi:10.64898/2026.09.29.754498.abstract: Understanding how the brain processes the everyday world is fundamental, yet laboratory paradigms exclude self-generated movement, unscripted events, and a continuously evolving multisensory environment. Wearable neuroimaging enables real-world measurement, but linking neural activity to uncontrolled sensory information remains challenging. Here, we extend a feature-based framework from naturalistic movie viewing to everyday behavior using wearable whole-head high-density fNIRS and participant-specific audiovisual recordings during movies and outdoor walking with no explicit task or scripted audiovisual sequence. Luminance- and sound-related cortical maps showed significant spatial correspondence, particularly in visual and auditory regions, whereas face-related correspondence was weaker. Luminance- and face-related maps were reproducible within individuals across repeated walks. Additional exploratory analysis demonstrated, to our knowledge, the first out-of-sample encoding of continuous environmental features during unconstrained real-world fNIRS, predicting cortical activity during held-out walking periods. Together, these findings establish a feature-based framework for linking cortical activity to naturally unfolding sensory experience in everyday behavior.

doi:10.64898/2026.10.01.755868.title: A dynamical attractor computes reward prediction in the basal forebrain
doi:10.64898/2026.10.01.755868.abstract: Phasic ensemble bursting in subcortical neuromodulatory systems such as the basal forebrain (BF) provides a powerful format for broadcasting reward-prediction signals. These bursts encode reward prediction by varying population amplitude, yet their internal structure, reflected in cell-to-cell amplitude relationships, remains conserved. How neural circuits reconcile these competing constraints remains unknown. Here we show that BF bursting is generated by a dynamical attractor: burst structure is imposed not by feedforward inputs but by recurrent circuit dynamics, while burst amplitude is determined by approximately linear integration across concurrent inputs. Optogenetic activation of BF neurons expressing natriuretic peptide receptor 3 (Npr3) outside the behavioral task reproduced the low-dimensional dynamics of natural cue-evoked bursting, preserving the temporal envelope and cell-to-cell amplitude relationships across stimulation patterns. Critically, unilateral activation of non-overlapping Npr3 populations in either hemisphere recruited the full bilateral ensemble into the same native trajectory, showing that restricted inputs can nevertheless recruit the full ensemble. Matched ipsilateral and contralateral onset latencies exceeding 25 ms implicated recurrent interactions beyond the BF. Despite the conserved structure, population burst amplitude varied with stimulation strength and summed approximately linearly across concurrent unilateral inputs. This linear summation extended to natural sensory input during behavior: adding Npr3 stimulation to auditory cues increased cue-evoked burst amplitude, improved detection, and reduced subsequent reward responses, consistent with stronger reward prediction producing smaller reward prediction errors. Thus, a low-dimensional dynamical attractor preserves a shared BF burst structure across diverse inputs while integrating concurrent inputs into a scalar burst amplitude that encodes reward prediction.

doi:10.64898/2026.10.01.755994.title: LLM-powered automatic scoring tools for memory recall
doi:10.64898/2026.10.01.755994.authors: Tang, R. S.; Born, S. J.; Delarazan, A. I.; Demarest, P. L.; Karagoz, A. B.; Reagh, Z. M.
doi:10.64898/2026.10.01.755994.abstract: Free recall of naturalistic stimuli, such as films and stories, reveals what people remember and how they organize it. Scoring such recall requires matching each recalled utterance to the encoded stimulus, and doing this manually often makes large studies impractical. Existing automated methods mostly return similarity or aggregate scores rather than explicit matches between recalled and stimulus content. Here we introduce an open-source, model-agnostic pipeline that uses a large language model (LLM) to divide the stimulus and the recall into information units and to match units between the two texts. The output is a table of unit-to-unit matches with accuracy labels, from which standard analysis scripts compute recall measures. We validated the pipeline with four LLMs (Claude Sonnet 4.5, GPT 5.4, Gemini 2.5 Pro, and Gemini 2.5 Flash) on three datasets. On typed recall of four short stories, agreement between each model and two trained raters ({phi} = .73-.79) was close to the agreement between the raters themselves ({phi} = .77). A second run reproduced each model's matches ({phi} = .91-.97) more closely than the raters agreed with each other. On spoken recall of 10 films, every model attributed recall to the correct film with high agreement. On uncorrected speech-to-text recall of a television episode, agreement varied more across models. The median cost was under $1 per participant for every model. These results suggest that the pipeline can serve as a reliable, low-cost alternative to manual scoring of free recall.
doi:10.64898/2026.10.01.755994.institution: Department of Psychological and Brain Sciences, Washington University in St. Louis

doi:10.1016/j.neuropsychologia.2026.1096.title: The roles of working memory and executive functioning in relational semantic processing tasks: Evidence from primary progressive aphasia.
doi:10.1016/j.neuropsychologia.2026.1096.authors: Meyer AM, Snider SF, Faria AV, Tippett DC, Turkeltaub PE, Hillis AE, Friedman RB.
doi:10.1016/j.neuropsychologia.2026.1096.abstract: Referential semantic processing tasks, such as word-picture matching (WPM), require the matching of stimuli that represent the same concept, while relational semantic processing tasks, such as Pyramids and Palm Trees (PPT), require the processing of relationships between concepts. Compared to referential tasks, relational tasks may be likely to place a greater demand on working memory and/or executive functioning. In the current study, we examined referential and relational semantic processing in all variants of primary progressive aphasia (PPA). We predicted that backward digit and spatial span tasks and/or Trails B would be significant predictors of accuracy on relational tasks, while similar tasks that place less significant demands on working memory or executive functioning, such as forward digit and spatial span tasks and Trails A, would not be significant predictors of accuracy on relational tasks. In behavioral regression analyses, neither backward span task was a significant predictor of accuracy on referential tasks, but accuracy on 5 out of 6 relational tasks was predicted by at least one backward span task. In a second set of behavioral analyses, neither Trails task was a significant predictor of accuracy on referential tasks. Conversely, accuracy on 5 out of 6 relational tasks was predicted by Trails B. In regression analyses involving grey matter volume, three ROIs (left middle temporal gyrus, left insula, right middle temporal pole) were significant positive predictors of accuracy on a referential task (Auditory WPM). The same three ROIs were significant positive predictors of accuracy on a relational task (PPT-Pictures), along with one additional ROI - the left pars triangularis. The findings of this study suggest that performance on relational semantic processing tasks is affected by working memory capacity and executive functioning, which are supported by the left pars triangularis.

doi:10.64898/2026.09.17.752393.title: Sleep spindle deficits in childhood absence epilepsy improve with antiseizure treatment and disease resolution
doi:10.64898/2026.09.17.752393.authors: Goodman SK, Yi S, Chinappen DM, Kramer MA, Chu CJ, Kwon H.
doi:10.64898/2026.09.17.752393.abstract: Childhood absence epilepsy (CAE), the most common childhood epilepsy syndrome, is associated with bursts of generalized thalamocortical spike-wave discharges and cognitive impairment, yet the physiological mechanisms linking disease activity, treatment, and cognition remain unclear. Sleep spindles, generated by thalamocortical circuits, are associated with cognitive function and may be disrupted by epileptic activity. Here, we retrospectively studied 87 EEGs from 53 children with active and resolved CAE and 87 age- and sex-matched controls to evaluate sleep spindle activity across disease states and its association with antiseizure medication (ASM) exposure. We found that children with active CAE had reduced spindle rates across all cortical regions compared to those with resolved CAE and controls, with the largest reduction in the frontal region, where epileptic spike activity was also most prominent. Spindle rate was inversely correlated with epileptic spike rate, consistent with a shared thalamocortical circuitry. The association between ASM exposure and spindle rate varied by disease state. In active CAE, treated children had higher spindle rates than untreated children. In resolved CAE, treated children had lower spindle rates than untreated children. In contrast, ASM-related differences in spike rate were more limited, although a medication-specific reduction was observed in active CAE. These findings support sleep spindle rate as a candidate physiological marker of disease state and ASM exposure in children with CAE. Given the established role of sleep spindles in memory consolidation, these findings support testing of whether spindle disruption provides a mechanistic link between epileptic thalamocortical activity and cognitive vulnerability in CAE. Significance Statement Childhood absence epilepsy (CAE) is a common childhood generalized epilepsy characterized by abnormal thalamocortical activity and cognitive difficulties. Here, we show that sleep spindle activity is globally reduced during active CAE, particularly in frontal regions, and normalizes after disease resolution. Spindle activity was anticorrelated with epileptic spike rate and impacted by antiseizure medication exposure. These results support the hypothesis that epileptic spikes and sleep spindles share thalamocortical circuitry and promote sleep spindles as a candidate physiological biomarker to link epileptic activity with cognitive vulnerability in CAE.

doi:10.64898/2026.10.01.755903.title: Cellular and molecular coding of habit-driven behavior in the dorsal raphe nucleus
doi:10.64898/2026.10.01.755903.authors: Chalençon L, Rahn RM, Chottekalapanda RU, Lenz A, Zhang T, Donatelle A, Stujenske JM, Fetcho RN, Parekh PK, Roshgadol J, Wright MA, Liston C.
doi:10.64898/2026.10.01.755903.abstract: Chronic stress has potent effects on reward-seeking behavior, reducing hedonic drive but also biasing individuals toward habitual responding at the expense of goal-directed action. While prior studies have implicated corticostriatal circuits in these shifts, the contribution of the dorsal raphe nucleus (DRN) - a central neuromodulatory hub that regulates motivational states - remains poorly understood. Here, we identify a key role for DRN neurons in mediating stress-induced transitions from goal-directed to habit-driven behavior. Using two-photon calcium imaging in awake behaving mice, we show that DRN neurons encode representations of both effort expenditures and reward acquisition that are integrated at the single-neuron level. Chronic stress selectively enhances reward-related responses in habit-driven individuals, and deficits in reward-related activity in DRN neurons predict future habit formation after chronic stress. Single-nucleus transcriptional profiling revealed that chronic stress drives habit-related gene expression changes in GABAergic DRN neurons, including upregulation of genes implicated in synapse function and inhibitory signaling, and identified potential pharmacological treatment targets. Optogenetic inhibition of DRN GABA neurons rescued stress effects on habit formation, driving stable shifts in operant responding that persisted for days. Together, these findings establish the DRN as a critical modulator of stress-induced behavioral inflexibility, and identify a new role for DRN GABAergic neurons in determining stress susceptibility and driving stable and persistent switches in operant responding during recovery from chronic stress.

doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11174-3.title: Targeted stimulation of motor cortex ensembles drives learned movements.
doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11174-3.authors: Chen Q, Wu A, Yu B, Chae S, Tan Z, Ramot A, Aljadeff J, Komiyama T.
doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11174-3.abstract: During the execution of learned motor skills, the neural population in layer 2/3 (L2/3) of primary motor cortex (M1) expresses a reproducible spatiotemporal activity pattern 1 . It is debated whether M1 actively participates in generating this learned pattern and whether this pattern causally drives the learned movement 2-5 . Here we combined in vivo two-photon calcium imaging and holographic optogenetic stimulation of functionally defined M1 L2/3 ensembles in mice performing a skilled lever-pressing task. Brief synchronous stimulation of about 20 neurons whose activity onset precedes voluntary movement onset induced movements resembling the learned movement, while producing activity patterns in other M1 neurons resembling the learned activity. Moreover, trial-by-trial variability of optogenetically triggered population activity correlated with variability in the induced movements. These variabilities were predicted by the initial state of M1 activity preceding stimulation. In some trials, stimulation induced the learned activity without inducing movements, indicating that the learned activity is not simply a reflection of movements but can arise internally. Stimulation failed to generate movements or learned activity in task-disengaged mice. Stimulation of neurons whose activity followed movement onsets failed to induce the learned movement in task-engaged mice. Together, the learned activity in M1 L2/3 can be generated when M1 is prepared at the optimal initial state and receives precise triggering inputs, supporting the active role of M1 in generating learned activity and learned movements.

doi:10.64898/2026.10.13.758534.title: A gαq signaling pathway in dopaminergic neurons suppresses memory
doi:10.64898/2026.10.13.758534.authors: Martinez-Cervantes, J. C.; Shah, P.; Cervantes Sandoval, I.
doi:10.64898/2026.10.13.758534.abstract: Which experiences persist as memories is a fundamental question in neurobiology. The balance between memory persistence and suppression is thought to be optimal for an organism to adapt to the ever-changing environment. Memory suppression is a process by which the brain limits the strength and expression of memories. Memory suppressors are genes whose disruption can enhance memory at different stages: acquisition, consolidation, forgetting, or recall. Here, using aversive classical conditioning in Drosophila, we show that Gq acts as a memory suppressor in PPL1 dopaminergic neurons. Knockdown of gq in dopaminergic neurons enhances acquisition, strengthens anesthesia-resistant memory, and impairs reversal learning. In vivo functional imaging revealed that gq knockdown amplifies shock-evoked responses in a type of PPL1 neuron. Additionally, using ex vivo imaging and pharmacological experiments, we reveal that both Gq and the OAMB receptor alter octopamine-evoked ER calcium responses in PPL1 neurons. Our results uncover a new role of Gq signaling within dopaminergic neurons that suppresses memory.

doi:10.64898/2026.10.10.756925.title: Primate Gaze Behavior Reflects Change of Mind in a Naturalistic Navigation Task
doi:10.64898/2026.10.10.756925.authors: Choi, W.; Alefantis, P.; Andreadakis, G.; Angelaki, D. E.
doi:10.64898/2026.10.10.756925.abstract: Revising a decision while acting on it is a fundamental aspect of natural behavior, yet the underlying computations are difficult to track in real time. To explore how such belief updates unfold, we tested whether eye movements reveal a subject's change of mind during a naturalistic navigation task with a binary target choice. Humans and monkeys were required to navigate to one of two goal locations presented either simultaneously or sequentially in a virtual environment where explicit position cues were absent. Our findings reveal that gaze continuously tracks the latent variable, including changes of mind. We found that the target tracking accuracy before the second target is even presented during sequential target trials predicts whether the subject's navigational goal persists (first target choice) or changes (second target choice). These results underscore the importance of gaze in action planning and changes of mind, supporting the hypothesis that eye movements embody not only the current latent variable but also its uncertainty.

doi:10.64898/2026.09.20.752934.title: Abstract representation in the hippocampus predicts spontaneously adopted structure-based behavioral strategy
doi:10.64898/2026.09.20.752934.authors: Jiang, Y.; Liu, Y.; Zhao, X.
doi:10.64898/2026.09.20.752934.abstract: Animals can solve the same problem using distinct strategies, ranging from memorization of specific sensory details to inference based on abstract task structure. Although the hippocampus has been implicated in cognitive map formation, how the structural information emerges in the hippocampus through learning and whether it is associated with behavioral strategies remain poorly understood. Here, we developed a structured cue-guided navigation task in virtual reality and performed longitudinal two-photon calcium imaging of hippocampal CA1 neurons throughout learning in mice. Although the task did not explicitly require learning of latent structure, most animals progressively transformed hippocampal map from sensory-oriented representations into cue-invariant representations of reward sequences. Strikingly, the emergence of such abstract hippocampal maps predicted whether individual animals adopted structure-based behavioral strategies when sensory information became partially unavailable. At the population level, reward-sequence representations formed a latent-state map capable for predicting future state transitions, generating a parsimonious Markov graph. Computational modeling further identified next-state prediction and representational regularization as two computational principles essential for generating similar latent-state structures across distinct architectures. Together, our findings suggest that the hippocampus spontaneously extracts abstract task structure through learning and that the geometry of hippocampal representations predicts problem-solving strategies.

doi:10.64898/2026.10.02.755501.title: Thalamocortical credit routing from the basal ganglia and cerebellum: anatomical constraints and circuit principles
doi:10.64898/2026.10.02.755501.authors: Tanno S, Morishima M, Fujita K, Kato S, Kobayashi K, Kawaguchi Y, Isomura Y, Hira R.
doi:10.64898/2026.10.02.755501.abstract: Animals learn to select actions that maximize reward in complex environments. A central challenge in this process is credit routing: behavioral outcomes must be routed back to the neural populations that contributed to generating the relevant actions. One possible route is through thalamocortical pathways conveying learning signals from the basal ganglia and cerebellum, where plasticity is shaped by reward-prediction errors. However, how these pathways route such signals back to specific cortical circuits remains unclear. To address this question, we combined anatomical circuit mapping in mice with closed-loop circuit modeling. Anterograde transsynaptic tracing revealed that thalamic neurons receiving input from the substantia nigra pars reticulata or the lateral cerebellar nucleus were largely segregated, with partial overlap in the ventromedial thalamus. Nevertheless, their cortical axons shared a pronounced enrichment in layer 1a, most prominently in secondary motor cortex. In a brain- wide synergistic loop-circuit model, learning was enhanced when both pathways delivered additive and gain-modulating feedback aligned with the cortical action readout. Local activity- based calibration established this alignment, whereas dendritic-spike- and reward-prediction- error-dependent thalamocortical plasticity further refined behavioral output. Module-specific feedback was essential for a brain–machine interface task requiring the simultaneous conditioning of multiple target neurons. Together, these findings define a credit-routing architecture in which laminar convergence, plastic alignment, and modular feedback link parallel subcortical learning systems to cortical action representations.

doi:10.1371/journal.pcbi.1014796.title: Modeling decision dynamics disentangles working memory, cognitive control and reinforcement learning and reveals clinical differences.
doi:10.1371/journal.pcbi.1014796.authors: Bera K, Fengler A, Boudewyn MA, Carter CS, Erickson MA, Gold JM, Luck SJ, Ragland JD, Yonelinas AP, MacDonald Iii AW, Barch DM, Frank MJ.
doi:10.1371/journal.pcbi.1014796.abstract: Various neurocognitive processes contribute to reinforcement learning (RL) and decision making, requiring careful task designs and computational modeling to disentangle them. People rely on capacity-limited working memory (WM) to rapidly and flexibly adapt behavior during learning, together with slower incremental RL processes that support robust long-term retention. The RLWM paradigm was developed to isolate these contributions by manipulating WM demands during learning. Empirical and computational advances support the separability of such processes, but only imperfectly, because a given choice can often equally be attributed to use of WM vs. RL. Here, we show that jointly modeling decision dynamics - accounting not only for choices but also response time distributions, together with hierarchical Bayesian parameter estimation - improves the ability to disentangle separable learning and cognitive control processes. Despite added complexity, models with decision dynamics improved parameter recovery and yielded accurate out-of-sample prediction for choices in a held-out test phase after learning. In contrast, models fit only to choices produced an inflation of RL learning rates and failed the out-of-sample test. Moreover, joint modeling also revealed a novel neurocognitive process by which participants proactively widen decision boundaries to increase response caution under increased WM load. Applying our model to patients with schizophrenia revealed a deficit in proactive control mechanisms as well as slowed incremental RL, which were masked by previous choice-only models, while replicating previously established WM deficits. In summary, we show how joint modeling enables accurate, model-based and mechanism-oriented computational phenotyping of psychopathologies.

doi:10.64898/2026.09.26.754627.title: A cascade of attentional and default mode network dynamics following the resolution of perceptual ambiguity
doi:10.64898/2026.09.26.754627.authors: Ponzi, A.; Miyahara, K.; Suzuki, K.
doi:10.64898/2026.09.26.754627.abstract: The neural mechanisms underlying spontaneous perceptual switches during bistable perception, particularly the dynamic interplay between large-scale brain networks, remain incompletely understood. Here, using functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) in six participants and a bistable kinetic depth effect (KDE) stimulus, we investigated the spatiotemporal dynamics of brain activity associated with spontaneous perceptual reversals compared to physically induced (replayed) switches. Leveraging a fine-grained functional brain parcellation (MD758) and time-resolved analysis including noise correlations, we identified a distributed network encompassing occipital (MT/MST, LOC), parietal (IPS), and frontal (FEF, IFC, DLPFC) regions showing differential activity during spontaneous versus replayed switches. This network topography qualitatively overlapped a prior review-derived synthesis of perceptual-switching regions. Temporal decomposition of the differential fMRI signal further revealed a characteristic network cascade after the perceptual report: positive dorsal attention (DAN) and visual (VIS) network contrasts peaked approximately 4 s after the report alongside a negative default mode network (DMN) contrast; a slower, more modest ventral attention (VAN)-frontoparietal (FPN) component was observed around 10 s post-report but was weak and is treated as preliminary. The early 4 s profile was recovered across raw-signal, PCA-denoised, and noise-correlation analyses (three related, not fully independent analyses), with the noise-correlation analysis indicating that it is not fully attributable to shared motor-report signals. These findings delineate the temporal sequence of network recruitment following spontaneous perceptual transitions and suggest that interplay between attentional control and default mode networks accompanies the resolution of perceptual ambiguity.

doi:10.64898/2026.10.01.755396.title: Eccentricity, but not category, organizes infant ventral temporal cortex
doi:10.64898/2026.10.01.755396.authors: Tung, S. S.; Chen, E. M.; Tay, C.; Szymanski, K.; Ellis, C. T.
doi:10.64898/2026.10.01.755396.abstract: Scene- and word-selective regions in adult ventral temporal cortex occupy consistent locations across individuals and align with eccentricity biases for peripheral versus central parts of the visual field, respectively. This relationship may reflect a developmental sequence in which initial preferences for visual field location influence the emergence of category-selectivity in these regions, driven by where each category appears in the visual field. To test this account, we used fMRI in awake, behaving infants aged 2-10 months, independently manipulating stimulus size (40{degrees} versus 6{degrees}) and category (scenes versus letters). We found eccentricity gradients across early visual cortex and ventral temporal cortex. Crucially, the collateral sulcus -- a scene-selective, peripherally-biased region in adults -- showed greater responses to big over small stimuli in infants, but no reliable preference for scenes over letters. These findings suggest that an eccentricity bias could provide a scaffold for later category specialization.

doi:10.21203/rs.3.rs-11314069/v1.title: A Rigorous Statistical Framework for Long Short-Term Memory Networks: State-Space Operator Dynamics, Continuous-Time Neural SDEs, and Informational Efficiency
doi:10.21203/rs.3.rs-11314069/v1.abstract: Abstract The statistical elucidations of Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) models are usually distinct from their dynamical and information processing capabilities, even though LSTM models have drawn a lot of attention and become popular for modelling time series with dependent sequential data. This paper develops a unified framework in which an LSTM is treated as a nonlinear stochastic state-space system, an operator acting on latent memory, and, under an explicit diffusion scaling, a continuous-time stochastic dynamical system. The framework has four components. First, the discrete LSTM recursion is formulated as a measurable Markov state-space model with bounded gates and a potentially unbounded cell state. Second, a continuous-time neural stochastic differential equation (SDE) is introduced through a well-defined scaling limit rather than by an informal division of the discrete recursion by the sampling interval. Third, statistical inference is analysed through recursive parameter sensitivities, a conditional likelihood, the Fisher information matrix, and a martingale central limit argument under stationarity, mixing, and non-singularity assumptions. Fourth, sequential PAC-Bayesian bounds are used to relate predictive risk to posterior complexity and information divergence. We prove existence and uniqueness of the neural SDE under global Lipschitz and linear-growth conditions, derive a sufficient mean-square stability condition for a dissipative continuous-time model, establish consistency and asymptotic normality of the score-based estimator under standard geometric-ergodicity assumptions, and state a sequential PAC-Bayesian risk bound. The paper is deliberately careful about scope: none of the theoretical results implies that every LSTM is automatically stable, statistically efficient, or optimal. Those properties follow only under the assumptions stated in the corresponding results. The proposed simulation protocol is therefore presented as a validation design rather than as completed empirical evidence.

doi:10.64898/2026.09.15.751731.title: Hunger and sleep recruit distinct brain systems to form spatial memory
doi:10.64898/2026.09.15.751731.authors: Tosadori, E.; Bou, J.; Dimitrov, S.; Ocampo-Garces, A.; Valdes, J.; Inostroza, M.; Born, J.; Sawangjit, A.
doi:10.64898/2026.09.15.751731.abstract: By demonstrating that hunger consolidates spatial memory via a non-hippocampal mechanism that critically involves the retrosplenial cortex, we identify a mode of memory formation that is distinct from well-known hippocampus-dependent memory formation during sleep. Food-deprived rats encoded object locations and, during a subsequent 2-h consolidation phase, either received food and slept (Sleep-Fed) or stayed awake (Wake-Fed), or remained hungry and stayed awake (Wake-Hungry). At later retrieval testing, both Wake-Hungry and Sleep-Fed rats exhibited robust spatial memory, whereas Wake-Fed rats did not. Blocking neuropeptide-Y (NPY) signaling during the consolidation phase abolished hunger-consolidated memory. Unlike sleep-dependent consolidation, hunger-consolidated memory did not require the hippocampus during consolidation or retrieval, and not even during encoding. In contrast, inhibiting retrosplenial cortex during retrieval abolished hunger-consolidated memory but spared memory formed during sleep. Thus, recruitment of brain systems to form spatial memory is tuned to specific brain states, and fundamentally differs between sleep and hunger.

doi:10.1016/j.neuroscience.2026.10.001.title: Cue-responsive mPFC neuronal populations are associated with response execution and response withholding in a Go/No-Go task.
doi:10.1016/j.neuroscience.2026.10.001.authors: Wang S, Li Y, Cai Y, Yang X, Sun C, Ma C.
doi:10.1016/j.neuroscience.2026.10.001.abstract: Response inhibition is an important component of behavioral control that enables organisms to withhold inappropriate or prepotent responses under specific environmental contingencies. The prefrontal cortex (PFC) has been widely implicated in this process, yet how populations of PFC neurons are differentially recruited during response withholding and response execution remains incompletely understood. In this study, rats were trained on a Go/No-Go task, and calcium activity in medial PFC (mPFC) pyramidal neurons was monitored using a miniscope during freely behaving performance. The results revealed that distinct cue-responsive populations of mPFC pyramidal neurons were associated with Go and No-Go conditions, with both increased and decreased calcium activity observed following the corresponding auditory cues. Some neurons exhibited transient cue-related activity, whereas others showed more sustained or temporally distributed activity during the defined response-withholding period. Some neurons exhibited transient cue-related activity, whereas others showed more sustained or temporally distributed activity during the defined response-withholding period. Notably, subsets of neurons responded to both Go and No-Go cues, indicating overlapping as well as cue-dependent response profiles across task conditions. At the population level, cue-responsive neuronal populations showed associations with behavioral outcome. However, these functionally defined populations do not establish specific co-active neuronal populations or causal contributions to behavior. Together, these findings provide a population-level characterization of mPFC neuronal dynamics associated with response withholding and response execution and highlight the heterogeneous and cue-dependent organization of prefrontal activity during behavioral control.

doi:10.1523/jneurosci.0619-26.2026.title: Estradiol-dependent memory and hippocampal spine remodeling require proteasomal protein degradation.
doi:10.1523/jneurosci.0619-26.2026.authors: Beamish SB, Gross KS, Kuehn RK, Frank K, Valentine EP, Jarome TJ, Frick KM.
doi:10.1523/jneurosci.0619-26.2026.abstract: Although 17β-estradiol (E 2 ) is a critical neuromodulator of hippocampus-dependent memory and synaptic plasticity, the molecular mechanisms underlying these effects remain incompletely understood. Previous studies showed that E 2 enhances dorsal hippocampus-dependent memory consolidation by activating signaling pathways that promote protein synthesis and dendritic spine formation. However, these studies largely overlooked the contribution of protein degradation mediated by the ubiquitin proteasome system (UPS), despite extensive evidence implicating UPS activity in long-term memory and synaptic plasticity. Here, we combined temporally specific dorsal hippocampal infusions of the proteasome inhibitor β-lactone with three-dimensional spine morphometry to examine the role of UPS-mediated protein degradation in E 2 -induced memory consolidation and CA1 spinogenesis. Immediate post-training bilateral infusion of β-lactone into the dorsal hippocampus of ovariectomized female mice blocked E 2 -induced enhancement of object recognition memory and attenuated E 2 -associated improvements in spatial memory. Arbor-wide Golgi-based analyses revealed robust E 2 -induced increases in spine number across the apical dendritic tree and smaller parallel effects within the basal arbor. Segment-level analyses showed that E 2 produced the greatest structural changes on tertiary apical dendritic segments, increasing total, mushroom, and thin spine density and enhancing multiple morphometric features, including mushroom spine surface area and head-to-neck ratio. Secondary basal dendritic segments exhibited smaller, more variable changes. Many E 2 -associated structural effects were attenuated or abolished by β-lactone. Together, these findings provide the first evidence that proteasomal protein degradation contributes to estrogenic enhancement of hippocampus-dependent memory and CA1 dendritic spine remodeling, identifying UPS-mediated protein degradation as a previously unrecognized mechanism regulating estrogenic memory consolidation and structural plasticity. Significance Statement 17β-estradiol (E 2 ) rapidly enhances hippocampal memory consolidation and promotes CA1 dendritic spinogenesis, yet the molecular mechanisms that support these effects remain unclear. Here, we combine temporally specific dorsal hippocampal proteasome inhibition with three-dimensional Golgi-based spine analyses to show that proteasomal protein degradation is required for E 2 -induced enhancement of object recognition memory and contributes to E 2 -associated improvements in spatial memory in ovariectomized female mice. We further demonstrate that proteasome activity contributes to E 2 -induced increases in apical CA1 spine density and morphology. These findings reveal new insights into estrogenic modulation of cognition that may provide novel protein targets whose levels could be regulated to reduce memory dysfunction related to menopause, depression, and other conditions for which women are at greater risk.

doi:10.1007/s00221-026-07408-5.title: Acute unilateral DBS of the basolateral amygdala does not affect motricity, anxiety-like behavior, or fear memory consolidation in rats.
doi:10.1007/s00221-026-07408-5.authors: Formolo DA, Drabowski NR, Mello HM, Hoeller AA, de Carvalho CR, Neto AT, Walz R.
doi:10.1007/s00221-026-07408-5.abstract: Deep brain stimulation (DBS) is an alternative to ablative functional neurosurgeries. The basolateral amygdala (BLA) is a potential DBS target for treating psychiatric disorders. However, understanding the associated behavioral and cognitive effects is necessary for safety and tolerability concerns. Therefore, we investigated potential acute effects of unilateral BLA DBS. Adult male Wistar rats were implanted with monopolar electrodes in the right BLA. In Experiment 1, different groups of animals were stimulated for 10 min with either high-frequency (HFS, 130 Hz) or low-frequency (LFS, 20 Hz) stimulation using different stimulation intensities (0 [Control], 10, 50, or 100 µA). Immediately after stimulation, animals were tested in the elevated plus-maze (EPM) and subsequently in the open field test (OFT). In Experiment 2, two groups of animals were subjected to a fear-conditioning protocol and stimulated with HFS or LFS (50 µA) immediately after conditioning. Animals were then tested for short- (2 h) and long-term (24 h) fear memory consolidation. BLA DBS showed no significant effects on: (i) anxiety-like behavior expression for HFS (p = 0.46) or LFS (p = 0.37); (ii) locomotor activity (HFS, p = 0.12; LFS, p = 0.60), in terms of distance traveled in the OFT, or (iii) fear memory consolidation (HFS, p = 0.31; LFS, p = 0.68). Under the stimulation parameters and experimental conditions tested, acute unilateral BLA DBS did not significantly affect spontaneous locomotor activity, anxiety-like behavior, or fear memory consolidation in rats. These results provide information relevant to the tolerability and safety of amygdala DBS.

doi:10.1007/s12035-026-06264-2.title: Ayahuasca Impairs Fear Memory Reconsolidation and Promotes Rapid Structural Plasticity in the Hippocampus and Prelimbic Cortex.
doi:10.1007/s12035-026-06264-2.authors: Daneluz DM, Dos Santos AS, de Melo SR, de Oliveira RMW, Stern CAJ.
doi:10.1007/s12035-026-06264-2.abstract: Psychedelic drugs promote rapid neuroplasticity in brain regions affected by trauma exposure, such as the prelimbic (PL) cortex and the dorsal hippocampus (DH), being investigated as potential treatments for posttraumatic stress disorder. Ayahuasca (Aya) contains N,N-dimethyltryptamine, a classic psychedelic. Our previous work showed that Aya reduces fear expression by impairing fear memory reconsolidation. We hypothesized that Aya administration during reconsolidation induces neuroplastic changes in DH and PL cortex associated with its behavioral effects. Adult male Wistar rats underwent contextual fear conditioning and received Aya (60 mg/kg, oral gavage) or H₂O (vehicle) 20 min before or 3 h after fear memory retrieval. To confirm the reconsolidation-impairing effect of Aya, animals were re-exposed to the conditioned context 24 h later. Structural plasticity was assessed 24 h after retrieval and drug administration by Golgi-Cox staining of the DH and the PL cortex. Neurogenesis was evaluated 10 days later by doublecortin (DCX) immunohistochemistry of dentate gyrus. Aya significantly reduced freezing behavior, confirming the reconsolidation-impairing effect. This outcome was accompanied by increased dendritic spine density in the CA1, CA3, and dentate gyrus regions of the DH, as well as in the PL cortex. In the PL cortex, Aya altered dendritic branching and length depending on the timing of administration. In contrast, Aya did not affect adult hippocampal neurogenesis. Together, these findings suggest that rapid synaptic remodeling in the DH and PL cortex, rather than changes in adult hippocampal neurogenesis, is associated with the reconsolidation-impairing effect of Aya.

doi:10.64898/2026.10.06.756930.title: Attentional modulation of persistent visual representations after stimulus offset is coordinated across primary visual and anterior cingulate cortices
doi:10.64898/2026.10.06.756930.authors: Safaryan K, Bhalodia RR, Shenassa J, Golshani P.
doi:10.64898/2026.10.06.756930.abstract: Flexible behavior in complex environments requires animals to infer which sensory inputs are relevant for guiding action and which need to be ignored. Yet, how cognitive control circuits apply contextual knowledge during decision-making is poorly understood. To address this question, we trained head-fixed mice on a cross-modal, context-dependent two-alternative forced-choice (2-AFC) decision-making task. In this task, animals simultaneously received visual and auditory inputs, and the behaviorally relevant modality switched covertly between blocks of trials, requiring animals to infer rule changes from reward feedback alone. Mice successfully adapted their behavior after rule switches and recovered to expert performance. Using simultaneous Neuropixels recordings in the primary visual cortex (V1) and the anterior cingulate cortex (ACC) during task performance, we found that neuronal responses in both regions showed mixed selectivity, multiplexing sensory, choice, and outcome signals. However, V1 neural responses more strongly encoded visual stimulus orientation, while ACC neural responses preferentially encoded outcome. Population decoding further revealed that V1 and ACC neurons maintained a persistent representation of task context throughout the trial, occupying a subspace approximately orthogonal to visual stimulus coding. This contextual representation strengthened progressively as mice adapted their behavior following each switch. Critically, context representations emerged in parallel in V1 and ACC, and decoding accuracies in these two regions were strongly correlated with each other and with behavioral performance across trial blocks. Orthogonal to this shared emergent and sustained context signal, visual stimulus decoding was enhanced when vision was task-relevant. This attentional enhancement in V1 occurred not only during the stimulus presentation period but also after stimulus offset. Similarly, in ACC, a persistent increase of visual stimulus identity encoding in visually relevant session blocks was present after stimulus offset. Taken together, these findings reveal a distributed, inter-areal representation of task context spanning sensory and frontal cortices, suggesting that V1 and ACC contribute to maintaining task-relevant sensory information beyond the immediate sensory response period to provide a circuit-level mechanism for cross-modal attentional control.

doi:10.1162/imag.a.1378.title: Oxygen extraction fraction mapping between normal cognition and mild cognitive impairment in older adults using quantitative BOLD.
doi:10.1162/imag.a.1378.authors: Le LNN, Wheeler GJ, Blockley NP, Fletcher E, Jung Y, Farias SET, Gavett B, DeCarli C, Fan AP.
doi:10.1162/imag.a.1378.abstract: Oxygen extraction fraction (OEF) represents the proportion of oxygen utilized by the brain from the blood and is a sensitive biomarker in understanding the vascular interplay between oxygen supply and demand. Alterations in OEF are increasingly recognized in normal aging and the pathophysiology of many neurological disorders, including Alzheimer's disease and cognitive impairment. Here, we aimed to assess regional OEF MRI in older adults and investigate its relationship with mild cognitive impairment (MCI) and normal aging using a Variational Bayesian quantitative BOLD (qBOLD) framework. The qBOLD model leverages a biophysical relationship between OEF, deoxygenated blood volume (DBV), and the reversible transverse relaxation rate (R 2 ' ) to extract parameter values from asymmetric spin echo (ASE) MRI scans. The reliability of these parameter estimates was enhanced by Variational Bayesian inference, which incorporates prior distributions that we optimized in numerical simulation. We then applied this model to a cohort of older adults (N = 70) from the Alzheimer's Disease Research Center (ADRC) at the University of California, Davis, including 58 cognitively normal (CN) and 12 amnestic mild cognitive impaired (MCI) participants. Our findings revealed a trend of elevated OEF across many cortical brain regions in the MCI group. Additionally, we identified regional positive associations between OEF and age in the MCI group, significantly in the left inferior parietal region ( β=0.88±0.23, T=3.75, P=0.0004 ). Furthermore, the relationship between OEF and episodic memory in the right parahippocampal region differed significantly between two diagnostic groups (negative for CN and positive for MCI) ( β=0.09±0.02, T=3.77, P=0.0004 ). This work adopts a novel qBOLD MRI framework for studying OEF changes in cognitive impairment as a potential biomarker for monitoring pathophysiology in aging and dementia.

doi:10.1162/imag.a.1314.title: The Philadelphia Theta Burst Project: A novel fMRI-guided electric field modeling dataset with reliability metrics.
doi:10.1162/imag.a.1314.authors: Gregory DF, Sun I, Teferi M, Gura H, Patel M, Casalvera A, Chandrashekar S, Lynch KG, Schultz DH, Jeyapratap A, Tate Q, Makhoul W, Deng ZD, Oathes DJ, Sheline YI, Balderston NL.
doi:10.1162/imag.a.1314.abstract: Recent neuromodulation studies suggest that theta burst stimulation (TBS) applied to the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (dlPFC) can influence neural circuits involved in cognitive control and emotion-related processing, with relevance for psychiatric disorders. However, large-scale datasets characterizing variability, reliability, and multimodal neural responses to TBS remain limited. To address this gap, we established the Philadelphia Theta Burst Project, a dataset of 100 healthy participants who completed 4 fMRI sessions following cumulatively increasing doses of intermittent or continuous TBS, with participants randomized to one protocol or the other. Each session includes multiband, multi-echo resting-state (16 minutes) and task-based fMRI (16 minutes) during a Sternberg working memory paradigm. TMS targeting was guided by task-evoked activation in the left dlPFC. Structural T1-weighted, T2-weighted, and diffusion-weighted imaging were also acquired. Here, we describe the dataset design, acquisition protocol, and data characteristics, and report initial measures of data quality and reliability. The completed dataset can be accessed at https://openneuro.org/datasets/ds008893, providing an open resource for future investigations of TBS mechanisms and individualized neuromodulation strategies.

doi:10.64898/2026.10.01.755613.title: Phase-targeted Poisson closed-loop peripheral nerve stimulation modulates sensorimotor oscillations in human MEG
doi:10.64898/2026.10.01.755613.abstract: Closed-loop brain stimulation offers a promising approach for modulating neural oscillations, but the mechanisms of phase-dependent neuromodulation remain poorly understood. We developed a real-time MEG-based closed-loop system delivering median nerve stimulation using a phase-modulated Poisson process. Sixteen healthy participants (11 female, 5 male) underwent open-loop characterization followed by closed-loop testing of eight phase-offset conditions (0 degrees-315 degrees), each paired with a statistically matched replay control. Closed-loop stimulation induced robust phase-dependent modulation (14.21 +/- 8.24%) versus replay (7.03 +/- 2.95%; p = 0.0003), with consistent phase specificity across participants (circular mean: 70.2 degrees, referenced to each individual's dominant frequency). At the group level, alpha oscillations (8-12 Hz) showed bidirectional modulation (mean boost: +21.0 +/- 19.9% at 0 degrees-135 degrees; mean suppression: -13.3 +/- 10.8% at 180 degrees-315 degrees), while beta oscillations (13-30 Hz) showed predominantly unidirectional suppression (-9.3 +/- 9.6%). Successful fixed-frequency targeting required alignment with each individual's natural peak. Misalignment led to different phase shifts producing power at different frequencies, a phenomenon we term phase-frequency coupling. Dynamic frequency tracking (8-30 Hz) automatically identified and targeted each individual's natural peak, achieving robust bidirectional modulation without prior knowledge of peak location. These findings demonstrate that real-time phase-locked peripheral nerve stimulation selectively modulates sensorimotor oscillations beyond statistically matched open-loop stimulation. The distinct phase-excitability relationships of alpha and beta oscillations, together with the importance of aligning stimulation with individual natural peaks, establish principled guidelines for personalized closed-loop neuromodulation.

doi:10.64898/2026.10.08.757563.title: Disrupting the Right Inferior Frontal Gyrus Increases Social Brain Activity During Emotion Recognition
doi:10.64898/2026.10.08.757563.authors: Kucuk, E.; Gofton, H.; Smith, C.; Kaiser, D.; Pitcher, D.
doi:10.64898/2026.10.08.757563.abstract: Neuroimaging studies have identified a specialised social brain network that supports emotion recognition and social cognition. This network performs a range of functions that include facial expression recognition and inferring the mental states of others. Studies of neuropsychological patients report that damage to the right inferior frontal gyrus (IFG), the top-down control area in this network, impairs facial expression recognition. To investigate how transient disruption of the right IFG affects the wider social brain we combined transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) with functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI). Participants (n=20) were scanned across two sessions while performing a delayed match-to-sample emotion recognition task in which happy or fearful expressions were preceded by a congruent or incongruent word cue. Prior to each scan, thetaburst TMS was delivered over the right IFG or over the vertex control site (session order was balanced across participants). A group whole-brain analysis revealed that TMS to the IFG increased neural activity in multiple regions of the social brain network. These included the bilateral temporal pole, precuneus and medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC). This pattern of results shows that the disruption of top-down control mechanisms localised in the IFG alters the neural processing in remote nodes of the social brain network. Our findings are discussed within the wider context of how we recognise and understand the emotions of other people.

doi:10.64898/2026.10.06.757155.title: Context Shapes Alpha-Band Electrophysiological Signatures Under Psilocybin
doi:10.64898/2026.10.06.757155.authors: Dhanawansa, V.; Stoliker, D.; Novelli, L.; Biabani, M.; Razi, A.; Kuhlmann, L.
doi:10.64898/2026.10.06.757155.abstract: Background: Psilocybin is a serotonergic psychedelic that provides a pharmacological tool for examining neural activity associated with altered states of consciousness. Existing studies report reduced power (4-30 Hz) in posterior regions and altered functional connectivity (FC) at rest, but have typically involved small samples and coarse anatomical parcellations. Additionally, perceptual engagement has been shown to attenuate psilocybin-related whole-brain FC changes. However, how naturalistic context modifies psilocybin's frequency-specific electrophysiological effects remains incompletely characterised. Methods: We analysed the largest psilocybin electroencephalography (EEG) dataset to date (n = 56), with matched baseline recordings acquired before psilocybin administration. EEG was recorded during movie viewing, eyes-closed rest, guided meditation, and music listening. Cortical source activity was estimated using minimum-norm estimation and analysed across six canonical frequency bands (1-80 Hz). Spectral power, alpha peak frequency (APF), and magnitude-squared coherence within and between seven functional networks were quantified. Psilocybin effects were assessed using permutation testing with FDR correction, and linear mixed-effects models separated the contributions of drug, context, and their interaction to alpha-band connectivity. Results: At rest, psilocybin decreased alpha (8-13 Hz) power, increased gamma-range power, and elevated APF. Alpha-band FC decreased within and between higher-order networks implicated in top-down control. Relative to eyes-closed rest, psilocybin-context interactions showed that structured sensory environments attenuated or reversed psilocybin-related alpha-band connectivity changes. Conclusions: These findings identify alpha-band activity as a key electrophysiological correlate of psilocybin-related changes in cortical communication. Structured sensory input reshapes psilocybin-related cortical dynamics, particularly alpha-band connectivity across large-scale cortical networks, with the strength and direction of this modulation differing by context.

doi:10.1016/j.neubiorev.2026.107054.title: Reorienting TMS treatments for fear memories and posttraumatic stress disorder. The emerging potential of the anterior prefrontal cortex.
doi:10.1016/j.neubiorev.2026.107054.authors: La Pastina AC, Manassero E, Sacchetti B.
doi:10.1016/j.neubiorev.2026.107054.abstract: Posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD) is characterized by re-experiencing trauma through vivid and involuntary intrusions, avoidance of cues that could trigger traumatic memories, and alterations in mood and cognition. Transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) offers a promising approach to modulating activity and functional coupling within neural circuits underlying these processes. To date, TMS studies in fear-conditioning research and PTSD have mainly focused on dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (dlPFC) and ventromedial (vmPFC)-connected or broader medial-prefrontal (mPFC) targets, yielding encouraging but heterogeneous effects on posttraumatic symptoms. In parallel, emerging evidence has implicated the anterior prefrontal cortex (aPFC; Brodmann area 10) in threat- and trauma-related processes, including memory retrieval, higher-order control of defensive responding, adaptive strategy selection, and resilience. Whereas the dlPFC and vmPFC have been incorporated into mechanistic models of fear regulation, the aPFC has received limited attention in theoretical frameworks of fear and PTSD. Here, we review TMS studies organized around dlPFC, vmPFC-connected or mPFC, and aPFC neuroanatomical targets, integrating evidence from experimental and clinical research. Based on the hierarchical model of prefrontal organization, we argue that these regions represent potential TMS targets or circuit nodes, but likely act on partially distinct mechanisms. The vmPFC appears primarily involved in early automatic downregulation of defensive responses; the dlPFC may support cognitive control strategies such as reappraisal; and the aPFC may enable a supraordinate influence over higher-order representations and avoidance-related circuitry, as well as flexible selection of emotion-regulation strategies. We conclude that integrating the aPFC into this framework may guide next-generation, mechanistically-informed TMS treatments for PTSD.

doi:10.1016/j.bbr.2026.116493.title: Role of dopaminergic projections from ventral tegmental area to paraventricular thalamus in heroin-induced behavioural sensitization of rats.
doi:10.1016/j.bbr.2026.116493.authors: Zhu H, Zhou Y, Xu Z, Gao L, Li L, Hong Q, Xu W, Fu D, Lou Z, Liu H.
doi:10.1016/j.bbr.2026.116493.abstract: The ventral tegmental area (VTA) is involved in the behavioural sensitization to heroin, but the possible neural projections and molecular mechanisms remain unclear. Rats first underwent 8 days of heroin sensitization induction, followed by a 10-day drug-free period. Subsequently, a M5 muscarinic acetylcholine receptor antisense oligonucleotide was microinjected into the VTA, and the expression of heroin sensitization was assessed. Secondly, retrograde viral tracing combined with immunofluorescence labeling was used to characterize VTA neuronal populations projecting to the paraventricular thalamic (PVT) and the ventromedial hypothalamus (VMH). Finally, chemogenetic inhibition of VTA-PVT or VTA-VMH dopaminergic projections was performed to evaluate their effects on heroin sensitization. We found that microinjection of a M5 receptor antisense oligonucleotide into the VTA inhibited the expression of heroin sensitization. Furthermore, although the VTA sends dopaminergic projections to both the PVT and the VMH at varying densities, chemogenetic inhibition of VTA-PVT dopaminergic projection specifically attenuates heroin sensitization expression and leads to increased protein kinase B (Akt) phosphorylation and decreased cAMP response element binding protein (CREB) phosphorylation in the PVT. In contrast, inhibition of the VTA-VMH dopaminergic projection had no effect. Our results suggest that M5 receptor in the VTA is critically involved in regulating heroin sensitization. Furthermore, the VTA-PVT dopaminergic projection is essential for heroin sensitization expression and may act by modulating Akt and CREB phosphorylation.

doi:10.1007/s12035-026-06253-5.title: Neuronal IL-18 Signaling in the Medial Habenula Contributes to Schizophrenia-Like Behavioral Deficits via ERK-Associated BDNF Suppression.
doi:10.1007/s12035-026-06253-5.authors: Sun D, Zhang C, Hou M, Zhao H.
doi:10.1007/s12035-026-06253-5.abstract: Current antipsychotics for schizophrenia (SCZ) are notably ineffective against the debilitating cognitive and negative symptoms, creating a major therapeutic gap. Neuroinflammation in the medial habenula (MHb) is implicated in SCZ; however, the underlying cell-type-specific mechanisms remain unknown. This study aimed to determine whether pathologically elevated neuronal interleukin-18 (IL-18) in the MHb contributes to schizophrenia-like behavioral abnormalities through ERK-associated downregulation of brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF). Utilizing an MK-801-treated rat model, we adopted a multi-modal approach. Single-cell RNA sequencing was used to identify the cellular origin of pathological IL-18. We then combined neuron-specific viral manipulations to test functional involvement, chemogenetics to manipulate MHb neuronal activity, and ex vivo electrophysiology to measure neuronal excitability. Finally, targeted pharmacological interventions were used to test the functional contribution of this signaling pathway. MHb neurons exhibited marked hypoactivity and pathological changes in MK-801-treated rats. Single-cell RNA sequencing and histological analyses indicated that MHb neurons are the predominant cellular source of the pathological IL-18 signal in this model. Functionally, neuron-specific IL-18 overexpression was sufficient to induce schizophrenia-like behavioral abnormalities, whereas its knockdown ameliorated negative-like and cognitive deficits. Mechanistically, our data support a model in which elevated neuronal IL-18 is associated with ERK overactivation, reduced BDNF expression, and neuronal hypoactivity. Furthermore, pharmacological inhibition of the ERK pathway in the MHb ameliorated deficits at the molecular (BDNF), cellular (neuronal firing), and behavioral levels. Our findings support a neuron-centered IL-18/ERK/BDNF signaling framework in the MHb that contributes to schizophrenia-like pathological changes in this model and warrants further preclinical investigation as a potential target for cognitive and negative symptoms relevant to schizophrenia.

doi:10.1126/sciadv.aeh9563.title: Vitamin D binding protein in ventral CA3 of the hippocampus drives stress-induced depression.
doi:10.1126/sciadv.aeh9563.authors: Kong Y, Huang Z, Zeng C, Xu Y, Zhang Z.
doi:10.1126/sciadv.aeh9563.abstract: The ventral hippocampus plays a crucial role in regulating emotional and motivated behaviors. However, the molecular mechanisms underlying its dysfunction in major depressive disorder (MDD) remain poorly understood. Here, we identified elevated expression of vitamin D binding protein (VDBP) in the hippocampi of chronic unpredictable mild stress (CUMS)-susceptible mice, which correlated with the severity of depression-like behaviors. Notably, VDBP up-regulation was specifically in ventral CA3 excitatory (vCA3 CaMKIIα ) neurons. CA3 CaMKIIα VDBP overexpression led to inhibited neuronal activity, synaptic and dendritic impairments, and, ultimately, depression-like behaviors. Conversely, vCA3 CaMKIIα -specific VDBP knockdown enhanced resilience to chronic stress. Mechanistically, VDBP directly interacted with PIK3R3 to inhibit the PI3K-Akt-mTOR pathway in a cell-autonomous manner, leading to excessive autophagy and subsequent neuronal dysfunction. Chemogenetic activation, intervention using the Akt-specific activator SC79, and site-specific mutation disrupting the VDBP-PIK3R3 interaction ameliorated vCA3 CaMKIIα VDBP-induced depression-like phenotypes. Collectively, these findings underscore the critical involvement of vCA3 CaMKIIα neuron-derived VDBP in stress-induced depressive pathology and highlight its potential as a therapeutic target for MDD.

doi:10.1523/eneuro.0182-26.2026.title: Oxytocin signaling bidirectionally modulates serotonergic and dopaminergic neurons in the dorsal raphe nucleus.
doi:10.1523/eneuro.0182-26.2026.authors: Choi JE, Kim YK, Sung Y, Choi DI, Kim J, Lee C, Lee J, Yu NK, Choe HK, Kaang BK.
doi:10.1523/eneuro.0182-26.2026.abstract: The involvement of oxytocin in social behavior is well established, yet its interaction with neuromodulatory systems, such as serotonin and dopamine, remains incompletely understood. Here, we utilized immunohistochemistry, anatomical tracing, chemogenetic, and ex vivo electrophysiological approaches primarily in male mice, with female mice used only for an additional anatomical tracing control experiment, investigate how oxytocin modulates serotonergic and dopaminergic neuronal populations. Employing the dual-eGRASP tool, we visualized oxytocinergic projections from the paraventricular nucleus (PVN) to the serotonergic and dopaminergic neurons in dorsal raphe nucleus (DRN). Blocking oxytocin receptors in the DRN attenuated social interaction behavior. Additionally, analysis of c-Fos levels and neuronal excitability revealed that oxytocin inhibits serotonergic neurons while activating dopaminergic neurons in the DRN. Our findings suggest a bidirectional regulatory role of oxytocin signaling in the DRN serotonergic and dopaminergic neurons. Significance Statement Social behavior relies on interactions among neuromodulatory systems, yet how oxytocin communicates with serotonin and dopamine circuits remains unclear. We identify the DRN as a functionally relevant target of hypothalamic oxytocin neurons during social approach. Using dual-eGRASP, we visualize contacts from PVN oxytocin neurons onto both serotonergic and dopaminergic DRN. Blocking oxytocin receptors in the DRN reduces social interaction without affecting locomotion. Moreover, oxytocin suppresses serotonergic neuronal activity while increasing dopaminergic neuronal activation, revealing opposing control of two prosocial neuromodulatory populations within the same region. These findings provide a circuit framework for how oxytocin coordinates social behavior through bidirectional modulation of dorsal raphe neuromodulators.

doi:10.31234/osf.io/49q6t_v1.title: Quantifying context-dependent meaning representations: a novel procedure
doi:10.31234/osf.io/49q6t_v1.authors: Mainetto E, Ouden Hd, Merkx D, Horstman LI, de Haas N, Garvert M, Martin AE, Cools R, Zheng X.
doi:10.31234/osf.io/49q6t_v1.abstract: Our brains house representations of word meaning that are constrained by both the form and the sentence context of the word. For example, when hearing the sentence “They deposited cash at the bank”, we do not think about the bank of a river. These context-dependent meaning representations enable cognitive flexibility. Existing studies aimed at isolating such meaning representations have confounded them with operational processing requirements, due to reliance on inferential and surprisal effects during natural language comprehension. We introduce a novel symbol-based procedure for disentangling context-sensitive word meaning representations from the processing demands of word meaning inference. Participants were instructed to learn associations between sentence-constrained meanings of homonyms (“They deposited cash at the [bank]”) and symbols. Explicit word meaning representations were successfully captured by a task that required the spatial arrangement of these symbols based on their associated word meaning, with smaller distances between symbols representing the same meaning than between symbols representing different meanings. Contrary to the spatial arrangement task, in a priming task assessing implicit word meaning representations related to the same symbols, there was no evidence for semantic meaning priming of reaction times. This work provides a novel experimental procedure for measuring explicit word meaning representations in a manner that can be disentangled from changes in word meaning inference, but raises questions about the suitability of the priming task used for uncovering implicit meaning representations.

doi:10.1162/jocn.a.2725.title: Awareness-dependent Attentional Templates: Neural Mechanism Differentiation Driven by Visual Working Memory Load.
doi:10.1162/jocn.a.2725.authors: Zhang Y, Sun Y, Cai Y, Zhang X, Lu J.
doi:10.1162/jocn.a.2725.abstract: Visual working memory (VWM) guides attention via internal attentional templates, but whether this relies on a "single" or "multiple" templates and how awareness and VWM load regulate its neural mechanisms remain unclear.
