This study used a VWM-guided visual search paradigm with backward masking (awareness manipulation) and EEG. Behavioral results showed that aware VWM supported multi-template attention guidance, while subjectively unaware VWM only allowed single-template guidance. EEG revealed that alpha oscillations over posterior electrodes indexed attention allocation. Neural mechanisms differed by VWM load: Single-item maintenance relied on posterior alpha-alpha phase coupling, while multi-item maintenance depended on theta-alpha cross-frequency coupling between anterior and bilateral posterior regions. These findings clarify how awareness regulates VWM attentional template mode and reveal load-specific neural coupling, providing evidence for understanding working memory-attention-awareness interactions.

doi:10.7554/elife.108588.title: Bidirectional redistribution of actomyosin drives epithelial invagination in ascidian siphon tube morphogenesis.
doi:10.7554/elife.108588.authors: Qiao J, Yu P, Peng H, Shi W, Li B, Dong B.
doi:10.7554/elife.108588.abstract: How epithelia perform a spatiotemporal heterogeneous force-generating program to drive a sequential tissue morphogenesis remains unclear, particularly the underlying precise mechanical mechanisms. This study investigated dynamic actomyosin reorganization between apical and lateral membrane cortex regions during two sequentially invaginated stages of atrial siphon tube morphogenesis in the ascidian Ciona . At the initial invagination stage, the originally lateral-located actomyosin redistributed to the apical domains, while that actomyosin redistributed back to lateral domains at the accelerated invagination stage. Using genetic mutants to modulate myosin activities, the initial invagination was strengthened or abolished, indicating invagination is apical constriction-dependent. Optogenetic inhibition of myosin activities in lateral domains after initial invagination stage blocked the further processes, suggesting lateral constriction of actomyosin is required for the accelerated invagination. Vertex model simulations uncovered a coupled mechanism underlying epithelial invagination driven by apicobasal tension imbalance and lateral contraction. We thus propose an actomyosin redistribution mechanical model: lateral actomyosin first redistributes apically to drive apical constriction and shape the initial invagination, then apical actomyosin redistributes laterally to promote lateral contractility and accelerate invagination. Our findings reveal a bidirectional reorganization of the actomyosin network as a central mechanism driving epithelial invagination, providing insights on epithelial invagination and organ morphogenesis during development.

doi:10.1111/psyp.70416.title: Object Details Persist in Visual Working Memory Regardless of Category Sufficiency for Search.
doi:10.1111/psyp.70416.authors: Williams RS, Saito JM, Fukuda K, Ferber S.
doi:10.1111/psyp.70416.abstract: When searching for objects in complex environments, performance often improves with more specific target representations. Yet, sometimes a more general representation may be preferable. For example, when repeatedly searching for unique exemplars from the same object category, a shared category-based representation could help alleviate the cognitive burden of constantly encoding and maintaining new exemplar representations. We therefore examined whether the format of target representations used for search is sensitive to the sustained preservation of object-category membership. Across two experiments, observers searched consecutively for images of real-world objects from the same basic-level category. We recorded contralateral delay activity (CDA), an electrophysiological marker of visual working memory (VWM) maintenance, to assess whether the encoding of object-specific details diminished across category repetitions in favor of more generalized representations. In Experiment 1, we manipulated whether object-category membership alone sufficiently differentiated each unique target from nontargets in the search array. In Experiment 2, we preserved category sufficiency but allowed the targets to additionally repeat at the level of the exemplar to examine how repeatedly searching for the same object differs from repeatedly searching for the same kind of object. We found that while fewer object-specific details were maintained in VWM when category membership was sufficient, the amount of detail only diminished across repetitions of the exact same object. Moreover, observers exhibited sensitivity to the sustained preservation of the target category in the form of perceptual and semantic expectancy violations following category switches, as indexed by N2pc and N400 ERP components. Together, we show that, even though the sustained preservation of a target object category does not continuously reduce the encoding of object-specific details, categorical information is nonetheless represented in parallel. We speculate that object-specific representations principally serve attentional guidance, while categorical representations benefit target-match decisions.

doi:10.64898/2026.09.15.751737.title: Prefrontal control of hippocampal map reorganization during sleep
doi:10.64898/2026.09.15.751737.authors: Huang R, Nakano M, Clopath C, Born J, Bartsch T, Both M, Blanco-Hernández E, Burgalossi A.
doi:10.64898/2026.09.15.751737.abstract: During wakefulness, exposure to novel experiences induces hippocampal remapping, in which place cell ensembles reorganize to form distinct representations of new information. Classical models of systems consolidation posit that subsequent sleep stabilizes these wake-formed representations and supports their gradual transfer to medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC) networks primarily via bottom-up hippocampal reactivations. Using miniscope Ca 2+ imaging of CA1 place cells, we monitored hippocampal activity as mice explored a familiar environment followed by a similar novel one. As expected, place cells remapped in the novel context. However, a single episode of post-encoding sleep selectively reversed remapping dynamics by promoting the reinstatement of familiar place cell representations in the novel environment – an effect that was absent in the wake condition. This neural reinstatement was accompanied by behavioral indicators of familiarity, including reduced exploration and rearing. Chemogenetic inactivation of the mPFC during post-encoding sleep abolished this generalization effect, and instead preserved the novel hippocampal map. Thus, our results extend current models by showing that sleep not only consolidates wake-established hippocampal patterns, but actively shapes hippocampal maps via prefrontal control, thereby supporting memory generalization.

doi:10.64898/2026.09.25.754563.title: Reversible inhibition of medial septum interneurons abolishes initial acquisition of new place-reward associations and reveals a progressive reduction in dependence on medial septal function
doi:10.64898/2026.09.25.754563.authors: Alizadeh Z, Ferbinteanu J, Eckert M, Shobe J, McDonald RJ, McNaughton BL.
doi:10.64898/2026.09.25.754563.abstract: Hippocampal place cells encode spatial information within a theta-organized temporal framework paced by the medial septum (MS). Lesions or inactivation of the MS impair spatial learning and disrupt hippocampal theta rhythmicity, long-term potentiation, and plasticity-related gene expression, while often sparing spatially selective firing of CA1 neurons (but not CA3 neurons). Although many rodent studies argue against classical systems consolidation by showing persistent hippocampal dependence of spatial memories, other work has suggested that training structure, spaced vs. massed trials, can influence this dependence. To investigate this possibility, we used DREADD-based, reversible, inhibition of MS GABAergic neurons, some of which are known to project to hippocampus. DREADD activation reduced hippocampal theta power and spatial information encoded by hippocampal neurons while largely preserving overall neuronal firing. We then examined the effect of inhibition of medial septal GABAergic neurons on learning the correct goal arm in an 8-arm maze when the correct arm was randomly changed each day. On each day, the mice were given two ‘forced-choice’ trials indicating the correct arm and then 5 free-choice trials (without correction) and were always started from an opaque cylinder in the maze center, in a random orientation, to eliminate possible use of a simple response strategy. When the correct goal arm varied randomly daily, MS cell inhibition severely and repeatedly impaired acquisition. In contrast, when the correct goal arm was subsequently fixed across days, performance was initially impaired but became resistant to DREADD activation over time. Once performance reached asymptote, the goal arm was switched to a new (random) position. In this case, learning was no longer impaired by DREADD activation. This generalization suggests that repeated fixed-goal training in the same environment induces a broader reorganization of the neural systems supporting spatial behaviour. One possibility is that mice develop a septal-independent task-solving strategy that supports both retrieval of established goal locations and acquisition of new ones within a stable environment. This transition could reflect the gradual adoption of a ‘non-spatial’ strategy such as visual pattern recognition, or the use of a directional cue. Moving the most salient distal cue in the environment (a single room light) produced a substantial change in the visual configurations seen from the arm entry points, and disrupted performance; however, it did not produce a consistent directional shift relative to the cue, suggesting that the light contributed to an integrated visuo-spatial representation rather than serving as the reference frame origin. We conclude that the mice switched from a hippocampus/MS-dependent spatial strategy to a non-hippocampus-dependent visual pattern matching solution.

doi:10.1007/s00221-026-07401-y.title: Age-related changes in front-rear anisotropy of peripersonal space representation.
doi:10.1007/s00221-026-07401-y.authors: Teraoka R, Kuroda N, Teramoto W.
doi:10.1007/s00221-026-07401-y.abstract: Peripersonal space (PPS) refers to the multisensory space surrounding the body and plays an important role in interactions with external objects and the preparation of defensive responses. Recent studies suggest that PPS varies as a function of spatial direction. Since PPS is shaped by bodily action capabilities in nearby space, age-related declines in bodily and motor functions may alter PPS representation in older adults. However, whether older adults maintain front-rear anisotropy in PPS similar to that in younger adults, and such spatial characteristics are related to sensorimotor function remains unclear. Older adults performed an audio-tactile PPS task in the front and rear spaces; their performance was compared with data from younger adults. A vibrotactile stimulus was presented while a task-irrelevant sound approached the participant, and participants responded to the tactile stimulus. The Timed Up and Go (TUG) test was used to examine older adults' functional mobility. Auditory-facilitation effect was greater in the rear space than in the front space even in older adults, suggesting front-rear differences in PPS-related auditory facilitation. Importantly, this age-related change was direction-specific: no age-group difference was observed in the front space; conversely, the auditory-facilitation effect in the rear space was significantly greater in older adults. In addition, higher TUG scores were associated with a larger front-rear difference in facilitation, indicating relatively greater rear space facilitation in older adults with lower functional mobility. Thus, age-related changes in PPS-related auditory facilitation were particularly evident in the rear space, and functional mobility may be linked to front-rear asymmetry in this facilitation effect.

doi:10.31234/osf.io/a4vdb_v3.title: Semantic Interference in Blocked-Cyclic Word Production with Different Stimulus Types, Tasks, and Response Modalities
doi:10.31234/osf.io/a4vdb_v3.authors: Wöhner S, Widmann A, Forchner S, Schröger E, Jescheniak JD.
doi:10.31234/osf.io/a4vdb_v3.abstract: Theories of word production rely heavily on semantic context effects. For example, when pictures are named repeatedly and sorted by semantic category, it takes longer to name them than when they are named in an intermixed manner. Wöhner et al. (2021) found that semantic interference in blocked-cyclic naming was approximately three times greater for sounds (e.g., barking) than for pictures (e.g., a dog). This study explored possible reasons for this differential interference pattern. When the stimuli were presented briefly, the differential interference was replicated, ruling out the possibility that it results from a large overlap between stimulus processing and phonological response preparation. When the sounds and pictures were replaced with spoken and written words that the participants translated into their second language, the size of the interference was similar, showing that the differential pattern does not result from different stimulus modalities (auditory vs. visual). When participants typed their responses, the differential interference was replicated again, showing that it does not depend on a certain response modality (spoken vs. written). Additionally, pupil dilation data suggest that sounds, compared with pictures, may activate additional representations that contribute to the interference. Overall, the data imply that semantic interference in word production is shaped by early, stimulus-specific, perceptual and semantic “lead-in” processes that precede lexical selection. More attention should be given to these early processes in word production research.

doi:10.64898/2026.09.18.752313.title: LGR5 and SOX2 expressing progenitor cells in the adult and aged human and mouse inner ear have the potential to produce Myosin 7A positive cells in vitro
doi:10.64898/2026.09.18.752313.authors: Fenton GE, Pieper T, Cleypool C, Sgroi S, Rousset F, de Heus C, Liv N, Thomeer HG, Senn P, Stokroos RJ, Straatman LV, Smith-Cortinez N.
doi:10.64898/2026.09.18.752313.abstract: Summary Hearing loss and deafness as a result of hair cell loss cannot be restored due to the incapacity of spontaneous regeneration of these cells. Compounds that manipulate key signaling pathways can potentially regenerate cochlear hair cells. In order to test different compounds that promote hair cell regeneration in vitro models can be used. Three-dimensional cultures have allowed the expansion and experimentation of human and mouse inner ear organoids. This is mainly performed in the embryonic or the early postnatal developmental stage. However, since the majority of patients with hearing loss are adult, it is crucial to understand the adult inner ear regenerative capacity. Here, we evaluated progenitor cell markers in the adult human and mouse inner ear and the generation, expansion and differentiation of cochlear organoids derived from the adult human and mouse inner ear. Cochlear and vestibular sensory epithelium from adult humans; and from adult and aged mice express the progenitor markers SOX2 and LGR5; and can generate organoids in vitro . By optimizing the culture conditions, organoids derived from the cochlea and vestibular organ from adult human and adult and aged mouse differentiated to Myosin 7A positive cells. This indicates that the adult inner ear has regenerative capacity. These findings are encouraging for future regenerative therapies to cure hair cell-related hearing loss and deafness. Highlights Human adult cochlear and vestibular organ sensory epithelia possess progenitor potential and express LGR5 and SOX2 The adult and aged mouse cochlea possesses progenitor potential and express LGR5 and SOX2, By optimizing the culture conditions, the adult human and mouse inner ear sensory epithelium can generate organoids in vitro Human cochlear and vestibular organ derived organoids differentiate to Myosin 7A positive cells with polarized F-Actin. Mouse cochlear organoids differentiate to Myosin 7A positive cells with polarized F-Actin, FM1-43 uptake, and stereocilia-like structures

doi:10.64898/2026.09.24.26363961.title: Adult disability and mental/psychological illness in Somaliland socioeconomic inequalities and co-occurrence in the 2020 Somaliland Health and Demographic Survey
doi:10.64898/2026.09.24.26363961.authors: Saed AA, Osman OA, Adan AM, Suleiman YI, Mohamed AI.
doi:10.64898/2026.09.24.26363961.abstract: Disability is an important population-health concern, but adult-specific evidence on its distribution and socioeconomic patterning remains limited in Somaliland. This study estimated the prevalence and distribution of reported disability among adults in Somaliland and examined socioeconomic inequality, reported mental/psychological illness, and their co-occurrence. We conducted a cross-sectional secondary analysis of the 2020 Somaliland Health and Demographic Survey. The analysis included 14,579 adults aged ≥18 years who were usual residents, had the disability module administered, and had a defined reported mental/psychological illness measure. Reported disability was defined as at least one positive response across seven disability domains: sight, hearing, speech, learning, mobility, self-care, and mental. Survey-weighted prevalence estimates and design-based comparisons were calculated. Survey-weighted logistic regression assessed associations with household wealth and other covariates. Socioeconomic inequality was assessed using a concentration index and the normalized Erreygers concentration index. Co-occurrence was evaluated by comparing observed joint prevalence with that expected under statistical independence and by survey-weighted logistic regression. The survey-weighted prevalence of any reported disability was 7.30% (95% CI 6.65–8.02). Sight was the most frequently reported domain (3.83%, 95% CI 3.19–4.59), followed by hearing (1.54%, 95% CI 1.20–1.97) and mobility (1.39%, 95% CI 1.14–1.70). Disability prevalence increased markedly with age, from 4.15% among adults aged 18–29 years to 23.96% among those aged ≥60 years. The crude wealth pattern was non-monotonic and was not statistically detectable after adjustment for residence and region. The concentration index for reported disability was 0.0584 (SE 0.0284, p=0.0415). Reported mental/psychological illness had a weighted prevalence of 0.71% (95% CI 0.50–1.00). Both reported disability and reported mental/psychological illness occurred in 0.5032% of adults, compared with 0.05185% expected under statistical independence; the observed-to-expected ratio was 9.70 (95% CI 7.60–11.81). After adjustment for age group and sex, reported disability was strongly associated with reported mental/psychological illness (OR 42.99, 95% CI 18.45–100.18). Reported disability affected approximately one in fourteen adults in Somaliland and showed a marked age gradient and substantial geographic variation. The crude socioeconomic pattern was attenuated after adjustment for geographic context, while concentration analysis indicated modest marginal concentration toward higher wealth ranks. Reported mental/psychological illness was uncommon but co-occurred with reported disability more often than expected under independence. These findings provide an adult population baseline for Somaliland while highlighting the need to distinguish survey-reported disability from the separate mental/psychological illness construct and to interpret the findings within the limitations of cross-sectional, survey-reported measures. Author Summary Why was this study done? Evidence on disability among adults in Somaliland is limited, especially on its socioeconomic distribution and relationship with reported mental/psychological illness. We used the 2020 Somaliland Health and Demographic Survey to examine these patterns nationally. What did the researchers do and find? We analysed 14,579 adults aged 18 years or older using survey-weighted methods that accounted for the survey’s sampling design. Overall, 7.30% of adults reported at least one disability domain. Sight, hearing, and mobility were most frequently reported, and disability was much more common among older adults and varied across regions and residence settings. Reported mental/psychological illness was found in 0.71% of adults. Both conditions occurred together in 0.50%, substantially more than expected under statistical independence. What do these findings mean ? Our study provides an adult population baseline for reported disability in Somaliland and shows clear differences by age and geographic context. Our findings highlight the importance of keeping reported disability and reported mental/psychological illness as distinct measures. Because our data are cross-sectional and based on reported survey measures, the findings describe the 2020 survey period and do not establish clinical diagnoses or causal relationships.

doi:10.1016/j.neuroimage.2026.122274.title: HD-tACS at 40 Hz improves consciousness and brain connectivity in prolonged disorders of consciousness: a randomized sham-controlled clinical trial.
doi:10.1016/j.neuroimage.2026.122274.authors: Hu J, Mou C, Jiang X, Zhang L, Ling Y, Zhao J, Meng F, He F, Wang H, Peng F, Ning J, Gao J, Xu C, Xiao J, Zhao S, Yu J, Pan G, Luo B.
doi:10.1016/j.neuroimage.2026.122274.abstract: Background Frequency-specific high-definition transcranial alternating current stimulation (HD-tACS) may facilitate recovery in patients with prolonged disorders of consciousness (pDoC), but predictive biomarkers and mechanistic insights are limited. Objective To investigate the therapeutic efficacy of 40 Hz or 4 Hz HD-tACS in pDoC. Methods Sixty pDoC patients were randomized into four groups receiving 40 Hz or 4 Hz HD-tACS, each with a corresponding sham condition. Behavioral recovery was assessed via Coma Recovery Scale-Revised (CRS-R), network connectivity was analyzed with electroencephalography (EEG), and baseline 40 Hz auditory steady-state response (ASSR) was explored as a predictive biomarker. Results Five days of 40 Hz HD-tACS yielded greater improvements of total CRS-R scores than 4 Hz or sham, particularly in visual and arousal subscales. EEG revealed strengthened short- and long-range connectivity quantified by phase-locking value (PLV), correlating with behavioral gains. At six months, 37.5% of 40 Hz patients got a good outcome with Glasgow Outcome Scale-Extended (GOS-E) score ≥ 4, which was significantly higher than that observed in the sham group (P = 0.019). Higher baseline ASSR predicted stronger network enhancement and clinical improvement. Conclusions 40 Hz HD-tACS promotes recovery and network reorganization in pDoC. Baseline ASSR may provide complementary information for understanding individual variability in responses to frequency-specific neuromodulation.

doi:10.64898/2026.09.30.755799.title: Intracranial electrophysiology reveals distinct neural representations of nociception and salience in the human brain
doi:10.64898/2026.09.30.755799.authors: Joshi, S.; Polat, M.; Pantis, S.; Garg, R.; Ahmed, S.; Huang, Y.; McGeoch, P. D.; Keller, C. J.; Buch, V. P.; Mackey, S.; Parvizi, J.; Ramayya, A. G.
doi:10.64898/2026.09.30.755799.abstract: Neuroimaging studies have shown close overlap between neural representations of nociceptive stimuli and non-nociceptive, salient stimuli (such as low-probability sounds), leading to the proposal that nociception and salience share a common neural substrate in the human brain. Here we use high-resolution intracranial recordings from 13 neurosurgical patients (2,018 total electrodes) to show that neural representations of nociception and salience are anatomically and functionally distinct in the human brain. 77% of 107 electrodes that encoded nociceptive stimuli did not encode low-probability sounds ("nociceptive representations"), whereas 23% encoded both nociceptive and low-probability sounds ("salience representations"). Nociceptive representations were distinct from salience representations in terms of anatomical prevalence (posterior insula, inferior parietal, and perirolandic cortex vs. anterior insula, thalamus, and inferior frontal gyrus), timing (nociception preceded salience by 120 ms on a trial-by-trial basis), and function (intracranial electrical stimulation was more likely to cause sensory experience when applied near nociceptive representations, as compared to salience representations). These results provide strong evidence that nociception and salience have distinct neural substrates in the human brain, and that selective measurement of these distinct processes may help understand patient-to-patient variability in chronic pain and develop personalized brain stimulation treatments.

doi:10.21203/rs.3.rs-11142611/v1.title: Effect of Co-Alarming of Monitor Alarms on the Response Time and Accuracy of Recognition of Novel Hemodynamic Alarms
doi:10.21203/rs.3.rs-11142611/v1.authors: Essani S, Ghelmensaraei A, Ferguson M, Shive J, Epstein RH, Schlesinger J.
doi:10.21203/rs.3.rs-11142611/v1.abstract: Abstract Auditory alarms communicate critical patient information to clinicians, yet poor alarm design contributes to alarm fatigue, which can result in delayed clinician responses and compromised patient safety. This study evaluated novel auditory heart rate (HR) and blood pressure (BP) alarms that were designed using perceptually informed principles to improve alarm identification. We tested these novel alarms in realistic co-alarming conditions to better understand how proprietary General Electric (GE) and Philips alarms affect identification of the novel alarms. Thirty-nine adult participants completed a laboratory-based experiment in which the novel HR and BP alarms were presented in isolated and co-alarming conditions. Participants identified alarms they heard from choices shown on a computer screen and were evaluated for their response times and accuracy. Responses were 763 ms slower to HR alarms than BP alarms. The presence of proprietary alarms during co-alarming produced an 89 ms increase to reaction time and a 4% decrease in accuracy while identifying novel alarms. Compared to trials with no co-alarming, responses to ascending HR alarms were 183 ms slower during co-alarming and responses to descending HR alarms were 4 ms slower during co-alarming. Practically, these differences in reaction time and accuracy may influence clinical decision-making despite being brief relative to clinical response windows. These findings highlight the importance of temporal and spectral structure in auditory alarm design and suggest that carefully designed alarms can maintain perceptual clarity in complex acoustic environments to be tested and implemented.

doi:10.31234/osf.io/frwn7_v1.title: 〈’〉 in Tsimane’: a Preliminary Investigation
doi:10.31234/osf.io/frwn7_v1.authors: Havard WN, Sy Y, Scaff C, Peurey L, Cristia A.
doi:10.31234/osf.io/frwn7_v1.abstract: Tsimane’ is a language spoken in Bolivia by several thousand people. Yet, it has not been described in detail. We aim to take a step towards a better description by focusing on an aspect of language: the sound represented in spelling with 〈’〉, informally described as a glottal stop. We recorded two adult speakers of Tsimane’ producing (near-)minimal pairs involving this sound. Perceptual analyses suggested 〈’〉 is very rarely realised as a full glottal stop, and is more often cued by creaky-voiced vowels and nasals. Despite the variability in implementation, presentation of syllabic minimal pairs to these two informants and two other adult Tsimane’ listeners revealed evidence that they could easily perceive when 〈’〉 was intended. Together, these data suffice to rule out the hypothesis that 〈’〉 is systematically realised as a full stop, and suggests instead a more complex set of perceptual cues may be at speakers’ and listeners’ disposal.Index Terms: phonology, perception, production, adapted lab experiments

doi:10.21203/rs.3.rs-11321451/v1.title: Maand: Architecture, Empirical Performance, and Multimodal Decision Governance for AI-Driven Virtual Mental Healthcare
doi:10.21203/rs.3.rs-11321451/v1.abstract: Abstract Mental health disorders affect hundreds of millions of individuals globally, yet conventional psychological care remains severely bottlenecked by acute practitioner shortages, prohibitive financial costs, geographical disparities, and pervasive social stigma. In developing nations such as Pakistan, where over 50 million individuals suffer from psychological conditions with merely 500 licensed psychiatrists available (a critical ratio of 1:480,000 citizens), traditional healthcare delivery models fail to provide scalable intervention. Furthermore, existing digital mental health chatbots (e.g., Woebot, Wysa, Youper) remain fundamentally constrained to unimodal text exchanges, entirely excluding non-verbal, deaf, and hard-of-hearing populations while lacking real-time affective awareness and clinical immersion. To address these critical systemic deficiencies, this paper presents Maand: A Pocket Psychologist, a full-stack, multimodal, AI-driven virtual mental healthcare platform. Maand orchestrates four synchronized interaction modalities within a unified web environment: natural language text chat, voice interaction via the Web Speech API, real-time sign language and gesture recognition supporting 112 therapeutic hand and body movements via MediaPipe, and immersive emotional regulation environments rendered through Unreal Engine 5. Perceptual emotion recognition is governed by a hybrid Vision Transformer and Fusion Convolutional Neural Network (ViT-FCNN) trained on AffectNet ($C=8$ classes, achieving 64.8% Top-1 accuracy and 0.632 macro-$F_1$ under in-the-wild benchmarks) and a fine-tuned RoBERTa GoEmotions classifier (87.0% text classification accuracy, 0.865 macro-$F_1$), which dynamically steer a deliberative conversational agent powered by Google Gemini 2.5 Flash. All clinical dialogues are fortified with end-to-end field-level AES-256-GCM encryption, automatic 15-minute inactivity timeouts, and a deterministic safety filter providing immediate crisis keyword interception for high-severity lexicons. Rigorous empirical profiling via k6 load testing (500 concurrent users, 42,000 transactions) demonstrates an average end-to-end response latency of 1.85 s with a 0.5% error rate and 120 ms database access time. User acceptance testing across 35 pilot participants yielded a System Usability Scale (SUS) score of 78/100 and a WCAG 2.1 AA accessibility score of 92/100, verifying the architectural efficacy, clinical safety, and real-time viability of Maand as an accessible paradigm for digital psychotherapy.

doi:10.1016/j.cognition.2026.106739.title: Further predictors of iconicity.
doi:10.1016/j.cognition.2026.106739.abstract: Iconicity refers to a perceived resemblance between the form of a signal and its meaning (e.g., "meow" resembling the sound of a cat). Iconicity has been operationalized by having participants rate words in terms of their iconicity. This has enabled researchers to examine the lexical and semantic properties of words high and low in iconicity, for example finding that iconic words tend to be rich in sensory experience and semantically unique. In the present study I examined a suite of novel predictors that have not been examined in English iconicity. I discovered that while iconic words are low in frequency they are generally well known. They also tend to have more specific meanings, though this was moderated by concreteness and part of speech. Iconic words are also more polysemous and emotional. With one exception, there was no evidence that iconic words were more systematic. Together these results extend previous work, and reinforce the finding that iconicity must be understood through a lens of word use and of words as depictions.

doi:10.31234/osf.io/va7t2_v1.title: The Effects of Nature Walk on Positive and Negative Affect and Perceived Restorativeness in Deaf Adults
doi:10.31234/osf.io/va7t2_v1.abstract: Background: Exposure to natural environments has been associated with positive affective responses and perceived restorativeness. However, these experiences have primarily been investigated in hearing populations, and little is known about deaf adults’ affective and restorative experiences in relation to natural environments. Purpose: We examined whether deaf and hearing adults differed in post-walk positive and negative affect, perceived restorativeness, and nature relatedness. We also explored the sensory pathways associated with their affective and restorative experiences.Methodology: We conducted a mixed-methods study with 15 deaf and 14 hearing adults who completed an outdoor nature walk in a national forest park in Cyprus. Participants completed the Positive and Negative Affect Scale, the Perceived Restorativeness Scale, and the Nature Relatedness Scale, alongside semi-structured interviews. Hierarchical multiple regressions examined group associations with the quantitative outcomes after adjusting for relevant covariates. Deductive content analysis then explored affective and restorative experiences and their associated sensory pathways. Results: Deaf participants reported significantly higher post-walk positive affect than hearing participants (B = -3.82 for hearing relative to deaf group, 95% Confidence Interval [-6.89, -0.76], p = .017). No significant group associations were identified for negative affect, perceived restorativeness, or nature relatedness. Qualitative findings identified both high and low arousal positive affect experiences, alongside restorative experiences such as fascination and the feeling of being away. These experiences were linked to various sensory pathways in both groups, with visual pathways frequently described and auditory, tactile, and bodily/thermal experiences also contributing to participants’ accounts. Conclusion: Our study provides preliminary evidence of differences in post-walk positive affect between deaf and hearing adults while highlighting the diverse sensory experiences linked to affect and perceived restorativeness in natural environments. Larger studies are needed to clarify these findings and investigate the role of sensory experiences in nature restoration.

doi:10.21203/rs.3.rs-11148975/v1.title: Living with Verbal Abuse and Stigma: Psychosocial Experiences of Persons with Disabilities in Bangladesh
doi:10.21203/rs.3.rs-11148975/v1.authors: Urme SA, Islam MS, Fahad AHM, Nasrin S.
doi:10.21203/rs.3.rs-11148975/v1.abstract: Abstract Background Verbal abuse does not necessarily result in visible physical harm, but repetitive humiliation, verbal insults, threats, ridicule, stigma, and intimidation can compromise mental health, dignity, self-esteem, and social inclusion. Verbal abuse of Persons with Disabilities (PWDs) in Bangladesh is the most general and least visible type of abuse yet has so far received little research attention. This research aims to explore the experiences of verbal abuse among PWDs in Bangladesh and identify common perpetrators and psychosocial consequences. Methods This interpretive phenomenological qualitative study was conducted in Cumilla district of Bangladesh. Participants with physical, visual, speech, hearing, and intellectual disabilities, as well as cerebral palsy, were purposively recruited through government and non-government disability service organizations. This study conducted face-to-face interviews with respondents, and the data were thematically analyzed using NVivo 14. Results Three broad themes and ten subtopics were identified. Participants described being subject to systematic verbal insult and ridicule, along with moral or religious blame that merged into general social stigma. Abuse and victimization across family, peer/community, and public settings occurred, with family members acting as both the primary caregiver and a frequent perpetrator. Severe psychosocial harm, including depression, anxiety, avoidance of social participation, and self-isolation, was associated with chronic verbal abuse, and suicidal ideation or attempt was common among the PWDs. Women enumerated other gendered harms associated with marriageability, character attacks, and intimate partner violence. Conclusions Verbal abuse towards PWDs in Bangladesh is a largely invisible form of ableism that is normalized and damaging to mental health. This highlights the necessity of raising community awareness and establishing routine screening for emotional abuse and suicidality in disability service settings. Besides, more effective policy enforcement towards disability-inclusive development consistent with the Sustainable Development Goals is important.

doi:10.31234/osf.io/ywjv9_v1.title: Hallucination-proneness is associated with more extreme social evaluations of external voices
doi:10.31234/osf.io/ywjv9_v1.authors: Lavan N, Needham-Bennett G, Muñoz PRR, Greenfield NE.
doi:10.31234/osf.io/ywjv9_v1.abstract: Auditory verbal hallucinations are often experienced as the voices of entities who have a character and personality of their own. We asked whether hallucination-proneness in listeners affects how they evaluate the personality of external voices. 48 participants who self-reported a diagnosis of a psychotic disorder, and 50 participants without a similar diagnosis rated brief vowel recordings on attractiveness, competence, dominance, friendliness and trustworthiness. Hallucination-proneness was measured with the Cardiff Anomalous Perceptions Scale (CAPS) and the auditory hallucinations subscale of the Psychotic Symptom Rating Scales (PSYRATS-AH). Despite clearly higher symptom levels in listeners diagnosed with psychotic disorders, there was no group-level difference in average social trait evaluations, nor were average ratings associated with hallucination-proneness. There was, however, a numerical trend for listeners diagnosed with psychotic disorders to report more extreme social trait evaluations, where additionally, greater hallucination-proneness was also significantly associated with more extreme ratings across all social traits, on both measures. This association was, however, primarily present in controls but not in listeners diagnosed with psychotic disorders. Hallucination-proneness therefore appears to amplify, rather than directionally bias, social trait evaluations of voices. Our findings link proneness to experiencing internal voices, i.e. auditory verbal hallucinations, to how external voices are perceived. This finding is broadly consistent with previous work reporting that hallucination-prone individuals may be more likely to detect a signal (here: a salient social evaluation) in relatively ambiguous stimuli, speaking to mechanistic accounts that propose that stronger priors imbue stimuli with meaning.

doi:10.21203/rs.3.rs-10916152/v1.title: Pulsatile Tinnitus: A Multimodality Imaging Review of Etiology and Diagnostic Evaluation
doi:10.21203/rs.3.rs-10916152/v1.authors: V P, V S, C.V M, B.M S.
doi:10.21203/rs.3.rs-10916152/v1.abstract: Abstract Pulsatile tinnitus is a rhythmic, pulse-synchronous auditory perception that is frequently associated with an underlying vascular or structural abnormality. While tinnitus affects approximately 10–20% of adults, pulsatile tinnitus is relatively uncommon but clinically significant, with an identifiable and potentially treatable cause detected in over 70% of patients and in up to 90% in dedicated imaging cohorts. The etiologic spectrum is broad and includes vascular, structural, systemic, benign, and malignant conditions, some of which may result in serious morbidity if unrecognized. Imaging is central to diagnosis and management, with evaluation commonly performed using high-resolution temporal bone CT, CT angiography and venography, MRI with angiographic and venographic techniques, and digital subtraction angiography in selected cases. This pictorial review integrates multimodality imaging with representative case examples to provide a structured, physiology-based diagnostic approach. By emphasizing key imaging patterns across major etiologic categories, this review aims to enhance diagnostic confidence, streamline imaging workup, and facilitate recognition of actionable causes, thereby supporting timely intervention and improved patient outcomes.

doi:10.1126/sciadv.aed3930.title: Ultrasound-enhanced exosome secretion and antibody-free SERS profiling for Alzheimer's disease via iPSC-derived cortical organoids.
doi:10.1126/sciadv.aed3930.authors: Yoo J, Kim Y, Yu WJ, Kim S, Jo Y, Cho H, Park H, Lee LP, Park JC, Kim I, Park B.
doi:10.1126/sciadv.aed3930.abstract: Exosomes offer a promising vehicle for noninvasive diagnosis of neurodegenerative diseases by carrying multiple biomarkers across the blood-brain barrier. However, traditional exosome analysis often misses subtle genotype-specific variations because of weak signals from a few exosomes, reliance on markers, and limited understanding of disease signatures. Here, we present a sound way to understand Alzheimer's disease through label-free surface-enhanced Raman scattering (SERS) profiling of cortical organoid-derived exosomes. Initially, we enhanced exosomal SERS signal levels by optimizing ultrasound parameters to increase exosome secretion from cortical organoids. Using this strategy, we distinguished apolipoprotein E genotype-dependent differences in intact exosomal fingerprints. Transcriptome analysis confirmed that ultrasound stimulation increased exosome secretion and up-regulated exosome-related genes functionally linked to Alzheimer's pathology. Ultrasound-based stimulation and label-free exosome profiling reveal genotype-specific pathologies, providing a precision-diagnostic framework for Alzheimer's disease.

doi:10.3389/fncir.2026.1934104.title: Beyond heartbeats: re-thinking interoception in autism through virtual reality and computational modelling.
doi:10.3389/fncir.2026.1934104.authors: Savickaite S, Li R, Nagai Y.
doi:10.3389/fncir.2026.1934104.abstract: Interoception, the sensing and interpretation of internal bodily signals, is increasingly invoked to explain heterogeneity in autism, yet empirical findings remain inconsistent. A major reason is methodological: the field remains cardio-centric and relies heavily on heartbeat counting tasks and trait questionnaires, which are vulnerable to cognitive strategies, attention, expectancy effects, and confounds such as alexithymia and anxiety. Autism research further indicates that interoception is multidimensional (accuracy, sensibility, metacognitive awareness) and developmentally dynamic, with evidence for dissociations across components and compensation across the lifespan. We argue that progress requires reframing interoception as an inference problem: the brain estimates hidden physiological states from noisy sensory evidence under context-dependent precision weighting (predictive processing/active inference). Building on this framework, we propose a participatory, multimodal research program for autism that integrates (i) lived experience as hypothesis-shaping data, (ii) virtual reality (VR) as an experimental testbed to manipulate embodiment, sensory load, agency cues, and feedback, and (iii) computational physiological modelling to estimate latent cardiovascular-respiratory and autonomic-control parameters, which could subsequently constrain separately specified models of perceptual inference.

doi:10.64898/2026.09.29.755365.title: Two components of rapid temporal recalibration: a stimulus-driven shift and a decisional carryover dissociate across the senses
doi:10.64898/2026.09.29.755365.authors: Cass, J.; Van der Burg, E.
doi:10.64898/2026.09.29.755365.abstract: Multisensory synchrony judgments depend on recent history: the point of subjective simultaneity (PSS) shifts toward recently experienced timing relationships. This shift, known as rapid temporal recalibration, is almost always interpreted as perceptual, a change in when events appear simultaneous. Yet serial dependence in such judgments can arise from two mechanistically distinct sources that a raw PSS shift cannot separate: a genuine perceptual realignment, which slides the psychometric function sideways along the multisensory asynchrony axis (an odd effect), and a decisional carryover, a bias to repeat the previous verdict, which lifts the function vertically without moving the PSS (an even effect). We re-analysed eight published datasets investigating rapid recalibration spanning audiovisual, audiotactile, and visuotactile pairings and audiovisual speech, decomposing serial dependence into these two components within a single mixed-effects model. The components dissociated by modality: perceptual recalibration was robust for audiovisual pairs but weak for audiotactile and absent for visuotactile pairings, whereas the decisional carryover was largest for the tactile pairings and weak for audiovisual pairings, so that the two traded off across the senses. In audiovisual speech, the decisional carryover was gated by the spoken syllable but not by the talkers identity and did not persist beyond one trial, identifying it as a content-specific, one-step decision memory rather than a motor habit or a multi-trial store. Separating the perceptual and decisional contributions to a timing judgment thus re-draws the map of temporal recalibration and revises several conclusions drawn from the undecomposed PSS.

doi:10.64898/2026.09.28.754984.title: Altered Aperiodic EEG Activity in Adolescents with Neurofibromatosis Type 1
doi:10.64898/2026.09.28.754984.authors: Litwinczuk, M. C.; Donoghue, T.; Taylor, J.; Pobric, G.; Lea-Carnall, C.; Garg, S.
doi:10.64898/2026.09.28.754984.abstract: BackgroundThe balance between excitatory and inhibitory neuronal signalling (E/I balance), proposed as a key mechanism controlling neuronal activity, is disrupted in many neurodevelopmental conditions. One such condition is Neurofibromatosis Type 1, a monogenic neurodevelopmental disorder characterised by increased inhibitory tone. While previous research suggests that E/I balance may be altered in infancy, it is unknown whether E/I balance remains altered during adolescence in NF1. Here we investigated this question using the aperiodic exponent of the resting electroencephalogram (EEG) power spectrum, a proposed electrophysiological index of E/I balance. MethodThe aperiodic exponent of the EEG power spectrum ( 1/f) was estimated for 16 adolescents with NF1 diagnosis aged 11-16, and 16 age- and sex-matched neurotypical controls. General linear models (GLM) were fit to estimate effects of NF1 diagnosis, age and their interaction on aperiodic exponent. We also estimated the peak dominant frequency and power in oscillatory activity of the EEG signal and fitted the same structure of GLM models. Cognitive assessments across domains of memory, executive function and attention were also analysed with GLM to examine brain-cognition associations. ResultsThe NF1 group had higher aperiodic exponent compared to neurotypical controls, but the aperiodic exponent was not associated with cognitive performance. After accounting for aperiodic activity, the NF1 group also had lower dominant oscillatory frequency than the control group. There was no significant interaction between NF1 diagnosis and age on PAF. There were no group differences in peak alpha power. ConclusionsWe demonstrate for the first time that the alterations to aperiodic activity in NF1 are consistent with the proposed mechanism of increased inhibitory tone. These findings show the potential of this paradigm for future pharmacological and brain stimulation trials investigating treatment-related changes in cortical function.

doi:10.64898/2026.09.17.752150.title: Cx3cr1 -BAC-CRE-mediated knockout of toll-like receptor 4 alters mouse communicative behaviors, microglial morphology, and engulfment of synaptic material
doi:10.64898/2026.09.17.752150.authors: Bankowski IM, Bishnoi IR, Shin EE, Cashin MJ, Möhrle D, Norris HA, Barry DT, Slamin MM, Bordt EA.
doi:10.64898/2026.09.17.752150.abstract: ABSTRACT Microglia, the tissue resident immune cells of the central nervous system, are critical regulators of postnatal neural circuit refinement. Innate immune receptors on microglia such as toll-like receptor 4 (TLR4) are best characterized in the context of inflammation, however, endogenous TLR4 ligands are generated during typical developmental processes. Here, we investigated whether TLR4 signaling in CX3CR1-expressing myeloid cells contributes to microglial morphology, synaptic engulfment, and behavioral development in mice under basal conditions. TLR4 conditional knockout altered maternal separation-induced ultrasonic vocalizations without impacting social preference or anxiety-like behaviors. Conditional TLR4 knockout in CX3CR1-expressing myeloid cells markedly increased microglial ramification and cell volume within the paraventricular nucleus (PVN) of the hypothalamus. TLR4 conditional knockout also reduced microglial engulfment of vGlut2-positive presynaptic material, while overall excitatory synapse numbers remained unchanged. Together, these findings demonstrate that TLR4 signaling in CX3CR1-expressing myeloid cells contributes to microglial morphology, presynaptic engulfment, and neonatal communicative behavior under basal conditions.

doi:10.1016/j.neuron.2026.08.025.title: A basolateral amygdala to dorsolateral striatum projection modulates stimulus-evoked motor behavior.
doi:10.1016/j.neuron.2026.08.025.authors: Hobel ZB, Brechbill TR, Cruz AM, Yang LT, Jimenez K, Wu B, Liu Q, Kirsch SB, Fernandes NJ, Bock R, Alvarez VA, Blackwell KT, Plotkin JL.
doi:10.1016/j.neuron.2026.08.025.abstract: The dorsal striatum is divided into dorsomedial (DMS) and dorsolateral (DLS) subregions, which support distinct aspects of motor learning. The basolateral amygdala (BLA) encodes emotionally salient information and can influence striatal function, but its connection to the sensorimotor DLS remains poorly understood. Using mice, we identify a direct, functional BLA-DLS projection that arises from a neuronal population distinct from BLA neurons projecting to the DMS. Although sparser than BLA-DMS inputs, BLA-DLS synapses preferentially targeted the distal dendrites of striatal projection neurons, positioning them to modulate heterosynaptic integration. Repeated optogenetic activation of BLA-DLS inputs potentiated stimulus-evoked grooming and induced heterosynaptic plasticity. This projection was also pathologically strengthened in compulsively grooming Sapap3 null mice. Together, these findings reveal a direct mechanism through which limbic input from the amygdala shapes sensorimotor striatal circuits and motor output.

doi:10.21203/rs.3.rs-10612934/v1.title: Frontal population organization supports the behavioral expression of confidence
doi:10.21203/rs.3.rs-10612934/v1.authors: Ohnuki T, Osako Y, Shiotani K, Tanisumi Y, Takamiya S, Manabe H, Johansen J(, Minamimoto T, Sakurai Y, Hirokawa J.
doi:10.21203/rs.3.rs-10612934/v1.abstract: Abstract Internal cognitive representations are not necessarily expressed in behavior, yet the neuronal mechanisms determining their behavioral expression remain unclear. Here, we reveal a dissociation between robust confidence representations and their behavioral expression, with population organization bridging this dissociation. Using a perceptual decision-making task in rats, we varied how strongly confidence guided post-decision waiting by altering reward-timing predictability, while holding perceptual choice behavior constant. Confidence representations remained robust at the single-neuron level in orbitofrontal cortex (OFC) across reward-timing conditions, whereas their behavioral expression depended on population organization. When confidence guided post-decision waiting, temporal organization supported temporally generalized readout, whereas population geometry enabled linear readout across graded confidence levels. When behavioral expression was attenuated, both properties were disrupted despite preserved confidence representations. Optogenetic perturbation of OFC–striatal projections disrupted confidence-dependent waiting. These findings support a model in which population organization shapes the downstream accessibility of preserved cognitive representations, enabling their behavioral expression.

doi:10.64898/2026.09.28.754654.title: Medial septum glutamatergic neurons drive speed coding and grid cell spatial accuracy in the medial entorhinal cortex
doi:10.64898/2026.09.28.754654.authors: Robinson J, Carmichael JE, Brandon MP, Hasselmo ME.
doi:10.64898/2026.09.28.754654.abstract: ABSTRACT Successful navigation requires the integration of self-motion signals with spatial representations, yet the circuits that provide velocity information necessary for stable grid cell firing remain incompletely understood. Here, we identify medial septal (MS) glutamatergic neurons as a critical component of this pathway. Using cell-type-specific optogenetic silencing combined with in vivo electrophysiology in freely moving mice, we show that MS glutamatergic neurons support the fidelity of firing rate–based speed coding in the medial entorhinal cortex (MEC). Silencing this population reduced grid cell spatial periodicity and stability and produced distortions of grid firing fields. Silencing also reduced theta phase-locking strength in strongly theta-modulated MEC neurons. Model simulations of a hybrid oscillatory interference–continuous attractor network with reductions in speed-signal fidelity disrupted grid periodicity and reproduced features of the spatial distortions observed in vivo. Together, these findings identify a septo-entorhinal circuit that coordinates self-motion information with the spatial and temporal organization of MEC activity to maintain a stable neural representation of space. HIGHLIGHTS Medial septum glutamatergic neurons support the fidelity of speed coding in the medial entorhinal cortex Silencing MS glutamatergic neurons distorts grid periodicity and spatial stability Medial septum glutamatergic input regulates MEC theta phase locking Model simulations identify speed-signal fidelity as important for grid periodicity

doi:10.64898/2026.09.25.754485.title: Partial sleep deprivation diminishes and uncouples neuronal activity and energy metabolism in the live mouse hippocampus
doi:10.64898/2026.09.25.754485.authors: Lu, Z.; Mai, K.; Rivera, A. C.; Liu, C.; Li, Y.; Shah, P.; Zhang, K.; Spring, B. Q.; Yaseen, M. A.
doi:10.64898/2026.09.25.754485.abstract: Sleep disorders and wakefulness constitute a pronounced and pervasive health risk that contributes to numerous cerebral pathologies such as stroke, depression, and neurodegenerative disorders. The hippocampus (HC) plays vital roles in learning and memory and is especially susceptible to the pathological insults imposed by sleep deprivation (SD). While SD disrupts neuronal network signaling and triggers inflammatory processes, the impact of SD on metabolism within the HC presently remains poorly understood. In this study, we assessed the progressive and cumulative effects of partial SD in the live mouse HC CA1 region using two-photon microscopy. Using a custom-designed implantable cannula enabling direct HC visualization and administration of dyes and pharmacological agents directly to HC tissue, we longitudinally monitored spontaneous neuronal activity and partial pressure of oxygen (pO2) within HC CA1 tissue before and during a 7-day period of partial SD and after a 7- day period of recovery. Our results revealed a progressive decline in spontaneous neural activity, alongside sustained elevation in tissue pO2; during the 7-day partial SD period. Notably, after 7 days of recovery, neuronal activity did not return to baseline, and tissue oxygenation continued to increase. Our findings emphasize chronic SD's cumulative and enduring impairments to neuronal function and metabolism in the HC and reveal uncoupling between metabolic and functional recovery that outlasts the sleep restriction period.

doi:10.64898/2026.10.01.755874.title: Dopamine neurons drive basal forebrain reward prediction in milliseconds
doi:10.64898/2026.10.01.755874.authors: Jhong Y, Chiang M, Guillaumin A, Cheng C, Kuo M, Lee C, Scaglione A, Georges F, Lin S.
doi:10.64898/2026.10.01.755874.abstract: Phasic reward prediction signals in ventral tegmental area (VTA) dopamine (DA) neurons and basal forebrain (BF) noncholinergic bursting neurons are remarkably similar despite the distinct circuit organizations and functions of the two systems. Whether this similarity reflects independent computation within each system, inheritance from common upstream circuitry, or causal propagation from one system to the other remains unknown. Here we show that reward prediction signals are tightly coordinated across these two systems, with VTA DA activity causally driving BF bursting neurons on a millisecond timescale. Simultaneous recordings from freely moving rats revealed strong coupling between putative DA neurons and BF bursting neurons on individual trials, both in response amplitude and spike timing. DA activity consistently preceded BF bursting neuron activity by approximately 10 ms across well-trained behavior, learning, and even outside overt task events. In DAT-Cre mice, optogenetic activation of VTA DA neurons rapidly recruited BF bursting neurons at latencies matching those observed during natural DA-BF coupling, while activation of their BF terminals produced responses at still shorter latencies. Conversely, inhibition of DA neurons or their BF terminals suppressed both cue-evoked and, notably, ongoing activity in a substantial subset of BF bursting neurons. Fast DA-evoked BF recruitment persisted after D1/D2 receptor blockade, and anatomical tracing identified glutamatergic DA-to-BF synapses, supporting glutamate co-release as a candidate substrate. Together, these findings reveal a previously unrecognized causal link that enables rapid propagation of reward prediction signals between functionally distinct subcortical systems.

doi:10.64898/2026.09.29.755395.title: The basolateral amygdala dopamine system shapes dynamic drug seeking states
doi:10.64898/2026.09.29.755395.authors: Brickner, M. A.; Szot, W. E.; Prohofsky, J. M.; Wolff, A. R.; Thomas, M. J.; Saunders, B. T.
doi:10.64898/2026.09.29.755395.abstract: Drug-associated sensory cues and contexts exert powerful influence over drug seeking motivation, but in vivo brain mechanisms governing this process remain unclear. Here, we recorded and manipulated dopamine signaling and dopamine receptor D1+ neuronal activity in the basolateral amygdala (BLA) to investigate their contributions to dynamic sensory-guided cocaine seeking in rats. First, we show that cocaine exposure sensitizes dopamine transmission from ventral tegmental area dopamine neurons projecting to the BLA. We then employed an intermittent access cocaine self-administration paradigm that prompted robust binge-like cocaine seeking that was heavily guided by shifts in the sensory environment. Cued transitions to drug available states evoked large and sustained BLA dopamine signals and transient neuronal responses from BLA D1+ neurons. BLA dopamine signals and D1-neuron activity came to preferentially encode these drug availability states, which hierarchically modulated neural activity during drug seeking actions and predicted different aspects of behavior. Finally, we found that optogenetically enhancing BLA D1-neuron activity at drug availability state transitions potentiated cocaine binging. Our findings provide new insight into the neural control of addiction-related behavior, identifying the dopaminergic amygdala as a key interface between the environment and decisions to engage in vigorous drug use.

doi:10.64898/2026.10.05.756595.title: Large-scale all-optical electrophysiology links excitability and connectivity to circuit dynamics in vivo
doi:10.64898/2026.10.05.756595.authors: Ǫi Y, Parot V, Wu X, Plutkis SE, Lavis LD, Cohen AE.
doi:10.64898/2026.10.05.756595.abstract: To understand neural computations, one would like to relate circuit dynamics to neuronal intrinsic excitability and connectivity. We developed tools for large-scale all-optical electrophysiology and applied them to approximately 300 layer 1 interneurons per mouse in vivo . Across two mice, targeted stimulation and voltage imaging identified 1,469 inhibitory and 5,752 directed electrical connections among 14,312 tested pairs. Presynaptic identity was more strongly associated with inhibitory post-synaptic potential (IPSP) amplitude, whereas postsynaptic identity was more strongly associated with IPSP decay time. Gap junctional and synaptic interactions had distinct spatiotemporal kernels, with corresponding signatures in spontaneous activity. Excitability measured under optogenetic stimulus predicted spiking responses to subthreshold voltage, depolarization rate, and spike history during spontaneous firing. Genetic subtypes also showed different behavioral-state-dependent voltage-to-spike relationships despite similar population-average subthreshold voltages. These measurements link cellular properties and pairwise interactions to spontaneous circuit dynamics, establishing an approach for functional circuit mapping in vivo . Highlights All-optical mapping links excitability, connectivity, and spontaneous dynamics in vivo Presynaptic and postsynaptic identity relate differently to IPSP strength and decay Gap junctional and synaptic couplings reveal distinct spatiotemporal interactions Measured intrinsic excitability predicts features of spontaneous spiking in vivo

doi:10.1126/science.adz5323.title: Dendritic computation for abstract rule-based flexible decision-making.
doi:10.1126/science.adz5323.authors: Zhang Y, Liu Y, Hu Y, Zhang Z, Du J, Cui L, Liu Q, Zhong L, Xin Y, Chai R, Deng L, Pan J, Schiller J, Xu NL.
doi:10.1126/science.adz5323.abstract: Intelligent behavior involves flexible integration of sensory input and abstract rule knowledge. Dendritic computation has been shown to contribute to top-down modulation of sensory processing; however, whether and how it is involved in flexible cognitive processing remains to be elucidated. Combining a rule-based flexible decision-making task with in vivo two-photon imaging and optogenetics in mice, we found that within single layer 5 extratelencephalic neurons in the auditory cortex, apical dendrites preferentially encoded the inferred abstract rule and somata preferentially represented sensory stimuli, whereas choice signals were present in both compartments. Optogenetic dendritic inhibition impaired rule-dependent somatic choice coding, supporting a task-relevant integration across the dendritic and somatic compartments. These results indicate that dendritic computation in cortical neurons mediates flexible behavior.

doi:10.64898/2026.09.28.26364143.title: Diagnostic Utility of Multi-Domain Language Measures Across the Alzheimer Disease Continuum
doi:10.64898/2026.09.28.26364143.authors: Geng Z, Montembeault M, Coulombe V.
doi:10.64898/2026.09.28.26364143.abstract: Objectives Alzheimer’s disease (AD) progresses from a cognitively unimpaired stage through mild cognitive impairment (MCI) to dementia. Because language impairment often emerges before dementia, it is a candidate marker of disease stage. Yet the standard batteries of large AD research cohorts rely on a narrow set of tests that mainly evaluate the lexical-semantic domain (i.e., picture naming and verbal fluency), leaving other language domains, such as semantic memory, phonology, morphosyntax, and single-word reading, rarely assessed. We evaluated the diagnostic utility of standard and specialized language tests for distinguishing amyloid-positive MCI and dementia of the Alzheimer’s type (DAT) from healthy controls (HC) and from each other. Methods We included 286 participants from the National Alzheimer’s Coordinating Center (125 HC, 53 MCI Aβ+, 108 DAT Aβ+) assessed with three standard tests from UDSv3 (semantic fluency, letter fluency, and Multilingual Naming Test [MINT]) and nine specialized tests from the FTLD Module (regular and irregular word reading, semantic word-picture matching, semantic associates, Northwestern Anagram Test – Short Form [NAT-S], Northwestern Naming Battery noun and verb naming, sentence repetition, and sentence reading). For each test, the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) was computed for DAT vs. HC, MCI vs. HC, and DAT vs. MCI, and AUCs were compared between tests with DeLong’s test. Results Eight of 12 measures reached acceptable discrimination (AUC ≥ .700) for DAT vs. HC, five for MCI vs. HC, but only semantic fluency and NAT-S for DAT vs. MCI. Semantic fluency showed the highest discrimination in each contrast, though it did not significantly outperform the NAT-S for MCI vs. HC or DAT vs. MCI. MINT, letter fluency, and irregular word reading reached clinically meaningful accuracy in distinguishing MCI and DAT from HC, but not DAT from MCI. The remaining specialized tests reached it only for DAT vs. HC, or not at all. In a post hoc regression, adjusting for cognitive flexibility and working memory attenuated group differences; the DAT difference was no longer significant, whereas the MCI difference remained significant. Discussion Semantic fluency was the strongest single language marker across the AD continuum. Among specialized tests, NAT-S was the most informative, challenging the view that syntax is spared in early AD. Its performance was partly explained by executive function, mainly in DAT, whereas a residual morphosyntactic component remained in MCI, and several specialized tests were limited by ceiling effects. Clinically, the NAT-S may complement semantic fluency for staging, and specialized tests may help characterize heterogeneous language profiles in MCI and DAT.

doi:10.20944/preprints202609.1783.v1.title: From Generation to Access: On Artificial Dreaming as an Advanced Form of AI Art
doi:10.20944/preprints202609.1783.v1.abstract: The convergence of generative artificial intelligence and brain-computer interface technology is pushing artificial dreaming from science fiction into the scope of academic inquiry. Existing research has focused primarily on technical implementation pathways and sensory fidelity goals; while fragmented ethical and risk warnings exist, there remains a lack of systematic assessment of the physiological costs that artificial dreaming imposes on core sleep functions, a scarcity of theoretical refinement grounded in the dream system's own generative rules and aesthetic nature, and an absence of clear demarcation between different application paradigms. Taking a complete REM sleep–awakening boundary consciousness experience as its phenomenological point of departure, this paper draws on sleep neuroscience and neuroaesthetics to develop a theoretical inference that distills four layers of constraint in the human dream system: the visual bias of PGO wave conduction pathways, the functional auditory suppression of thalamic gating's "external-open, internal-closed" strategy, the emotional safety threshold of the auditory–amygdala short pathway, and the gating leakage effect during sleep-boundary transitions. On this basis, the paper assesses the impact of three levels of intervention—mild, moderate, and severe—on sleep restoration functions across four dimensions: neural repair, memory consolidation, emotional regulation, and somatic recovery, clarifying the upper limits of dream vividness corresponding to different intervention intensities. The study further proposes that artificial dreaming diverges into two paradigms: artistic dreaming and ludic dreaming. The former is an advanced form of AI art's transition from "exogenous generation" to "endogenous generation"—its core is not full-sensory realistic replication, but the continuous dynamic alignment of generated content with the subject's experience while protecting sleep's physiological functions. The latter targets open-world immersive experience, demanding higher intervention intensity and technical capability, and carrying higher health risks. The paper accordingly proposes the aesthetic concept of "dreamness," infers the design constraints of two layered technical pathways—non-invasive and invasive—and introduces the perspective of "consciousness ecology," arguing for four boundaries: neural safety, aesthetic value, sleep health, and ethical norms. It concludes that the "right of offline consciousness" should constitute the ultimate limit that artificial dreaming must never transgress. It should be noted that this paper is a cross-disciplinary theoretical construction; the relevant judgments regarding intervention effects and risks are hypothetical conclusions, and the cultural-symbolic and deep psychological dimensions of dreams are not yet covered.

doi:10.64898/2026.09.28.755101.title: Adaptive spatiotemporal filtering of social electrosensory signals by cerebellar feedback
doi:10.64898/2026.09.28.755101.authors: Miller, D. R.; Shinn, E. K.; Harrison, B.; Marsat, G.
doi:10.64898/2026.09.28.755101.abstract: Sensory feedback can suppress predictable input, yet most research on this mechanism used simplified stimuli that do not capture the spatial and temporal structure of natural signals. We examined how cerebellum-like feedback, in brown ghost knifefish, shapes the encoding of realistic social electrosensory signals. These naturalistic signals replicated the spatial structure of social signals, spanned the range of typical AM beat frequencies, and incorporated movement-related contrast envelopes. Single-unit recordings were obtained from electrosensory lateral line lobe pyramidal cells while a conspecific-like signal was delivered. Responses were compared before and after pharmacological blockade of descending cerebellar feedback. As expected, feedback strongly attenuated responses to spatially-realistic low-frequency beats but did not alter beat-cycle coding at higher frequencies. However, feedback reduced the neural representation of movement-related contrast envelopes across all beat frequencies. Using information-theoretic tools, we showed that feedback strength adapts dynamically to the stimulus contrast over the past few hundred ms. Furthermore, we examined how the spatial coding by the pyramidal cell population is influenced by feedback. We show that feedback enhances localization cues. This improvement arose because feedback reduces weak background responses while not affecting the strongest responses, thereby increasing spatial contrast. These findings show that the same descending pathway jointly filters temporal and spatial features of the full range of natural signals, adapting to recent input statistics. This process exemplifies a general mechanism by which a predictive feedback can improve the efficiency of natural sensory representations.

doi:10.64898/2026.10.06.757200.title: Stochastic Decision Policy Is Optimal Under Costly Control
doi:10.64898/2026.10.06.757200.authors: Li, J.; Louie, K.; Vittala, A.; Mattar, M.; Glimcher, P.; Shen, B.
doi:10.64898/2026.10.06.757200.abstract: Human and animal decisions are often noisy. This variability is usually attributed to noise that corrupts the decision evidence, a defect that an ideal decision maker would eliminate. Here we ask whether stochastic choice can instead be optimal once the cost of implementing prescribed policies is counted. We treat the decision maker as an ideal observer that maximizes expected gain but pays costs to sharpen its policy away from a random default. Using sequential sampling, a setting in which the optimal policy is precisely defined, we show that this trade-off makes a stochastic policy optimal, replacing the hard decision boundaries of classical theory with soft stopping zones whose softness is set by the price of control. This soft policy aligns with the strategy used in cutting-edge artificial learning agents for robustness. Noise that corrupts the agent's belief, an important confound of noisy behavior, produces superficially similar yet distinctive signatures in behavioral policies. Leveraging this, we recovered the policies of two macaques with low-dimensional recurrent neural networks and found that their behavior carries both a stochastic policy and belief noise. By separating variability in constructing a decision belief from stochasticity in selecting actions, these results establish that stochastic decision policies can themselves be optimal, offering a common principle for understanding behavioral variability in biological and artificial decision makers.

doi:10.64898/2026.10.13.758657.title: Dopamine Release from the Locus Coeruleus Enables Temporal Binding in the Hippocampus
doi:10.64898/2026.10.13.758657.authors: Crestani AP, Diniz CRAF, Carda D, Maw S, Wiltgen BJ.
doi:10.64898/2026.10.13.758657.abstract: The hippocampus forms memories by associating events that are separated in time. These associations can be studied using trace conditioning, a procedure where a temporal gap is inserted between a conditional stimulus and an unconditional stimulus. Here, we examined how dopaminergic projections to CA1 support trace fear conditioning. Using fiber photometry and genetic lesions, we demonstrate that locus coeruleus (LC)-derived dopamine, rather than VTA input, is the primary source of dopamine in CA1 and is essential for trace learning. LC lesions reduced CA1 principal neuron activity and c-Fos expression. In-vivo imaging revealed that successful learning requires post-shock reactivation of stimulus-specific ensembles, a process compromised by LC lesions or long trace intervals. Finally, optogenetic stimulation of LC-CA1 projections during the post-shock period was sufficient to rescue learning in long-trace protocols. These findings identify LC-CA1 dopamine as a critical regulator of temporal binding via the facilitation of hippocampal memory trace reactivation.

doi:10.1111/ejn.70715.title: Exploring Hippocampal Neural Network Dynamics in Rodents Using Virtual Reality: A Narrative Review on Systems, Spatial Coding, and Applications.
doi:10.1111/ejn.70715.authors: Ezgin N, Kurul F, Cetin AE, Hrnčić D.
doi:10.1111/ejn.70715.abstract: Virtual reality (VR) provides a highly controllable, immersive, and interactive platform for investigating hippocampal mechanisms underlying spatial learning and memory. In rodent models, VR-based paradigms have elucidated how hippocampal subregions including CA1, CA3, and the dentate gyrus support spatial representation, pattern separation, and memory consolidation. Within VR environments, place cells, grid cells, head-direction cells, and boundary vector cells exhibit characteristic remapping dynamics, reflecting both the experimental advantages and sensory constraints inherent to VR. Although VR enhances reproducibility and integrates seamlessly with advanced methodologies such as two-photon calcium imaging and optogenetics, reduced vestibular and multisensory inputs can limit the fidelity of spatial coding. This review synthesizes current evidence on hippocampal-retrosplenial interactions, synaptic plasticity, and multisensory integration in VR, highlighting mechanistic insights into spatial cognition.

doi:10.7554/elife.104862.title: Brief disruption of activity in a subset of dopaminergic neurons during consolidation impairs long-term memory by fragmenting sleep.
doi:10.7554/elife.104862.authors: Yan L, Wu L, Wiggin TD, Su X, Yan W, Li H, Li L, Lu Z, Guo F, Meng Z, Li Y, Li F, Griffith LC, Liu C.
doi:10.7554/elife.104862.abstract: Sleep disturbances are associated with poor long-term memory (LTM) formation, yet the underlying cell types and neural circuits involved have not been fully decoded. Dopamine neurons (DANs) are involved in memory processing at multiple stages. Here, using both male and female flies, Drosophila melanogaster , we show that, during the first few hours of memory consolidation, disruption of basal activity of a small subset of protocerebral anterior medial DANs (PAM-DANs), by either brief activation or inhibition of the two dorsal posterior medial (DPM) neurons, impairs 24 hr LTM. Interestingly, these brief changes in activity using female flies result in sleep loss and fragmentation, especially at night. Importantly, pharmacological rescue of sleep after manipulation restores LTM. A specific subset of PAM-DANs (PAM-α1) that synapse onto DPM neurons specify the microcircuit that links sleep and memory. MBON-α1 also contributes to the integration of sleep and memory by acting as an additional parallel circuit. PAM-DANs, including PAM-α1, form functional synapses onto DPM mainly via two dopamine receptor subtypes. Dop1R1 primarily mediates the link between sleep and memory. This PAM-α1 to DPM microcircuit exhibits a synchronized, transient, post-training change in activity during the critical memory consolidation window, suggesting an effect of this microcircuit on maintaining the sleep necessary for LTM consolidation. Our results provide a new molecular and circuit basis for the complex relationship between sleep and memory.

doi:10.64898/2026.09.19.752895.title: Ethanol withdrawal induces temporally distinct alterations in oxytocinergic, opioidergic, glutamatergic and neuroimmune systems associated with recognition memory deficits
doi:10.64898/2026.09.19.752895.authors: Zimmerman SA, Onisiforou A, Zanos P, Sklirou M, Garcia Carmona J, Pantouli F, Wells L, Bailey A, Georgiou P.
doi:10.64898/2026.09.19.752895.abstract: Alcohol use disorder is associated with persistent neuroadaptations and cognitive impairments, particularly during withdrawal, yet the temporal dynamics and interactions between these processes remain poorly understood. In the present study, we investigated time-dependent alterations in the oxytocin receptor (OTR), μ-opioid receptor (MOPr), metabotropic glutamate receptor 5 (mGlu5R), and translocator protein (TSPO) following chronic ethanol exposure and withdrawal, and their relationship to behavioral impairments. Male C57BL/6J mice were exposed to a 10-day escalating-dose ethanol liquid diet paradigm followed by 1, 4, or 7 days of withdrawal. Motor coordination and recognition memory were assessed using rotarod and novel object recognition tests, and receptor binding was quantified using autoradiography across multiple brain regions. Chronic ethanol exposure induced motor deficits that persisted during early withdrawal, whereas recognition memory impairments emerged after 7 days of withdrawal. Ethanol exposure and withdrawal produced region- and time-dependent alterations across all systems examined, with increased OTR binding in septal regions and transient reductions in basomedial amygdala OTR binding during intermediate withdrawal that normalized following prolonged withdrawal, transient increases in MOPr binding in striatal regions at 4 days of withdrawal, increased mGlu5R binding in the nucleus accumbens core, basolateral amygdala, and hippocampus, and early transient increases in TSPO binding indicative of neuroimmune activation. Notably, mGlu5R binding in the caudate-putamen and amygdala was associated with recognition memory deficits in a withdrawal stage-dependent manner.
